The Qur'an is described as "clear" for several reasons:

First: The Qur'an is an overpowering miracle and a manifest sign for Muhammad (ﷺ).

Second: It makes clear in it guidance and right conduct, and the lawful and the unlawful. Since these matters are made clear in it, the Book is clear regarding them.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may reason.﴾ In this there are several issues:

The first issue: It is related that the scholars of the Jews said to the leaders of the polytheists: "Ask Muhammad why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the manner of the story of Yusuf." So God, exalted is He, sent down this verse, and in it He mentioned that He expressed this story in Arabic words so that they could understand it and be able to attain knowledge of it. The meaning is: "Indeed, We have sent down this Book in which is the story of Yusuf, in the state of being an Arabic Qur'an." Some of the Qur'an was called "Qur'an," because the word Qur'an is a generic noun which applies to the whole and to a part.

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) argued from this verse that the Qur'an is created, from three aspects:

First: His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾ indicate this, for what is eternal cannot be sent down, caused to descend, or transferred from one state to another.

Second: He, exalted is He, described it as Arabic, and what is eternal cannot be Arabic or Persian.

Third: When He said ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, this indicates that He, exalted is He, was able to send it down not in Arabic, and that indicates that it is originated.

Fourth: His words ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ indicate

[Page 68]

that it is composed of verses and words, and whatever is composed is originated.

The answer to all these aspects together is that we say: they indicate that what is composed of letters, words, expressions and phrases is originated, and this is not disputed. What we claim to be eternal is something else, so this argument falls.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i argued from His words ﴿so that you may reason﴾, saying: The word "la'alla" must be understood as certainty. The meaning is: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand its meanings concerning matters of religion," since it is not permissible that "la'allakum ta'qilun" should mean doubt, for that is impossible for God. Thus it is established that the intended meaning is that He sent it down in order that they might come to know its proofs, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, desired from all servants that they understand His oneness and the matter of their religion, whether they know it or not, unlike the claim of the Jabriyya (determinists).

The answer: Grant that the matter is as you have said. It only indicates that He, exalted is He, sent down this surah and desired from them knowledge of the manner of this story. But why do you say that it indicates that He, exalted is He, desired from all of them faith and righteous deeds?

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verse 3:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories, by Our revelation to you of this Qur'an, though you were before it among the unaware.﴾

There are several issues (masa'il) concerning this:

The first issue: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that when the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and he recited it to his people, they said: "O Messenger of God, if only you would relate stories to us." So this surah was revealed and he recited it to them. They said: "If only you would tell us something (a report)." So He revealed: ﴿God has sent down the best of discourse, a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. They said: "If only you would admonish us." So He revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Hadid: 16].

The second issue: al-qasas (narrative account) is the following of one report by another, and its original meaning in the language is "following." He, exalted, said: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], meaning: follow his trail. And He said: ﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf: 64], meaning: following. The narration was called qasas only because the one who relates a story mentions its events one by one, just as it is said "talla al-Qur'an" (he recited the Qur'an) when he reads it, because he follows (yatlu, i.e., yatba'u) what he has memorized of it, verse after verse. The word qasas in this verse may be a verbal noun (masdar) meaning al-iqtisas (the relating), as it is said: "qassa al-hadith yaqussuhu qassan wa qasasan" when one drives and carries it along, just as it is said: "arsalahu yursiluhu irsalan." It may also be of the type of naming the object (maf'ul) by the verbal noun, as in your saying: "This is the power of God, the Exalted," meaning what is empowered (maqdur) by Him; "This book is the knowledge of so-and-so," meaning what is known (ma'lumuhu) of him; and "This is our hope," meaning what we hope for (marjuwwuna). If we take it as a verbal noun, the meaning is: "We relate to you the best of relating," and on this reading the excellence returns to the excellence of the expression, not to the story itself. What is meant by this excellence is that these words are eloquent, reaching in their eloquence the limit of inimitability (i'jaz). Do you not see that this story is mentioned in the books of history, yet none of it resembles this surah in eloquence and rhetorical force? If we take it as the object (maf'ul), the meaning of its being the best of stories is because of what it contains of lessons (ibar), subtleties (nukat), wisdom (hikam), and marvels that are not found in any other account. Among the benefits of this story is that there is no repeller of God's decree and no obstacle to God's destiny, and that when God, the Exalted, decrees for a person good and honor, even if the people of knowledge gathered together against it, they would not be able to repel it.

The second benefit: it shows that envy is a cause of abandonment and loss.

The third benefit: patience is the key to relief, as in the case of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for when he was patient he attained his aim. The same applies to Yusuf, peace be upon him.

As for His statement: ﴿by Our revelation to you of this Qur'an﴾, the meaning is "by Our revealing to you this Qur'an." This is the interpretation if we consider "ma" together with the verb as equivalent to a verbal noun.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿though you were before it﴾, meaning: before We revealed it to you, ﴿among the unaware﴾ of the story of Yusuf and his brothers, because he, peace be upon him, only knew that through revelation. Some said: the meaning is that he was among those unaware of the religion and the law before that, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 4:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾

Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The implied sense of the verse is: mention ﴿when Joseph said﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The correct view is that "Yusuf" is a Hebrew name, because if it were Arabic it would be diptote (not take tanwin), since it has no reason for being so other than being a proper noun. Some read "Yusifa" with a kasra on the sin, and "Yusafa" with a fatha. Also, these three forms are reported for "Yunus." From the Prophet (ﷺ) it is reported that he said: "When it is said, 'Who is the noble one?', say: 'The noble one is the son of the noble, the son of the noble, Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them.'"

**The second issue:** Ibn Amir read "Ya abata" with a fatha on the ta' throughout the Qur'an, while the others read it with a kasra on the ta'. As for the fatha, its basis is that originally it was "Ya abatah" as a nudba (a vocative used in lament or appeal, nudba), so the alif and the hā' were dropped. As for the kasra, its origin is "Ya abi," the ya' was dropped and the kasra was left to stand in its place. Then the pausal hā' (hā' al-waqf) was added, so it became ﴿Ya abati﴾. Its usage then became so frequent that it seemed to be part of the word itself, so they added the idafa (the genitive annexation of a noun to a following noun, idafa) to it. This is the view of Tha'lab and Ibn al-Anbari.

Know that the grammarians have extended discussion on this issue, and whoever wants their words should consult their books.

**The third issue:** Joseph, peace be upon him, saw in a dream that eleven stars, the sun, and the moon were prostrating to him. He had eleven brothers. He interpreted the stars as the brothers, the sun and moon as the father and mother, and the prostration as their humility before him and their submission to his command. We have understood his saying ﴿I saw eleven stars﴾ as referring to a dream for two reasons:

The first: the stars do not actually prostrate, so this speech must be understood as referring to a dream.

The second: the saying of Ya'qub, peace be upon him: ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾ [Yusuf: 5].

Regarding the verse there are questions:

**The first question:** His saying ﴿they prostrating to me﴾. The word ﴿prostrating﴾ is only fitting for rational beings, while the stars are inanimate. How then was this term, specific to rational beings, permitted for inanimate things?

We say: a group of philosophers who claim that the stars are living, rational beings have used this verse as evidence, and likewise they have used His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40], since the plural with the waw and nun is specific to rational beings. Al-Wahidi said: When He, exalted is He, described them with prostration, they became as if they understood, so He spoke of them as one speaks of those who understand, as He said in describing the idols: ﴿and you see them looking at you, but they do not see﴾ [al-A'raf: 198], and as in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

**The second question:** He said ﴿I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon﴾, then he repeated the word "saw" a second time and said ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾. What is the benefit of this repetition?

The answer: al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He mentioned the first seeing to indicate that he witnessed the stars, the sun, and the moon, and the second to indicate that he witnessed their prostrating to him. Some said: when he said ﴿I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon﴾, it was as if it were said to him: "How did you see them?" So he said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me.' Others said: It is possible that one of them is from seeing and the other from dreaming. This speaker did not clarify which of them is to be understood as seeing and which as dreaming, so he mentioned a general statement that was not made clear.

**The third question:** Why did he postpone the sun and the moon?

We say: He postponed them because of their superiority over the stars, since singling something out by mention indicates added nobility, as in His saying: ﴿whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

**The fourth question:** Does prostration mean actual prostration, or humility, as in the line:

*"You see the hills in it prostrating before the hooves."*

We say: Both are possible, but the original principle in speech is to take it in its literal sense. And there is no obstacle to his seeing in a dream that the sun, the moon, and the stars prostrated to him.

**The fifth question:** When did Joseph, peace be upon him, see this dream?

We say: There is no doubt that he saw it in childhood, but as for that exact time, it is only known through report. Wahb said: Joseph, peace be upon him, when he was seven years old, saw that eleven long staves were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and suddenly a small staff rose up over them until it swallowed them. He mentioned that to his father, who said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon, and the stars prostrating to him, and he related it to his father, who said: "Do not mention it to them, lest they plot a scheme against you." It was said: the period between Joseph's dream and his brothers' coming to him was forty years. It was also said: eighty years.

Know that the sages say that the bad dream's interpretation appears soon, while the good dream's interpretation appears only after a while. They said: the reason for this is that the mercy of Allah requires that the announcement of the arrival of evil not occur except near its arrival, so that grief and sorrow are less. As for the announcement of good, it occurs well in advance of its appearance by a long time, so that the joy resulting from anticipating that good is greater and more complete.

**The sixth question:** Some said: the sun and the moon mean his father and his maternal aunt. What is the reason for this?

We say: They only said that because it is reported in the narration that his mother had died and had not entered upon him while he was in Egypt. They said: If the sun and the moon meant his father and mother, she would not have died, because the dreams of the prophets, peace be upon them, must be revelation. This argument is not strong, because Joseph, peace be upon him, was not a prophet at that time.

**The seventh question:** What are those stars?

We say: The author of al-Kashshaf reported that a Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, tell me about the stars which Joseph saw." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent, and then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and informed him of that. Then the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, said to the Jew: "If I tell you, will you become Muslim?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jarban, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Qabis, 'Amudan, al-Fulayq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, al-Farigh, Wathsab, and Dhu al-Kaffayn: Joseph saw them, and the sun and the moon descended from the sky and prostrated to him." The Jew said: "By Allah, they are indeed their names."

Know that many of these names are not mentioned in the books written on the forms of the stars, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 5–6:

God Almighty says: ﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾ ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of events and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Hafs read "yā bunayya" (يا بُنَيَّ) with a fatha on the ya, while the others read it with a kasra.

The second issue: Jacob (peace be upon him) had an intense love for Joseph and his brother, and because of this his brothers envied them. This sentiment became apparent to Jacob (peace be upon him) through many signs. So when Joseph (peace be upon him) mentioned this dream, and its interpretation was that his brothers and his parents would submit to him, he said: "Do not inform them of your dream, for they will recognise its interpretation and plot against you a scheme."

The third issue: Al-Wahidi said: "Al-ru'ya (الرُّؤْيا) is a verbal noun, like al-bushra (البُشْرى), al-suqya (السُّقْيا), al-buqya (البُقْيا) and al-shura (الشُّورى). However, when it became a noun for this imagined thing in sleep, it took the course of nouns." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Al-ru'ya has the meaning of al-ru'yah (seeing), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep rather than in wakefulness. Hence it was distinguished from it by the two feminine letters, as it is said: al-qurbah and al-qurba." It was read as "ru'yāka" (رُوياكَ) with the hamza changed to waw. Al-Kisa'i was heard reading "ruyyāka" and "riyyāka" with assimilation, and with the ra' vowelled with damma and with kasra; and these are weak readings.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿fa-yakīdū laka kaydan﴾ ("so that they plot against you a scheme"), and it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (أنْ). The meaning is: if you relate it to them, they will scheme against you.

If it is asked: why did he not say "fa-yakīdūnaka" as in His saying ﴿fa-kīdūnī﴾ [Hud: 55]?

We say: this lam is for emphasising the complement, like His saying ﴿li-l-ru'yā ta'burūn﴾, and like your saying "naṣaḥtuka" and "naṣaḥtu laka", and "shakartuka" and "shakartu laka". It is also said that it belongs to the complement of the scheming, meaning "fa-yakīdū kaydan laka". The people of verification said: this indicates that they had knowledge of the interpretation of dreams, for otherwise they would not have known from this dream anything that would cause resentment and anger.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.﴾ The reason for this statement is that if they had proceeded to scheme, that would be attributed to Satan. Its parallel is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him): "This is of the work of Satan." Then Jacob (peace be upon him) intended by this advice the interpretation of that dream. They mentioned several matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾, meaning: just as He chose you through this great dream, indicating nobility, might and great station, thus He will choose you for great matters. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ijtibā' (الاجتباء) is derived from "jaba'tu al-shay'" when you purify it for yourself, and from it "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I collected the water in the pool). They differed regarding the intended meaning of this choosing. Al-Hasan said: your Lord will choose you with prophethood. Others said: what is meant is the elevation of rank and the magnifying of status. As for the specification of prophethood, there is no indication of it in the wording.

The second: His saying: ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, and in it there are several aspects:

The first: what is meant by it is the interpretation of dreams, which he called "interpretation" because it returns the matter to what he saw in the dream, meaning the interpretation of people's accounts concerning what they see in their dreams. They said: he (peace be upon him) had the utmost knowledge of the science of interpretation.

The second: the interpretation of accounts in the books of God Almighty and the reports transmitted from the earlier prophets, just as one of the scholars of our time occupies himself with the exegesis of the Qur'an and its interpretation, and the interpretation of the hadiths transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ.

The third: al-aḥādīth is the plural of ḥadīth, and ḥadīth is the ḥādith (that which occurs), and its interpretation is its outcome (māl), and the outcome of occurrences is to the power of God Almighty, His creating and His wisdom. What is meant by the interpretation of accounts is the manner of inferring, from the various kinds of created beings, both spiritual and corporeal, the power, wisdom and majesty of God Almighty.

The third: His saying: ﴿and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾.

Know that whoever interprets ijtibā' as prophethood cannot interpret the completion of favour here as prophethood as well, otherwise it would entail repetition. Rather, the completion of favour here is interpreted as the happinesses of this world and the happinesses of the Hereafter. As for the happinesses of this world: a large number of children, servants and followers, abundance of wealth, status and retinue, and his being revered in the hearts of creation, and good praise and commendation. As for the happinesses of the Hereafter: many sciences, virtuous character, and absorption in the knowledge of God Almighty. As for whoever interprets ijtibā' as attaining high ranks, here he interprets the completion of favour as prophethood, and this is reinforced by several matters:

The first: the completion of favour is an expression for that by which a favour becomes complete, perfect, free from aspects of deficiency. And for a human being this is nothing but prophethood, for all the stations of creation below the station of messengership are deficient in comparison with the perfection of prophethood. Thus absolute perfection and absolute completeness for a human being is nothing but prophethood.

The second: His saying: ﴿as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac﴾. It is well known that the complete favour by which Abraham and Isaac were distinguished from the rest of mankind is nothing but prophethood, so it is necessary that the meaning of the completion of favour be prophethood.

Know that when we interpreted this verse as prophethood, it follows that all the sons of Jacob were prophets, because He said: ﴿and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾, and this requires the attainment of complete favour for the family of Jacob. Since the meaning of completing the favour is prophethood, it follows that it was attained by the family of Jacob. We have abandoned applying this to those other than his sons, so it remains necessary that it be applied to his sons. Also, Joseph (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, and its interpretation was eleven persons who possess virtue and perfection, by whose knowledge and religion the people of the earth are illuminated, for there is nothing brighter than the stars and by them one is guided; and this requires that the totality of Jacob's sons were prophets and messengers.

If it is asked: how is it permissible that they were prophets, when they committed what they committed against Joseph (peace be upon him)?

We say: that occurred before prophethood, and in our view infallibility is considered only at the time of prophethood, not before it.

The second view: that what is meant by His saying ﴿and complete His favour upon you﴾ is his deliverance from trials, and the aspect of comparison in this with Abraham and Isaac (peace be upon them both) is God Almighty's bestowal upon Abraham by saving him from the fire, and upon his son Isaac by rescuing him from the slaughter.

The third view: that the completion of favour is connecting God's favour upon him in this world with the favour of the Hereafter, by making them prophets and kings in this world and transferring them from it to the high ranks in Paradise.

Know that the correct view is the first, because complete favour for a human being is nothing but prophethood, and everything else is deficient in comparison with it. Then, when He promised him these three degrees, He concluded the speech with His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾ His saying "Knowing" is an allusion to His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and His saying "Wise" is an allusion to the fact that God Almighty is exalted above folly and futility, and places prophethood only in a holy soul and a radiant, lofty jewel.

If it is asked: were these good tidings that Jacob (peace be upon him) mentioned something he was certain of or not? If he was certain of their truth, how did he grieve over Joseph (peace be upon him), how could it be that it was confused for him that the wolf had eaten him, how did he fear for him from his brothers that they would destroy him, and how did he say to his brothers: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him while you are heedless of him﴾, despite his knowledge that God, glorified be He, would choose him and make him a messenger? And if we say that he (peace be upon him) was not aware of the truth of these circumstances, how could he be certain of them, and how could he judge their occurrence with a firm judgment without any hesitation?

We say: it is not far-fetched that His saying "And thus will your Lord choose you" was conditional upon their not plotting against him, since the mention of that has already preceded. Also, on the assumption that he (peace be upon him) was certain that Joseph (peace be upon him) would reach these stations, it is nonetheless not impossible that he would fall into severe straits and then be delivered from them and reach those stations; so his fear was for this reason, and the meaning of his saying "And I fear that the wolf will eat him" [Yusuf: 13] is a warning against negligence in guarding him, even though he knew that the wolf would not reach him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 5–6:

God Almighty says: ﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾ ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of events and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Hafs read "yā bunayya" (يا بُنَيَّ) with a fatha on the ya, while the others read it with a kasra.

The second issue: Jacob (peace be upon him) had an intense love for Joseph and his brother, and because of this his brothers envied them. This sentiment became apparent to Jacob (peace be upon him) through many signs. So when Joseph (peace be upon him) mentioned this dream, and its interpretation was that his brothers and his parents would submit to him, he said: "Do not inform them of your dream, for they will recognise its interpretation and plot against you a scheme."

The third issue: Al-Wahidi said: "Al-ru'ya (الرُّؤْيا) is a verbal noun, like al-bushra (البُشْرى), al-suqya (السُّقْيا), al-buqya (البُقْيا) and al-shura (الشُّورى). However, when it became a noun for this imagined thing in sleep, it took the course of nouns." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Al-ru'ya has the meaning of al-ru'yah (seeing), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep rather than in wakefulness. Hence it was distinguished from it by the two feminine letters, as it is said: al-qurbah and al-qurba." It was read as "ru'yāka" (رُوياكَ) with the hamza changed to waw. Al-Kisa'i was heard reading "ruyyāka" and "riyyāka" with assimilation, and with the ra' vowelled with damma and with kasra; and these are weak readings.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿fa-yakīdū laka kaydan﴾ ("so that they plot against you a scheme"), and it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (أنْ). The meaning is: if you relate it to them, they will scheme against you.

If it is asked: why did he not say "fa-yakīdūnaka" as in His saying ﴿fa-kīdūnī﴾ [Hud: 55]?

We say: this lam is for emphasising the complement, like His saying ﴿li-l-ru'yā ta'burūn﴾, and like your saying "naṣaḥtuka" and "naṣaḥtu laka", and "shakartuka" and "shakartu laka". It is also said that it belongs to the complement of the scheming, meaning "fa-yakīdū kaydan laka". The people of verification said: this indicates that they had knowledge of the interpretation of dreams, for otherwise they would not have known from this dream anything that would cause resentment and anger.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.﴾ The reason for this statement is that if they had proceeded to scheme, that would be attributed to Satan. Its parallel is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him): "This is of the work of Satan." Then Jacob (peace be upon him) intended by this advice the interpretation of that dream. They mentioned several matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾, meaning: just as He chose you through this great dream, indicating nobility, might and great station, thus He will choose you for great matters. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ijtibā' (الاجتباء) is derived from "jaba'tu al-shay'" when you purify it for yourself, and from it "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I collected the water in the pool). They differed regarding the intended meaning of this choosing. Al-Hasan said: your Lord will choose you with prophethood. Others said: what is meant is the elevation of rank and the magnifying of status. As for the specification of prophethood, there is no indication of it in the wording.

The second: His saying: ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, and in it there are several aspects:

The first: what is meant by it is the interpretation of dreams, which he called "interpretation" because it returns the matter to what he saw in the dream, meaning the interpretation of people's accounts concerning what they see in their dreams. They said: he (peace be upon him) had the utmost knowledge of the science of interpretation.

The second: the interpretation of accounts in the books of God Almighty and the reports transmitted from the earlier prophets, just as one of the scholars of our time occupies himself with the exegesis of the Qur'an and its interpretation, and the interpretation of the hadiths transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ.

The third: al-aḥādīth is the plural of ḥadīth, and ḥadīth is the ḥādith (that which occurs), and its interpretation is its outcome (māl), and the outcome of occurrences is to the power of God Almighty, His creating and His wisdom. What is meant by the interpretation of accounts is the manner of inferring, from the various kinds of created beings, both spiritual and corporeal, the power, wisdom and majesty of God Almighty.

The third: His saying: ﴿and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾.

Know that whoever interprets ijtibā' as prophethood cannot interpret the completion of favour here as prophethood as well, otherwise it would entail repetition. Rather, the completion of favour here is interpreted as the happinesses of this world and the happinesses of the Hereafter. As for the happinesses of this world: a large number of children, servants and followers, abundance of wealth, status and retinue, and his being revered in the hearts of creation, and good praise and commendation. As for the happinesses of the Hereafter: many sciences, virtuous character, and absorption in the knowledge of God Almighty. As for whoever interprets ijtibā' as attaining high ranks, here he interprets the completion of favour as prophethood, and this is reinforced by several matters:

The first: the completion of favour is an expression for that by which a favour becomes complete, perfect, free from aspects of deficiency. And for a human being this is nothing but prophethood, for all the stations of creation below the station of messengership are deficient in comparison with the perfection of prophethood. Thus absolute perfection and absolute completeness for a human being is nothing but prophethood.

The second: His saying: ﴿as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac﴾. It is well known that the complete favour by which Abraham and Isaac were distinguished from the rest of mankind is nothing but prophethood, so it is necessary that the meaning of the completion of favour be prophethood.

Know that when we interpreted this verse as prophethood, it follows that all the sons of Jacob were prophets, because He said: ﴿and complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾, and this requires the attainment of complete favour for the family of Jacob. Since the meaning of completing the favour is prophethood, it follows that it was attained by the family of Jacob. We have abandoned applying this to those other than his sons, so it remains necessary that it be applied to his sons. Also, Joseph (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, and its interpretation was eleven persons who possess virtue and perfection, by whose knowledge and religion the people of the earth are illuminated, for there is nothing brighter than the stars and by them one is guided; and this requires that the totality of Jacob's sons were prophets and messengers.

If it is asked: how is it permissible that they were prophets, when they committed what they committed against Joseph (peace be upon him)?

We say: that occurred before prophethood, and in our view infallibility is considered only at the time of prophethood, not before it.

The second view: that what is meant by His saying ﴿and complete His favour upon you﴾ is his deliverance from trials, and the aspect of comparison in this with Abraham and Isaac (peace be upon them both) is God Almighty's bestowal upon Abraham by saving him from the fire, and upon his son Isaac by rescuing him from the slaughter.

The third view: that the completion of favour is connecting God's favour upon him in this world with the favour of the Hereafter, by making them prophets and kings in this world and transferring them from it to the high ranks in Paradise.

Know that the correct view is the first, because complete favour for a human being is nothing but prophethood, and everything else is deficient in comparison with it. Then, when He promised him these three degrees, He concluded the speech with His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾ His saying "Knowing" is an allusion to His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and His saying "Wise" is an allusion to the fact that God Almighty is exalted above folly and futility, and places prophethood only in a holy soul and a radiant, lofty jewel.

If it is asked: were these good tidings that Jacob (peace be upon him) mentioned something he was certain of or not? If he was certain of their truth, how did he grieve over Joseph (peace be upon him), how could it be that it was confused for him that the wolf had eaten him, how did he fear for him from his brothers that they would destroy him, and how did he say to his brothers: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him while you are heedless of him﴾, despite his knowledge that God, glorified be He, would choose him and make him a messenger? And if we say that he (peace be upon him) was not aware of the truth of these circumstances, how could he be certain of them, and how could he judge their occurrence with a firm judgment without any hesitation?

We say: it is not far-fetched that His saying "And thus will your Lord choose you" was conditional upon their not plotting against him, since the mention of that has already preceded. Also, on the assumption that he (peace be upon him) was certain that Joseph (peace be upon him) would reach these stations, it is nonetheless not impossible that he would fall into severe straits and then be delivered from them and reach those stations; so his fear was for this reason, and the meaning of his saying "And I fear that the wolf will eat him" [Yusuf: 13] is a warning against negligence in guarding him, even though he knew that the wolf would not reach him.

[Page 74]

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly there were in Joseph and his brothers signs for the inquirers.﴾ ﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a group. Indeed our father is in obvious error."﴾

Concerning this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) mentioned the names of Joseph's brothers: Yahuda, Ruwbil, Shim'un, Lawi, Rabalun, Yashjur, Dina, Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Ashir. Then he said: "The first seven are from Layya, the daughter of Ya'qub's maternal aunt, and the other four are from two concubines, Zilfa and Bilha. When Layya died, Ya'qub married her sister Rahil, and she bore him Binyamin and Yusuf."

**The second issue:** His statement ﴿signs for the inquirers﴾. Ibn Kathir read "āyatun" without an alif, taking it as referring to the matter of Joseph. The rest read "āyātun" in the plural, because Joseph's affairs were many and each of them was a sign in itself.

**The third issue:** The scholars mentioned several interpretations of His statement ﴿signs for the inquirers﴾:

The first: Ibn Abbas said: "A Jewish rabbi entered upon the Prophet ﷺ and heard from him the recitation of [the story of] Joseph. He returned to the Jews and informed them that he had heard it from him exactly as it is in the Torah. So a group of them went and heard it as he had heard it, and they said to him: 'Who taught you this story?' He said: 'Allah taught me.' Then there was revealed: ﴿Certainly there were in Joseph and his brothers signs for the inquirers.﴾" This interpretation seems to me far-fetched, because what is understood from the verse is that in the event of Joseph there were signs for the inquirers. According to this interpretation which we have related, the signs were not in the story of Joseph; rather, the signs were in Muhammad's ﷺ report of it without prior learning or study, and there is a clear difference between the two statements.

The second: Most of the people of Makkah were relatives of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and they denied his prophethood and showed severe enmity toward him out of envy. So Allah, exalted is He, related this story and clarified that Joseph's brothers went to great lengths in harming him out of envy. In the end, Allah, exalted is He, gave him victory, strengthened him, and placed them under his authority and banner. When a sensible person hears such an event, it is a deterrent for him from engaging in envy.

The third: When Ya'qub interpreted Joseph's dream, that interpretation came to pass and entered into existence after eighty years. Likewise, when Allah, exalted is He, promised Muhammad (peace be upon him) victory and triumph over his enemies, if that promised matter is delayed for a period of time, this does not indicate that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was lying in it. Thus this story is beneficial from this angle.

The fourth: Joseph's brothers went to great lengths in nullifying his affair, but when Allah, exalted is He, promised him victory and triumph, the matter occurred as Allah, exalted is He, decreed and not as the enemies strove for. Likewise is the case of Muhammad ﷺ, for when Allah guaranteed him the elevation of rank, the efforts of the disbelievers to nullify his affair did not harm him.

* * *

As for His statement ﴿for the inquirers﴾: know that in this story there are many signs for whoever asks about it. It is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿in four days, equal for the inquirers﴾.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a group."﴾ Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** His statement ﴿Joseph (Yusuf)﴾: the lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and in it there is emphasis and confirmation of the content of the sentence. They meant that the increase of his love for the two of them is a fixed matter with no doubt about it. "And his brother" is Binyamin. They said "his brother" although they were all brothers, because their mother was one. The "'uṣbah" and the "'iṣābah" are ten or more, and it was said up to forty. They were named so because they are a group by whom affairs are bound (ta'ṣubu bihimu al-umūr). It is related from Ali (peace be upon him) that he read "wa naḥnu 'uṣbatan" with the accusative case, and it was said: its meaning is "and we gather as a group."

**The second issue:** The purpose of this is to explain the cause for which they intended to harm Joseph. That is because Ya'qub used to prefer

[Page 75]

Joseph and his brother over the rest of the children in love, and they were hurt by him for several reasons:

The first: They were older in age than the two of them.

The second: They were stronger and more active in attending to the father's interests than the two of them.

The third: They said: "We are the ones who repel harms and calamities, and who busy ourselves with obtaining benefits and goods."

Since it is established what we have mentioned, that they were ahead of Joseph and his brother in these virtues, yet he (peace be upon him) used to prefer Joseph and his brother over them, therefore they said: ﴿Indeed our father is in obvious error﴾, meaning: this is clear injustice and manifest misguidance. Here there are questions:

**The first question:** It is one of the known matters that preferring some children over others produces hatred and envy, and produces calamities. Since Ya'qub (peace be upon him) knew this, why did he proceed with this preference? Also, the elder, the more knowledgeable, and the more beneficial are more excellent, so why did he reverse this principle?

The answer: He (peace be upon him) preferred the two of them over the rest of the children only in love, and love is not within human capacity. So he was excused in it, and no blame attaches to him because of it.

**The second question:** If the children of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) believed that he was truly a messenger from Allah, exalted is He, how did they object to him, how did they find fault with his way and criticize his action? And if they were denying his prophethood, this would necessitate their disbelief.

The answer: They were believers in the prophethood of their father, acknowledging that he was truly a messenger from Allah, exalted is He. However, perhaps they permitted that prophets (peace be upon them) might do particular actions merely by ijtihad (independent reasoning). Then their own ijtihad led them to judge their father's ijtihad in that matter as erroneous. That is because they used to say: "These two are boys who have not reached full intellect, and we are ahead of them in age, intellect, sufficiency, benefit, abundance of service, and undertaking of important tasks. His insistence on preferring Joseph over us contradicts this evidence." As for Ya'qub (peace be upon him), perhaps he would say: "Increase in love is not within capacity and power, so Allah has no obligation upon me regarding it." As for his singling out the two of them with greater kindness, it may be that this was for several reasons:

One: Their mother died while they were young.

Two: Because he saw in him signs of right guidance and nobility that he did not find in the rest of the children.

Three: Perhaps he (peace be upon him), although young, used to serve his father with kinds of service more noble and exalted than what the rest of the children produced.

The summary is that this matter was a matter of ijtihad, and it was mixed with the inclination of the soul and the requirements of human nature. Therefore, the occurrence of disagreement in it does not necessitate that one of the two opponents attack the religion of the other or his honor.

**The third question:** They attributed their father to "obvious misguidance," and that is exaggeration in blame and attack. Whoever exaggerates in attacking a messenger disbelieves, especially if the attacker is a son, since the right of fatherhood requires greater reverence.

The answer: What is meant by it is misguidance from taking care of worldly interests, not distance from the path of right guidance and correctness.

**The fourth question:** Their statement ﴿Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are﴾ is pure envy, and envy is among the mothers of the major sins, especially since they committed lying because of that envy, and neglected that righteous brother, threw him into the humiliation of slavery, and distanced him from his compassionate father. They also cast their father into perpetual grief and great sorrow, and they committed lying. Thus no blameworthy trait or course of evil and corruption remained except that they carried it out, and all of this detracts from infallibility and prophethood.

The answer: The matter is as you have mentioned, except that what is considered by us is the infallibility of the prophets (peace be upon them) at the time the prophethood is attained. As for before it, that is not obligatory. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 9–10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Kill Joseph, or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face may be free for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾ ﴿A speaker among them said: Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the depths of the well (ghayabat al-jubb), that some of the travelers may pick him up, if you are going to do something.﴾

Know that when envy grew strong and reached its extreme, they said: there is no escape from keeping Joseph away from his father, and this can only be achieved by one of two ways: killing him, or banishing him to a land where there is despair of his reuniting with his father. There is no evil the envious man can reach greater than this. Then they mentioned the reason for it, which is their saying: ﴿so that your father's face may be free for you﴾, meaning: Joseph has occupied him away from us and turned his face toward himself; so when he is lost to him, he will turn toward us with inclination and love. ﴿And after him you will be a righteous people﴾. In this there are several aspects:

First: they knew that what they had resolved upon was among the major sins, so they said: if we do that, we will repent to God and become among the righteous people.

Second: the intended meaning here is not the righteousness of religion; rather the meaning is: your affair will be set right in the eyes of your father, and your father will become loving toward you, occupied with your affairs.

Third: the meaning is that because of this estrangement you have become confused, not free to set right an important matter; when this estrangement departs, you will be free to set right your important matters. They differed as to who this speaker was who commanded the killing, on two views:

One: that some of his brothers said this.

Two: that they consulted a stranger, and he advised them to kill him, and none of his brothers said that.

As for those who held the first view, they differed. Wahb said: he was Shim'un; Muqatil said: Ruben.

If it is said: how is this fitting for them, when they were prophets?

We say: some people answered this by saying that they were adolescents at that time and not yet mature. This is weak, because it is far-fetched that a prophet of God, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, would send a group of boys without some sensible person with them to prevent them from ugly deeds. Also, they said: ﴿and after him you will be a righteous people﴾, and this indicates that before repentance they would not be righteous, and that contradicts their being children. Some answered that this falls under minor sins, and this too is far-fetched, because harming a father who is a sinless prophet, lying about him, and striving to destroy a young brother are each among the mothers of major sins. Rather, the correct answer is to say: they were not prophets at that time; and even if they were prophets, they undertook this incident before prophethood.

Then God related that a speaker said: ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾. It was said that he was Ruben, who was Joseph's maternal cousin, and was the best of them in opinion regarding him, so he prevented them from killing him. It was also said: Yahuda, who was the foremost of them in opinion, virtue and age.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿and throw him into the depths of the well﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' read "fi ghayabat al-jubb" in the plural in both places, this one and the following one; the rest read "ghayabat" in the singular in both places. As for the reading of the plural, it is because the well has sides and directions, so there are depths in it; and whoever reads the singular says: the intended meaning is one place in the well where Joseph would be hidden, so the singular is more specific and more indicative of the intended meaning. Al-Jahdari read "fi ghaybat al-jubb."

The second issue: the people of the language said: al-ghayaba is everything that conceals a thing and covers it; so ghayabat al-jubb is its depth, and that part of it which is hidden from the eye of the viewer and grows dark at its bottom. Al-jubb is the well that is not lined with stone; it was called jubb because it was cut (qata'a) out, and nothing other than cutting occurred in it, such as lining (tayy) or the like. The mention of al-ghayaba with al-jubb is to indicate that the one who suggested it advised casting him in a dark place of the well that the gaze of onlookers would not reach; so the mention of ghayaba conveyed this meaning, since it could have been understood that he would be thrown in a place of the well that does not prevent him from being seen by onlookers.

The third issue: the "al" in "al-jubb" indicates a previously known referent. They differed about which well it was. Qatadah said: it was a well in Bayt al-Maqdis; Wahb said: it was in the land of the Urdunn; Muqatil said: it was three farsakh from Ya'qub's dwelling. They specified that well because of the reason they mentioned, which is their saying: ﴿that some of the travelers may pick him up﴾. That well was well known and they used to come to it frequently, and he (the advisor) knew that if he were cast into it, he would be nearer to safety, because when the caravan passed by and came to the water, they would see the person in it, and upon seeing him they would take him out and carry him away; so casting him into it was further from destruction.

The fourth issue: al-iltiqat is taking up a thing from the road, and from it come luqatah (lost property) and laqit (foundling). Al-Hasan read "taltaqit-hu" with the feminine ta', according to the meaning, because some of the caravan is also a caravan; and al-sayyarah is the group of people who travel the road for a journey. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the passers-by.

His saying: ﴿if you are going to do something﴾ contains an indication that the better course is that you do none of that; but if it must be done, then confine yourselves to this extent. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with﴾, meaning: the better course is that you do not do that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 9–10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Kill Joseph, or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face may be free for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾ ﴿A speaker among them said: Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the depths of the well (ghayabat al-jubb), that some of the travelers may pick him up, if you are going to do something.﴾

Know that when envy grew strong and reached its extreme, they said: there is no escape from keeping Joseph away from his father, and this can only be achieved by one of two ways: killing him, or banishing him to a land where there is despair of his reuniting with his father. There is no evil the envious man can reach greater than this. Then they mentioned the reason for it, which is their saying: ﴿so that your father's face may be free for you﴾, meaning: Joseph has occupied him away from us and turned his face toward himself; so when he is lost to him, he will turn toward us with inclination and love. ﴿And after him you will be a righteous people﴾. In this there are several aspects:

First: they knew that what they had resolved upon was among the major sins, so they said: if we do that, we will repent to God and become among the righteous people.

Second: the intended meaning here is not the righteousness of religion; rather the meaning is: your affair will be set right in the eyes of your father, and your father will become loving toward you, occupied with your affairs.

Third: the meaning is that because of this estrangement you have become confused, not free to set right an important matter; when this estrangement departs, you will be free to set right your important matters. They differed as to who this speaker was who commanded the killing, on two views:

One: that some of his brothers said this.

Two: that they consulted a stranger, and he advised them to kill him, and none of his brothers said that.

As for those who held the first view, they differed. Wahb said: he was Shim'un; Muqatil said: Ruben.

If it is said: how is this fitting for them, when they were prophets?

We say: some people answered this by saying that they were adolescents at that time and not yet mature. This is weak, because it is far-fetched that a prophet of God, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, would send a group of boys without some sensible person with them to prevent them from ugly deeds. Also, they said: ﴿and after him you will be a righteous people﴾, and this indicates that before repentance they would not be righteous, and that contradicts their being children. Some answered that this falls under minor sins, and this too is far-fetched, because harming a father who is a sinless prophet, lying about him, and striving to destroy a young brother are each among the mothers of major sins. Rather, the correct answer is to say: they were not prophets at that time; and even if they were prophets, they undertook this incident before prophethood.

Then God related that a speaker said: ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾. It was said that he was Ruben, who was Joseph's maternal cousin, and was the best of them in opinion regarding him, so he prevented them from killing him. It was also said: Yahuda, who was the foremost of them in opinion, virtue and age.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 11–12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O our father, what is [wrong] with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph while we are indeed sincere toward him?"﴾ ﴿Send him with us tomorrow to eat and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.﴾

Know that this speech indicates that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, feared for Joseph at their hands, and had it not been so, they would not have said this statement.

Know also that when they had firmly resolved, they uttered this speech and showed their father that they had the utmost love for Joseph and the utmost compassion toward him. Their custom was to be away from him for a period to pasture the animals, so they asked him to send him with them. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, loved to comfort Joseph's heart, so he was deceived by their words and sent him with them. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "La ta'manna" (لا تأمنا) was read with the two nuns made clear, and with idgham (assimilation) with ishmam (partial rounding) and without ishmam. The meaning is: why do you fear for him from us, while we love him and desire good for him?

Page 78
The second issue: In ﴿yartaʿ wa-yalʿab﴾ (يَرْتَعْ ويَلْعَبْ) there are five readings:

The first reading: Ibn Kathir read "nartaʿ" (نَرْتَعِ) with the nun and with kasra on the ʿayn, from al-irtiʿa' (الِارْتِعاء), and "yalʿab" with the ya'. Al-irtiʿa' is an iftiʿal form from raʿaytu (رَعَيْتُ). It is said: the livestock "rataʿat al-kala'" (رَعَتِ الماشِيَةُ الكَلَأ), "tarʿāhu raʿyan" (تَرْعاهُ رَعْيًا), meaning when they ate it. His saying "nartaʿ": al-irtiʿa' is for camels and livestock, and they attributed it to themselves, because the meaning is "we pasture our camels," then they ascribed it to themselves because they were the cause of that pasturing. The summary is that they attributed the pasturing and the task of guarding the property to themselves, because they were adult and complete, and they attributed the play to Joseph because of his youth.

The second reading: Nafi' read both with the ya' and with kasra on the ʿayn of "yartaʿ," attributing the pasturing to Joseph, meaning that he would engage in pasturing the camels in order to train himself in it; so once "yartaʿ" and once "yalʿab," like the act of children.

The third reading: Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read "nartaʿ" with the nun and with jazm (sukun) on the ʿayn, and likewise "nalʿab." Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-rataʿ is eating with greed. It was said: it is abundance. It was said: what is meant by play is undertaking permissible things, and this is a quality that can be attributed to a human being. As for "nalʿab," it is narrated that it was said to Abu ʿAmr: how do they say "we play" when they are prophets? He said: they were not prophets at that time. Also, it is possible that what is meant by play is undertaking permissible things for the sake of gladdening the heart, as it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said to Jabir: "Why not a virgin, you playing with her and she playing with you?" Also, their play was racing, and its purpose was learning warfare and fighting against the disbelievers. The evidence for this is their saying: "We went racing" (إنّا ذَهَبْنا نَسْتَبِقُ). They named it play only because it resembles it in form.

The fourth reading: The people of Kufa read both with the ya' and with sukun on the ʿayn, and its meaning is attributing the pasturing and the play to Joseph, peace be upon him.

The fifth reading: "yartaʿ" with the ya' and "nalʿab" with the nun, and this is far-fetched, because they only asked to send Joseph with them so that he would rejoice in play, not so that they would rejoice in play. And Allah knows best.

He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him." They said, "If the wolf devours him while we are a band, then indeed we would be losers."

Know that when they asked him to send Yusuf with them, he gave them an excuse on two grounds:

The first: their taking him away and parting from him would grieve him, because he could not bear to be apart from him for even an hour.

The second: his fear for him from the wolf, if they became heedless of him while tending their flocks or playing, because of their lack of concern for him.

It is said: he had seen in a dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, so he was warning them. It is from this that he mentioned it. It is as if he had taught them the argument. And among their sayings: "Calamity is entrusted to speech." It is also said: the wolves were numerous in their lands. The word "al-dhi'b" (الذِّئْبُ) was read with a hamza, according to the original form, and also with lightening (al-takhfif). It is also said: its derivation is from "tadhā'abat al-rīḥ" (تَذاءَبَتِ الرِّيحُ), when the wind blows from every direction. When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said these words, they answered with their saying: ﴿If the wolf devours him while we are a band, then indeed we would be losers.﴾ In this there are questions:

The first question: What is the benefit of the lam (اللّامُ) in his saying: ﴿If the wolf devours him﴾?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: the word "in" (إنْ) indicates that the condition necessitates the consequence, i.e., if this event occurs, then we are losers. So this lam entered to emphasize this necessitation.

The second: the author of al-Kashshaf said: this lam indicates an implied oath, its estimated form being: "By God, if the wolf devours him, we would indeed be losers."

The second question: What is the benefit of the waw (الواوُ) in his saying: ﴿while we are a band﴾?

The answer: it is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal). They swore that if what he feared of the wolf snatching their brother from among them occurred, and their condition was that they were ten men, by the likes of whom affairs are strengthened and difficulties are relieved, then they would indeed be a people of losers.

The third question: What is meant by their saying: ﴿Indeed we would be losers﴾?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: "losers" means those who perish in weakness and incapacity. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey a human like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 34], meaning: indeed you would be incapable.

The second: that they would be deserving that loss and ruin be invoked against them, and that it be said: God caused them loss and destruction when the wolf devoured their brother while they were present.

The third: the meaning is that if we fail to protect our brother, then our livestock would have perished and we would have lost them.

The fourth: they had exhausted themselves in serving their father and strove in carrying out his affairs, and they bore those hardships only so that they might gain from him prayers and praise. So they said: if we fall short in this service, we have nullified all those deeds and lost everything of the kinds of service that proceeded from us.

The fourth question: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, gave two excuses, so why did they answer one of them and not the other?

The answer: their spite and rage were caused by the first excuse, which was the intensity of his love for him. So when they heard the mention of that meaning, they feigned heedlessness of it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verse 15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they took him away and resolved to put him at the bottom of the well, We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive."﴾

Know that in this verse there must be an ellipsis (idmar, the omission of words understood from context) in two places:

The first: the sense of the verse is that they said: ﴿"If the wolf eats him while we are a group, then we would indeed be losers."﴾ Then he (Jacob) gave him permission and sent him with them, and then his saying connects: ﴿"So when they took him away."﴾

The second: the phrase ﴿"So when they took him away and resolved to put him at the bottom of the well"﴾ must have an answer (jawab), since the answer to *lamma* (when) is not mentioned. Its implied meaning is "then they put him in it." Omitting the answer is common in the Qur'an, on condition that what is mentioned indicates it, and here this is the case.

As-Suddi said: When Joseph, peace be upon him, went out with his brothers, they showed him intense hostility. This brother (of his) began to strike him, so he cried out to another, who struck him too, and he found none of them merciful. They beat him until they nearly killed him, while he was saying: "O Jacob, if only you knew what is being done to your son!" Then Judah said: "Did you not give me a covenant that you would not kill him?" So they took him to the well, lowering him into it while he was clinging to its edge. They stripped off his shirt, and their aim was to smear it with blood and present it to Jacob. He said to them: "Return my shirt to me so that I may cover myself with it." They said: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the eleven stars so that they may keep you company." Then they lowered him into the well until, when he reached halfway down, they dropped him so that he would die.

There was water in the well, so he fell into it, then he rested on a rock and stood upon it, weeping. They called out to him, and he thought that mercy had come to them, so he answered them. They then wanted to crush him with a rock, but Judah stood up and prevented them. Judah used to bring him food.

It is narrated that when he was thrown into the well he said: "O You who are a witness not absent, O You who are near not distant, O You who are victorious not defeated, make for me a way out and an exit from my affair." It is also narrated that when Abraham, peace be upon him, was thrown into the fire, he was stripped of his garments, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought him a shirt of the silk of Paradise and dressed him in it. Abraham passed it to Isaac, and Isaac to Jacob. Jacob placed it in an amulet (tamimah) and hung it around Joseph's neck, peace be upon him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and took it out and dressed him in it.

\* \* \*

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive."﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning His saying ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them: what is meant is revelation (wahy), prophethood and messengership. This is the view of a great group of the scholars who verify (muhaqqiqun). Then those who hold this view differed as to whether he, peace be upon him, was at that time an adult or a child. Some said that he was an adult at that time, and his age was seventeen years. Others said that he was a child, but God, exalted is He, perfected his intellect and made him fit to receive revelation and prophethood, as in the case of Jesus, peace be upon him.

The second opinion: what is meant by this revelation is inspiration (ilham), as in His saying: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ (Qur'an 28:7) and His saying: ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾ (Qur'an 16:68). The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of wahy is that.

If it is said: How can He make him a prophet at that time when there is no one there to convey the message to him?

We say: There is nothing impossible in His honouring him with revelation and scripture and commanding him to convey the message after some time, and the benefit of advancing the revelation is to console him, to calm his soul, and to remove grief and loneliness from his heart.

The second issue: concerning His saying ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: what is meant is that God, exalted is He, revealed to Joseph: "You will surely inform your brothers of their deed after this day, while they do not perceive at that time that you are Joseph." The purpose is to strengthen his heart by assuring him that he will attain deliverance from this trial, that he will become dominant over them, and that they will be under his power and authority. It is narrated that when they entered upon him to request grain, and he recognised them while they did not recognise him, he called for the drinking-cup (suwa'), placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This cup informs me that you had a brother of your father's named Joseph, whom you threw into the well and told your father: 'The wolf ate him.'"

The second: what is meant is that We revealed to Joseph, peace be upon him, in the well, that you will inform your brothers of these deeds, while they were not aware of the descent of the revelation upon him. The third issue: if we take His saying ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ according to the first interpretation, then this is a command from God, exalted is He, to Joseph that he should conceal himself from his father and not inform him of his own circumstances. For this reason he kept news of himself from his father throughout that period, although he knew of his father's grief over him, out of fear of disobeying the command of God, exalted and glorified is He, and he endured the bitterness of that. God, glorified and exalted is He, had decreed for Jacob, peace be upon him, that these severe sorrows and great anxieties should reach him, so that his turning back to God, exalted is He, would increase and the attachment of his thought to this world would be severed, so that he would reach a high rank in servitude that cannot be attained except by bearing severe trials. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another, and we left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. The point is that although we are truthful, you will not believe us, because you suspect us. [p. 82]

[p. 83]

Then Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, said: ﴿So patience is beautiful.﴾ On this there are issues:

The first issue: some said it is in the nominative by the inchoative (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is omitted, and the sense is: "So patient endurance is beautiful, better than lamentation." Others omitted the subject. Al-Khalīl said: "What I do is beautiful patience." Qaṭrub said: its meaning is "So my patience is beautiful patience." Al-Farrāʾ said: "So it is beautiful patience."

The second issue: Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, had lost his eyebrows, and he used to lift them with a cloth. It was said to him: "What is this?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of griefs." Then Allah, exalted, revealed to him: "O Yaʿqūb, do you complain about Me?" He said: "O my Lord, it is a sin I committed, so forgive it for me."

It is also narrated from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, in the story of the slander, that she said: "By Allah, if I swear, you will not believe me, and if I give an excuse, you will not accept my excuse. My example and yours is like the example of Yaʿqūb and his sons: ﴿So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ (12:18)." Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed in her defense what He revealed.

The third issue: it is narrated from al-Ḥasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about His saying: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, and he said: "Patience in which there is no complaint. Whoever makes his distress known has not been patient." Evidence for this from the Qurʾān is His saying, exalted: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾ (12:86). Mujāhid said: "So patience is beautiful" means without impatience (jazaʿ). Al-Thawrī said: part of patience is that you do not speak of your pain or your calamity, and that you do not praise yourself.

Here there is a discussion. Patience with the decree of Allah, exalted, is obligatory. As for patience with the oppression of oppressors and the schemes of schemers, it is not obligatory; rather what is obligatory is to remove it, especially when the harm returns to others. Here is the point: when the lies and treachery of Joseph's brothers became manifest, why did Yaʿqūb remain patient about that? Why did he not strive greatly in searching and inquiry, seeking to rescue Joseph, peace be upon him, from the trial and hardship if he was alive, and to establish retaliation if it is sound that they killed him? So it is established that patience in this situation is blameworthy.

What strengthens this question is that he, peace be upon him, knew that Joseph was alive and sound, because he had said to him: ﴿and thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events﴾ (12:6). The apparent meaning is that he said this by revelation. And if he knew that Joseph was alive and sound, it was obligatory for him to strive to seek him. Also, Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, was a man of great standing in himself, from a great and noble house, and the people of knowledge knew him, believed in him, and revered him. Had he exerted himself greatly in the search and inquiry, that would have become known and widely spread, and the matter of deception would have been dispelled. So what is the reason that he, peace be upon him, despite the intensity of his desire to have Joseph present and the utmost of his love for him, did not seek him, although seeking him was among the obligations? So it is established that this patience in this situation is blameworthy, by reason and by the Sharīʿa.

[p. 84]

The answer to this: we say there is no answer to it except that it may be said that He, glorified and exalted, prevented him from seeking, to intensify the trial upon him and to make the matter more severe for him. Also, perhaps he knew from circumstantial evidence that his sons were strong and that they would not allow him to search and inquire, and that if he exerted himself much in the search, they might proceed to harm him and kill him. Also, perhaps he, peace be upon him, knew that Allah, exalted, would protect Joseph from calamity and trial, and that his matter would be magnified in the Hereafter. Then he did not wish to tear away the veils from the secrets of his sons, nor did he consent to exposing them to the tongues of people. That is because if one of two sons wrongs the other, the father falls into severe torment: if he does not take revenge, his heart burns for the wronged son; and if he takes revenge, his heart burns for the son against whom he takes revenge. So when Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, fell into this trial, he judged that the more correct course was patience, silence, and entrusting the matter entirely to Allah, exalted.

Fourth issue: His saying, exalted: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ indicates that patience is of two kinds: some of it may be beautiful and some of it may be not beautiful. Beautiful patience is that a person knows that the one who sent down this trial is Allah, exalted, and then he knows that Allah, glorified, is the Owner of the dominion, and there is no objection to the Owner who disposes of what is His own. Thus his heart's absorption in this station prevents him from expressing complaint.

The second aspect: he knows that the one who sent down this trial is wise and does not err, all-knowing and does not forget, merciful and does not wrong. When this is so, and everything that proceeds from Him is wisdom and rightness, then at that point he is silent and does not object.

The third aspect: it becomes clear to him that this trial is from the Real (al-Haqq), and his being absorbed in witnessing the light of the One who tests him prevents him from occupying himself with complaining about the trial. For this reason it was said: "Perfect love does not increase through fidelity nor decrease through estrangement, for if it increased through fidelity, the beloved would be the benefit and the portion (*nasīb* wa-ḥaẓẓ). What brings about a portion is not loved in itself but only accidentally." This is the beautiful patience (*al-ṣabr al-jamīl*). As for when patience is not for the sake of contentment with the decree of the Real, glorified is He, but is for other aims, that patience is not beautiful. The governing principle for all acts, sayings, and beliefs is that whatever is done to seek servanthood (*ʿubūdiyya*) to God, exalted is He, is good, and otherwise it is not. Here the truth of what is narrated in the report appears: "Consult your heart, even if the mufti has given you a fatwa." So let the person reflect with a thorough reflection: is what he has undertaken driven and motivated by the pursuit of servanthood or not? For if the scholars gave us a ruling about something that is not in itself such, no benefit at all would appear from it.

When Jacob said, ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, he said, ﴿And God is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾. The meaning is that his undertaking of patience is not possible except by God's help, because the carnal impulses call him to show distress, and they are strong, while the spiritual impulses call him to patience and contentment. So it is as if a battle occurred between the two groups, and unless God's help is obtained, victory is not achieved. Thus His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ run parallel to His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5], and His words ﴿And God is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ run parallel to His words ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5].

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 16–18 (part 1 of 2)]

Why did he not strive greatly in searching and inquiry, seeking to rescue Joseph, peace be upon him, from the trial and hardship if he was alive, and to establish retaliation if it is sound that they killed him? So it is established that patience in this situation is blameworthy.

What strengthens this question is that he, peace be upon him, knew that Joseph was alive and sound, because he had said to him: ﴿and thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events﴾ (12:6). The apparent meaning is that he said this by revelation. And if he knew that Joseph was alive and sound, it was obligatory for him to strive to seek him. Also, Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, was a man of great standing in himself, from a great and noble house, and the people of knowledge knew him, believed in him, and revered him. Had he exerted himself greatly in the search and inquiry, that would have become known and widely spread, and the matter of deception would have been dispelled. So what is the reason that he, peace be upon him, despite the intensity of his desire to have Joseph present and the utmost of his love for him, did not seek him, although seeking him was among the obligations? So it is established that this patience in this situation is blameworthy, by reason and by the Sharīʿa.

[p. 84]

The answer to this: we say there is no answer to it except that it may be said that He, glorified and exalted, prevented him from seeking, to intensify the trial upon him and to make the matter more severe for him. Also, perhaps he knew from circumstantial evidence that his sons were strong and that they would not allow him to search and inquire, and that if he exerted himself much in the search, they might proceed to harm him and kill him. Also, perhaps he, peace be upon him, knew that Allah, exalted, would protect Joseph from calamity and trial, and that his matter would be magnified in the Hereafter. Then he did not wish to tear away the veils from the secrets of his sons, nor did he consent to exposing them to the tongues of people. That is because if one of two sons wrongs the other, the father falls into severe torment: if he does not take revenge, his heart burns for the wronged son; and if he takes revenge, his heart burns for the son against whom he takes revenge.
