His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another, and we left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said: "Rather, your souls have embellished a matter for you. So patience is beautiful. And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

Know that when they cast Joseph into the well, they returned to their father at the time of ʿishāʾ (nightfall), weeping. Ibn Jinnī narrated it as ʿushan, with a damma on the ʿayn and without the long vowel. He said: "They had become blind (ʿashaw) from weeping." At that, Yaʿqūb was alarmed and said: "Has anything befallen your flocks?" They said: "No." He said: "Then what has Joseph done?" They said: ﴿"We went off racing one another, and we left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him."﴾ He wept and cried out and said: "Where is the shirt?" He placed it over his face until his face was stained with the blood of the shirt.

It is also narrated that a woman brought a dispute before Shurayh, and she wept. Al-Shaʿbī said: "O Abū Umayya, do you not see that she is weeping?" He said: "The brothers of Joseph came weeping, and they were wrongdoers and liars. It is not fitting for a person to judge except with the truth."

They differed over the meaning of al-istibāq (racing). Al-Zajjāj said: some of them race one another in shooting. From this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace: "There is no racing except in camel, arrow, or horse." By "arrow" he means shooting. The original meaning of sabq in shooting with arrows is that two people shoot so that it becomes clear which of them has the faster arrow and the farther throw (ghalwa). Then the two who shoot are described by this, so it is said: istabaqā and tasābaqā when they do this, to make clear which of them has the faster arrow. What supports the correctness of this interpretation is that in the recitation of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) it is: "Innā dhahabnā nantadil" (we went off shooting at targets).

The second view on the meaning of istibāq is what al-Suddī and Muqātil said: "nastabiq" means we run and race on foot, so that it becomes clear which of us is faster in running.

If it is said: how could they race, when they were grown men, and this is the act of children?

We say: their racing was like racing with horses. They would test themselves by it and train themselves in running, because it was for them like a tool in fighting the enemy and in repelling the wolf when it snatches a sheep. As for his saying: ﴿and the wolf devoured him﴾, it was said that the wolf devoured Joseph; and it was said that they were speaking indirectly, and meant that the wolf devoured the belongings. The first view is the sounder.

Then they said: ﴿But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful.﴾ On this there are issues:

The first issue: the meaning is not that Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, would not believe one whom he knew to be truthful. Rather the meaning is: if we had been among those trusted and truthful in your sight, you would have suspected us regarding Joseph because of the intensity of your love for him, and you would have thought that we had lied. The point is that although we are truthful, you will not believe us, because you suspect us. It was also said: the meaning is that although we are truthful, you will not believe us, because no sign has appeared to you that indicates our truthfulness.

[p. 82]

The second issue: the scholars of our school (the Ashʿarīs) used this verse as evidence that īmān (faith), in the original language, means taṣdīq (affirmation/believing as true), because the meaning of his saying ﴿you will not believe us﴾ is: you will not affirm us as true. When this is established in the original language, it must remain so in the usage of the Sharīʿa. The full discussion of this has already preceded at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara, in the commentary on his saying: ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ (2:3).

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood.﴾ On this there are issues:

The first issue: they brought this shirt smeared with blood only to give the impression that they were truthful in their statement. It was said: they slaughtered a young goat and smeared that shirt with its blood. The judge (al-Qāḍī) said: Perhaps their purpose in removing his shirt when they cast him into the depths of the well was that they would do this as an affirmation of their truthfulness, because it is unlikely that they did that out of desire for the shirt itself. Disobedience must be accompanied by this kind of abandonment; so if they had torn it while smearing it with blood, the deception would have been stronger. When he saw the shirt intact, he knew that they were lying.

The second issue: his saying ﴿and they brought upon his shirt﴾ means: they brought with blood upon his shirt, as one says: "They came upon their camels with loads."

The third issue: the grammarians, namely al-Farrāʾ, al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjāj, and Ibn al-Anbārī, said: ﴿with false blood﴾ means blood that is falsely claimed (maksūb fīhi). However, it was described by a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the assumption of "blood with falsehood," but it made the thing itself "falsehood" for emphasis. They said: both the passive participle and the active participle are called by the verbal noun, as one says: "māʾ sakb" (poured water), meaning "maskūb" (poured); "dirham ḍarb al-amīr" (a coin of the ruler's minting); "thawb nasj al-Yaman" (a garment of Yemeni weaving). And the active participle is like his saying: ﴿if your water becomes sunken﴾ (67:30), and "rajul ʿadl" (a just man), "ṣawm" (a fasting person), and "nisāʾ nawḥ" (women who wail). When these two were called by the verbal noun, the verbal noun was also called by them. So they say "al-ʿaql al-maʿqūl" (intellect that is understood) and "al-jild al-majlūd" (hide that is flogged). From this is His saying, exalted: ﴿which of you is the afflicted one (al-maftūn)﴾ (68:6), and His saying: ﴿when you are torn into utter pieces (kull mumazzaq)﴾ (34:7).

Al-Shaʿbī said: the whole story of Joseph is in his shirt. This is because when they threw him into the well, they removed his shirt, smeared it with blood, and presented it to his father. When the witness testified, he said: ﴿if his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken truly, and he is one of the liars﴾ (12:26). When the shirt was brought to Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, and it was placed over his face, he regained his sight.

Then He, exalted, mentioned that when the brothers of Joseph made that statement and argued for their truthfulness with the blood-stained shirt, Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Rather, your souls have embellished a matter for you.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbās said: its meaning is: rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you. Taswīl is the imagining of a meaning in the soul together with the desire to complete it. Al-Azharī said: it is as if taswīl is a form (tafʿīl) derived from the request (suʾāl) of a person, which is his wish that he seeks, and which makes falsehood and other things appealing to the one who seeks it. Its root is hamzated, but the Arabs found the hamza burdensome in it. The author of al-Kashshāf said: "sawwalat" means "made easy," from sawl, which is slackness.

Having understood this, we say: his saying "Rather" (bal) is a rejection of their statement: ﴿the wolf devoured him.﴾ It is as if he said: it is not as you say; rather, ﴿your souls have embellished a matter﴾ regarding him, namely, your souls have made attractive to you a matter other than what you describe. They differed about the cause by which he knew that they were lying, in several ways:

The first: he knew this because he knew the intense envy in their hearts.

The second: he knew that Joseph was alive, because he, peace be upon him, had said to Joseph: ﴿and thus your Lord will choose you﴾ (12:6).

[p. 83]

That is decisive evidence that they were lying in this.

The third view: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: when they brought his shirt stained with false blood, and it was not torn, he said: "You have lied. If the wolf had devoured him, it would have torn his shirt." It is narrated from al-Suddī that he said: Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, said: "This wolf was merciful. How did it eat his flesh and not tear his shirt?" It was also said: when he, peace be upon him, said that, some of them said: "Rather, robbers killed him." He said: "How could they kill him and leave his shirt, when they had more need of his shirt than of killing him?" When their statements contradicted one another, he knew through this that they were lying.

* * *

Others omitted the subject. Al-Khalīl said: "What I do is beautiful patience." Qaṭrub said: its meaning is "So my patience is beautiful patience." Al-Farrāʾ said: "So it is beautiful patience."

The second issue: Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, had lost his eyebrows, and he used to lift them with a cloth. It was said to him: "What is this?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of griefs." Then Allah, exalted, revealed to him: "O Yaʿqūb, do you complain about Me?" He said: "O my Lord, it is a sin I committed, so forgive it for me."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 19–20:

Page 85

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "Good news! This is a boy!" And they concealed him as merchandise, and Allah was Knowing of what they did.﴾ ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out; and they were of those who had no desire for him.﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, explained how He facilitated the way to Yusuf's deliverance from that trial, so He said: ﴿And there came a caravan﴾, meaning a company traveling for a journey. Ibn 'Abbas said: "A caravan came," that is, a people traveling from Madyan to Egypt who lost their way and went wandering off the road, and they descended upon a land in which was the well of Yusuf, peace be upon him. The well was in a distant desert far from habitation and was used only by shepherds. It was also said that its water was salty, but it became sweet when Yusuf, peace be upon him, was cast into it. They sent a man called Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i to seek water for them. The "warid" is the one who comes to the water so that the people may draw from it. ﴿And he let down his bucket﴾. Al-Wahidi reported from the general body of lexicographers that it is said: "adla dalwahu" when one lowers it into the well, and "dallaha" when one pulls it out of the well. It is said: "adla yudlli idlaan" when one sends down, and "dalla yadlu dalwan" when one draws up and brings out. The "dalw" is well known, and its plural is "dilaa'". ﴿He said, "Good news! This is a boy!"﴾ Here there is an ellipsis, and the implied sense is: then Yusuf appeared. The commentators said: When the water-drawer let down his bucket, and Yusuf was in one side of the bottom of the well, he clung to the rope; the water-drawer looked at him, saw his beauty, and called out, saying: "Good news!" There are two issues concerning this:

The first issue: 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Bushra" without the alif and with a sukun on the ya', while the rest read "ya bushraya" with the alif and a fatha on the ya', as an idafa (possessive construction).

The second issue: concerning His saying "Ya bushra" there are two views:

The first view: that it is a word uttered at the time of good news, and its parallel is the saying of people: "ya 'ajaban min kadha" (O wonder at such-and-such), and His saying: ﴿Alas, my grief over Yusuf!﴾ [Yusuf: 84]. On this view, there are two explanations of the address:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the address in these matters, which do not answer, is to alert the listeners and to affirm the account. So when you say "ya 'ajabaah" (O wonder!), it is as if you said: "Be amazed!"

The second: Abu 'Ali said: it is as if he says: "O good news, this is your time; if you were one who is addressed, you would be addressed now and commanded to be present."

Know that the cause of the good news was that they found a boy of extreme beauty, and they said: "We will sell him for a great price, and that will become a cause of wealth."

The second view, which al-Suddi mentioned, is that the one who called out addressed his companion, whose name was Bushra, saying "Ya Bushra," as you say "Ya Zayd." It is reported from al-A'mash that he said: he called a woman whose name was Bushra, "Ya Bushra." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: if we take "bushra" as a noun for good news, which is the preferred view, it may be in the place of nominative case, as it is said "ya rajul" because it is specific to address; and it may be in the place of accusative case, on the assumption that he made that address common to the genus of good news and did not restrict it, as you say "ya rajulan" and "ya hasratan 'ala al-'ibad" (O regret over the servants).

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: To whom does the pronoun in "wa-asarruhu" refer? There are two views. The first: that it refers to the water-drawer, and his companions concealed from the caravan that they had found him in the well, because they said: "If we tell the caravan that we picked him up, they will share in him, and if we say we bought him, they will ask us for a share. So the most correct course is to say that the people of the water made him merchandise deposited with us, on condition that we sell him for them in Egypt."

The second: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "wa-asarruhu" means: the brothers of Yusuf concealed his affair, meaning that they hid the fact that he was their brother; rather they said that he was a slave of ours who had run away from us, and Yusuf went along with them in that, because they had threatened him with death in the Hebrew tongue. The first view is preferable, because His saying "wa-asarruhu bidha'ah" indicates that the intended meaning is that they concealed him at the time they ruled that he was merchandise, and that fits only the water-drawer, not the brothers of Yusuf.

The second issue: "bidha'ah" is a portion of wealth set aside for trade, from "bada'tu al-lahm" when I cut the meat. Al-Zajjaj said: "bidha'ah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "and they concealed him at the time they made him merchandise."

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah was Knowing of what they did﴾, and what is meant by it is that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, saw in the dream the stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him, and mentioned that, his brothers envied him and devised schemes to nullify that matter for him, so they cast him into severe trial so that this aim would not be easily attained for him. And He, may He be exalted, made his falling into that trial a means to his arrival in Egypt. Then his circumstances extended and the matter followed on until he became king of Egypt, and that which he had seen in the dream came to pass. So the deed that the enemies performed to keep him from that goal, Allah, may He be exalted, turned into a means to attaining that goal. For this meaning He said: ﴿And Allah was Knowing of what they did﴾.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams counted out﴾. As for His saying "wa-shaarawhu," there are two views:

The first view: that by "shira'" is meant "bay'" (selling). On this interpretation, there are two views concerning the seller:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: when the brothers of Yusuf threw Yusuf into the well and went back, after three days they returned seeking news of him. When they did not find him in the well and saw the traces of the caravan, they pursued them. When they saw Yusuf, they said: "This is our slave who ran away from us." The caravan said to them: "Then sell him to us," so they sold him to them. The meaning of His saying "wa-shaarawhu" is: they sold him. It is said: "shareetu al-shay'" when I sold it. The reason this purchase must be taken as sale is that the pronoun in His saying "wa-shaarawhu" and in His saying "wa-kanu fihi min az-zahidin" refers to one thing. But the pronoun in "wa-kanu fihi min az-zahidin" refers to the brothers, so likewise in "wa-shaarawhu" it must refer to the brothers. If that is so, they sold him, and therefore this purchase must be taken as sale.

The second view: that the seller of Yusuf were those who drew him out of the well. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "Your Lord knows best whether his brothers sold him or the caravan." Here there is another view, namely that it is possible to say that by "shira'" is meant the act of buying itself, and the meaning is that the people bought him and were among those who had no desire for him, because from circumstantial evidence they knew that the brothers of Yusuf were liars in their claim that he was their slave, and perhaps they also recognized that he was the son of Ya'qub, so they disliked buying him, fearing Allah, may He be exalted, and the exposure of that affair. Yet despite that they bought him in the end, because they bought him for a small price, even though they showed themselves to be among those without desire for him, and their aim was to reach through that a reduction of the price. It is also possible to say that when the brothers said, "He is our slave who ran away," the buyer became without desire for him. Mujahid said: "They used to say: secure him, lest he run away."

Then know that He, may He be exalted, described that price with three attributes:

The first attribute: that it was "bakhs." Ibn 'Abbas said: it means unlawful, because the price of a free man is unlawful. He also said: every "bakhs" in the Book of Allah means deficiency, except this one, which is unlawful. Al-Wahidi said: they called the unlawful "bakhs" because it lacks blessing. Qatadah said: "bakhs" is injustice, and injustice is deficiency; it is said "zalamahu," meaning he diminished him. 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: it means little. It was also said: it was a deficiency below its true value by an evident shortfall. It was also said: the dirhams were debased coins, lacking in standard weight. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to all these views, "bakhs" is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and the meaning is "for a price that is diminished."

The second attribute: His saying: "a few dirhams counted out." It was said: they were counted by number and not weighed, because they did not weigh except when it reached an uqiyyah, which is forty, and they counted what was below that. So a small amount was called "ma'dud" (counted), because a large amount would be impractical to count because of its abundance. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were twenty dirhams, and from al-Suddi that they were twenty-two dirhams. They said: the brothers were eleven, so each one of them took two dirhams, except Yahudha, who took nothing.

The third attribute: His saying: "and they were of those who had no desire for him." The meaning of zuhd is lack of desire; it is said: "zahida fulan fi kadha" when he did not desire it, and its origin is paucity; it is said: "rajulun zahid" when he is one of little greed. And in this there are several aspects:

One of them: that the brothers of Yusuf sold him, because they were among those who had no desire for him.

The second: that the caravan who sold him were among those who had no desire for him, because they had picked him up, and one who picks up a thing treats it lightly and does not care for what he sells it for; or because they feared that the rightful owner might appear and take him from their hands, so they sold him at the lowest of prices.

The third: that those who bought him were among those who had no desire for him. The direction of these views has been explained previously. The pronoun in His saying "fihi" may refer to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and it may refer to the paltry price. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the one who had bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son."﴾ ﴿And thus did We establish Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant in His affair, but most of the people do not know.﴾

Among its issues:

The first issue: Know that it is established in the reports that the one who bought him, whether from the brothers or from the travelers who came to the water, took him to Egypt and sold him there. It is said that the one who bought him was Qitfir or Itfir, who was the 'Aziz (minister) in charge of the treasuries of Egypt. The king at that time was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, a man from the 'Amaliq, who believed in Joseph and died during Joseph's lifetime. After him, Qabus ibn Mus'ab ruled, and Joseph invited him to Islam, but he refused. The 'Aziz bought him when he was seventeen years old, and he remained in his house for thirteen years. Al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid appointed him as minister when he was thirty years old, Allah gave him kingship and wisdom when he was thirty-three years old, and he died when he was one hundred and twenty years old. It is also said that the king in his days was Pharaoh of Moses, who lived four hundred years, based on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. It is also said that the Pharaoh of Moses was among the descendants of the Pharaoh of Joseph. It is said that the 'Aziz bought him for twenty dinars. It is said that they took him into the market, displaying him, and they bid against one another over his price until his price reached what equaled his weight in musk, silver and silk, and Qitfir bought him at that price. They said: the name of that woman was Zulaykha, and it is said Ra'il.

Know that none of these narrations is indicated by the Qur'an, nor has any of them been established in a sound report. The tafsir of the Book of Allah, exalted is He, does not depend on any of these narrations, so the most fitting course for a sensible person is to refrain from mentioning them.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿Make his residence comfortable﴾, meaning his dwelling and his station with you, from your saying "thawaytu bil-makan" when you stay in a place, and its verbal noun is ath-thawa'. The meaning: make his dwelling with you noble, good and pleasing, based on the saying: ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my residence excellent﴾ [Yusuf: 23]. The scholars who investigate said: the 'Aziz ordered his wife to honour his residence rather than honouring himself, which indicates that he regarded him with reverence and esteem, as one says: "Peace of Allah upon the exalted assembly." When he ordered her to honour his residence, he gave the reason by saying: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾, meaning: he will take charge of our affairs, or we will take him as a son, because he had no child, and he was impotent (ḥaṣūr).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus did We establish Joseph in the land﴾, meaning: just as We bestowed upon him safety from the well, We established him by turning the heart of the 'Aziz toward him, until through that he attained being empowered to command and forbid in the land of Egypt.

Know that true perfections are nothing but power and knowledge, and when He, glorified is He, sought to elevate Joseph's status, He mentioned these two attributes. As for his perfection in the attribute of power and capacity, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾; and as for his perfection in the attribute of knowledge, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿and that We might teach him the interpretation of events﴾. The explanation of this word has already been given.

Know that we mentioned that when he was thrown into the well, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We revealed to him that you will surely inform them of this affair of theirs﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and this apparently indicates that He revealed to him at that time. According to us, the irhas (preparatory sign before prophethood) is permissible, so it is not far-fetched to say that this revelation to him at that time was not for the sake of his being sent to the creation, but for strengthening his heart, removing grief from his chest, and so that he would be at ease with the presence of Jibril, peace be upon him. Then He, exalted is He, said here: ﴿and that We might teach him the interpretation of events﴾, and what is meant by it is his being sent to the creation to convey the obligations and to call the creation to the true religion. It is also possible to say that this first revelation was for the sake of messengership and prophethood, and His saying: ﴿and that We might teach him the interpretation of events﴾ is taken to mean that He revealed to him increments and degrees by which he becomes, each day, higher in state than what was before. Ibn Mas'ud said: the three most perceptive people are: the 'Aziz, when he perceived in Joseph and said to his wife, "Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us"; and the woman, when she saw Moses and said, "O father, hire him" [al-Qasas: 26]; and Abu Bakr, when he appointed 'Umar as successor.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is predominant in His affair﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: He is predominant over His own affair, because He is the doer of what He wills; none can repel His decree, nor prevent His judgment in His earth and His heavens.

The second: And Allah is predominant over Joseph's affair, meaning that the orderliness of his affairs was divine, and was not by his own effort; his brothers intended for him every evil and harm, while Allah intended for him good, so it happened as Allah, exalted is He, willed and arranged. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ that the whole matter is in the hand of Allah.

Know that whoever reflects upon the conditions of this world and the wonders of its states comes to know and be certain that the whole matter belongs to Allah, and that the decree of Allah prevails.

[Page 89]

**The Words of the Exalted: "And when he reached his full maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers." In this verse there are several issues.**

**First issue:** The coherence (*nazm*) of the passage can be explained as follows. God Most High explained that when his brothers mistreated him, and he endured those hardships and trials, God established him in the land. Then, when he reached his full maturity (*ashudd*), God gave him judgment and knowledge. The purpose is to show that all the blessings he attained were a reward for his patience through those trials. Some people said that prophethood is a reward for good deeds. Others said that whoever strives, is patient under God's trial, and gives thanks for God's favours attains the rank of messengerhood. They argued for the correctness of their view by saying that when God mentioned Joseph's patience through those trials, He mentioned that He gave him prophethood and messengerhood.

* * *

Then God Most High said: "Thus do We reward the good-doers." This indicates that everyone who performs the good acts that Joseph performed will be given those same ranks by God. This is far-fetched, because the scholars agree that prophethood is not something acquired through effort.

Know that whoever said that Joseph was neither a messenger nor a prophet at all, but merely a servant who obeyed God and whom God favoured, has a view that is invalid by consensus. Al-Hasan said that he was a prophet from the time about which God said: "And We revealed to him that you will inform them of this affair of theirs" [Yusuf: 15], but he was not yet a messenger. Then he became a messenger from this point, namely His words: "And when he reached his full maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge." Others said that he was a messenger from the time he was thrown into the depths of the well.

**Second issue:** Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say, "So-and-so reached his *ashudd*" when he attains its limit in youth and strength, before he begins to decline. This word is used for both the singular and the plural: one says "he reached his *ashudd*" and "they reached their *ashudd*." We have already explained the meaning of *ashudd* in Surat al-An'am at His words: "until he reaches his *ashudd*" [al-An'am: 152]. As for the exegesis, Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding "And when he reached his *ashudd*," that he said: thirty-three years.

I say: This report fits very closely with the medical principles, because physicians say that a human being comes into existence at first and grows little by little each day until he reaches the peak of perfection, and then he begins to recede and diminish until nothing of him remains. His condition is thus similar to that of the moon, which appears as a weak crescent, then continues to grow until it becomes a full moon, then recedes until it reaches nonexistence and disappearance.

Having understood this, we say: The period of the moon's cycle is twenty-eight days and a fraction. If this cycle is divided into four parts, each part is seven days. Therefore, they arranged the states of bodies according to weeks. A human, when born, is weak in constitution and slight in structure until he completes seven years. Then, when he enters the second seven, the signs of understanding, intelligence, and strength appear in him, and he continues to advance until he completes fourteen years. When he enters his fifteenth year, he enters the third week, and there the intellect is perfected, he reaches the limit of responsibility (*taklif*), and desire is stirred in him. He continues to rise in this state until he completes his twenty-first year. There the third week is completed, and he enters his twenty-second year. This week is the last of the weeks of growth and development. When his twenty-eighth year is complete, the period of growth and development is complete, and the human passes from it to the time of standing still, which is the time when a human reaches his *ashudd*. With the completion of this fifth week, the human attains thirty-five years. However, these stages vary in increase and decrease. This fifth week, which is the week of strength and perfection, begins from the twenty-ninth year until the thirty-third year, and it may extend to the thirty-fifth year. This is the reasonable path in this matter, and God knows the realities of things.

**Third issue:** Concerning the explanation of *judgment* (*hukm*) and *knowledge* (*'ilm*), there are several views:

[Page 90]

**The first view:** The root of *hukm* and *hikmah* (wisdom) is restraining the soul from its desires and preventing it from what disgraces it. Therefore, *hukm* here means practical wisdom (*al-hikmah al-'amaliyyah*), and *'ilm* means theoretical wisdom (*al-hikmah al-nazariyyah*). Practical wisdom is mentioned first here before theoretical wisdom, because those who undertake spiritual disciplines (*riyadat*) occupy themselves with practical wisdom, then ascend from it to theoretical wisdom. As for those who pursue rational reflection and spiritual contemplation, they reach theoretical wisdom first, and then descend from it to practical wisdom. Joseph's path, peace be upon him, was the first, because he endured tribulation and trial, so God opened for him the doors of unveilings (*mukashafat*). For this reason, He said: "We gave him judgment and knowledge."

**The second view:** *Hukm* is prophethood, because a prophet is a judge over creation, and *'ilm* is the knowledge of religion.

**The third view:** It is possible that *hukm* means that his tranquil soul (*al-nafs al-mutma'innah*) becomes a judge over his commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su'*), dominant over it and subduing it. When the appetitive and irascible powers become subdued and weak, the holy lights and divine illuminations pour from the world of holiness upon the essence of the soul. The reality of this matter is that the essence of the rational soul was created capable of universal knowledge and intellectual lights. However, it has been established for us, according to rational proofs and according to lofty unveilings, that the essences of human spirits differ in their realities. Some are intelligent and some are dull, some are free and some are base, some are noble and some are lowly, and some have a great inclination toward the spiritual realm while others have a great desire for the corporeal. These categories are many, and each of these stations is capable of being more intense or weaker, more perfect or less perfect. If it happens that the essence of the rational soul is a luminous, noble essence, highly prepared to receive intellectual lights and divine radiances, then this soul does not display these states in childhood, because the rational soul can only act through the use of bodily instruments. In childhood these instruments are dominated by moisture. When a person grows and the innate heat (*al-hararah al-gharizziyyah*) spreads through the body, those moistures ripen, decrease, and become balanced, and those bodily instruments become fit for the human soul to use. If the soul is noble in its original essence, then when the bodily instruments reach maturity, its knowledge is perfected, its lights strengthen, and the brilliance of its illuminations increases. Thus, His words "when he reached his *ashudd*" indicate the balance of the bodily instruments, and His words "We gave him judgment and knowledge" indicate the perfection of the soul in its practical and theoretical powers. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence good. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

Know that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was at the utmost of beauty and goodliness, so when the woman saw him she desired him. It is also said that her husband was impotent. It is said: "So-and-so sought to seduce his slave-girl from herself (rawada fulanun jariyatahu 'an nafsiha), and she sought to seduce him from himself (rawadat-hu hiya 'an nafsihi)," when each of the two sought intercourse and coition. ﴿And she closed the doors﴾: the reason is that such an act is not performed except in concealed places, especially when it is forbidden, and with intense fear present. His saying ﴿and she closed the doors﴾ means she locked them (aghlaqat). Al-Wahidi said: the origin of this is from their saying of anything that clings to a thing and becomes bound to it: ghaliqa (he became fixed/obsessed). It is said: ghaliqa fi al-batil (he persisted in falsehood) and ghaliqa fi ghadabihi (he was consumed by his anger), and from it comes ghalq al-rahn (the forfeiture of a pledge). Then it is transitive with the alif, so it is said: ughliqa al-bab (the door was closed) when he made it such that it is difficult to open. The exegetes said: the intensive form ghallaqat came because she locked seven doors, then she invited him to herself.
* * *
Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And she said, "Come, you"﴾, and regarding this there are issues:

The first issue: Al-Wahidi said: haita laka (هَيْتَ لَكَ) is a verb-word, like ruwaydan (slowly), sah (be quiet), and mah (stop). Its meaning is "come here" (halumma) according to the consensus of the people of language. Al-Akhfash said: "haita laka" is with the ha and the ta both fatha; it is also permissible to kasra the ta and to damma it. Al-Wahidi said: Abu al-Fadl al-Mundhiri said: Ibn al-Tabrizi informed me from Abu Zayd, who said: haita laka in Hebrew is hayya lakh, meaning "come"; the Qur'an arabicized it. Al-Farra' said: it is a dialect of the people of Hawran, who fell into Makka and so they spoke it. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is a point of agreement between the dialect of Quraysh and the people of Hawran, just as the language of the Arabs and the Romans agreed on "qistas" (balance), the language of the Arabs and the Persians on "sijjil", the language of the Arabs and the Turks on "ghassaq", and the language of the Arabs and the Abyssinians on "nashi'at al-layl" (the rising of the night).

The second issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, read "hiyta" with a kasra on the ha and fatha on the ta. Ibn Kathir read "haytu laka" like "haythu". Hisham ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Amir, read "hi'tu laka" with a kasra on the ha, a hamza on the ya, and a damma on the ta, like "ji'tu" from "tahayya'tu laka" (I have prepared myself for you). The rest read with a fatha on the ha, sukun on the ya, and fatha on the ta. Then He, exalted, said: when the woman mentioned this statement, Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence good﴾. His saying ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾ means I take refuge in Allah as a refuge (a'udhu billah ma'adhan). The pronoun in His saying ﴿indeed (innahu)﴾ is for the matter and the affair. ﴿My lord; he has made my residence good﴾ means: my lord, my master and my owner has made my residence good when he said to you: "Honour his residence." It is not fitting for reason that I repay him for that kindness with this vile betrayal. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾: those who repay kindness with evil. It was said: he meant adulterers, because they wrong themselves, or because their act requires placing a thing in other than its place. Here there are questions:

The first question: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was free and was not a slave of anyone, so his saying ﴿he is my lord﴾ would be a lie, and that is a sin and a major offence.

The answer: He, peace be upon him, spoke this according to the outward meaning and in accordance with what they believed about him, that he was her slave. Also, he (her husband) had raised him and bestowed upon him many favours, so by his being a lord to him he meant his being his nurturer. This is among the fine allusions (ma'arid hasana), for the outward people take it to mean that he was a lord to him, whereas he meant by it that he was his nurturer and benefactor.

The second question: Does the saying of Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾ indicate the soundness of our doctrine on decree and destiny?

The answer: It clearly indicates it, because his saying, peace be upon him, "I seek refuge in Allah as a refuge," is a request from Allah that He protect him from that act. That protection is not an expression for giving power, reason and instrument, removing excuses, removing obstacles and doing kindnesses, because whatever was within Allah's power of this kind He has already done. So it would be either a request for obtaining what is already obtained, or a request for obtaining the impossible, and that is absurd. We therefore know that the protection that Yusuf requested from Allah has no meaning unless He creates in him a decisive motive toward obedience and removes from his heart the motive toward disobedience, and that is what is sought. The evidence that what we have mentioned is the intended meaning is what is transmitted: that when the Prophet ﷺ's gaze fell upon Zaynab he said: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion." What was meant by it was strengthening the motive toward obedience and removing the motive toward disobedience. So it is here too. Likewise is his saying, peace be upon him: "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful." So what is meant by the two fingers is the motive to act and the motive to abstain, and these two motives are not obtained except by the creation of Allah, the Exalted; otherwise they would require another motive and an infinite regress would follow. Thus it is established that the saying of Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾ is among the strongest proofs for our position. And Allah knows best.

The third question: Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned three things in answer to her speech:

One of them: his saying ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, about him: ﴿Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence good﴾.

The third: his saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾. What is the connection of some of this answer with some?

The answer: This order is in the utmost goodness, because submission to the command of Allah, exalted is He, and His obligation is the most important of things given the abundance of His bounties and kindnesses toward the servant. So his saying ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾ points to the fact that the right of Allah, exalted is He, prevents him from this act. Also, the rights of creatures must be observed; since this man has bestowed favours upon me, it is ugly to repay his favour and kindness with evil. Also, preserving the self from harm is obligatory, and this pleasure is a small pleasure followed by disgrace in this world and severe punishment in the Hereafter; when a small pleasure entails a severe harm, reason requires abandoning it and keeping away from it. So his saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ points to this. Thus it is established that these three answers are arranged in the best possible order.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [was it], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾

Know that this verse is one of the important matters that requires careful investigation, and in this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: whether a sin proceeded from him, peace be upon him, or not. On this issue there are two views.

The first: that Yusuf, peace be upon him, did resolve upon immorality. Al-Wahidi said in his book al-Basit: The exegetes whose knowledge is trusted and whose reports are relied upon said: Yusuf also resolved upon this woman with a genuine resolve, and he sat from her in the position of a man with a woman. Then when he saw the proof from his Lord, every desire left him. Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, related with his chain of narration: From Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: She desired him and he desired her, and his desire for her was that he intended to untie the belt. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: He untied the money-belt and sat from her in the position of a betrayer. And also from him: that she lay down for him and he sat between her legs, taking off his clothes. Then al-Wahidi went on at length with words devoid of benefit on this subject, and he did not mention a verse to argue with, nor a sound hadith to rely upon to authenticate this view. Nor did he reflect deeply on those words devoid of benefit. It is related that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: "Nor when you resolved, O Yusuf?" Thereupon Yusuf said: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾ [Yusuf: 53]. Then he said: Those who affirmed this act for Yusuf were more knowledgeable of the rights of the prophets, peace be upon them, and of the elevation of their ranks with Allah the Exalted, than those who negated the resolve from him. This is the summary of his speech on this subject.

Page 93

The second view: that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was free of the vain act and the forbidden resolve. This is the view of the research-oriented exegetes and theologians, and it is what we say, and it is what we defend.

Know that the proofs indicating the obligation of the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, are numerous, and we have thoroughly examined them in Surat al-Baqarah in the story of Adam, peace be upon him, so we will not repeat them, except that we add here several points:

The first argument: adultery is among the greatest of the grave sins, and betrayal in the context of a trust is also among the reprehensible sins. Also, returning a great kindness with an injury that brings complete disgrace and severe shame is also among the reprehensible sins. Also, a boy who is raised in the house of a person, remaining provided for and protected in honor from the beginning of his childhood until the time of his youth and full strength, then his undertaking to inflict the most vile kind of injury upon that great benefactor is among the most reprehensible deeds.

Having established this, we say: this disobedience that they attributed to Yusuf, peace be upon him, possessed all four of these aspects. A sin of this kind, if attributed to the most debauched of Allah's creatures and the furthest from all good, he would be repulsed by it. How then is it permissible to ascribe it to the Messenger, peace be upon him, who was supported by overpowering and dazzling miracles! Moreover, the Exalted said in another incident: ﴿Thus [was it], that We might avert from him evil and immorality﴾, and this indicates that the essence of evil and immorality is turned away from him. There is no doubt that the disobedience they attributed to him is the greatest of disobediences and the most vile category of immorality. How then is it fitting for the Lord of the worlds to testify, in this very incident, to his being free from evil, while he had committed the greatest kinds of evil and immorality?!

Also, the verse indicates our view in another respect, for we say: even if this verse does not indicate the negation of this disobedience from him, there is no doubt that it conveys great praise and abundant commendation. It is not fitting for the wisdom of Allah the Exalted to relate of a person his undertaking a great disobedience, then immediately praise him and extol him with the greatest praises and commendations after relating that grave sin about him. Its example is like when a sultan relates of one of his slaves the most vile sins and the most reprehensible deeds, then immediately mentions him with great praise and abundant commendation. Such a thing is greatly disapproved of, so likewise here. And Allah knows best.

The third: whenever a slip or lapse proceeds from the prophets, peace be upon them, they regard it as grave and follow it with the manifestation of remorse, repentance and humility. Had Yusuf, peace be upon him, committed this great and reprehensible sin here, it would have been impossible for him not to follow it with repentance and seeking forgiveness. And if he had repented, Allah the Exalted would have related his repentance about him, as in other places. Since nothing of that is found, we know that no sin or disobedience proceeded from him in this incident.

The fourth: everyone who had a connection to that incident has testified to the innocence of Yusuf, peace be upon him, from disobedience.

Know that those who had a connection to this incident are: Yusuf, peace be upon him, that woman and her husband, the women and the witnesses, and the Lord of the worlds has testified to his innocence from sin, and Iblis also acknowledged his innocence from disobedience. When this is the case, there remains for the Muslim no hesitation in this matter. As for the demonstration that Yusuf, peace be upon him, claimed innocence from sin, it is his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿She sought to seduce me from myself﴾, and his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. As for the demonstration that the woman acknowledged this, it is because she said to the women: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him from himself, but he refused﴾ [Yusuf: 32], and also she said: ﴿Now the truth has become evident; it was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51].

As for the demonstration that the woman's husband acknowledged this, it is his saying: ﴿Indeed, it is [a plot] of your women; indeed, the plot of you women is great﴾ ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾

Page 94

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 28]. As for the witnesses, it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And a witness from her family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars"﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. As for the testimony of Allah the Exalted to this, it is His saying: ﴿Thus [was it], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ In this verse, Allah the Exalted has testified to his purity four times:

The first: His saying: ﴿that We might avert from him evil﴾, where the lam is for emphasis and intensification.

The second: His saying: ﴿and immorality﴾, meaning: thus that We might avert from him evil and immorality.

The third: His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our servants﴾, although He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [Al-Furqan: 63].

The fourth: His saying: ﴿chosen﴾ (al-mukhlasin), and in it there are two readings: once with the active participle and once with the passive participle. Its occurrence with the active participle indicates that he performed acts of obedience and devotions together with the attribute of sincerity, and its occurrence with the passive participle indicates that Allah the Exalted chose him for Himself and selected him for His presence. On both readings, it is among the most indicative expressions that he is exalted above what they attributed to him. As for the demonstration that Iblis acknowledged his purity, it is because he said: ﴿So by Your might, I will surely mislead them all, ﴾ ﴿except Your chosen servants among them﴾, so he acknowledged that he is not able to mislead the sincere ones, and Yusuf is among the sincere ones by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants﴾. So this is an acknowledgment from Iblis that he did not mislead him nor lead him astray from the path of guidance.

At this point we say: those ignorant people who attributed this disgrace to Yusuf, peace be upon him, if they are among the followers of the religion of Allah the Exalted, then let them accept the testimony of Allah the Exalted to his purity; and if they are among the followers of Iblis and his soldiers, then let them accept the testimony of Iblis to his purity. Perhaps they will say: "At the beginning we were students of Iblis, until we graduated under him, and we surpassed him in foolishness," as al-Kharazmi said:

I was a man from the soldiers of Iblis, until time raised me until Iblis became one of my soldiers.
Had he died before me, I would have excelled after him
in the ways of wickedness, which no one excels in after me.

Thus it is established by these proofs that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was innocent of what those ignorant people say.

Having understood this, we say: speaking about the apparent meaning of this verse falls under two stations.

The first station: we say we do not concede that Yusuf, peace be upon him, resolved upon her. The evidence for this is that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, and the answer of "law-la" (lawla) here is preposed, as one says: "You would have been among the perished had not so-and-so rescued you."

Al-Zajjaj criticized this answer from two angles:

The first: that preposing the answer of "lawla" is anomalous and not found in eloquent speech.

The second: that the answer of "lawla" is introduced by the lam, so if the matter were as you claim, it would say: "And she certainly desired him, and he would certainly have desired her, had it not been..."

Someone other than al-Zajjaj raised a third objection, namely that if the resolve did not exist, then His saying: ﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ would have no purpose.

Know that what al-Zajjaj mentioned is far-fetched, for we concede that delaying the answer of "lawla" is good and permissible, but its permissibility does not prevent the permissibility of preposing this answer. And how could it be, when it is related from Sibawayh that he said: They prefer to place first what is more important, and what they are concerned with is more prominent; so the matter of permitting preposing and postponing is tied to the intensity of concern. As for specifying some expressions by prohibition, that is something not befitting wisdom. Also, mentioning the answer of "lawla" with the lam is permissible, but this does not indicate that mentioning it without the lam is not permissible. Furthermore, we mention another verse that shows the invalidity of al-Zajjaj's view regarding these two objections, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She had almost revealed it, had We not fortified her heart﴾ [Al-Qasas: 10].

Page 95

As for the third objection, that if the resolve did not exist, the saying "had he not seen the proof of his Lord" would have no purpose: we say, rather it contains the greatest benefits, namely the clarification that his abandonment of the resolve toward her was not due to his lack of desire for women or his inability over them, but rather because the proofs of the religion of Allah prevented him from that act. Then we say: what indicates that the answer of "lawla" is what we mentioned is that "lawla" requires an answer, and this mentioned element is suitable to be its answer, so it is obligatory to rule that it is its answer. It cannot be said that we posit an implied answer for it, and omitting the answer is common in the Qur'an, because we say: there is no dispute that it is common in the Qur'an, but the original principle is that it should not be omitted. Also, omitting and deleting the answer is only good when something in the wording indicates its specificity, and here, even assuming the answer is omitted, there is nothing in the wording that indicates the specificity of that answer, for there are here several types of implied elements each of which is suitable to be implied, and implying some of them is not more preferable than implying the rest. Thus the difference becomes clear. And Allah knows best.

The second station in discussing this verse: we say, granting that the resolve did occur, we still say that His saying ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ cannot be taken in its apparent sense, because attaching the resolve to the woman's very person is impossible, since resolve is of the genus of intention, and intention does not attach to persisting entities. Thus it is established that there must be an implied specific verb that makes the object of that resolve and that act unmentioned. They claimed that this implied element is committing immorality with her, whereas we imply something else different from what they mentioned, and its explanation is through several aspects:

**First issue:** The first (interpretation): The meaning is that he (peace be upon him) *intended* to push her away from himself and to prevent her from that vile act, because *hamm* means intention. So it must be understood, for every person, according to the intention that befits them. What befits a woman is the intention to obtain pleasure, luxury and enjoyment, while what befits a Messenger sent to creation is the intention to restrain the disobedient from disobedience and to enjoin good and forbid evil. It is said: "I *hammattu* (intended) with so-and-so," meaning, I intended to strike him and push him away.

If they say: On this interpretation, the words "had he not seen the proof of his Lord" would have no benefit?

We say: On the contrary, they have the greatest benefit, and this is explained in two ways:

The first: God Most High informed Joseph (peace be upon him) that if he had intended to push her away, she would have killed him, or she would have ordered those present to kill him. So God informed him that refraining from striking her was better, to preserve the self from destruction.

The second: If he (peace be upon him) had busied himself with pushing her away from himself, she might have clung to him, and his garment would have been torn from the front. It was known to God Most High that the witness would testify that if his garment had been torn from the front, Joseph would be the one who was treacherous, but if his garment had been torn from behind, the woman would be the treacherous one. So God Most High informed him of this meaning, and therefore he did not busy himself with pushing her away from himself, but turned and fled from her, until the witness's testimony became a proof for him of his innocence from sin.

The second answer: *Hamm* is interpreted as desire (*al-shahwah*), and this is used in common language. A person says of something he has no desire for: "This does not concern me (*ma yuhimmuni*)," and of something he desires: "This is the most important thing to me (*ahamm al-ashya' ilayya*)." So God Most High named Joseph's desire a *hamm*. The meaning of the verse is therefore: "She desired him and he desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord, that act would have come into existence."

The third: *Hamm* is interpreted as the soul's inner discourse (*hadith al-nafs*). This is because a woman who surpasses others in beauty and loveliness, when she adorns herself and prepares herself for a young, strong man, there must inevitably occur, between wisdom and natural desire, and between the soul and the intellect, pullings and conflicts. Sometimes the call of nature and desire prevails, and sometimes the call of intellect and wisdom prevails. So *hamm* is an expression for the pulls of nature, and seeing the proof is an expression for the pulls of servitude (*ubudiyyah*). An example of this: a righteous man, fasting on a scorching summer day, sees a chilled, iced drink; his nature drives him to drink it, but his religion and guidance prevent him from doing so. This does not indicate that a sin has occurred. Rather, the stronger this state is, the more perfect is the strength in fulfilling the requirements of servitude. Thus, by the praise of God Most High, the soundness of this view that we have adopted has become evident, and nothing remains in the hand of al-Wahidi except mere boasting and the enumeration of names of exegetes (*mufassirin*). Had he mentioned a doubt in establishing that view, we would have answered it. But he added nothing beyond narrating from some exegetes.

Know that some of the *Hashwiyyah* (literalists) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Abraham (peace be upon him) told no lies except three lies." I said: The better course is that we do not accept such reports. He said, in a tone of disapproval: If we do not accept it, we would be obliged to reject the narrators. I said to him: Poor fellow! If we accept it, we are obliged to judge that Abraham (peace be upon him) told lies, and if we reject it, we are obliged to judge that the narrators are liars. There is no doubt that preserving Abraham (peace be upon him) from lying is more fitting than preserving a group of unknown persons from lying.

Having understood this principle, we say to al-Wahidi: Who guarantees for us that those who transmitted this view from these exegetes were truthful rather than liars? And God knows best.

\* \* \*

**Second issue:** Regarding what the proof of that *burhan* is: Those scholars who affirm infallibility (*al-'ismah*) have interpreted the seeing of the proof in several ways:

The first: It is the proof of God Most High concerning the prohibition of fornication, and the knowledge of the punishment that awaits the fornicator.

The second: God Most High purified the souls of the prophets (peace be upon them) from blameworthy traits. Rather, we say: He purified the souls of those connected to Him from them, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah intends only to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with [complete] purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. So the meaning of seeing the proof is the presence of those traits and the reminder of the circumstances that restrain them from committing forbidden acts.

The third: He saw written on the ceiling of the house: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and is evil as a way﴾ [al-Isra: 32].

The fourth: It is the prophethood that prevents one from committing grave sins. The evidence for this is that the prophets (peace be upon them) were sent to prevent people from ugly deeds and scandals. If they prevented people from them and then committed the most abominable kinds of them and the most vile of their categories, they would fall under His words: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3]. Also, God Most High rebuked the Jews with His words: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. If this is a defect with regard to the Jews, how could it be attributed to the Messenger who was supported by miracles?

As for those who attributed sin to Joseph (peace be upon him), they mentioned several matters regarding the explanation of that proof:

The first: They said: The woman went to an idol adorned with pearls and rubies in a corner of the house and covered it with a cloth. Joseph said: Why did you do that? She said: I am ashamed before my god that he should see me in sin. Joseph said: Are you ashamed before an idol that does not understand, hear, or see, and I am not ashamed before my God who watches over every soul for what it has earned? By God, I will never do that! They said: This is the proof.

The second: They reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that Ya'qub appeared to him, and he saw him biting his fingers and saying to him: Will you do the deed of the wicked while you are recorded among the prophets? So he felt shame before him. He said: This is also the view of 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and Ibn Sirin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ya'qub appeared to him and struck him in the chest, and his desire came out through his fingertips.

The third: They said that he heard in the air a voice saying: O son of Ya'qub, do not be like the bird that has feathers, which, when it commits fornication, loses its feathers.

The fourth: They reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that Joseph (peace be upon him) was not restrained by seeing the image of Ya'qub until Jibril (peace be upon him) pushed him, and nothing of desire remained in him but it came out.

When al-Wahidi transmitted these reports, he boasted and said: What we have mentioned is the view of the leading exegetes who took the interpretation from those who witnessed the revelation. It is said to him: You never bring us anything except these boastful claims, which have no benefit. Where is this from proof and evidence? Furthermore, the accumulation of proofs for one matter is permissible, and he (peace be upon him) was refraining from fornication on the basis of the original proofs. When these admonitions were added to them, the restraint grew stronger and the avoidance became complete. What is remarkable is that they reported that "a puppy entered the room of the Prophet (ﷺ) and remained there without his knowledge. They said: So Jibril (peace be upon him) refrained from entering upon him for forty days." And here they claim that while Joseph (peace be upon him) was engaged in indecency, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him. What is remarkable is that they claim he did not refrain from that deed because of the presence of Jibril (peace be upon him). Yet if the most wicked and disbelieving of creatures were engaged in indecency, and a man in the guise of the righteous entered upon him, he would feel shame before him, flee, and abandon that act. Here, he saw Ya'qub (peace be upon him) biting his fingers and paid him no attention; then Jibril (peace be upon him), despite his high rank, entered upon him, and he still did not refrain from that ugly act because of his presence, until Jibril (peace be upon him) had to push him on his back. So we ask God to preserve us from error in religion and from abandonment in seeking certainty. This is the clear discussion of this issue. And God knows best.

**Third issue:** On the difference between *su'* (evil) and *fahsha'* (indecency), there are several views:

The first: *Su'* is the offence of the hand, and *fahsha'* is fornication.

The second: *Su'* is the preliminaries of indecency, such as kissing and looking with desire, and *fahsha'* is fornication.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾, meaning those who made their religion sincerely for God Most High. Whoever reads the *lam* with a fatha (*al-mukhlasin*) means those whom God has delivered from evils. It is also possible that the intended meaning is that he was of the descendants of Abraham (peace be upon him), concerning whom God said: ﴿Indeed, We chose them with an exclusive quality﴾ [Sad: 46].

**Fourth issue:** Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read *al-mukhlisin* (with a kasra on the *lam*) throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatha on the *lam*.

The Exalted said: ﴿And they raced each other to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her husband at the door. She said, "What is the punishment for one who intended evil against your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought to seduce me," and a witness from her household testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken the truth and he is among the liars."﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied and he is among the truthful.﴾ ﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said, "Indeed, it is a scheme of you women; surely your scheming is great."﴾ ﴿"Joseph, turn away from this. And you, ask forgiveness for your sin, for you were among the sinners."﴾

Know that when the Exalted related her having "intended" (hamma), He followed it with the manner of her pursuit and his flight, saying: ﴿And they raced each other to the door.﴾ The meaning is that he fled from her and tried to get out through the door, and the woman ran behind him to pull him towards herself. Al-istibaq (racing, competing) is seeking to be first to a thing. Its meaning is that each of them rushed to the door, striving to get ahead of the other. If Joseph got ahead, he would open the door and go out; if the woman got ahead, she would hold the door closed so that he could not leave. His words ﴿they raced each other to the door﴾ mean "they raced toward the door," like His words: ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men﴾ [Al-A'raf: 155], meaning "from among his people."

Know that Joseph, peace be upon him, got to the door first and wanted to go out, while the woman ran after him. She could not reach him except to the back of the shirt, so she tore it, that is, cut it lengthwise. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 30–31 (part 1 of 2)**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And women in the city said, "The wife of the chief minister is seeking to seduce her young slave from himself. He has captivated her heart with love. Indeed, we see her in obvious error."﴾ ﴿So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet, and she gave each one of them a knife, and said, "Come out before them." And when they saw him, they were amazed by him and cut their hands, and they said, "Perfect is Allah! This is not a human being. This is none but a noble angel."﴾ [p. 101]

In the verse there are issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah):

**First issue:** Why did it not say "wa qalat niswatun" (and women said), with the feminine verb form?

We answer with two reasons:

First: *al-niswah* is a singular noun used as a collective for *al-mar'ah* (woman), and its feminine marking is not real (*ghayr haqiqi*). Therefore the verb does not take the feminine *ta'* (ta' al-ta'nith).

Second: al-Wahidi said: placing the verb before its subject calls for dropping the feminine marker, on the analogy of dropping the marker of the dual and plural.

**Second issue:** Al-Kalbi said: they were four women: the wife of the cupbearer of the chief minister, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his prison, and the wife of the keeper of his animals. Muqatil added: the wife of the chamberlain.

The more likely view is that this affair spread in the land, became well known, and women talked about it. The wife of the chief minister is this well-known woman. ﴿Seeking to seduce her young slave from himself.﴾ *Al-fata* means the young man, and *al-fataah* means the young female servant. ﴿He has captivated her heart with love.﴾ On this there are two issues:

When they saw him and were struck with that bewilderment, she said: "This is the one you have seen, he is that Canaanite slave about whom you blamed me," meaning: you did not imagine him as he truly is, and had his image been present in your imagination you would have abandoned this blame.

And unless You turn their scheming away from me, I may incline toward them and become one of the ignorant."﴾ ﴿So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their scheming. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

Know that when the woman said: ﴿And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will surely be among the humiliated﴾, and the rest of the women heard this threat, it is apparent that they gathered around Yusuf, peace be upon him, and said: "There is no benefit for you in opposing her command, or else you will fall into prison and into humiliation." At that point, various kinds of whisperings (waswasah) gathered in the case of Yusuf, peace be upon him:

The first: Zulaykha was at the utmost of beauty.

The second: She possessed wealth and property, and she was determined to give everything to Yusuf on the condition that he assist her in what she desired.

The third: The women gathered against him, and each one of them was enticing him and frightening him by a different means, and the scheming of women in this matter is severe.

The fourth: He, peace be upon him, was afraid of her evil and of her resolve to kill him and destroy him. Thus, all the aspects of enticement toward agreeing with her and all the aspects of intimidation toward opposing her gathered in the case of Yusuf, and he, peace be upon him, feared that these strong and numerous causes would have an effect upon him.

Know that human power and human capacity are not sufficient to attain this strong protection (ʿiṣmah). Therefore, at this point he turned to Allah, Exalted is He, and said: ﴿My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to.﴾ It was also read as "as-Sijnu" with a fatha, as a verbal noun (maṣdar). In this there are two questions:

The first question: Prison is in the utmost of undesirability, while what they invited him to is in the utmost of desirability. How then could he say: "Hardship is dearer to me than pleasure"?

The answer: That pleasure would entail great pains, namely blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, whereas that undesirable thing, which is choosing prison, would entail great felicities, namely praise in this world and lasting reward in the Hereafter. For this reason he said: ﴿Prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to.﴾

The second question: Their confining him is a sin just as adultery is a sin. How then is it permissible for him to love prison when it is a sin?

The answer: The sense of the statement is that if it is necessary to adopt one of two matters, namely adultery or prison, then this one is preferable, because whenever it is necessary to adopt one of two things, each of which is an evil, the lesser of the two is the more appropriate to bear.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿And unless You turn their scheming away from me, I may incline toward them and become one of the ignorant.﴾ "Aṣbu ilayhinna" means "I incline toward them," as one says: "ṣabā ilā al-lahw yaṣbū ṣabwan" when he inclines. Our companions (the Ashʿarite theologians) used this verse as evidence that a person does not turn away from disobedience except when Allah, Exalted is He, turns him away from it. They said: This verse indicates that if He does not turn him away from that abomination, he falls into it. Its explanation: If the capacity (qudrah) and the motive (dāʿī) toward the act and the abandonment are equal, the act is impossible, because the act is the preponderance of one of the two sides and the subordination of the other side. Their coexistence while the two sides are equal is a combination of two contradictories, and that is impossible. If the preponderance occurs on one side, that preponderance is not from the servant, otherwise the chain of causes would go on without end. Rather, it is from Allah, Exalted is He. So "turning away" (ṣarf) means making the act subordinate, because when it becomes subordinate it becomes impossible to occur, since occurrence is preponderance. So if it occurred while it was subordinate, preponderance would coexist with subordination, and this entails the combination of two contradictories, which is impossible.

Thus it has been established by this that the servant's turning away from abomination is only from Allah, Exalted is He.

This statement can also be explained in another way: In the case of Yusuf, peace be upon him, all the causes that encouraged that disobedience had gathered, namely benefiting from wealth and status, and enjoying what is to be married and what is to be eaten. And in turning away from it, all the causes that repelled had gathered. When this is the case, the motives for the act have grown strong and the motives for abandoning it have weakened. So he asked Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, to produce in his heart various opposing motives that negate the motives of disobedience, because if this opposing factor did not occur, the inclining factor toward falling into disobedience would occur unopposed by anything that counters it, and that necessitates the occurrence of the act. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿I may incline toward them and become one of the ignorant.﴾
