Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah Yusuf, verses 35–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾ ﴿Two young men entered the prison with him. One of them said, "I see myself pressing wine," and the other said, "I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers."﴾

On the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when the wife's husband (al-Aziz) became clear about the innocence of Yusuf, peace be upon him, he did not pursue the matter with him. The woman then employed every kind of scheme to bring Yusuf, peace be upon him, to agree to her desire, but Yusuf did not turn to her. When she despaired of him, she devised another way and said to her husband: "This Hebrew slave has disgraced me among the people. He tells them that I solicited him, and I cannot show my innocence. So either you permit me to go out and make my excuse, or you imprison him as you imprisoned me." At that point it entered the heart of the Aziz that the best course was to imprison him until mention of this story fell from people's tongues and the scandal lessened. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾ Because al-Bada' (a change of decision) means a change of opinion from what it was at first. The "signs" refer to his innocence shown by the tearing of the shirt from behind, the scratching of the face, and the judge's pronouncement against her: ﴿Indeed, it is from your guile; surely your guile is great.﴾ We have mentioned that other kinds of signs appeared there which reached the level of certainty, but the people kept silent about them in an effort to conceal the scandal.

The second issue: His saying ﴿it occurred﴾ is a verb, and its subject in this place is His saying ﴿that they should imprison him﴾. The apparent sense of this statement requires attributing a verb to another verb, but the grammarians agreed that attributing a verb to a verb is not permissible; if you say "went out struck," it conveys nothing at all. Therefore they said: the sense of the sentence is "then it occurred to them to imprison him," but this verb was placed in the position of that noun. I say: good taste testifies that making a verb the subject of a predication is not permissible. No one may say that the verb is a predicate, and making a predicate the subject of a predication is not permissible. For we say: a noun may be a predicate, as in your saying "Zayd is standing": "standing" is a noun and a predicate. So we know that a thing being a predicate does not preclude its being the subject of a predication. Rather, we raise doubts in this regard:

One of them: when we say "struck is a verb," the thing predicated as a verb is "struck," so the verb has become the subject of the predication.
If they say: the subject of the predication is this form, which is a noun, we say: according to this assumption it follows that the thing predicated as a verb is a noun and not a verb, and that is false and invalid. Rather, we say: the thing predicated as a verb, if it is a verb, then it has been established that a verb may be the subject of a predication; and if it is a noun, its meaning would be that we predicated of the noun that it is a verb, and it is known that this is invalid. In this subject there are deep investigations which we have mentioned in the books of the rational sciences.

The third issue: The people of language said: al-Hin is a period of time, not specified, which applies to a short span and to a long one. Ibn Abbas said: it means until the talk ceased and the indecency that had spread in the city subsided. It was then said: al-Hin here means five years; it was also said: seven years; and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: Yusuf was imprisoned for twelve years. The correct view is that these measures are not known; the only known matter is that he remained imprisoned for a long period, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he remembered after a period [of time].﴾ (Yusuf 45)

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Two young men entered the prison with him,﴾ there is an omitted element here. The sense is: "When they intended to imprison him, they imprisoned him," and this was omitted because of the indication given by His saying ﴿Two young men entered the prison with him.﴾ It was said: they were two servants who belonged to the greatest king in Egypt, one of whom was his cupbearer and the other his baker. It was reported to the king that his baker intended to poison him, and he thought the other was assisting him in that. So he ordered that both be imprisoned. Questions remain regarding the verse:

The first question: How did they know that he, peace be upon him, had knowledge of ta'bir (interpretation of dreams)?

The answer: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, asked them about their sorrow and distress, and they mentioned: "We saw this dream," and it is possible that they saw him displaying his knowledge of various matters, among them the interpretation of dreams, and so at that point they mentioned it to him.

The second question: How did he know that they were servants of the king?

The answer: From His saying: ﴿so he will give his lord wine to drink﴾ (Yusuf 41), that is, his master, and from His saying: ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾ (Yusuf 42).

The third question: How did he know that one of them was the king's cupbearer and the other his baker?

The answer: The dream of each of them corresponds to his occupation, for one of them saw that he was pressing wine, and the other seemed to be carrying bread on his head.

The fourth question: How did the dreams occur?

The answer: On this there are two views:

The first view: When Yusuf, peace be upon him, entered the prison, he said to his companions, "I interpret dreams." One of the two young men said, "Come, let us test this Hebrew slave with a dream we invent for him," and so they questioned him without having seen anything at all. Ibn Mas'ud said: they had not seen anything; they only dreamed up dreams in order to test his knowledge.

The second view: Mujahid said: when they entered the prison, they had seen dreams, so they came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and asked him about them. The cupbearer said: "O learned one, I saw myself in a garden, and there was a fine vine with three branches upon which were three bunches of grapes. I picked them, and it was as if the king's cup was in my hand. I pressed them into it and gave it to the king, and he drank it." That is His saying: ﴿I see myself pressing wine.﴾ The one who was the baker said: "I saw myself as though above my head were three baskets containing bread, various foods and dishes, and suddenly the birds of prey were pecking at them." That is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the other said, "I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat."﴾

The fifth question: How did Yusuf, peace be upon him, know that His saying ﴿I see myself pressing wine﴾ meant a dream?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: if he had not intended sleep, then the mention of ﴿pressing﴾ would have made the mention of ﴿I see myself﴾ unnecessary.

The second: His saying ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾ indicates it.

The sixth question: How can the pressing of wine be understood?

The answer has three views:

One: the meaning is "I press grapes of wine," that is, grapes whose juice becomes wine, and the modifier has been omitted.

The second: the Arabs name a thing by what it turns into when the meaning has become clear and is not ambiguous. They say: "So-and-so is cooking date-syrup," when he is in fact cooking grape-juice.

The third: Abu Salih said: the people of Oman call grapes "khamr" (wine), and this term reached the people of Mecca, and they used it. Al-Dahhak said: the Qur'an was revealed in the tongues of all the Arabs.

The seventh question: What is the meaning of ta'wil (ultimate meaning or interpretation) in His saying ﴿Inform us of its ta'wil﴾?

The answer: The ta'wil of a thing is that to which it returns, which is what it ultimately becomes at the end of that matter.

The eighth question: What is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: its meaning is: "Indeed, we see you preferring goodness and bringing noble qualities and all praiseworthy acts." It was said: he used to visit their sick and comfort their grieving, so they said, "You are indeed one of the good-doers," that is, toward companions and associates. It was also said: he was highly persistent in acts of worship, such as fasting and prayer, so they said, "You are indeed one of the good-doers in matters of religion," and whoever is like this is trusted in what he says about interpreting dreams and in all other matters. It was also said: the meaning is ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾ in the knowledge of ta'bir, for whenever he interpreted, he did not err, as he said: ﴿and You have taught me something of the interpretation of events﴾ (Yusuf 101).

The ninth question: What is the reality of the science of ta'bir?

The answer: The Qur'an and demonstrative proof both show its soundness. As for the Qur'an, it is this verse. As for proof, it is that it has been established that He, glorified be He, created the essence of the rational soul in such a way that it is enabled to ascend to the world of the spheres and to contemplate the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and what prevents it from this is its preoccupation with managing the body. At the time of sleep, this preoccupation diminishes, so it becomes capable of this contemplation. When the spirit reaches a certain state, it leaves particular traces suited to that spiritual perception in the world of imagination. So the interpreter infers those imaginal traces to those intellectual perceptions. This is a general statement, and its detail is mentioned in the rational books, and the Sharia confirms it. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Dreams are of three kinds: a dream in which a man speaks to himself, a dream caused by Satan, and a dream which is the true dream, which is truth." This is a sound division in the rational sciences. He, peace be upon him, also said: "The dream of a righteous man is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

God the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "No food will come to you that you are provided with except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who, concerning the Hereafter, are disbelievers. And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Know that what is mentioned in this verse is not an answer to what the two had asked about, so it is necessary here to explain the reason why he turned away from giving the answer to this speech. The scholars have mentioned several reasons for this:

The first: When the answer to one of the two questioners was that he would be crucified, and there is no doubt that when he heard that his grief greatly increased and his aversion to hearing this speech intensified, he saw that it was right to first present before that what would have an effect on them through his knowledge and speech, so that when he afterwards gave them the interpretation, his answer would not be attributed to accusation or enmity.

The second: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, wanted to show that his rank in knowledge is higher and greater than what they believed about him. That is because they asked him for the knowledge of ta'bir (dream interpretation), and there is no doubt that this knowledge is based on conjecture and guesswork. So he made clear to them that he could not inform about the unseen with certainty and conviction, since all creation is incapable of that. If this is the case, then it is more fitting that he would surpass all people in the knowledge of ta'bir. So the purpose of mentioning that preface was to establish that he surpasses others in the knowledge of ta'bir and has attained what no one else has attained.

The third: al-Suddi said: ﴿No food will come to you that you are provided with﴾ in sleep. By this he showed that his knowledge of the interpretation of dreams is not restricted to one thing rather than another. For this reason he said: ﴿except that I will inform you of its interpretation﴾.

The fourth: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, when he knew that they believed in him and accepted his word, presented to them what indicates that he is a messenger from Allah, the Exalted, since occupying oneself with setting right the important matters of religion is better than occupying oneself with the important matters of this world.

The fifth: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, when he knew that that man would be crucified, strove to bring him into Islam, so that he would not die in disbelief and would not deserve severe punishment: ﴿So that whoever perishes would perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lives would live upon clear evidence﴾ [al-Anfal: 42].

The sixth: His saying, ﴿No food will come to you that you are provided with except that I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ is to be understood as referring to the waking state. The meaning is: No food will come to you that you are provided with except that I will inform you what kind of food it is, what color it is, how much it is, and what its outcome will be; that is, if a person eats it, whether it brings health or sickness. There is another interpretation: It was said that when the king wanted to kill a person, he would prepare food for him and send it to him. So Yusuf said: No food will come to you except that I will inform you whether there is poison in it or not. This is what is meant by his saying: ﴿No food will come to you that you are provided with except that I will inform you of its interpretation﴾. Its essence goes back to his claim to inform about the unseen, and this runs along the lines of the saying of Jesus, peace be upon him:

[p. 110]

﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾. So the first three reasons are to establish that he surpasses others in the knowledge of ta'bir, and the last three reasons are to establish that he is a truthful prophet from Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: How is it permissible to take the verse as referring to a claim of a miracle, when no claim to prophethood had preceded it?

We say: Although he did not mention it, one knows that it must be said that he had mentioned it. Also, in his saying, ﴿That is from what my Lord has taught me﴾ and in his saying, ﴿And I have followed the religion of my fathers﴾, there is what indicates that.

\* \* \*

Then the Exalted said: ﴿That is from what my Lord has taught me﴾, meaning: I do not inform you by way of kahana (soothsaying) and astrology; rather I inform you by revelation from Allah and by knowledge that was obtained through the teaching of Allah.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who, concerning the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

First issue: One might say: In his saying, ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah﴾ there is an assumption that he, peace be upon him, had been in this religion (millah). We say, its answer is in several respects:

The first: Leaving (tark) is an expression for not engaging with something, and it is not a condition of it that one must have been immersed in it.

The second, which is the most correct: It may be said that he, peace be upon him, had been a slave to them according to their assumption and their corrupt belief. Perhaps before that he did not manifest tawhid (monotheism) and faith, out of fear of them, by way of taqiyya (precautionary concealment). Then he manifested it at this time, so this was in the manner of leaving the religion of those disbelievers in outward appearance.

Second issue: The repetition of the word ﴿هم﴾ in his saying, ﴿and who, concerning the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾ is to specify that disbelief is restricted to them. Perhaps their denial of the ma'ad (return/resurrection) is more severe than their denial of the mabda' (origin/creator), so because of their exaggeration in denying the ma'ad, he repeated this word for emphasis.

Know that his saying, ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah﴾ is an indication of knowledge of the mabda'. And his saying, ﴿and who, concerning the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾ is an indication of knowledge of the ma'ad. Whoever reflects upon the Glorious Qur'an and contemplates how the prophets, peace be upon them, called people, will know that the purpose of sending the messengers and sending down the books is to turn people toward acknowledging tawhid, the mabda' and the ma'ad, and that whatever lies beyond that is futile.

\* \* \*

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾. Concerning this there are questions:

First question: What is the benefit of mentioning this statement?

The answer: When he, peace be upon him, claimed prophethood and challenged with a miracle, which is knowledge of the unseen, he coupled with it that he was from the household of prophethood, and that his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather were prophets and messengers of Allah. For when a person claims the profession of his father and grandfather, it is not considered far-fetched from him. Also, just as the rank of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, peace be upon them, was a well-known matter in the world, when it became clear that he was their son, they venerated him and regarded him with an eye of reverence. So their submission to him was more general and their hearts were more perfectly affected by his speech.

Second question: Since he was a prophet, how could he say: "Indeed, I have followed the religion of my fathers," when a prophet must be specific to his own sharia (law)?

We say: Perhaps his intended meaning is the tawhid that did not change. Also, perhaps he was a messenger from Allah, but he was upon the sharia of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Third question: Why did he say: ﴿It was not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾, when the state of all the responsible persons is like that?

[p. 111]

The answer: The meaning of his saying ﴿It was not for us﴾ is not that He prohibited that for them. Rather the meaning is that the Exalted purified his fathers from disbelief. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

Fourth question: What is the benefit of his saying ﴿anything﴾?

The answer: The kinds of shirk are many. Some of them worship idols, some worship fire, some worship the stars, and some worship the intellect, the soul, and nature. So His saying ﴿It was not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾ is a refutation of all these groups and sects, and a guidance to the true religion, which is that there is no originator except Allah, no creator except Allah, and no provider except Allah.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind﴾. Concerning this there is an issue, namely that He said: ﴿It was not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah﴾. His saying ﴿That﴾ is an indication of what preceded, namely not associating others with Allah. This indicates that not associating others with Allah and the attainment of faith are from Allah. Then he made clear that the matter is the same in his own case and in the case of people. Then he made clear that most people do not give thanks, and it must be that the meaning is that they do not thank Allah for the blessing of faith.

It is reported that one of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunnah) entered upon Bishr ibn al-Mu'tamir and said: "Do you thank Allah for faith or not? If you say no, you have opposed the ijma' (scholarly consensus), and if you thank Him, how can you thank Him for something that is not an act of yours?" Bishr said to him: "We thank Him for the fact that He gave us power, intellect, and instruments. So it is obligatory upon us to thank Him for giving us power and instruments. As for thanking Him for faith, when faith is not an act of His, that is false." The discussion became difficult for Bishr. Then Thumama ibn al-Ashras entered upon them and said: "We do not thank Allah for faith; rather Allah thanks us for it, as He said: ﴿Then those, their striving was appreciated﴾ [al-Isra: 19]." Bishr said: "When the discussion became difficult, it became easy."

Know that what Thumama imposed upon him is false by the explicit text of this verse. That is because He, the Exalted, made clear that not associating others with Allah is from the bounty of Allah, then He made clear that most people do not give thanks for this blessing, and He mentioned it by way of blame. This indicates that it is obligatory for every believer to thank Allah, the Exalted, for the blessing of faith, and then the proof is strengthened and the indication is complete.

The Qadi said: His saying ﴿That﴾, if we take it as an indication of adherence to tawhid, then it is from the bounty of Allah, the Exalted, because it came about through His kindnesses and facilitation. It may also be an indication of prophethood.

The answer: That is an indication of what was mentioned before, and that is the abandonment of shirk. So it is necessary that the abandonment of shirk be from the bounty of Allah, the Exalted. The Qadi turns it toward kindnesses and facilitation, so this is abandoning the apparent meaning. As for turning it toward prophethood, that is far-fetched, because the word that indicates a demonstrative reference must be turned to the nearest of what was mentioned, and here that is the non-association of others with Allah.

[Page 112]

The Exalted said: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners! Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: His saying ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ means "my two companions in the prison." It is also possible that, because their companionship in the prison lasted only a short time, they were attributed to him. If a brief companionship is enough to make someone a companion, then whoever knows Allah and loves Him all his life is more deserving that the name of a believer who knows and loves Him should remain upon him.

The second issue: When he (peace be upon him) claimed prophethood in the earlier verse, and the establishment of prophethood rests on the establishment of divinity (ilahiyyat), he therefore began in this verse to establish the matters of divinity. Since most of creation acknowledges the existence of a God who is knowing and powerful, but the real issue is that they take idols in the form of celestial spirits (al-arwah al-falakiyyah), worship them, and expect benefit and harm from them, the efforts of most prophets were directed at preventing the worship of idols. The matter was the same in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him). For this reason he here began to mention what indicates the corruption of the claim of worshipping idols, and he mentioned several kinds of proofs and arguments.

The first argument: His saying ﴿Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ The explanation of this argument is that we say: Allah the Exalted has shown that the multiplicity of gods brings about disorder and corruption in this world, as in His saying ﴿Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. So the multiplicity of gods necessitates corruption and disorder, while the oneness of the God requires the attainment of order and good arrangement. When He had established this meaning in the other verses, He said here ﴿scattered lords are better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ and the intent is a question in the manner of denunciation (istifham 'ala sabil al-inkar).

The second argument: These idols are made, not makers, and subdued, not subduers. When a person wants to break them and destroy them, he is able to do so. So they are subdued and have no influence, and one does not expect benefit or harm from them. But the God of the world is the Doer, the Subduer, the Powerful, who is able to bring about good and repel evils and calamities. So the meaning is: is the worship of subdued and humiliated gods better, or the worship of Allah, the One, the Subduer? His saying ﴿lords﴾ points to multiplicity, so He placed in opposition to it the fact that He, the Exalted, is One. His saying ﴿scattered﴾ points to their being different in size, shape and color, and all of that happens only because the carver and the craftsman make them in that form. So His saying ﴿scattered﴾ points to their being subdued and powerless, and He placed in opposition to it the fact that He, the Exalted, is the Subduer. By this way that we have explained, this verse includes these two apparent kinds.

The third argument: The oneness of Him, the Exalted, necessitates worshipping Him, because if He had a second, we would not know who created us, provided for us, and repelled evils and calamities from us, and doubt would arise as to whether we worship this one or that one. In this there is an indication of what shows the corruption of the claim of worshipping idols. That is because, even assuming agreement that they benefit and harm but are many, then we would not know whether our benefit and the repelling of harm from us came from this idol or from that other one, or came through their partnership and mutual help. In that case doubt arises as to whether the one deserving worship is this one or that one. But if the one worshipped is one, this doubt is removed and certainty is attained in

[Page 113]

that He alone deserves worship, and there is no one worthy of worship by created beings and existents but Him. So this is also a subtle point derived from this verse.

The fourth argument: Even assuming that someone agrees that these idols benefit and harm according to what the astrologers (ashab al-talsamat) claim, there is no dispute that they benefit only at specific times and according to specific effects, whereas Allah the Exalted is capable of all things that are capable of being done. He is the Subduer absolutely, with executing will and power over all possibilities absolutely. So occupying oneself with His worship is more fitting.

The fifth argument, and it is noble and lofty: This is because the condition of the Subduer is that no one else subdues Him, and that He is the subduer of everything other than Himself. This requires that God be necessary of existence in His essence, for if He were possible, He would be subdued and not a subduer. And it is necessary that He be one, for if two necessary beings came into existence, neither would be the subduer of everything other than itself. So God is not a subduer except when He is necessary in His essence and is one. And when the one worshipped must be like this, this requires that God be something other than the sphere, other than the stars, other than light and darkness, and other than intellect and soul. As for whoever holds to the stars, they are "scattered lords," and they are not described as subduers. The same applies to natures, spirits, intellects and souls. So this single letter (al-harf al-wahid) is sufficient to establish this absolute monotheism and that it is a lofty station. This is the totality of the proofs derived from this verse. Two questions remain concerning it:

The first question: Why did He call them lords when they are not so?

The answer: Because of their belief that they are so. Also, the speech came in the manner of supposition and assumption (al-farḍ wa-l-taqdir), and the meaning is that if they are lords, then are they better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

The second question: Is it permissible to make a comparison between the idols and Allah, the Exalted, such that it is said that they are better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

The answer: It came in the manner of supposition, and the meaning is: even if we grant that they produced something that entails good, are they better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ In this there is a question: He, the Exalted, said in the verse before this: ﴿Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ and that indicates the existence of these named things. Then He said right after that verse: ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named,﴾ and this indicates that the named thing is not existent, and between the two there is contradiction.

The answer: The essence is existent and present, but what is named "god" is not present. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: Although the essences of the idols exist, they are not described by the attributes of divinity. Since this is so, the thing that is named "god" in reality is not existent or present.

The second: It is reported that the idol-worshippers were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah), and they believed that God is the Greatest Light, and that the angels are small lights, and they made idols in the form of those lights. Their real object of worship is those heavenly lights. This is the doctrine of the anthropomorphists, for they imagined a great body settled upon the Throne and worship it, and this imagined thing does not exist at all. So it is correct that they worship nothing but mere names.

[Page 114]

Know that a group of those who worship idols said: "We do not say that these idols are gods of the world in the sense that they are the ones who created the world. Rather, we apply the name of god to them and worship them and glorify them, because we believe that Allah commanded us to do so." So Allah the Exalted answered this, saying: As for naming them "gods," Allah the Exalted has not commanded that, and He has not sent down in the establishment of this naming any proof, argument, evidence, or authority. And there is no judgment for other than Allah that must be accepted, nor any command that must be obeyed. Rather, judgment, command and obligation belong to Him alone. Then He commanded that you worship none but Him. That is because worship is the utmost of glorification and reverence, so it is not fitting except for one from whom comes the utmost of bounty, and that is the God, the Exalted, for from Him come creation, giving life, intellect, provision and guidance. The blessings of Allah are many, and the aspects of His kindness to creation are without end.

Then, when He, the Exalted, had clarified these matters, He said ﴿But most people do not know.﴾ Its explanation is that most of creation attributes the occurrence of earthly events to celestial connections and stellar correspondences, because it is established in minds that every occurrence must have a cause. When they see that the change of conditions in this world, in heat and cold and the four seasons, occurs only with the change of the sun's positions in the quarters of the sphere, they link the four seasons to the movement of the sun. Then, when they witness that the conditions of plants and animals differ according to the difference of the four seasons, they link the growth of plants and the change of animals' conditions to the alternation of the four seasons. By this way it dominated the natures of most creation that the one governing the occurrence of events in this world is the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars. Then, when Allah grants success to a person so that he rises above this level and knows that these, in their essences and attributes, are in need of a originator, creator, subduer, powerful, knowing and wise, such a person is extremely rare. Therefore He said: ﴿But most people do not know.﴾

[Page 112]

The Exalted said: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners! Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: His saying ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ means "my two companions in the prison." It is also possible that, because their companionship in the prison lasted only a short time, they were attributed to him. If a brief companionship is enough to make someone a companion, then whoever knows Allah and loves Him all his life is more deserving that the name of a believer who knows and loves Him should remain upon him.

The second issue: When he (peace be upon him) claimed prophethood in the earlier verse, and the establishment of prophethood rests on the establishment of divinity (ilahiyyat), he therefore began in this verse to establish the matters of divinity. Since most of creation acknowledges the existence of a God who is knowing and powerful, but the real issue is that they take idols in the form of celestial spirits (al-arwah al-falakiyyah), worship them, and expect benefit and harm from them, the efforts of most prophets were directed at preventing the worship of idols. The matter was the same in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him). For this reason he here began to mention what indicates the corruption of the claim of worshipping idols, and he mentioned several kinds of proofs and arguments.

The first argument: His saying ﴿Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ The explanation of this argument is that we say: Allah the Exalted has shown that the multiplicity of gods brings about disorder and corruption in this world, as in His saying ﴿Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. So the multiplicity of gods necessitates corruption and disorder, while the oneness of the God requires the attainment of order and good arrangement. When He had established this meaning in the other verses, He said here ﴿scattered lords are better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ and the intent is a question in the manner of denunciation (istifham 'ala sabil al-inkar).

The second argument: These idols are made, not makers, and subdued, not subduers. When a person wants to break them and destroy them, he is able to do so. So they are subdued and have no influence, and one does not expect benefit or harm from them. But the God of the world is the Doer, the Subduer, the Powerful, who is able to bring about good and repel evils and calamities. So the meaning is: is the worship of subdued and humiliated gods better, or the worship of Allah, the One, the Subduer? His saying ﴿lords﴾ points to multiplicity, so He placed in opposition to it the fact that He, the Exalted, is One. His saying ﴿scattered﴾ points to their being different in size, shape and color, and all of that happens only because the carver and the craftsman make them in that form. So His saying ﴿scattered﴾ points to their being subdued and powerless, and He placed in opposition to it the fact that He, the Exalted, is the Subduer. By this way that we have explained, this verse includes these two apparent kinds.

The third argument: The oneness of Him, the Exalted, necessitates worshipping Him, because if He had a second, we would not know who created us, provided for us, and repelled evils and calamities from us, and doubt would arise as to whether we worship this one or that one. In this there is an indication of what shows the corruption of the claim of worshipping idols. That is because, even assuming agreement that they benefit and harm but are many, then we would not know whether our benefit and the repelling of harm from us came from this idol or from that other one, or came through their partnership and mutual help. In that case doubt arises as to whether the one deserving worship is this one or that one. But if the one worshipped is one, this doubt is removed and certainty is attained in

[Page 113]

that He alone deserves worship, and there is no one worthy of worship by created beings and existents but Him. So this is also a subtle point derived from this verse.

The fourth argument: Even assuming that someone agrees that these idols benefit and harm according to what the astrologers (ashab al-talsamat) claim, there is no dispute that they benefit only at specific times and according to specific effects, whereas Allah the Exalted is capable of all things that are capable of being done. He is the Subduer absolutely, with executing will and power over all possibilities absolutely. So occupying oneself with His worship is more fitting.

The fifth argument, and it is noble and lofty: This is because the condition of the Subduer is that no one else subdues Him, and that He is the subduer of everything other than Himself. This requires that God be necessary of existence in His essence, for if He were possible, He would be subdued and not a subduer. And it is necessary that He be one, for if two necessary beings came into existence, neither would be the subduer of everything other than itself. So God is not a subduer except when He is necessary in His essence and is one. And when the one worshipped must be like this, this requires that God be something other than the sphere, other than the stars, other than light and darkness, and other than intellect and soul. As for whoever holds to the stars, they are "scattered lords," and they are not described as subduers. The same applies to natures, spirits, intellects and souls. So this single letter (al-harf al-wahid) is sufficient to establish this absolute monotheism and that it is a lofty station. This is the totality of the proofs derived from this verse. Two questions remain concerning it:

The first question: Why did He call them lords when they are not so?

The answer: Because of their belief that they are so. Also, the speech came in the manner of supposition and assumption (al-farḍ wa-l-taqdir), and the meaning is that if they are lords, then are they better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

The second question: Is it permissible to make a comparison between the idols and Allah, the Exalted, such that it is said that they are better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

The answer: It came in the manner of supposition, and the meaning is: even if we grant that they produced something that entails good, are they better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ In this there is a question: He, the Exalted, said in the verse before this: ﴿Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ and that indicates the existence of these named things. Then He said right after that verse: ﴿You worship not besides Him but names you have named,﴾ and this indicates that the named thing is not existent, and between the two there is contradiction.

The answer: The essence is existent and present, but what is named "god" is not present. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: Although the essences of the idols exist, they are not described by the attributes of divinity. Since this is so, the thing that is named "god" in reality is not existent or present.

The second: It is reported that the idol-worshippers were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah), and they believed that God is the Greatest Light, and that the angels are small lights, and they made idols in the form of those lights. Their real object of worship is those heavenly lights. This is the doctrine of the anthropomorphists, for they imagined a great body settled upon the Throne and worship it, and this imagined thing does not exist at all. So it is correct that they worship nothing but mere names.

[Page 114]

Know that a group of those who worship idols said: "We do not say that these idols are gods of the world in the sense that they are the ones who created the world. Rather, we apply the name of god to them and worship them and glorify them, because we believe that Allah commanded us to do so." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 41:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink; but as for the other, he will be crucified and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.﴾

Know that when he (peace be upon him) had established the matter of tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood, he returned to answering the question that the two had asked him about. The meaning is clear. This is because the cupbearer, when he related his dream to Yusuf, and we have mentioned how he related it to him, Yusuf said to him: "How good is what you saw! As for the good grape cluster, it is the goodness of your condition; and as for the three branches, they are three days after which the king will summon you, and will return you to your position, so you will be as you were, rather better." And he said to the baker, when he related to him: "How evil is what you saw! The three baskets are three days after which the king will summon you, and will crucify you, and birds will eat from your head."

Then the commentators relate that the two of them said: "We saw nothing." So he said: ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.﴾ It has been disputed concerning the reason they said "We saw nothing." It is said that they had composed this statement in order to test his knowledge of interpretation, even though they had seen nothing. It is also said that when they disliked that answer, they said "We saw nothing."

If it is said: This answer which Yusuf (peace be upon him) gave was either based on revelation from God, the Exalted, or based on the science of ta'bir (interpretation of dreams). The first is invalid, because Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with both of them) reported that he only mentioned it by way of interpretation. Also, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved﴾. If that interpretation had been based on revelation, what would result from it would have been certainty and conviction, not conjecture and guesswork. The second is also invalid, because the science of ta'bir is based on conjecture and supposition.

The answer: It is not far-fetched to say that when they asked him about that dream, whether they were truthful in it or lying, God, the Exalted, revealed to him that the outcome of each of them would be in the specific manner, so when the revelation descended with that unseen matter at that question, it came to be thought that he had mentioned it by way of interpretation. It is also not far-fetched to say that he based that answer on the science of ta'bir. As for his saying: ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire﴾, he did not mean by it that what the two of them mentioned is inevitably going to happen; rather he meant that He decided it in the interpretation of what they asked him about, that which he mentioned.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved, "Mention me before your lord." But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord, so he remained in the prison several years.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The First Issue: The scholars differed over whether the one described with "thought" (ẓann) is Yusuf, peace be upon him, or the one who would be saved. According to the first view, the meaning is: the man whom Yusuf, peace be upon him, thought would be saved. On this view there are two aspects:

The first: that this ẓann is taken to mean knowledge and certainty. This applies if we say that he, peace be upon him, made that statement on the basis of revelation. The one who holds this said: the use of the word ẓann in the sense of certainty is common in the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who think (yaẓunnūna) that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46], and He said: ﴿Indeed, I thought (ẓanantu) that I would meet my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20].

The second: that this ẓann is taken in its literal sense of supposition. This applies if we say that he, peace be upon him, made that statement not on the basis of revelation, but on the principles mentioned in that field of knowledge (ta'bir al-ru'ya), which yield only supposition and conjecture.

The second view: that this ẓann is an attribute of the one who would be saved. The two inquirers did not believe in the prophethood and message of Yusuf, but they held a good opinion of him, so his words did not produce for them anything beyond mere supposition.

The Second Issue: Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to that man who had been judged to be released from prison and return to the service of the king: ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾, that is, before the king. The meaning: mention to him that I was wronged by my brothers when they expelled me and sold me, and then that I was wronged in this affair for which I was imprisoned. This is what is meant by the "mention."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾, and concerning this there are two views:

The first: that it refers to Yusuf, and the meaning is that Satan made Yusuf forget to mention his lord. On this view there are two aspects:

One of them: that his relying on other than Allah was something that warranted rebuke, and its explanation is in several ways:

The first: that his welfare lay in not turning in that affair to any of the creatures, and not presenting his need to anyone besides Allah, and in following the example of his grandfather Ibrahim, peace be upon him, for when he was placed in the catapult to be thrown into the fire, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." So when Yusuf returned to a creature, without doubt Allah described that as Satan having made him forget that entrusting (tafwid) and that tawhid, and having called him to present his need to the creatures. Then, when He described him with that, He mentioned that he remained in prison for several years for that cause, meaning that when he turned away from devoting himself to his Lord to this creature, he was punished by remaining in prison several years. The essential matter is that Yusuf's turning to the creature became a cause for two things:

One of them: that it became a cause for Satan's dominion over him, to the point that he made him forget the mention of his lord.

The second: that it became a cause for the trial remaining upon him for a long period.

The second aspect: that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, refuted the worship of idols, he said: ﴿Are scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ Then here he affirmed another lord besides Him when he said: ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾. Far be it from Allah that it be said that he judged him to be a lord in the sense of being a god; rather he judged him to lordship in the way one says "lord of the house" or "lord of the garment." Moreover, applying the word "lord" to him in its apparent sense contradicts the negation of multiple lords.

The third aspect: that he said in that verse: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾, and that is a negation of association absolutely and a complete entrusting of affairs to Allah, exalted is He; so here, turning to other than Allah, exalted is He, is as if contradicting that tawhid.

Know that seeking help from people in repelling injustice is permissible in the Sharia, but the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near. So although this is permissible for the general mass of creation, it is more fitting for the truthful (siddiqin) to cut off their regard for means entirely and to occupy themselves only with the Causer of causes.

The second aspect in interpreting the verse is to say: grant that he relied on other than Allah and asked that cupbearer to explain his condition before that king; nevertheless, it was obligatory for him not to leave that speech empty of the mention of Allah, such as saying "if Allah wills" or "Allah has decreed." When he left it empty of this mention, this rebuke came.

The second view: it is said that His saying ﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾ refers to the one who would be saved, and the meaning is: Satan made that youth forget to mention Yusuf to the king, until the matter lengthened, ﴿so he remained in the prison several years﴾ because of this cause. Some people said: the first view is preferable because of what is reported from him, peace be upon him, who said: "May Allah have mercy on Yusuf; had he not said 'Mention me before your lord,' he would not have remained in prison." And it is reported from Qatadah that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was punished because of his turning to other than Allah. And it is reported from Ibrahim al-Taymi that when he reached the prison door, his companion said to him: "What is your need?" He said: "That you mention me before a lord other than the Lord whom Yusuf mentioned." And it is reported from Malik: when Yusuf said to the cupbearer, "Mention me before your lord," it was said: "O Yusuf, you have taken other than Me as a guardian; I will indeed prolong your imprisonment." Yusuf wept and said: "The length of the trial made me forget the mention of my Master, so I uttered this word, and woe to my brothers."

The author of the book, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What I have tested from the beginning of my life to its end is that whenever a person relies in any matter on other than Allah, that becomes a cause of trial, affliction, hardship and calamity; and when the servant relies upon Allah and does not turn to any of the creatures, that desired outcome is achieved in the best of ways. This experience has continued for me from the beginning of my life until this time, when I have reached fifty-seven years, and at this point my heart has settled on the conviction that there is no benefit for a human being in relying on anything other than the grace and kindness of Allah, exalted is He. Some people preferred the second view, because diverting Satan's whispering to that man is better than diverting it to Yusuf the truthful, and because seeking help from servants in escaping injustice is permissible.

Know that the truth is the first view. What this second speaker mentioned is an adherence to the outward of the Sharia, while what the first speaker established is an adherence to the secrets of the Reality and the noble qualities of the Sharia. Whoever has a taste for the station of servanthood and has drunk from the spring of tawhid knows that the matter is as we have mentioned. Moreover, there is in the wording of the verse what indicates that this second view is weak, for if that were the intended meaning, it would have said: "So Satan made him forget the mention of his lord (dhikrahu li-rabbihi)."

The Third Issue: Seeking help from other than Allah in repelling injustice is permissible in the Sharia and there is no objection to it. However, since that was regarded as a fault by the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) who immerse themselves in the seas of servanthood, Yusuf, peace be upon him, was indeed held to account for it. At this point we say: whoever is held to account for this degree would more certainly be held to account for undertaking to seek illicit intercourse and for repaying good with evil. So when we see that Allah, exalted is He, took him to account for this degree and did not hold him to account at all in that affair, and did not blame him but rather mentioned him with the greatest forms of praise and commendation, we know that he, peace be upon him, was free of what the ignorant and the literalists (hashwiyya) attributed to him.

The Fourth Issue: Satan can cast whisperings, but as for forgetfulness, he cannot, because it is an expression for the removal of knowledge from the heart, and Satan has no power over it; otherwise he would have removed knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, from the hearts of the children of Adam.

The answer to this: he can do so insofar as through his whispering he calls to all other deeds, and a person's occupation with other deeds prevents him from recalling that knowledge and that awareness.

The Fifth Issue: As for His saying ﴿so he remained in the prison several years﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first discussion, according to the language: al-Zajjaj said: its derivation is from "bada'tu" in the sense of "I cut," and its meaning is a portion of the number. Al-Farra' said: al-bid' is not mentioned except with ten or twenty up to ninety. This implies that it is specific to what lies between three and nine. He said: "Thus I have seen the Arabs say, and I have not seen them say 'bid' and a hundred." And al-Sha'bi narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to his companions: "How much is the bid'?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "What is less than ten." The majority agreed that what is meant here by "several years" (bid' sinin) is seven years. They said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to that man, "Mention me before your lord," he had remained in prison five years, and then he remained after that seven years. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, humbled himself before that man, the time of his release had drawn near, but when he mentioned that, he remained in prison after it seven years. And it is reported that al-Hasan narrated his saying, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him: "May Allah have mercy on Yusuf; had it not been for the word he uttered, he would not have remained in prison this long a period." Then al-Hasan wept and said: "When a matter befalls us, we humble ourselves before people."

Page 118

Its statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And the king said, "Indeed I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green spikes and others dry. O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you can interpret visions."﴾ ﴿They said, "Confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."﴾

Know that when God, may He be exalted, wills something, He prepares causes for it. When the relief of Yusuf (peace be upon him) drew near, the king of Egypt saw in his sleep seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and seven lean cows, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones. He also saw seven green spikes whose grain had formed, and seven others that were dry, and the dry ones coiled around the green ones until they overcame them. He gathered the soothsayers (kahana) and told them of it, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿O eminent ones, explain to me my vision﴾. The people said, "This vision is mixed up, so we cannot interpret it or explain it." This is the apparent meaning of the speech, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: al-Layth said: al-'ajaf is the loss of fatness. The verb is 'ajifa, ya'jafu; the masculine is a'jaf, the feminine is 'ajfa', and the plural is 'ijaf for both masculine and feminine. In the speech of the Arabs there is no form af'al and fa'la' as a plural on fi'al except a'jaf and 'ijaf, and this is anomalous. They treated it according to the form of simān (fat), so they said simān and 'ijāf, because the two are opposites. It is among their habits to apply the counterpart to the counterpart, and the opposite to the opposite.

As for the lām in His words ﴿li-l-ru'yā ta'burūn﴾ (for dreams you interpret), according to some it is extra (zā'ida), because the object has been placed before the verb. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is permissible that al-ru'yā be the predicate of kāna, as when you say, "Fulān was for this matter," if he was independent in it and capable of it, and ta'burūn is another predicate or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is said: 'abartu al-ru'yā a'buruhā 'ibāratan and 'abbartuhā ta'bīran when you explain it. Al-Azhari related that this is derived from al-'ubr, which is the side of a river. The meaning of 'abartu al-nahr and al-ṭarīq is that I crossed it to the other side. So the interpreter of a dream is called 'ābir, because he considers both sides of the dream, reflects on its extremities, and moves from one of the two ends to the other. And al-aḍghāth (confused dreams) is the plural of ḍighth, which is a bundle of various kinds of plants and grass, on condition that it is of what stands on a stalk and has grown long. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [Sad: 44]﴾.

Having known this, we say: if the dream is mixed from things that are not harmonious, it resembles a bundle.

The second issue: God, the Exalted, made that dream a cause for the release of Yusuf (peace be upon him) from prison. This is because when the king became anxious and disturbed by it, since he witnessed that the weak and deficient had overcome the strong and complete, his nature testified that this was not good and that it warned of some kind of evil, but he did not know the nature of the matter. When a thing becomes known from one aspect and remains unknown from another, people's eagerness to complete that knowledge greatly increases, and the desire to complete what is deficient grows stronger, especially if the person is of great rank and wide dominion, and that thing indicates evil in some respects. By this means God strengthened the king's motive to acquire knowledge of the interpretation of this dream. Then God rendered the interpreters who were present with that king unable to answer this question, and concealed it from them, so that this would become the cause of Yusuf's release from that trial.

Know that the people did not deny for themselves being knowledgeable in the science of interpretation. Rather they said: the science of interpretation is of two kinds. Among it is that in which the dream is coherent and orderly, so that it is easy to move from imagined matters to spiritual rational realities. And among it is that in which the dream is mixed and disturbed, with no known arrangement, and this is what is called al-aḍghāth. The people said that the king's dream belongs to the category of al-aḍghāth, then they informed that they were not knowledgeable in the interpretation of this category. It is as if they said: this dream is mixed from many things, and whatever is like that, we are not guided to it and our intellect does not encompass it. There is also an implication that the scholar in this science and the one who is deeply versed in it may be guided to it. At this statement, that cupbearer (al-sharābī) remembered the incident of Yusuf, for he used to believe that Yusuf was deeply versed in this science.

As for the lām in His words ﴿li-l-ru'yā ta'burūn﴾ (for dreams you interpret), according to some it is extra (zā'ida), because the object has been placed before the verb. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is permissible that al-ru'yā be the predicate of kāna, as when you say, "Fulān was for this matter," if he was independent in it and capable of it, and ta'burūn is another predicate or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is said: 'abartu al-ru'yā a'buruhā 'ibāratan and 'abbartuhā ta'bīran when you explain it. Al-Azhari related that this is derived from al-'ubr, which is the side of a river. The meaning of 'abartu al-nahr and al-ṭarīq is that I crossed it to the other side. So the interpreter of a dream is called 'ābir, because he considers both sides of the dream, reflects on its extremities, and moves from one of the two ends to the other. And al-aḍghāth (confused dreams) is the plural of ḍighth, which is a bundle of various kinds of plants and grass, on condition that it is of what stands on a stalk and has grown long. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [Sad: 44]﴾.

Having known this, we say: if the dream is mixed from things that are not harmonious, it resembles a bundle.

The second issue: God, the Exalted, made that dream a cause for the release of Yusuf (peace be upon him) from prison. This is because when the king became anxious and disturbed by it, since he witnessed that the weak and deficient had overcome the strong and complete, his nature testified that this was not good and that it warned of some kind of evil, but he did not know the nature of the matter. When a thing becomes known from one aspect and remains unknown from another, people's eagerness to complete that knowledge greatly increases, and the desire to complete what is deficient grows stronger, especially if the person is of great rank and wide dominion, and that thing indicates evil in some respects. By this means God strengthened the king's motive to acquire knowledge of the interpretation of this dream. Then God rendered the interpreters who were present with that king unable to answer this question, and concealed it from them, so that this would become the cause of Yusuf's release from that trial.

Know that the people did not deny for themselves being knowledgeable in the science of interpretation. Rather they said: the science of interpretation is of two kinds. Among it is that in which the dream is coherent and orderly, so that it is easy to move from imagined matters to spiritual rational realities. And among it is that in which the dream is mixed and disturbed, with no known arrangement, and this is what is called al-aḍghāth. The people said that the king's dream belongs to the category of al-aḍghāth, then they informed that they were not knowledgeable in the interpretation of this category. It is as if they said: this dream is mixed from many things, and whatever is like that, we are not guided to it and our intellect does not encompass it. There is also an implication that the scholar in this science and the one who is deeply versed in it may be guided to it. At this statement, that cupbearer (al-sharābī) remembered the incident of Yusuf, for he used to believe that Yusuf was deeply versed in this science.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the one of the two who was saved and remembered after a period said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾ ﴿"Joseph, O truthful one, give us a ruling concerning seven fat cows, which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, that perhaps I may return to the people, that perhaps they may know."﴾

Know that when the king asked the chiefs about the vision, and those present acknowledged their inability to answer, the cupbearer said: "In the prison there is a virtuous, righteous man, abundant in knowledge and abundant in worship. I and the baker related two dreams to him, and he explained their interpretation (ta'wil), and he was right in all of it and did not err in a single letter. So if you permit, I will go to him and bring you the answer." This is His saying: ﴿And the one of the two who was saved said﴾.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and remembered after a period﴾, we say: the word iddakara will come up in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ in Surat al-Qamar. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Iddakara" with the dal is the eloquent form, related from al-Hasan. "Adhdhakara" with the dhal means "tadhakkara" (remembered). As for "ummah" (a period), there are several interpretations:

The first: "after ummah" means after a while (hin), because a while is only formed by the gathering of many days, just as a community (ummah) is only formed by the gathering of a great multitude. So the while was an ummah of days and hours.

The second: al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read "ba'da immah" with a kasra on the hamza, and immah means blessing. 'Adi said:

"Then after the prosperity and the kingdom and the blessing, the graves covered them there."

The meaning is: after he had been blessed with deliverance.

The third: it was read "ba'da amah", meaning after forgetfulness. One says "amiha, ya'mahu, amahan" when one forgets. The correct form is with a fatha on the mim, and Abu 'Ubayda mentioned it with a sukun on the mim. The summary of the matter is that either the intended meaning is that he remembered after the passage of many periods from the time when Joseph (peace be upon him) had instructed him to mention him to the king; or the intended meaning is that he remembered after finding favour with that king; or the intended meaning is that he remembered after forgetting.

If it is said: His saying "and remembered after a period" indicates that the one who forgot was the cupbearer, while you claim that the one who forgot was Joseph (peace be upon him).

We say: Ibn al-Anbari said: "iddakara" means "dhakara" and "akhbara" (remembered and informed). This does not indicate that forgetting came first. Perhaps the cupbearer did not mention him to the king out of fear that this would remind the king of his crime, for which he had been imprisoned, and the evil would increase. It is also possible to say: forgetting occurred to Joseph (peace be upon him), and it also occurred to that cupbearer.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿so send me forth﴾, it is addressed either to the king and his company (in the plural), or to the king alone out of reverence.

As for His saying: ﴿Joseph, O truthful one﴾, there is an omitted element in it, and the sense is: so he was sent, and he came to him and said, "O truthful one." The truthful one (al-siddiq) is one who is extremely truthful. He described him with this attribute because he had never tested him in a lie. It was also said: because he was truthful in interpreting his dream. This indicates that whoever wishes to learn something from a man must honour him, and address him with words that convey reverence. Then he repeated the question using the very same wording that the king had used, and how excellent was what he did, for the interpretation of dreams may differ according to the difference in wording, as is mentioned in that science.

[Page 120]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 47–50:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, words: ﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years, consistently. Then what you reap, leave it in its ears, except for a little that you eat."﴾ ﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored for them, except for a little that you keep.﴾ ﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain, and in which they will press (juice and oil).﴾

Know that peace be upon him mentioned the interpretation of that dream, saying: ﴿You will sow﴾. It is a statement with the meaning of a command, like His words: ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:228], and ﴿And mothers shall nurse﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:233]. A statement may come with the meaning of a command, and a command may come in the form of a statement, for emphasis on obligation, so that it is treated as if it has already occurred, and so he reports it. The evidence that it has the meaning of a command is His words: ﴿so leave it in its ears﴾.

As for His words ﴿consistently (da'aban)﴾, the linguists said: "Da'ab" means the continuation of a thing in one state. One is "da'ib" at doing something when he continues in doing it, and it is said "dA'aba, yad'abu, da'aban and da'aban", meaning sowing in succession during these years.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: Most of them read "da'ab" with a sukun, and perhaps the fatha is a dialect form, so it is like "sham'" and "sham'a", and "nahr" and "nahar". Al-Zajjaj said: "Da'aban" is in the accusative in the sense of "you will continue (taduʾabuna) da'aban." It was also said: it is a verbal noun placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and its estimated meaning is "you will sow persistently. Then what you reap, leave it in its ears, except for a little that you eat." Everything you wish to eat, thresh it, and leave the rest in its ears so that it does not spoil and weevils do not get into it, because leaving the grain in its ear keeps it in good condition.

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years﴾, that is, seven years of drought. "Al-shidad" means the hardships that bear heavily on people.

His words ﴿which will consume what you have stored for them﴾ are a metaphor, for a year does not eat, so the eating of the people of those years is attributed to the years.

His words ﴿except for a little that you keep﴾: "al-ihsan" means preserving, which is placing a thing in a fortress (ḥiṣn). It is said "ahṣanahu ihsanan" when he put it in safekeeping. The meaning is "except for a little that you store away." All these wordings are from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

As for His words ﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain﴾, the exegetes said: The first seven years are years of fertility and abundant blessings, and the second seven are years of famine and scarcity, which are known from the dream. As for the condition of this year, nothing in that dream indicates it. Rather, it was known through revelation. So it is as if peace be upon him mentioned that after the seven fertile years and the seven barren years there will come a blessed year, abundant in good and blessings. It is reported from Qatada: "May Allah increase him in knowledge (zādahu Allāh ʿilm) of a year."

If it is said: Since the lean ones were seven, this indicates that the years of drought do not exceed this number. It is known that what occurs after the end of the famine is fertility, and this was also among the implications of the dream. So why do you say it came through revelation and inspiration?

We reply: Grant that the change from famine to fertility is known from the dream. But the details of the condition in it, namely His words ﴿in which the people will be given rain﴾,

[Page 121]

﴿and in which they will press﴾, cannot be known except through revelation. Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said "ghāth Allāh al-bilād, yaghīthuhā ghaythan" when Allah sends rain upon the lands. "Ghīthat al-arḍ, tughāth" is used of the land when it is rained upon. His words ﴿the people will be given rain﴾ mean "they will be rained upon." It could also be from their saying "aghāthahu Allah" when He rescued him from distress or grief, and the meaning would be that the people are rescued in it from the hardship of drought. His words ﴿and in which they will press﴾ mean they will press sesame for oil, grapes for wine, and olives for oil, and this indicates the removal of drought and the arrival of fertility and goodness. It was also said: they will milk the udders. It was read "ya'ṣirūn" from "aṣarahu," meaning he saved him. It was also said: its meaning is "they will be rained upon," from "a'ṣarat al-saḥāba," when the cloud gave rain, and from this is His words: ﴿And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds (al-muʿṣirāt) abundant water﴾ [al-Naba' 78:14].

Everything you wish to eat, thresh it, and leave the rest in its ears so that it does not spoil and weevils do not get into it, because leaving the grain in its ear keeps it in good condition.

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years﴾, that is, seven years of drought. "Al-shidad" means the hardships that bear heavily on people.

His words ﴿which will consume what you have stored for them﴾ are a metaphor, for a year does not eat, so the eating of the people of those years is attributed to the years.

His words ﴿except for a little that you keep﴾: "al-ihsan" means preserving, which is placing a thing in a fortress (ḥiṣn). It is said "ahṣanahu ihsanan" when he put it in safekeeping. The meaning is "except for a little that you store away." All these wordings are from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

As for His words ﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain﴾, the exegetes said: The first seven years are years of fertility and abundant blessings, and the second seven are years of famine and scarcity, which are known from the dream. As for the condition of this year, nothing in that dream indicates it. Rather, it was known through revelation. So it is as if peace be upon him mentioned that after the seven fertile years and the seven barren years there will come a blessed year, abundant in good and blessings. It is reported from Qatada: "May Allah increase him in knowledge (zādahu Allāh ʿilm) of a year."

If it is said: Since the lean ones were seven, this indicates that the years of drought do not exceed this number. It is known that what occurs after the end of the famine is fertility, and this was also among the implications of the dream. So why do you say it came through revelation and inspiration?

We reply: Grant that the change from famine to fertility is known from the dream. But the details of the condition in it, namely His words ﴿in which the people will be given rain﴾,

[Page 121]

﴿and in which they will press﴾, cannot be known except through revelation. Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said "ghāth Allāh al-bilād, yaghīthuhā ghaythan" when Allah sends rain upon the lands. "Ghīthat al-arḍ, tughāth" is used of the land when it is rained upon. His words ﴿the people will be given rain﴾ mean "they will be rained upon." It could also be from their saying "aghāthahu Allah" when He rescued him from distress or grief, and the meaning would be that the people are rescued in it from the hardship of drought. His words ﴿and in which they will press﴾ mean they will press sesame for oil, grapes for wine, and olives for oil, and this indicates the removal of drought and the arrival of fertility and goodness. It was also said: they will milk the udders. It was read "ya'ṣirūn" from "aṣarahu," meaning he saved him. It was also said: its meaning is "they will be rained upon," from "a'ṣarat al-saḥāba," when the cloud gave rain, and from this is His words: ﴿And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds (al-muʿṣirāt) abundant water﴾ [al-Naba' 78:14].
