His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him about the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting."﴾ ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Far be God from imperfection! We know of him no evil." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that God does not guide the plot of the betrayers.﴾

Know that when the cupbearer returned to the king and presented the interpretation that Joseph (peace be upon him) had mentioned, the king approved of it and said, "Bring him to me." This indicates the virtue of knowledge, for He, glorified is He, made his knowledge the means of his deliverance from worldly trial. How then would knowledge not be the means of deliverance from the trials of the Hereafter? So the cupbearer returned to Joseph (peace be upon him) and said, "Answer the king." But Joseph (peace be upon him) refused to leave the prison until his case had been made clear and the accusation had been entirely removed from him.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I marvel at Joseph and his generosity and his patience, and God forgive him, when he was asked about the lean cows and the fat ones. Had I been in his place, I would not have informed them until I had stipulated that they bring me out. And I marvelled at him when the messenger came to him and he said, 'Return to your lord.' Had I been in his place and remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to respond and rushed to the door, and I would not have sought an excuse. Indeed, he was forbearing and possessed of deliberation."

Know that what Joseph did, namely patience and restraint until the king investigated his condition, is what befits resolve and intellect. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: had he come out immediately, the trace of that accusation might have remained in the king's heart. But when he asked the king to investigate the circumstances of that incident, this indicated his innocence of that accusation. After his release, no one could then stain him with that vice or use it as a pretext to attack him.

The second: a person who had remained in prison for twelve years, when the king sought him and ordered his release, would ordinarily hasten to come out. Since he did not come out, and since it was known of him that he possessed the utmost intellect, patience and steadfastness, this became a cause for the belief in his innocence of all kinds of accusations, and for the judgment that everything said about him was a lie and a calumny.

The third: his request that the king investigate his condition regarding those women also indicates the extreme purity of his character, for had he been tainted in any way, he would have feared that what had preceded would be mentioned.

The fourth: when he said to the cupbearer, ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾, he remained in prison for several years because of this statement. Now the king sought him, but he did not turn to him, nor did he give weight to his request, and he occupied himself with demonstrating his innocence of the accusation. Perhaps his purpose, peace be upon him, in this was that no inclination toward the king's response and acceptance should remain in his heart. This act served as a remedy for what had proceeded from him in the request he made to the cupbearer in his saying, ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾, so that this meaning might also become evident to that cupbearer, for he was the intermediary in both situations.

As for His saying, ﴿Ask him about the case of the women who cut their hands﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: they recited ﴿فَسَلْهُ﴾ (fa-salhu, without a hamza) and the rest recited ﴿فاسْألْهُ﴾ (fa-s'alhu, with a hamza). Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i recited the former, and the others recited the latter. ʿAsim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him, recited ﴿النُّسْوَةِ﴾ (al-nuswati) with a dammah on the nun, while the rest recited it with a kasrah on the nun. Both are dialectal variants.

The second issue: know that this verse contains several kinds of subtleties:

The first of them: the meaning of the verse is, "Ask the king so that he inquires what the affair of those women is and what their condition is, so that he may know my innocence of that accusation." However, he limited himself to asking the king about that incident, so that the wording would not include anything resembling a command to the king to do a deed or an action.

The second: he did not mention his mistress, although she was the one who strove to have him cast into the long imprisonment, but he limited himself to mentioning the rest of the women.

The third: it is apparent that those women attributed to him an ugly act and a shameful deed in the king's presence, so Joseph (peace be upon him) limited himself to the mere statement, ﴿the case of the women who cut their hands﴾, and did not complain of them specifically or in detail.

Then Joseph said after that, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting.﴾ Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿my Lord﴾ there are two views:

The first: it is God Most High, because He is the One who knows hidden matters.

The second: the intended one is the king, and he called him "lord" because he was his nurturer, and this contains an indication that the king was knowing of their plotting and deceit.

Know that their plotting against him may have several meanings:

One of them: each of them may have desired him, and when she did not find what she wanted, she began to slander him and attribute to him the ugly.

The second: perhaps each of them exerted great effort in encouraging Joseph to comply with his mistress's wishes, and Joseph knew that such betrayal toward a master who had shown him kindness is not permissible. So by his saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting﴾, he pointed to their extreme persistence in encouraging that betrayal.

The third: he extracted from them various aspects of deceit and stratagems aimed at distorting the image of Joseph (peace be upon him) before the king, and so the intended meaning of this expression was that.

Then God Most High relates that when Joseph (peace be upon him) requested this, the king ordered that the women be brought, and said to them: ﴿What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

The first: although his saying ﴿when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself﴾ is in the plural form, what is meant by it is the singular, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173].

The second: what is meant by it is addressing the group.

Then there are two views here:

The first: each of them sought to seduce Joseph from himself.

The second: each of them sought to seduce Joseph on account of the wife of the chief. The wording admits all these meanings. At this question they said, ﴿Far be God from imperfection! We know of him no evil.﴾ This is like an affirmation of what they had said at the beginning concerning him, namely their saying: ﴿This is not a mortal; this is none other than a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31].

Know that the wife of the chief was present, and she knew that these debates and investigations had arisen because of her and on her account. So she uncovered the veil, declared the true word, and said: ﴿Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: this is a definite testimony from that woman that Joseph, may God's blessings be upon him, was free of all sins and purified of all defects. Here there is a subtle point: Joseph (peace be upon him) had observed the side of the wife of the chief, when he said, ﴿the case of the women who cut their hands﴾. He mentioned them and did not mention that woman at all. So the woman understood that he had left mentioning her only out of consideration for her rights, honoring her side, and concealing the matter from her. She therefore wished to reward him for this good act. Accordingly, she removed the covering and the concealment, and acknowledged that the whole sin had been on her side, and that Joseph (peace be upon him) was innocent of all of it. I have seen in some books that a woman brought her husband before a judge and claimed from him her dower. The judge ordered that she uncover her face so that the witnesses could give their testimony. The husband said, "There is no need for that, for I acknowledge the truth of her claim." The woman said, "Since you have honored me to this extent, then bear witness that I have released you from every right I had against you."

The second issue: the lexicographers said: ﴿حَصْحَصَ الحَقُّ﴾ (haṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq) means: it became clear, was uncovered, and became firmly established in hearts and souls, from the saying: "haṣḥaṣa al-baʿīr fī burūkihi," when the camel settled and became fixed on the ground. Al-Zajjaj said: its derivation in the language is from al-ḥiṣṣah (portion), i.e., the portion of truth became separated from the portion of falsehood.

The third issue: they differed regarding whose statement is ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. There are several views:

The first view, which is the view of the majority, is that it is the statement of Joseph (peace be upon him). Al-Farra' said: it is not far-fetched to join the speech of one person with the speech of another when context indicates it. An example of this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the honored among its people humiliated﴾ [al-Naml: 34], and this is the statement of Bilqis. Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [al-Naml: 34]. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of people for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al ʿImran: 9] is the statement of the one who supplicates. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, God does not fail in His promise﴾.

Remaining on this view are some questions:

The first question: His saying ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to something absent, whereas what is meant here is a demonstrative referring to that present incident.

The answer: we addressed this in His saying ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. It has also been said that ﴿That﴾ refers to what he did of refusing the messenger, as if he were saying: "That which I did in refusing the messenger was only so that the king would know that I did not betray him in his absence."

The second question: when did Joseph (peace be upon him) say this statement?

The answer: ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that when Joseph (peace be upon him) entered upon the king, he said that so that he would know. He stated it in the form of the third person out of reverence for the king, so as to avoid addressing him directly. The more likely view is that he (peace be upon him) said that when the messenger returned to him, because uttering this statement in the presence of the king would be a breach of etiquette.

The third question: this betrayal occurred against the chief, so how can he say, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾?

The answer: it has been said that the meaning is: so that the king may know that I did not betray the chief by backbiting. It has also been said that if one betrays his minister, he has in some respect betrayed him. It has also been said that when the cupbearer returned to Joseph (peace be upon him) while he was in prison, he said: "That is so that the chief may know that I did not betray him in his absence." Then he concluded the statement with His saying: ﴿and that God does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾. Perhaps what is meant by it is: "If I had been a betrayer, God, Exalted is He, would not have delivered me from this predicament. And since He delivered me from it, it became evident that I was free of what they attributed to me."

The second view: that His saying ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾ is the statement of the wife of the chief. The meaning is: "Although I shifted the blame onto him in his presence, I did not shift the blame onto him in his absence, that is, I did not say about him while he was in prison what was contrary to the truth." Then she emphasized the truth further with this statement and said: ﴿and that God does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾, meaning: "Since I undertook plotting and deceit, I was inevitably disgraced; and since he was innocent of the sin, God, Exalted is He, inevitably purified him of it." The proponent of this view said: What indicates its soundness is that Joseph (peace be upon him) was not present in that assembly, so that it could be said that when the woman made her statement, ﴿Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾, Joseph would then say at that moment, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence.﴾ Rather, it would require that the messenger return from that assembly to the prison and relate that account to him. Then Joseph would say, starting afresh: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence.﴾ Such a connection between two unrelated statements has never occurred in prose or in verse. So we know that this is part of the woman's speech.

The fourth issue: this verse indicates the purity of Joseph (peace be upon him) from sin in many respects:

The first point: when the king sent for Joseph, peace be upon him, and requested him, had Joseph been accused of a shameful act, and had a sin and indecency actually proceeded from him, then by custom and habit it would be impossible for him to ask the king to investigate that incident. For if he had committed the sin, and then he asked the king to investigate that incident, that would be a striving on his part toward disgracing himself and renewing the defects that had become effaced and hidden. And a sensible person does not do that. Suppose that some people did doubt his infallibility (ʿiṣmah) or his prophethood, still there is no doubt that he was sensible, and a sensible person refrains from striving to disgrace himself and from driving his enemies to exaggerate in displaying his defects.

The second point: the women testified in the first instance to his purity and integrity, when they said: ﴿Holy God! This is not a human being. This is nothing but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. And in the second instance, when they said: ﴿Holy God! We know no evil of him﴾.

The third point: the wife of the chief minister (al-ʿAzīz) acknowledged his purity in the first instance, when she said: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him, but he steadfastly refused﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. And in the second instance, in this verse.

Know that this verse indicates his purity in several respects:

The first: the woman's saying: ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾.

The second: her saying: ﴿And he is certainly among the truthful﴾, which is an indication that he was truthful in his saying: ﴿She sought to seduce me﴾ [Yusuf: 26].

The third: Joseph's, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿That he (al-ʿAzīz) may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾. The Ḥashwiyyah (literalist anthropomorphists) mention that when Joseph said these words, Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "Nor when you did desire (her)?" This is among their corrupt narrations, and this report is not authenticated in any reliable book. Rather, they attach it to this place in an endeavour to distort the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

The fourth: his saying: ﴿And that God does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning that the one who commits treachery must inevitably be exposed. So had I been treacherous, I would have been exposed. Since I was not exposed, and God delivered me from this predicament, all of that indicates that I was not among the treacherous.

Here is another aspect, which is stronger than all of these: at this time that incident had become effaced and that trial had come to an end. So his undertaking to say: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾, even though he had betrayed him in the greatest forms of betrayal, would be an undertaking of great audacity and great falsehood, without any benefit whatsoever attached to it. Undertaking such audacity without any benefit at all does not befit anyone among the sensible; so how could it befit being attributed to the chief of the sensible and the exemplar of the chosen ones? Thus it is established that this verse indicates with decisive clarity his innocence of what the ignorant and the Ḥashwiyyah say.

It has also been said that ﴿That﴾ refers to what he did of refusing the messenger, as if he were saying: "That which I did in refusing the messenger was only so that the king would know that I did not betray him in his absence."

The second question: when did Joseph (peace be upon him) say this statement?

The answer: ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that when Joseph (peace be upon him) entered upon the king, he said that so that he would know. He stated it in the form of the third person out of reverence for the king, so as to avoid addressing him directly. The more likely view is that he (peace be upon him) said that when the messenger returned to him, because uttering this statement in the presence of the king would be a breach of etiquette.

The third question: this betrayal occurred against the chief, so how can he say, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾?

The answer: it has been said that the meaning is: so that the king may know that I did not betray the chief by backbiting. It has also been said that if one betrays his minister, he has in some respect betrayed him. It has also been said that when the cupbearer returned to Joseph (peace be upon him) while he was in prison, he said: "That is so that the chief may know that I did not betray him in his absence." Then he concluded the statement with His saying: ﴿and that God does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾. Perhaps what is meant by it is: "If I had been a betrayer, God, Exalted is He, would not have delivered me from this predicament. And since He delivered me from it, it became evident that I was free of what they attributed to me."

The second view: that His saying ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾ is the statement of the wife of the chief. The meaning is: "Although I shifted the blame onto him in his presence, I did not shift the blame onto him in his absence, that is, I did not say about him while he was in prison what was contrary to the truth." Then she emphasized the truth further with this statement and said: ﴿and that God does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾, meaning: "Since I undertook plotting and deceit, I was inevitably disgraced; and since he was innocent of the sin, God, Exalted is He, inevitably purified him of it." The proponent of this view said: What indicates its soundness is that Joseph (peace be upon him) was not present in that assembly, so that it could be said that when the woman made her statement, ﴿Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾, Joseph would then say at that moment, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence.﴾ Rather, it would require that the messenger return from that assembly to the prison and relate that account to him. Then Joseph would say, starting afresh: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence.﴾ Such a connection between two unrelated statements has never occurred in prose or in verse. So we know that this is part of the woman's speech.

The fourth issue: this verse indicates the purity of Joseph (peace be upon him) from sin in many respects:

The first point: when the king sent for Joseph, peace be upon him, and requested him, had Joseph been accused of a shameful act, and had a sin and indecency actually proceeded from him, then by custom and habit it would be impossible for him to ask the king to investigate that incident. For if he had committed the sin, and then he asked the king to investigate that incident, that would be a striving on his part toward disgracing himself and renewing the defects that had become effaced and hidden. And a sensible person does not do that. Suppose that some people did doubt his infallibility (ʿiṣmah) or his prophethood, still there is no doubt that he was sensible, and a sensible person refrains from striving to disgrace himself and from driving his enemies to exaggerate in displaying his defects.

The second point: the women testified in the first instance to his purity and integrity, when they said: ﴿Holy God! This is not a human being. This is nothing but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. And in the second instance, when they said: ﴿Holy God! We know no evil of him﴾.

The third point: the wife of the chief minister (al-ʿAzīz) acknowledged his purity in the first instance, when she said: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him, but he steadfastly refused﴾ [Yusuf: 32]. And in the second instance, in this verse.

Know that this verse indicates his purity in several respects:

The first: the woman's saying: ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾.

The second: her saying: ﴿And he is certainly among the truthful﴾, which is an indication that he was truthful in his saying: ﴿She sought to seduce me﴾ [Yusuf: 26].

The third: Joseph's, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿That he (al-ʿAzīz) may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾. The Ḥashwiyyah (literalist anthropomorphists) mention that when Joseph said these words, Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "Nor when you did desire (her)?" This is among their corrupt narrations, and this report is not authenticated in any reliable book. Rather, they attach it to this place in an endeavour to distort the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

The fourth: his saying: ﴿And that God does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning that the one who commits treachery must inevitably be exposed. So had I been treacherous, I would have been exposed. Since I was not exposed, and God delivered me from this predicament, all of that indicates that I was not among the treacherous.

Here is another aspect, which is stronger than all of these: at this time that incident had become effaced and that trial had come to an end. So his undertaking to say: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾, even though he had betrayed him in the greatest forms of betrayal, would be an undertaking of great audacity and great falsehood, without any benefit whatsoever attached to it. Undertaking such audacity without any benefit at all does not befit anyone among the sensible; so how could it befit being attributed to the chief of the sensible and the exemplar of the chosen ones? Thus it is established that this verse indicates with decisive clarity his innocence of what the ignorant and the Ḥashwiyyah say.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 53:

[Page 125]
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is certainly one that commands evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: Know that the interpretation of this verse varies according to the variation of what precedes it. For if we say that His saying, ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ (Yusuf: 52), is the speech of Yusuf, then this too is from the speech of Yusuf; and if we say that this is part of the speech of the woman, then this too is likewise. We shall interpret this verse according to both assumptions. As for when we say that this is the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, the Hashwiyya (literalist extremists) have clung to it and said: When he, peace be upon him, said, ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret,﴾ Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "Nor when you resolved to undo your trousers?" At that, Yusuf said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is certainly one that commands evil﴾, i.e., to fornication, ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy﴾, i.e., whom my Lord has protected, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving﴾ for the desire with which I desired, ﴿Merciful﴾, i.e., if I had done it, He would have turned in acceptance toward me.

Know that this statement is weak, for we have shown that the preceding verse is a decisive proof of his innocence from sin. It remains to be asked: "What is your answer concerning this verse?" We say: there are two aspects to it.

The first aspect: When he, peace be upon him, said, ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret,﴾ that was in the manner of praising oneself and commending it, and God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not attribute purity to yourselves﴾ (al-Najm: 32). So he corrected that about himself by his saying, ﴿And I do not absolve myself,﴾ and the meaning is: "And I do not commend myself. Indeed, the soul is certainly one that commands evil, inclined toward ugliness, eager for disobedience."

The second aspect in the answer: The verse does not at all indicate anything of what they mentioned. That is because when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said, ﴿that I did not betray him in secret,﴾ he made clear that the abstention from betrayal was not due to lack of desire or lack of inclination of the soul and nature, because the soul commands evil and the nature yearns for pleasures. So by this statement he made clear that the abstention was not due to lack of desire, but due to the presence of fear of God, exalted is He.

As for when we say that this statement is part of the speech of the woman, then there are two aspects:

The first: "And I do not absolve myself of his seduction," and her intent is to confirm Yusuf, peace be upon him, in his saying: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾ (Yusuf: 26).

The second: When she said, ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ (Yusuf: 52), she said: "And I do not absolve myself of betrayal absolutely, for I have betrayed him when I shifted the blame onto him and said: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾ (Yusuf: 25) and I placed him in prison." It is as if she intended to make an excuse for what had happened.

If it is said: Is it better to make this statement the speech of Yusuf or to make it the speech of the woman?

We say: Making it the speech of Yusuf is problematic, because His saying, ﴿The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become manifest,"﴾ is a speech connected part to part through to its end, so the claim that part of it is the speech of the woman and part is the speech of Yusuf, with many intervening separations between the two statements and between the two sessions, is remote. Also, making it the speech of the woman is problematic as well, because His saying, ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is certainly one that commands evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy,﴾ is a statement that is fitting only to come from one who has guarded himself against sins; then this statement is mentioned by way of breaking the self, and that is not befitting for a woman who has exhausted her effort in disobedience.

The second issue: They said: "mā" in His saying, ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy,﴾ has the meaning of "man" (who), and the estimated reading is: "except whom my Lord has mercy upon." Each of "mā" and "man" stands in place of the other, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾ (al-Nisa: 3), and He said: [Page 126] ﴿And of them is one who walks on four﴾ (al-Nur: 45). His saying, ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy,﴾ is an exception that is either connected or disconnected, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: that it is connected, and in its explanation there are two aspects:

The first: that His saying, ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy,﴾ means: except the portion that my Lord has shown mercy to by infallibility, like the angels.

The second: except what my Lord has mercy upon, i.e., except at the time of my Lord's mercy, meaning that she is one who commands evil at every time except at the time of infallibility.

The second view: that it is a disconnected exception, i.e., "but rather, the mercy of my Lord is what turns away the evil," as in His saying: ﴿Nor will they be saved﴾ ﴿except by a mercy from Us﴾ (Ya Sin: 44).

The third issue: The philosophers have differed regarding what the soul that commands evil actually is.

The verifiers said: The human soul is one thing, and it has many attributes. When it inclines toward the divine world, it is a tranquil soul; and when it inclines toward desire and anger, it is one that commands evil. Its being one that commands evil conveys emphasis, and the reason for this is that the soul, from the first moment of its origination, has become accustomed to sensible things, has delighted in them and become enamored of them. As for its awareness of the world of immaterial things and its inclination toward it, that does not occur except rarely, in the case of one person after another, and that one attains such detachment and unveiling only at rare times throughout his life. Since the predominant state is its being drawn toward the corporeal world, and its inclination to ascend to the higher world is rare, it is therefore judged to be one that commands evil. Some people have claimed that the tranquil soul is the rational, speaking soul, and that the appetitive and irascible souls are distinct from the rational soul. The discussion of establishing the truth in this matter is mentioned in the works on rational sciences.

The fourth issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) held that obedience and faith come about only from God, by His saying: ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy.﴾ They said: the verse indicates that the turning of the soul away from evil does not happen except by His mercy, and the wording of the verse implies that whenever that mercy occurs, that turning away occurs.

We say: It is not possible to interpret this mercy as the granting of intellect, power and graces, as al-Qadi (al-Baydawi/ the Mu'tazili judge) said, because all of that is shared between the disbeliever and the believer. Therefore it must be interpreted as something else, namely, the preponderance of the motive to obedience over the motive to disobedience. We have also established this by a decisive proof, and in that case the intended meaning results from it.

[p. 127]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trustworthy in our presence."﴾ ﴿He said, "Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian."﴾**

There are several issues in the verse.

**The first issue:** The scholars differed about this king. Some said he was the ʿAzīz. Others said he was al-Rayyān, who was the greatest king. This second view is the more apparent, for two reasons.

The first reason is that Yusuf's words, ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land﴾, indicate it.

The second reason is that his words, ﴿I will take him for myself﴾, indicate that before this he had not been exclusively his. Yusuf, peace be upon him, had previously been exclusively the ʿAzīz's. This shows that this king was the greatest king.

[p. 127 continues]

**The second issue:** They mentioned that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, while he was in prison and said: "Say: O Allah, grant me from You a relief and a way out, and provide for me from where I do not expect." Allah accepted his supplication and manifested this cause in his release from prison.

The summary of the matter is that the king's confidence in Yusuf grew greatly, for several reasons.

The first is that his confidence in Yusuf's knowledge grew greatly. This is because, when the people were unable to answer and Yusuf was able to give the correct answer, which reason testifies to be sound, the king's inclination toward him grew.

The second is that his confidence in Yusuf's patience and steadfastness grew greatly. This is because, after Yusuf had remained in prison for several years, when he was given permission to leave, he did not hasten to leave. Rather, he showed patience, paused, and first requested what would indicate the innocence of his condition from all accusations.

The third is that his confidence in Yusuf's good manners grew greatly. This is because he limited himself to saying: ﴿What is the matter with the women who cut their hands?﴾ (Yusuf: 50), and although his purpose was to mention the wife of the ʿAzīz, he concealed her mention and addressed the matter of the other women, even though great kinds of affliction had reached him from her side. This is a wondrous form of good manners.

The fourth is the clearing of his condition from all kinds of accusations, for the adversary acknowledged for him purity, integrity, and innocence from wrongdoing.

The fifth is that the cupbearer described to the king his diligence in acts of obedience and his striving in doing good to those who were in prison.

The sixth is that he remained in prison for several years.

Each of these matters, individually, necessitates a good opinion of a person. How, then, when they are combined? For this reason the king's opinion of him was good. When Allah wills something, He gathers its causes and strengthens them.

Having understood this, we say: When these qualities of Yusuf, peace be upon him, became apparent to the king, he desired to take him for himself, and he said: ﴿Bring him to me; I will take him for myself.﴾ It is related that the messenger said to Yusuf, peace be upon him: "Stand before the king cleansed of the filth of the prison, in clean clothes and good appearance." Yusuf wrote upon the prison gate: "These are the dwellings of affliction, the graves of the living, the gloating of enemies, and the trial of friends." When he entered upon the king, he said: "O Allah, I ask You for Your good through his good, and I seek refuge in Your might and power from his evil." Then he entered upon him and greeted him, and he supplicated for him in Hebrew.

[p. 128]

*Istikhlāṣ* (taking something exclusively for oneself) is seeking the purity of a thing from the impurities of sharing. This king sought that Yusuf be his alone, and that no one else share him in it, because the custom of kings is to keep exclusive possession of precious and elevated things. When the king knew that he was the unique one of his age and the matchless one among his peers, he wished to have him exclusively.

It is related that the king said to Yusuf, peace be upon him: "There is nothing that I do not love for you to share with me except my family, and that you not eat with me." Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: "Do you not see that I should eat with you, when I am Yusuf son of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq the sacrificed, son of Ibrāhīm the Friend, peace be upon them?" Then he said: ﴿So when he spoke with him﴾, and about this there are two views.

One of them is that what is meant is: when the king spoke with Yusuf, peace be upon him. They said this because in the assemblies of kings it is not proper for anyone to begin speaking; rather, the one who begins is the king.

The second is that what is meant is: when Yusuf spoke with the king. It is said: when Yusuf came to the king, at that time he was thirty years old. When the king saw him as a young man, he said to the cupbearer: "Is this the one who knew the interpretation of my dream, when the magicians and soothsayers did not know it?" He said: "Yes." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "I love to hear the interpretation of the dream from you directly." Yusuf answered with that answer directly, and his heart bore witness to its soundness. At that point the king said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are today established and trustworthy in our presence.﴾ It is said: "So-and-so is established with so-and-so," meaning clear standing, that is, rank, and it is a state by which its possessor is empowered to do what he wishes.

His saying: ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: we have known your trustworthiness and your innocence from what you have been accused of.

Know that his saying: ﴿established and trustworthy﴾ is a comprehensive expression for everything needed of virtues and excellent qualities, because it is necessary for him to be established, and that requires power and knowledge.

As for power, it is by it that empowerment is attained. As for knowledge, it is because his being empowered to do good deeds cannot be attained except by it. For if he did not know what is fitting and what is not fitting, he could not specify what is fitting by action and specify what is not fitting by abstention. Thus it is established that being established cannot be attained except by power and knowledge.

As for his being trustworthy, it is an expression for his being wise, not acting from the impulse of desire but acting only from the impulse of wisdom. Thus it is established that his being established and trustworthy indicates his being capable, his being knowledgeable of the places of good and evil, of righteousness and corruption, and his being disposed to act from the impulse of wisdom and not from the impulse of desire. Whoever is like this, no evil or foolishness proceeds from him. For this reason, when the Muʿtazilah ("those who withdrew," a theological school) sought to establish that Allah, exalted is He, does not do what is ugly, they said: Allah does not do what is ugly, because He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of the ugly and knows that He is independent of it. Whoever is like this does not do what is ugly.

They said: He is independent of what is ugly only if He is capable, and if He is free from the impulse of foolishness. Thus it is established that describing him as established and trustworthy is the furthest that can be mentioned in this matter.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said in this position: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian.﴾ There are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** The exegetes said: When Yusuf, peace be upon him, interpreted the king's dream in his presence, the king said to him: "What do you see, O truthful one?" He said: "I see that you should sow a large amount of crops in these fertile years, build storehouses, and gather food in them. Then, when the years of drought come, we will sell the harvests, and thereby a great wealth will be obtained." The king said: "Who will take care of this task for me?" Yusuf said: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land﴾, that is, over the storehouses of the land of Egypt. He put the definite article on "the land," and what is meant is the known and previously mentioned one.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this verse that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Set me over the storehouses of the land,' he would have employed him at that very moment. But when he said that, Allah delayed it for him by a year."

I say: This is among the wonders. When Yusuf refused to leave the prison, Allah made that easy for him in the best manner. When he hastened in mentioning the request, Allah, exalted is He, delayed that sought matter for him. This indicates that leaving disposal and entrusting everything entirely to Allah, exalted is He, is better.

**The second issue:** Someone may say: Why did Yusuf request leadership, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: "Do not ask for leadership"? Also, how did he request leadership from a disbelieving sultan? Also, why did he not wait for a period? Why did he show the desire for leadership immediately? Also, why did he request the matter of the storehouses at the outset, even though this produces a kind of suspicion? Also, how did he permit himself to praise himself with his saying: ﴿indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾, even though Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So do not attest to your own purity﴾ (al-Najm: 32)? Also, what is the benefit of his saying: ﴿indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾? Also, why did he omit the exception in this matter? For the better course would have been for him to say: "indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian, if Allah wills," based on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," unless [adding], "If Allah wills"﴾ (al-Kahf: 23–24).

These are seven questions, and each must be answered.

The principle in answering these issues is that managing the affairs of creatures was obligatory upon him, so it was permissible for him to reach it by whatever means. We say that this management was obligatory upon him for several reasons.

The first is that he was a true messenger from Allah, exalted is He, to creation, and it is obligatory upon a messenger to safeguard the welfare of the community to the extent possible.

The second is that he, peace be upon him, knew by revelation that drought and severe hardship would occur, which might perhaps lead to the destruction of a great number of people. Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to plan for this and to devise a means by which the harm of that drought would be lessened for the creatures.

The third is that striving to bring benefit to those deserving it and to repel harm from them is something the intellects deem good.

[p. 129]

When this is established, we say: he, peace be upon him, was charged with safeguarding the welfare of creation for these reasons, and he could not safeguard it except by this means. What the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. So this means was obligatory upon him. Since it was obligatory, the questions are entirely dropped.

As for omitting the exception, al-Wāḥidī said: that was an error which entailed a punishment, namely that Allah, exalted is He, delayed the attainment of that intended goal for him by a year. I say: Perhaps the reason for it is that if he had mentioned this exception, the king would have believed that he mentioned it because he knew he had no ability to manage this interest as it should be managed. For this reason, he omitted the exception.

As for the question of why he praised himself: its answer has several aspects.

The first: We do not concede that he praised himself. Rather, he explained that he was described by these two beneficial attributes in attaining this sought matter. There is a difference between the two matters. It seems that he had concluded that he needed to mention this attribute, because although the king knew his perfection in the sciences of religion, he did not know that he would fulfill this task.

Then we say: Grant that he praised himself. Praising oneself is blameworthy only when a man intends by it arrogance, boasting, and reaching what is not lawful. But apart from this aspect, we do not concede that it is prohibited. The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So do not attest to your own purity﴾ (al-Najm: 32) means attesting purity to oneself while one knows that one is not pure. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾. As for when a person knows that what he says is true and right, this is not forbidden to him. And Allah knows best.

His saying: What is the benefit of describing himself as a knowledgeable guardian?

We say: It is like saying: "a guardian of all the aspects through which income and wealth can be obtained, knowledgeable of the directions in which wealth can be properly spent." It may also be said: "a guardian of all the welfare of the people, knowledgeable of the directions of their needs." Or it may be said: "a guardian of the aspects of your favors and generosity, knowledgeable of the obligation to repay them with obedience and submission." This is a broad topic, which can be expanded for whoever wishes.

[p. 127]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trustworthy in our presence."﴾ ﴿He said, "Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian."﴾**

This king sought that Yusuf be his alone, and that no one else share him in it, because the custom of kings is to keep exclusive possession of precious and elevated things. When the king knew that he was the unique one of his age and the matchless one among his peers, he wished to have him exclusively.

It is related that the king said to Yusuf, peace be upon him: "There is nothing that I do not love for you to share with me except my family, and that you not eat with me." Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: "Do you not see that I should eat with you, when I am Yusuf son of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq the sacrificed, son of Ibrāhīm the Friend, peace be upon them?" Then he said: ﴿So when he spoke with him﴾, and about this there are two views.

One of them is that what is meant is: when the king spoke with Yusuf, peace be upon him. They said this because in the assemblies of kings it is not proper for anyone to begin speaking; rather, the one who begins is the king.

The second is that what is meant is: when Yusuf spoke with the king. It is said: when Yusuf came to the king, at that time he was thirty years old. When the king saw him as a young man, he said to the cupbearer: "Is this the one who knew the interpretation of my dream, when the magicians and soothsayers did not know it?" He said: "Yes." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "I love to hear the interpretation of the dream from you directly." Yusuf answered with that answer directly, and his heart bore witness to its soundness. At that point the king said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are today established and trustworthy in our presence.﴾ It is said: "So-and-so is established with so-and-so," meaning clear standing, that is, rank, and it is a state by which its possessor is empowered to do what he wishes.

His saying: ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: we have known your trustworthiness and your innocence from what you have been accused of.

Know that his saying: ﴿established and trustworthy﴾ is a comprehensive expression for everything needed of virtues and excellent qualities, because it is necessary for him to be established, and that requires power and knowledge.

As for power, it is by it that empowerment is attained. As for knowledge, it is because his being empowered to do good deeds cannot be attained except by it. For if he did not know what is fitting and what is not fitting, he could not specify what is fitting by action and specify what is not fitting by abstention. Thus it is established that being established cannot be attained except by power and knowledge.

As for his being trustworthy, it is an expression for his being wise, not acting from the impulse of desire but acting only from the impulse of wisdom. Thus it is established that his being established and trustworthy indicates his being capable, his being knowledgeable of the places of good and evil, of righteousness and corruption, and his being disposed to act from the impulse of wisdom and not from the impulse of desire. Whoever is like this, no evil or foolishness proceeds from him. For this reason, when the Muʿtazilah ("those who withdrew," a theological school) sought to establish that Allah, exalted is He, does not do what is ugly, they said: Allah does not do what is ugly, because He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of the ugly and knows that He is independent of it. Whoever is like this does not do what is ugly.

They said: He is independent of what is ugly only if He is capable, and if He is free from the impulse of foolishness. Thus it is established that describing him as established and trustworthy is the furthest that can be mentioned in this matter.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said in this position: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian.﴾ There are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** The exegetes said: When Yusuf, peace be upon him, interpreted the king's dream in his presence, the king said to him: "What do you see, O truthful one?" He said: "I see that you should sow a large amount of crops in these fertile years, build storehouses, and gather food in them. Then, when the years of drought come, we will sell the harvests, and thereby a great wealth will be obtained." The king said: "Who will take care of this task for me?" Yusuf said: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land﴾, that is, over the storehouses of the land of Egypt. He put the definite article on "the land," and what is meant is the known and previously mentioned one.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this verse that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Set me over the storehouses of the land,' he would have employed him at that very moment. But when he said that, Allah delayed it for him by a year."

I say: This is among the wonders. When Yusuf refused to leave the prison, Allah made that easy for him in the best manner. When he hastened in mentioning the request, Allah, exalted is He, delayed that sought matter for him. This indicates that leaving disposal and entrusting everything entirely to Allah, exalted is He, is better.

**The second issue:** Someone may say: Why did Yusuf request leadership, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: "Do not ask for leadership"? Also, how did he request leadership from a disbelieving sultan? Also, why did he not wait for a period? Why did he show the desire for leadership immediately? Also, why did he request the matter of the storehouses at the outset, even though this produces a kind of suspicion? Also, how did he permit himself to praise himself with his saying: ﴿indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾, even though Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So do not attest to your own purity﴾ (al-Najm: 32)? Also, what is the benefit of his saying: ﴿indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾? Also, why did he omit the exception in this matter? For the better course would have been for him to say: "indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian, if Allah wills," based on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," unless [adding], "If Allah wills"﴾ (al-Kahf: 23–24).

These are seven questions, and each must be answered.

The principle in answering these issues is that managing the affairs of creatures was obligatory upon him, so it was permissible for him to reach it by whatever means. We say that this management was obligatory upon him for several reasons.

The first is that he was a true messenger from Allah, exalted is He, to creation, and it is obligatory upon a messenger to safeguard the welfare of the community to the extent possible.

The second is that he, peace be upon him, knew by revelation that drought and severe hardship would occur, which might perhaps lead to the destruction of a great number of people. Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to plan for this and to devise a means by which the harm of that drought would be lessened for the creatures.

The third is that striving to bring benefit to those deserving it and to repel harm from them is something the intellects deem good.

[p. 129]

When this is established, we say: he, peace be upon him, was charged with safeguarding the welfare of creation for these reasons, and he could not safeguard it except by this means. What the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. So this means was obligatory upon him. Since it was obligatory, the questions are entirely dropped.

As for omitting the exception, al-Wāḥidī said: that was an error which entailed a punishment, namely that Allah, exalted is He, delayed the attainment of that intended goal for him by a year. I say: Perhaps the reason for it is that if he had mentioned this exception, the king would have believed that he mentioned it because he knew he had no ability to manage this interest as it should be managed. For this reason, he omitted the exception.

As for the question of why he praised himself: its answer has several aspects.

The first: We do not concede that he praised himself. Rather, he explained that he was described by these two beneficial attributes in attaining this sought matter. There is a difference between the two matters. It seems that he had concluded that he needed to mention this attribute, because although the king knew his perfection in the sciences of religion, he did not know that he would fulfill this task.

Then we say: Grant that he praised himself. Praising oneself is blameworthy only when a man intends by it arrogance, boasting, and reaching what is not lawful. But apart from this aspect, we do not concede that it is prohibited. The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So do not attest to your own purity﴾ (al-Najm: 32) means attesting purity to oneself while one knows that one is not pure. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾. As for when a person knows that what he says is true and right, this is not forbidden to him. And Allah knows best.

His saying: What is the benefit of describing himself as a knowledgeable guardian?

We say: It is like saying: "a guardian of all the aspects through which income and wealth can be obtained, knowledgeable of the directions in which wealth can be properly spent." It may also be said: "a guardian of all the welfare of the people, knowledgeable of the directions of their needs." Or it may be said: "a guardian of the aspects of your favors and generosity, knowledgeable of the obligation to repay them with obedience and submission." This is a broad topic, which can be expanded for whoever wishes.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land, that he might settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and used to be mindful of God.﴾

In this are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Joseph, peace be upon him, asked the king to appoint him over the treasuries of the land, God did not relate from the king that he said, "I have done so." Rather, God, glorified is He, said: ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land.﴾ Here the exegetes said that there is an omitted element in the speech, and its implied sense is: the king said, "I have done so," but God's establishing him in the land indicates that the king had granted what he requested.

I say: What they said is good, but here there is something better than it, namely that the king's granting his request is a cause in the observable world, whereas the true determinant is nothing other than that God established him in the land. This is because that king was able to accept or to reject, so the relation of his power to acceptance and to rejection was equal. As long as this equality remains, acceptance cannot occur; therefore acceptance must be preponderant over rejection in the mind of that king. That preponderance cannot occur except by a preponderating factor which God creates. When God creates that preponderating factor, acceptance inevitably occurs. Thus the establishment of Joseph in the land is nothing other than God's creation, in the heart of that king, of the combination of power and the firm motive, upon whose occurrence the effect necessarily follows. For this reason God, exalted is He, omitted mention of the king's granting and confined Himself to mention of the divine establishment, because the true determinant is nothing other than Him.

The second issue: It is related that the king crowned him, took out the ring of sovereignty and placed it on his finger, invested him with his sword, and set up for him a throne of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. Joseph, peace be upon him, said: "As for the throne, I will strengthen your kingdom by it; as for the ring, I will manage your affairs by it; as for the crown, it is not of my garments nor the garments of my fathers." He sat upon the throne and the people submitted to him. The king dismissed Qitfir, the husband of the woman well known, and he died after that, and the king married him to his wife. When he went in to her he said, "Is this not better than what you sought?" He found her a virgin, and she bore him two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. He established justice in Egypt, and men and women loved him, and the king and many people embraced Islam at his hand. In the years of famine he sold food to the people of Egypt for dirhams and dinars in the first year, then for jewelry and precious stones in the second year, then for livestock, then for lands and estates, then for their persons, until he enslaved them for years. They said, "By God, we have never seen a king greater in dignity than this king, for all creation has become his slaves." When he heard that he said, "I call God to witness that I have freed the people of Egypt, all of them, and returned to them their possessions." He would not sell to anyone who asked for food more than a camel's load, lest the food run short for the rest. This is how the author of al-Kashshaf related it, and God knows best.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿Thus﴾: the kaf is in the accusative governed by "establishment" (التمكين). "That" refers to what preceded, meaning: like that favour which We bestowed upon him by bringing him close to the king's heart and rescuing him from the distress of imprisonment. His saying ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾ means We empowered him to do what he wished by removing obstacles. His saying ﴿that he might settle therein wherever he willed﴾: "yatabawwa'" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, its sense being: We established him as one settling. Ibn Kathir read (نشاء) with the nun, attributed to God, exalted is He, while the rest read it with the ya', attributed to Joseph.

Know that His saying ﴿he might settle therein wherever he willed﴾ indicates that he attained to a position in the kingdom such that no one could oppose him or dispute with him; rather he became independent in everything he willed and desired. Then God clarified what confirms that this came from Him, saying: ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will.﴾

Know that God first mentioned that this establishment was from God and from no one other than Him, which is His saying ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land﴾; then He affirmed this a second time by His saying ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will.﴾ In this there are two benefits:

The first benefit: this indicates that the whole matter is from God, exalted is He.

The judge [al-Qadi] said: Since that kingdom was not complete except through matters which God did, it became as though it had come from Him, exalted is He.

His reply: We maintain that the very kingdom itself came into being from God, exalted is He, because the wording of the Qur'an indicates our view, and the decisive proof we have mentioned strengthens our view. So turning this wording toward metaphor has no path.

The second benefit: that it came to him purely by divine will and all-prevailing power.

The judge said: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, carries out the matter of His blessings according to what welfare requires.

We say: The verse indicates that matters are contingent upon divine will and pure power. As for observing the condition of welfare, this is a matter you have introduced from yourself, although the wording does not indicate it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ This is because the wasting of reward is either due to incapacity, or ignorance, or miserliness, and all of these are impossible with respect to God, exalted is He; so waste is impossible.

Know that this is a testimony from God, exalted is He, that Joseph, peace be upon him, was among the good-doers. Had the claim been true that he sat between her four legs, it would be impossible to say that he was among the good-doers. Here, then, it follows either that God is being called a liar in His judgment on Joseph that he was among the good-doers, which is outright disbelief, or that the literalist (al-Hashwi) is being called a liar in what he related, which is pure faith and truth.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and used to be mindful of God.﴾ In this are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this verse there are two opinions.

The first opinion: its meaning is that Joseph, peace be upon him, although he had reached lofty positions and high ranks in this world, the reward God has prepared for him in the Hereafter is better, more excellent and more complete. The aspects of preference have been mentioned in this book many times and in various ways; the sum of those aspects is that absolute good is that which is pure benefit, lasting, accompanied by exaltation; and all these four conditions are present in the goods of the Hereafter and absent from the goods of this world.

The second opinion: the word "good" (khayr) may be used to indicate that one of two goods is more excellent than the other, as one says: "JulLab (rosewater) is better than water." It may also be used to indicate that a thing is good in itself without the intention being to express preference, as one says: "Tharid (broth with bread) is better than God's (goodness)," meaning: tharid is among the goods which came about by God's bounty.

Given this, if we take His saying ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better﴾ in the first sense, it follows that the pleasures of this world must also be described as good. If we take it in the second sense, it follows that one should not say that the benefits of this world are also goods; rather it may indicate that the good of the Hereafter is the good, and whatever else is futile.

The second issue: There is no doubt that the intent of His saying ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and used to be mindful of God﴾ is a description of Joseph's state, peace be upon him. Therefore it must be affirmed concerning him that he was among "those who believe and used to be mindful of God." This is an explicit statement from God, glorified and exalted, that he was among the God-fearing in the earlier time. There is no earlier time for Joseph, peace be upon him, requiring a statement that he was among the God-fearing in it, except that time about which God said: ﴿And she desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ (Joseph: 24). So this was a testimony from God, exalted is He, that at that time he, peace be upon him, was among the God-fearing. Also His saying ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ is a testimony from God, exalted is He, that he, peace be upon him, was among the good-doers; and His saying ﴿Indeed he was of Our sincere servants﴾ (Joseph: 24) is a testimony from God, exalted is He, that he was among the sincere. Thus it is established that God, exalted is He, bore witness that Joseph, peace be upon him, was among the God-fearing, the good-doers and the sincere. The ignorant literalist says that he was among the losers, the sinners; and there is no doubt that whoever does not accept the word of God, glorified is He, with these emphases is among the losers.

The third issue: The judge said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and used to be mindful of God﴾ indicates the invalidity of the view of the Murji'ah, who claim that reward is obtained in the Hereafter by one who does not avoid major sins.

Response: This is weak. For if we take the word "khayr" as the comparative form, it follows that the reward obtained by the God-fearing is more excellent, and it does not follow that it is not obtained by others at all. And if we take it in the basic sense of goodness, this indicates that this good is obtained by the God-fearing, and does not indicate that this good is not obtained by others.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 58–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾ ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"﴾ ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ ﴿They said, "We will seek to get him from his father, and we will surely do it."﴾

Know that when the famine spread through the lands, and reached also the town in which Ya'qub (peace be upon him) lived, and times became hard for them, he said to his sons: "Indeed, in Egypt there is a righteous man who supplies people with grain. So go to him with your silver and take food." So they set out to him, and they were ten, and they entered upon Yusuf (peace be upon him). This event became, as it were, the means of the gathering of Yusuf (peace be upon him) with his brothers, and of the manifestation of the truth of what Allah, exalted is He, had reported about him in His saying to Yusuf (peace be upon him) at the time they cast him into the well: ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they will not perceive﴾ (Yusuf: 15). Allah, exalted is He, reported that Yusuf recognized them while they did not recognize him at all. As for his recognizing them, it was because Allah, exalted is He, had informed him in His saying: ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾ (Yusuf: 15) that they would reach him and enter upon him. Also, the dream he had seen was a sign that they would reach him. For this reason Yusuf (peace be upon him) was watchful for that matter, and every one who arrived at his gate from distant lands he would examine and inquire about their conditions, so that he might know whether these arrivals were his brothers or not. When the brothers of Yusuf arrived at the gate of his house, he examined their conditions with an examination that made it clear to him that they were his brothers. As for their not recognizing him, it was for several reasons:

Know that there must be a preceding speech so that this speech becomes a cause for Yusuf's asking about the condition of their brother, and they mentioned for it several explanations:

The first, which is the best of them: the custom of Yusuf (peace be upon him) with everyone was to give him the load of one camel, neither more nor less. The brothers of Yusuf who went to him were ten, so he gave them ten loads. They said: "We have an aged old father and another brother who remained with him." They mentioned that their father, because of his age and the severity of his grief, had not come, and that their brother had remained in the service of their father, and that both of them also needed some of the food. So he furnished for both of them two other camels of food. When they mentioned that, Yusuf said: "This indicates that your father's love for him is greater than his love for you. This is a strange thing, for you, with your beauty, intellect and good manners, if your father's love for that brother is greater than his love for you, this shows that this is a marvel in intellect, in virtue and in good manners. So bring him to me that I may see him." This cause is plausible and fitting.

The second: when they entered upon him (peace be upon him) and he gave them food, he said to them: "Who are you?" They said: "We are a people of herdsmen from the people of Syria; hardship has afflicted us, so we have come seeking grain." He said: "Perhaps you have come as spies." They said: "God forbid! We are brothers, sons of one father, an aged, truthful prophet whose name is Ya'qub." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "We were twelve; one of us perished, and one remained with the father to console himself with him for the one who perished. We are ten, and we have come to you." He said: "Leave some of you with me as a pledge, and bring me a brother of yours from your father so that he may convey to me the message of your father." At this, they cast lots among themselves, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, who was the best of them in opinion regarding Yusuf, so they left him with him.

The third: perhaps when they mentioned their father, Yusuf said: "Why did you leave him alone and solitary?" They said: "We did not leave him alone; rather, one remained with him." He said to them: "Why did he single him out for himself, and why did he specify him with this meaning? Is it because of a defect in his body?" They said: "No. Rather, because he loves him more than his love for the rest of the children." At this Yusuf said: "As you have mentioned, that your father is a wise, knowledgeable man far from rashness, and then he specified him with increased love, it must be that he is superior to you in virtue and in the attributes of perfection, although I see you as eminent, learned and wise. So my soul longs to see that brother; so bring him to me."

The second cause was mentioned by the commentators, and the first and third are plausible; and Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, related of him that he said: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it and do not diminish it, and I will add to you the load of another camel for the sake of your brother; ﴿and that I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, the best of hosts, because when he lodged them he treated them with the best hospitality. I say: this statement weakens the second cause, which is the one we have transmitted from the commentators, because the basis of that cause is that he accused them and attributed to them that they were spies; and if he had addressed them with that speech, it would not befit him to say to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾. Also, it is far-fetched that Yusuf (peace be upon him), being a truthful one, would say to them: "You are spies and informers," while he knows their innocence of this accusation, for slander does not befit the state of the truthful.

* * *

Then he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾
Know that when he (peace be upon him) asked them to bring that brother, he combined encouragement and intimidation.

As for encouragement, it is his saying: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾. As for intimidation, it is his saying: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ This is because they were in extreme need of obtaining food, and they could not obtain it except from him; so when he prevented them from coming to him, that was the utmost of intimidation and frightening. Then, when they heard this speech from Yusuf, they said: ﴿We will seek to get him from his father, and we will surely do it.﴾ That is: we will strive and devise to take him away from his hand, and we will surely do this seeking. The purpose of the repetition is emphasis. It may be that ﴿and we will surely do it﴾ means that we will bring him to you; and it may be that ﴿and we will surely do it﴾ means every effort within our power in this matter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 62–64:

50. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family; perhaps they will come back."﴾ ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us, that we may receive measure. And indeed, we will be his guardians."﴾ ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust you with him except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read (لِفِتْيانِهِ, li-fityānihi) with an alif and nun, while the rest read (لِفِتْيَتِهِ, li-fityatihi) with a ta' and without an alif. These are two dialects, like al-ṣibyān and al-ṣibyah, and al-ikhwān and al-ikhwah. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: al-fityah is the plural of fatan (young man) for a small number, and al-fityān is for a large number. The reasoning for the form that indicates a small number is that those who surround this matter, in which they place their merchandise in their saddlebags, are few, because this is a matter of secrecy, so it must be guarded except from a small number. The reasoning for the form indicating a large plural is that He said: ﴿Put their merchandise into their saddlebags﴾, and "al-rihāl" (saddlebags) indicates a large number, so those who carry out that task must be many.

The second issue: The majority agree that the brothers of Joseph did not know that the merchandise had been placed in their saddlebags. Some said they were aware of it, but this is weak, because His saying: ﴿so that they may recognize it﴾ refutes that. Then they differed concerning the reason for which Joseph commanded that their merchandise be placed in their saddlebags, in several ways:

The first: when they opened the baggage and found their merchandise in it, they would know that this was generosity from Joseph and pure bounty, which would move them to return to him and to be eager to deal with him.

The second: he feared that his father would not have enough silver to return with them a second time.

The third: he intended to provide for his father, because the time was a time of famine.

The fourth: he saw that taking the price of food from his father and his brothers, while they were in great need of food, would be baseness.

The fifth: al-Farra' said: when they witnessed their merchandise in their saddlebags, it would fall upon their hearts that they had placed that merchandise in their saddlebags out of forgetfulness, and they were prophets and sons of prophets, so they would return to find out the reason for it, or they would return to give the money back to its owner.

The sixth: he intended to do them a kindness in a manner that would not bring them shame or obligation.

The seventh: his aim was that they should know that he did not seek that brother for the sake of harm and injustice, nor to seek an increase in the price.

The eighth: he intended that his father should know that he had honored them, and that his request for the brother was for greater honor, so that sending his brother would not be burdensome to his father.

The ninth: he intended that this money be a support for them in the hardship of the time, and he feared thieves on the road, so he placed those dirhams in their saddlebags so that they would remain hidden until they reached their father.

The tenth: he intended to counter their excess in harming him with his excess in kindness toward them.

Then He, exalted is He, related of them that when they returned to their father they said: ﴿O our father, measure has been withheld from us﴾, and concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: that when they asked for food for their father and for the brother who remained with him, they were prevented from it, so their saying ﴿measure has been withheld from us﴾ refers to this.

The second: that measure was withheld for the future, and it refers to the saying of Joseph: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾. The evidence that the intended meaning is this is their saying: ﴿so send our brother with us, that we may receive measure.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (yaktal, "he will receive measure") with a ya', while the rest read it with a nun. The first reading supports the first opinion, and the second reading supports the second opinion.

Then they said: ﴿And indeed, we will be his guardians.﴾ They guaranteed that they would be guardians of him. When they said that, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Shall I entrust you with him except as I entrusted you with his brother before?﴾ The meaning is that you mentioned this statement before concerning Joseph, and you guaranteed me his protection when you said: ﴿And indeed, we will be his guardians﴾ (Yusuf: 12). Then here you mention this very phrase, so will there be any security here other than what there was there? That is, since security was not achieved there, likewise it will not be achieved here.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (ḥāfiẓan, "guardian") with an alif as a specification (tamyīz) and explanation, with the implied sense: He is better for you as a guardian, like their saying: "He is the best of them as a man," and "Praise be to Allah, what a horseman he is." It was also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). The rest read (ḥifẓan, "guarding") without an alif, as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: the best of you in guarding, i.e., Allah's guarding of Benjamin is better than your guarding. Al-A'mash read: (fa-Allāhu khayru ḥāfiẓ, "Allah is the best guardian"), and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, read: (khayru al-ḥāfiẓīn wa-huwa arḥamu al-rāḥimīn, "the best of guardians, and He is the most merciful of the merciful").

It was also said: the meaning is: I trusted you with the guarding of Joseph, peace be upon him, and what happened happened; now I entrust Benjamin's guarding to Allah.

If it is asked: why did he send him with them when he had witnessed what he had witnessed?

We say: for several reasons:

First: they had grown old and inclined toward goodness and righteousness.

Second: he witnessed that between them and Benjamin there was no envy or resentment like what there had been between them and Joseph, peace be upon him.

Third: the necessity of the famine compelled him to that.

Fourth: perhaps Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him and guaranteed his protection and his return to him.

If it is asked: does His saying ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ indicate that he gave permission for his son Benjamin to go at that time?

We say: most of them said it indicates that. Others said it does not indicate that, and concerning this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that even if he had permitted his going out with them, it would be in Allah's guarding, not in their guarding.

The second: when he mentioned Joseph, he said: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾, that is, for Joseph, because he knew that he was alive.
