The statement of God Most High: ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾

Know that al-*mata'* (goods, or belongings) is whatever is fit to be enjoyed, and it is general to everything. It is permissible that it here means the food they had carried, and it is permissible that it means the containers of the food.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾. The reciters differed concerning ﴿ruddat﴾ (was returned). Most read it with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ*, while ʿAlqama read it with a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: the *kasra* of the doubled *dāl* (in the original *rudda*) was transferred to the *rāʾ*, as in *qīla* and *bīʿa*.

Quṭrub related that they said, in our saying *ḍuriba Zaydun* (Zayd was struck), that the *kasra* of the *rāʾ* is transferred to the *ḍād* for those who make the letter quiescent. As for His words ﴿mā nabghī﴾ (what more could we desire), there are two views concerning the word *mā*:

The first view: it is a negation. On this reading there are several explanations:

The first: they had described Yusuf as generous and gentle, and said: "We have come upon a man of the utmost generosity, who lodged us and honoured us with a hospitality that, had he been a man of the family of Yaʿqub, he would not have done." So their words ﴿mā nabghī﴾ mean: "with this description which we have mentioned, we are not lying, and there is no mention of a thing that did not exist."

The second: he went so far in honouring us that there is nothing beyond it. After he had gone to such lengths in honouring us, he ordered our merchandise to be returned to us.

The third: the meaning is that he returned our merchandise to us, so when we return to him we do not seek from him any other merchandise, for this which is with us is sufficient for us.

The second view: the word *mā* here is interrogative, and the meaning is: when they saw that he had returned their merchandise to them, they said: "What more could we desire after this?" That is, he gave us the food, and then he returned to us the price of the food in the best manner. So what could we desire beyond that?

Know that if we take *mā* as interrogative, the sense becomes: "What could we desire above this honour? The man has returned our silver to us. So when we go to him, we will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load because of the presence of our brother."

Al-Asmaʿi said: it is said *māra yamīru mayran* when one comes back with provisions (*mīra*), that is, with food. From this comes the saying "he has neither goodness nor provision" (*mayr*). As for His words ﴿wa nazdādu kayla baʿīr﴾ (and gain an extra camel-load), their meaning is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, used to measure out to each man the load of one camel. So when his brother is present, that load must be increased. As for taking *mā* as negation, the meaning would be: "We do not seek anything else; this is our merchandise returned to us, and it is sufficient for the price of the food on the second journey. Then we will do such and such."

* * *

As for His words ﴿That is an easy measure﴾, there are several explanations:

The first: Muqatil said: "That is an easy measure for this good man, because of his generosity and his eagerness to give." This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj.

The second: "That is an easy measure," that is, short in duration; it is not the way of such a thing that its period should be prolonged by detention and delay.

The third: the intended meaning is: what is given to us without our brother is a small, slight amount; so send our brother with us, so that we may exchange that paucity for abundance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in Allah's name that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded (by some calamity)." And when they gave him their solemn pledge, he said, "Allah is Guardian over what we say."﴾

Know that al-mawthiq (the solemn covenant) is a verbal noun meaning trust (al-thiqah), and its meaning is the pledge by which one is trusted. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle. The meaning is: "I will never send him with you until you give me a pledge that is trusted." His words ﴿from Allah﴾ mean a pledge trusted because it is confirmed by calling Allah as witness and by swearing an oath by Allah upon it. His words ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾: the lam (la-) entered here because we have explained that what is meant by a covenant from Allah is an oath. So its implied sense is: "until you swear by Allah that you will surely bring him back to me."

His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ contain two discussions:

The first discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this exception is connected (istithna' muttasil). So His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ are an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the affirmative statement, which is His words ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾, is in the sense of a negative. So the meaning is: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back for any reason among the reasons, except for one reason."

The second discussion: al-Wahidi said: the commentators have two opinions regarding it:

The first opinion: that His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ mean destruction. Mujahid said: "Unless you all die, and that would be an excuse for me." The Arabs say: "uhीta bi-fulan" (he was surrounded) when his destruction drew near, as He, exalted, says: ﴿and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾ (al-Kahf: 42), meaning that what destroyed him befell him. And He, exalted, says: ﴿and they thought that they were encompassed﴾ (Yunus: 22). The origin of this is that whoever is surrounded by an enemy and the paths of escape are closed to him, his destruction draws near, so it is said of everyone who perishes: "he has been encompassed."

The second opinion: what Qatadah mentioned: ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ means unless you become overpowered and subdued, so that you are unable to return.

* * *
Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And when they gave him their solemn pledge, he said, "Allah is Guardian over what we say."﴾ He means: "Witness," because the witness is a guardian (wakil) in the sense that this covenant is entrusted to him. So if you fulfill it, He will reward you with the best reward, and if you betray it, He will requite you with the greatest punishments.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verse 67:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates. Yet I cannot avail you against Allah at all. Judgment belongs only to Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely put their trust."﴾

Know that when the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob) resolved to leave for Egypt, they were described as possessing perfection and beauty, and they were the sons of one man. So he said to them: ﴿Do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of the *mufassirun* (Qur'anic exegetes), is that he feared the evil eye (*al-'ayn*) for them. Here we have two standpoints.

The first standpoint: establishing that the evil eye is real. What indicates this are several considerations:

The first: the consensus (*ijma'*) of the earlier exegetes that this verse refers to that.

The second: what has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "used to seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, saying: 'I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and venomous creature, and from every envious evil eye.' And he would say: 'Thus Ibrahim used to seek refuge for Isma'il and Ishaq, may the blessings of Allah be upon them.'"

The third: what 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated, saying: "I entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of the day and saw him in severe pain. Then I returned to him at the end of the day and saw him well. He said: 'Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me and recited over me, saying: In the name of Allah I recite over you from everything that harms you, and from every evil eye and envier. Allah will cure you.'" He said: "So I was cured."

The fourth: it is narrated that "the children of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib were fair-skinned boys, and Asma' said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the evil eye hastens to them. Shall I seek a recitation (ruqyah) for them against the evil eye?' He said: 'Yes.'"

The fifth: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the house of Umm Salamah, where there was a child who was ailing. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the evil eye has struck him.' He said: 'Will you not seek a recitation for him against the evil eye?'"

The sixth: his (peace be upon him) saying: "The evil eye is real. If anything could outrun the decree, the evil eye would outrun the decree."

The seventh: 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He used to order the one who had caused the evil eye to perform ablution, and then the one affected by it would be washed with that water."

The second standpoint: in explaining its reality. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) denied this meaning with strong denial, and in his denial he did not mention a doubt, let alone a proof. As for those who acknowledged it and affirmed its existence, they mentioned several explanations:

The first: the *Hafiz* said: "It extends from the eye as particles which connect with the person who is admired, and they affect him and spread through him, like the effect of a sting, poison, or fire, though it differs in the manner of its effect from these things."

The *Qadi* said: "This is weak, because if the matter were as he said, it would have to affect the person who is not admired in the same way as it affects the admired one."

Know that this objection is weak, because when a person admires something, he may love its continuation, as when one admires his own child or his own garden. And he may also dislike its continuation, as when an envious person perceives something that has happened to his enemy. If it is the first, then at that admiration there arises in him a severe fear of its loss, and severe fear necessitates the confinement of the spirit within the heart, so the heart and spirit become very hot, and a strong heating quality arises in the seeing spirit. If it is the second, then at that admiration there arises intense envy and great grief because that blessing has come to his enemy.

Grief also necessitates the confinement of the spirit within the heart, and there arises in it intense heat. So it is established that at strong admiration the spirit becomes very hot, and thus the ray of the eye becomes hot. This is unlike when there is no admiration, for then this heat does not arise. Thus the difference between the two cases is evident. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) ordered the one who causes the evil eye to perform ablution, and the one afflicted by it to bathe.

The second: Abu Hashim and Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi said: "It is not impossible that the evil eye is real, and its meaning is that when the possessor of the evil eye sees a thing and is impressed by it with admiration, it is in the interest of that person, in his obligation, that Allah should change that person and that thing, so that the heart of that obligated person no longer remains attached to it. This meaning is not impossible. Then it is also not far-fetched that if he mentions his Lord at that moment, turns away from admiration, and asks his Lord for protection from its effect, then the interest is secured. And since this custom is consistent, it is rightly said: 'The evil eye is real.'"

The third: this is the statement of the philosophers (*hukama'*), who said: "This discourse is based upon a premise, namely that it is not a condition of an influence that its effect should be in accordance with these sensible qualities, i.e., heat, cold, moisture and dryness. Rather, the effect may be purely psychic, with no connection to bodily powers. What indicates this is that a plank of narrow width, when placed on the ground, a person can walk upon it, but if it were placed between two high walls, the person would be unable to walk upon it. This is only because his fear of falling from it causes him to fall. So we know that psychic effects exist. Also, when a person imagines that someone is harming him, anger arises in his heart, and his temperament becomes very hot. The source of that heat is nothing but that psychic imagining. And because the source of bodily movements is nothing but psychic perceptions, when it is established that the imagining of the soul causes a change in its particular body, it is not far-fetched that some souls may be such that their effects extend to other bodies. Thus it is established that it is not impossible by reason that the soul should affect other bodies. Also, the essences of souls differ in reality, so it is not impossible that some souls should affect the change in the body of another living being, on condition that it sees it and is amazed by it. Thus it is established that this meaning is a possibility, and experiences from ancient times support it, and the prophetic souls have spoken of it. Therefore, regarding its occurrence, no doubt remains."

When this is established, it is established that what the earlier exegetes agreed upon in interpreting this verse as referring to the striking of the evil eye is a true statement that cannot be rejected.

The second opinion: which is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, is that the sons of Ya'qub had become well known in Egypt, and people talked about them and their beauty and perfection. So he said: ﴿Do not enter﴾ that city ﴿from one gate﴾ in the form of your number and appearance. Thus he did not feel safe from the envy of the people. Or it is said: he did not feel safe that the great king might fear them for his kingdom and imprison them.

Know that this view is a possibility without denial. However, we have already shown that the first opinion has no impossibility according to reason, and the exegetes agreed upon it, so it is necessary to adopt it.

It is also reported from al-Hasan that he said: "He feared the evil eye for them, so he said: ﴿Do not enter from one gate﴾; then he returned to his knowledge and said: ﴿Yet I cannot avail you against Allah at all﴾, and he knew that the evil eye is nothing." Qatadah interpreted the verse as referring to the striking of the evil eye, and said: "The statement ﴿Yet I cannot avail you against Allah at all﴾ does not negate it, because even if the evil eye is real, Allah is capable of repelling its effect."

The third opinion: that he (peace be upon him) knew that the king of Egypt was his son Yusuf, but Allah did not permit him to reveal that. So when he sent his sons to him, he said: ﴿Do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates.﴾ His purpose was that Binyamin should reach Yusuf in private. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. As for his saying: ﴿Yet I cannot avail you against Allah at all﴾, know that a person is commanded to observe the means that are recognized in this world, and he is also commanded to believe and be certain that nothing reaches him except what Allah has decreed, and that caution does not save one from the decree. For a person is commanded to be cautious against deadly things and harmful foods, and to strive to obtain benefits and repel harms as far as possible. Yet despite that, he should be certain that nothing reaches him except what Allah has decreed, and nothing comes into existence except what Allah wills. So his (peace be upon him) saying: ﴿Do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates﴾ is an indication toward observing the means that are recognized in this world, and his saying: ﴿Yet I cannot avail you against Allah at all﴾ is an indication toward not relying upon the means, and toward pure monotheism and disavowal of everything other than Allah the Exalted.

As for the question of someone who asks: how can these two statements be reconciled? This question is not specific to this matter. For there is no dispute that one must perform acts of obedience and avoid sins and misdeeds, while we also believe that the one who is happy is the one who was made happy in his mother's womb, and the one who is wretched is the one who was made wretched in his mother's womb. Likewise here: we eat and drink and guard against poisons and against entering the fire, although life and death occur only by the decree of Allah the Exalted. Likewise here. It is evident that this question is not specific to this context, but is rather an inquiry into the secret of the question of compulsion (*jabr*) and divine decree (*qadar*). Rather, the truth is that the servant is obligated to strive with the utmost effort and capacity, and after that earnest striving and diligent exertion, he knows that everything that comes into existence must be by the decree of Allah the Exalted, His will, His prior judgment, and His wisdom. Then the Exalted emphasized this meaning, saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah.﴾

Know that this is among the strongest proofs for the correctness of our position regarding destiny and decree. For judgment (*hukm*) is an expression for obligation and prevention from the opposite. The term *hikmah* (bridle) of the beast was named by this name because it restrains the beast from corrupt movements. And judgment is named *hukm* because it requires preferring one of the two possibilities over the other, such that the other possibility becomes impossible to occur. So the Exalted made clear that judgment in this sense belongs only to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. This indicates that all possible things are ascribed to His decree, His destiny, His will, and His judgment, either directly or through intermediaries. Then He said: ﴿Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely put their trust.﴾ Its meaning is that since it is established that everything is from Allah, it is established that there is no reliance except upon Allah. And that desire is nothing but the preponderance of the existence of possible things over their non-existence, and that preponderance which prevents the opposite is judgment. And it has been established by proof that judgment belongs only to Allah. Therefore it follows with certainty that the attainment of all good and the repelling of all calamities are from Allah, and this necessitates that there is no reliance except upon Allah. This is a noble and elevated station. We have indicated what is the true proof in it. And the Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, elaborated at length on the explanation of this meaning in the Book of Trust (*Kitab al-Tawakkul*) from his work *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din* (The Revival of the Religious Sciences). So whoever wishes to investigate it thoroughly, let him consult that book.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them anything against Allah; it was but a need within the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled. And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.﴾

The exegetes said: When Ya'qub said, ﴿I can avail you nothing against Allah.﴾ Allah affirmed him in that, saying: That separation did not avail anything against Allah. In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: That separation did not repel the decree of Allah, nor any matter that Allah had predestined.

Al-Zajjaj said: If the evil eye had been decreed to strike them, it would have struck them whether they were separated or gathered, just as it would strike them while gathered.

Ibn al-Anbari said: If it had preceded in the knowledge of Allah that the evil eye would destroy them when they were gathered, their separation would have been the same as their gathering. These statements are close in meaning, and their summary is that caution does not repel destiny.

The second discussion: His saying, ﴿anything (min shay'in)﴾, may be parsed as an object in the accusative (naṣb bi-l-maf'ūliyyah) or as a subject in the nominative (raf' bi-l-fā'iliyyah).

As for the first: it is like his saying, "I did not see from anyone," meaning, "I did not see anyone." Similarly here, the sense of the verse is: that their separation did not avail anything against the decree of Allah, that is, that separation did not remove anything from under the decree of Allah, exalted is He.

As for the second: it is like your saying, "Nothing came to me from anyone," meaning, "No one came to me." Similarly here, the sense is: nothing from Allah availed them in the presence of His decree.

As for His saying, ﴿but it was a need within the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾, al-Zajjaj said: It is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), and the meaning is: "But a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled," meaning that entering in the manner of separation was the fulfilling of a need within the soul of Ya'qub. Then they mentioned several views on the explanation of that need:

The first: his fear for them of the striking of the evil eye.

The second: his fear for them of the envy of the people of Egypt.

The third: his fear for them that the king of Egypt would intend them harm.

The fourth: his fear for them that they would not return to him. All of these views are close in meaning.

* * *
As for His saying, ﴿And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾, al-Wahidi said: It is possible that "ma" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), and the pronoun refers to Ya'qub, and the sense is: "And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge because of Our teaching him." It is also possible that "ma" means "that which" (alladhi), and the pronoun refers to it, and the interpretation is: "And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge of the thing which We had taught him," meaning that when We taught him something, knowledge of that thing came to be his. In the verse there are two further statements:

The first: that by knowledge is meant memorization, that is, he was one who preserved what We had taught him and watched over it.

The second: he was a possessor of knowledge of the benefits of what We had taught him and of its good effects, and this is an indication that he acted upon what he knew. Then He said: ﴿but most of the people do not know﴾, and in this there are two views:

The first: but most of the people do not know the like of what Ya'qub knew.

The second: they do not know that Ya'qub was characterized by this attribute and knowledge.

What is meant by "most of the people" is the polytheists, for they do not know how Allah guided His friends to the sciences that benefit them in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 69–72:

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother close to himself and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup (al-siqayah) in the baggage of his brother. Then a caller called out, "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾ ﴿They said, while turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We are missing the king's measuring cup (sua', al-suwa'), and for whoever brings it is a camel's load, and I am its guarantor (za'im)."﴾

Know that when they came to him with his brother Binyamin, he honoured them, hosted them, and seated every two of them at a table. Binyamin was left alone, so he wept and said, "If only my brother Yusuf were alive, he would have seated me with him." Yusuf said, "Your brother has been left alone," and so he seated him with himself at a table. Then he ordered that every two of them should lodge in a house, and said, "This one has no second, so leave him with me," and so he took him to himself. When Yusuf saw his grief over a brother of his who had perished, he said to him, "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said, "Who would find a brother like you? But you were not born to Ya'qub and Rahil." Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."

Having understood this, we say: His words, ﴿he drew his brother close to himself﴾, mean that he settled him in the place where he used to lodge.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, I am your brother﴾, there are two views. Wahb said: he did not mean that he was his brother by lineage, but meant, "I shall stand in for your brother in companionship, so that you do not feel lonely in being alone."

The correct view, held by the majority of the exegetes, is that he meant to declare the lineage, because that is more effective in removing loneliness and bringing about intimacy; and because the basic sense of speech is its literal meaning, so there is no reason to turn it away from that to a figurative meaning without necessity.

* * *
As for His words, ﴿so do not grieve (tabtais)﴾, the lexicographers said: "tabtais" is from the form "tif'tal" of al-bu's, which is harm and hardship, and al-ibti'as is bringing upon oneself sorrow and distress.

His words, ﴿over what they used to do﴾, have several interpretations:

The first: what is meant by "what they used to do" is their persistence in envying us and their eagerness to turn our father's face away from us.

The second: Yusuf, peace be upon him, had no enmity left in his heart and was pure with his brothers, so he wished to make his brother's heart pure towards him as well. Thus he said, ﴿so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾, meaning: do not dwell on what they did previously, nor on their reprehensible deeds that they undertook.

The third: they only did to Yusuf what they did because they envied him for the father's attention to him and his being singled out for greater honour. Binyamin feared that they would envy him for the reason that the king had singled him out for greater honour, so he gave him assurance and said: do not dwell on that, for Allah has joined me and you together.

The fourth: al-Kalbi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, used to reproach Yusuf and his brother because their maternal grandfather used to worship idols; and that the mother of Yusuf ordered Yusuf to steal a basket belonging to her father in which were idols, in hope that he would give up worshipping them if he lost them. So he said to him: ﴿so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾, meaning: over their reproaching us for what our grandfather was upon. And Allah knows best.

* * *
Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup in the baggage of his brother.﴾ The discussion of "provisions" and "baggage" has already passed. As for the siqayah, the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is a drinking vessel from which one is given to drink, and it is the sua'. It was said: the king used to drink from it, and then it was made into a measure by which grain was measured. He said this is far-fetched, because the vessel from which the great king drinks is not suitable to be made into a measure. It was said: animals were given drink from it and grain was measured with it too, and this is closer. Then he said: It was said it was of silver overlaid with gold; it was said it was of gold; it was said it was set with jewels. This too is far-fetched, because a vessel from which animals drink is not like that. The better view is that this vessel was something of value, but not to the extent they mentioned.

* * *
Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Then a caller called out, "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾ It is said: "adhdhana-hu" means "a'lamahu," informed him. Regarding the difference between adhdhana and adhana there are two views. Ibn al-Anbari said: adhdhana means informing repeatedly, since it is a verb that requires repetition of the action; he said it is also possible that it is a single announcement, in that the Arabs often use fa''ala in the sense of af'ala in many contexts. Sibawayh said: adhdhantu and adhantu both mean a'lamtu, there is no difference between them, and ta'dhin means calling and raising the voice with an announcement.

* * *
As for His words, Exalted, ﴿O caravan, indeed you are thieves!﴾, Abu al-Haytham said: whatever is travelled upon with camels, donkeys and mules is an 'ir. The saying of one who says that al-'ir refers only to camels is false. It was said: al-'ir are the camels that carry loads, because they go back and forth (ta'iru), that is they go and come; it was said: it is a caravan of donkeys. Then this became common, until every caravan was called 'ir, as if it were the plural of 'ayr, whose plural pattern is fu'ul, like saqf and suquf.

Having understood this, we say: ﴿O caravan﴾ means: the people of the caravan, like His saying: "O horses of Allah, ride!" Ibn Mas'ud recited: (wa-ja'ala al-siqayah), with the answer of lamma omitted, as if it were said: "So when he furnished them with their provisions and placed the drinking-cup in the baggage of his brother; he gave them time until they set off, ﴿then a caller called out, O caravan, indeed you are thieves!﴾."

If it is asked: was that calling by the command of Yusuf, or was it not by his command? If it was by his command, how is it fitting for a true messenger from Allah to accuse people and attribute theft to them falsely and deceitfully? And if the second is the case, namely that it was not by his command, then why did he not deny it, and why did he not make clear their innocence of that accusation?

We say: the scholars mentioned several answers to this:

The first: when he, peace be upon him, revealed to his brother that he was Yusuf, he said to him: "I wish to hold you here, and there is no way to do so except by this stratagem; if you agree to it, the matter is yours." So he agreed that such a thing be said against him. On this basis, his heart was not pained by this statement, so it did not count as a sin.

The second: what is meant by "indeed you are thieves" is that you are thieves of Yusuf from his father, but they did not openly state this; and ma'arid (allusive speech) is only like that.

The third: that caller may have uttered that call in the form of a question, and on this basis it would not be a lie.

The fourth: the Qur'an does not say that they called out with that call by the command of Yusuf, peace be upon him. What is closer to the apparent situation is that they did it of their own accord, because when they sought the drinking-cup and did not find it, and there was no one there but them, it prevailed upon their assumption that they were the ones who had taken it. Then the brothers of Yusuf said, ﴿they said, while turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited: (tufqidun), from afqadtuhu when you find him lost. They said: "We are missing the king's measuring cup."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was read as sua', sa', saw' and suw', with the sad vowelled with fatha and with damma, and the 'ayn being dotted and undotted. Some said: the plural of suwa' is siy'an, like ghurab and ghirban, and the plural of sa' is as'wa', like bab and abwab. Others said: there is no difference between sa' and suwa', and the proof of this is the reading of Abu Hurayrah: (qalu nafqidu sa'a al-malik). Some said: suwa' is a noun, and siqayah is a descriptive term, like their saying: kuz and siqa'; kuz is a noun and siqa' is a descriptive term.

* * *
Then he said: ﴿and for whoever brings it is a camel's load﴾, meaning of food, ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾. Mujahid said: the za'im is the caller who called out. The explanation of za'im is kafil (guarantor). Al-Kalbi said: al-za'im: the guarantor, in the language of the people of Yemen.

Abu 'Ubaydah related from al-Kisa'i: za'amat bihi, ta'zumu, za'man and za'amah, meaning: she stood surety for it. This verse indicates that suretyship was valid in their law, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled by it in his saying: "The guarantor is liable."

If it is asked: is this a suretyship for something unknown?

We say: a camel's load of food was known to them, so suretyship for it was valid. However, this is a suretyship of property for returning a theft, and it is a suretyship for what is not obligatory, because it is not lawful for a thief to take anything in return for returning what was stolen. Perhaps such suretyship was valid among them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 69–72:

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother close to himself and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup (al-siqayah) in the baggage of his brother. Then a caller called out, "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾ ﴿They said, while turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We are missing the king's measuring cup (sua', al-suwa'), and for whoever brings it is a camel's load, and I am its guarantor (za'im)."﴾

Know that when they came to him with his brother Binyamin, he honoured them, hosted them, and seated every two of them at a table. Binyamin was left alone, so he wept and said, "If only my brother Yusuf were alive, he would have seated me with him." Yusuf said, "Your brother has been left alone," and so he seated him with himself at a table. Then he ordered that every two of them should lodge in a house, and said, "This one has no second, so leave him with me," and so he took him to himself. When Yusuf saw his grief over a brother of his who had perished, he said to him, "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said, "Who would find a brother like you? But you were not born to Ya'qub and Rahil." Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."

Having understood this, we say: His words, ﴿he drew his brother close to himself﴾, mean that he settled him in the place where he used to lodge.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, I am your brother﴾, there are two views. Wahb said: he did not mean that he was his brother by lineage, but meant, "I shall stand in for your brother in companionship, so that you do not feel lonely in being alone."

The correct view, held by the majority of the exegetes, is that he meant to declare the lineage, because that is more effective in removing loneliness and bringing about intimacy; and because the basic sense of speech is its literal meaning, so there is no reason to turn it away from that to a figurative meaning without necessity.

* * *
As for His words, ﴿so do not grieve (tabtais)﴾, the lexicographers said: "tabtais" is from the form "tif'tal" of al-bu's, which is harm and hardship, and al-ibti'as is bringing upon oneself sorrow and distress.

His words, ﴿over what they used to do﴾, have several interpretations:

The first: what is meant by "what they used to do" is their persistence in envying us and their eagerness to turn our father's face away from us.

The second: Yusuf, peace be upon him, had no enmity left in his heart and was pure with his brothers, so he wished to make his brother's heart pure towards him as well. Thus he said, ﴿so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾, meaning: do not dwell on what they did previously, nor on their reprehensible deeds that they undertook.

The third: they only did to Yusuf what they did because they envied him for the father's attention to him and his being singled out for greater honour. Binyamin feared that they would envy him for the reason that the king had singled him out for greater honour, so he gave him assurance and said: do not dwell on that, for Allah has joined me and you together.

The fourth: al-Kalbi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, used to reproach Yusuf and his brother because their maternal grandfather used to worship idols; and that the mother of Yusuf ordered Yusuf to steal a basket belonging to her father in which were idols, in hope that he would give up worshipping them if he lost them. So he said to him: ﴿so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾, meaning: over their reproaching us for what our grandfather was upon. And Allah knows best.

* * *
Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup in the baggage of his brother.﴾ The discussion of "provisions" and "baggage" has already passed. As for the siqayah, the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is a drinking vessel from which one is given to drink, and it is the sua'. It was said: the king used to drink from it, and then it was made into a measure by which grain was measured. He said this is far-fetched, because the vessel from which the great king drinks is not suitable to be made into a measure. It was said: animals were given drink from it and grain was measured with it too, and this is closer. Then he said: It was said it was of silver overlaid with gold; it was said it was of gold; it was said it was set with jewels. This too is far-fetched, because a vessel from which animals drink is not like that. The better view is that this vessel was something of value, but not to the extent they mentioned.

* * *
Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Then a caller called out, "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾ It is said: "adhdhana-hu" means "a'lamahu," informed him. Regarding the difference between adhdhana and adhana there are two views. Ibn al-Anbari said: adhdhana means informing repeatedly, since it is a verb that requires repetition of the action; he said it is also possible that it is a single announcement, in that the Arabs often use fa''ala in the sense of af'ala in many contexts. Sibawayh said: adhdhantu and adhantu both mean a'lamtu, there is no difference between them, and ta'dhin means calling and raising the voice with an announcement.

* * *
As for His words, Exalted, ﴿O caravan, indeed you are thieves!﴾, Abu al-Haytham said: whatever is travelled upon with camels, donkeys and mules is an 'ir. The saying of one who says that al-'ir refers only to camels is false. It was said: al-'ir are the camels that carry loads, because they go back and forth (ta'iru), that is they go and come; it was said: it is a caravan of donkeys. Then this became common, until every caravan was called 'ir, as if it were the plural of 'ayr, whose plural pattern is fu'ul, like saqf and suquf.

Having understood this, we say: ﴿O caravan﴾ means: the people of the caravan, like His saying: "O horses of Allah, ride!" Ibn Mas'ud recited: (wa-ja'ala al-siqayah), with the answer of lamma omitted, as if it were said: "So when he furnished them with their provisions and placed the drinking-cup in the baggage of his brother; he gave them time until they set off, ﴿then a caller called out, O caravan, indeed you are thieves!﴾."

If it is asked: was that calling by the command of Yusuf, or was it not by his command? If it was by his command, how is it fitting for a true messenger from Allah to accuse people and attribute theft to them falsely and deceitfully? And if the second is the case, namely that it was not by his command, then why did he not deny it, and why did he not make clear their innocence of that accusation?

We say: the scholars mentioned several answers to this:

The first: when he, peace be upon him, revealed to his brother that he was Yusuf, he said to him: "I wish to hold you here, and there is no way to do so except by this stratagem; if you agree to it, the matter is yours." So he agreed that such a thing be said against him. On this basis, his heart was not pained by this statement, so it did not count as a sin.

The second: what is meant by "indeed you are thieves" is that you are thieves of Yusuf from his father, but they did not openly state this; and ma'arid (allusive speech) is only like that.

The third: that caller may have uttered that call in the form of a question, and on this basis it would not be a lie.

The fourth: the Qur'an does not say that they called out with that call by the command of Yusuf, peace be upon him. What is closer to the apparent situation is that they did it of their own accord, because when they sought the drinking-cup and did not find it, and there was no one there but them, it prevailed upon their assumption that they were the ones who had taken it. Then the brothers of Yusuf said, ﴿they said, while turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited: (tufqidun), from afqadtuhu when you find him lost. They said: "We are missing the king's measuring cup."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was read as sua', sa', saw' and suw', with the sad vowelled with fatha and with damma, and the 'ayn being dotted and undotted. Some said: the plural of suwa' is siy'an, like ghurab and ghirban, and the plural of sa' is as'wa', like bab and abwab. Others said: there is no difference between sa' and suwa', and the proof of this is the reading of Abu Hurayrah: (qalu nafqidu sa'a al-malik). Some said: suwa' is a noun, and siqayah is a descriptive term, like their saying: kuz and siqa'; kuz is a noun and siqa' is a descriptive term.

* * *
Then he said: ﴿and for whoever brings it is a camel's load﴾, meaning of food, ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾. Mujahid said: the za'im is the caller who called out. The explanation of za'im is kafil (guarantor). Al-Kalbi said: al-za'im: the guarantor, in the language of the people of Yemen.

Abu 'Ubaydah related from al-Kisa'i: za'amat bihi, ta'zumu, za'man and za'amah, meaning: she stood surety for it. This verse indicates that suretyship was valid in their law, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled by it in his saying: "The guarantor is liable."

If it is asked: is this a suretyship for something unknown?

We say: a camel's load of food was known to them, so suretyship for it was valid. However, this is a suretyship of property for returning a theft, and it is a suretyship for what is not obligatory, because it is not lawful for a thief to take anything in return for returning what was stolen. Perhaps such suretyship was valid among them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother; then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. Al-awiyah (الأوعية) is the plural of al-wi'a (الوعاء), which is anything that, when something is placed in it, encloses it. ﴿He brought it out from his brother's bag.﴾ Al-Hasan read (وُعاءِ أخِيهِ) with a ḍammah on the wāw, and this is a dialect form. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (إعاءِ أخِيهِ), changing the wāw into a hamzah.

If it is asked: why did he use the masculine pronoun for the drinking vessel (al-ṣuwā') several times, and then the feminine?

We say: they said that the feminine pronoun refers to al-siqayah (السقاية, "the drinking cup"), and the masculine pronoun refers to al-ṣuwā' (الصواع, "the measuring cup"). Or it may be said: al-ṣuwā' may be feminine or masculine, so each of them is permissible. Or it may be said: perhaps Joseph called it siqayah, while his servants called it ṣuwā'. Thus in the speech connected to him the word siqayah occurs, and in the speech connected to them the word ṣuwā' occurs.

On the authority of Qatadah, he said: Joseph would not look into any bag without seeking forgiveness from God, repenting from what they had falsely attributed to him. Until, when only his brother remained, he said: "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said: "We will not leave until you examine his condition as well." When they looked into his belongings, they brought out the ṣuwā' from his bag. The people had already ruled that whoever steals is to be enslaved, so they seized him by the neck and dragged him to the house of Joseph.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law.﴾ There are two discussions here.

The first: the meaning is: "In the like of that plan (al-kayd), We devised for Joseph." That refers to the ruling on enslaving the thief; that is, like this ruling which Joseph's brothers stated, We ruled for Joseph.

The second: the word (al-kayd) (الكيد, "plotting, scheming") suggests cunning and deception, and this is impossible with regard to God, exalted is He. However, we have stated a principle that is accepted in this matter: such expressions are to be understood in terms of the final purposes of actions, not their initial purposes. We established this principle in explaining His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed﴾ (al-Baqarah: 26). So al-kayd is the pursuit of a stratagem and deception, and its end is the bringing about of a person, without his knowing it, into a disliked matter from which he has no way of defending himself. So al-kayd with regard to God, exalted is He, is understood in this sense.

Then they differed about what is meant by al-kayd here. Some said: what is meant is that Joseph's brothers strove to nullify Joseph's affair, while God, exalted is He, supported him, strengthened him, and raised his affair.

Others said: what is meant by this kayd is that He, exalted is He, cast into the hearts of his brothers that they should rule that the recompense for a thief is that he be enslaved. Therefore, when the ṣuwā' appeared in his baggage, they ruled that he be enslaved, and this became the cause of Joseph, peace be upon him, being able to keep his brother with himself.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law.﴾ The meaning is that the king's ruling concerning a thief was that he be beaten and made to pay twice the value of what he stole. Joseph was not able to keep his brother with himself based on the king's religion and ruling. However, God, exalted is He, devised for him what was said by the tongues of his brothers, that the recompense for a thief is enslavement. We have explained that this statement was used as a means to take his brother and keep him with himself. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except that God willed.﴾ Then He said: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ There are two issues here.

The first issue: Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisā'ī read (دَرَجاتٍ) with tanwīn, not as an idafah. The rest read it as an idafah.

The second issue: what is meant by His saying ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ is that He, exalted is He, shows him the ways of correctness in reaching the goal, and singles him out with kinds of knowledge and types of virtue. What is meant here is that He, exalted is He, raised Joseph's degrees above his brothers in everything.

Know that this verse indicates that knowledge is the most noble of stations and the highest of ranks, because when He, exalted is He, guided Joseph to this stratagem and insight, He praised him for that, saying: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ Also, He described Abraham, peace be upon him, with His saying: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ (al-An'am: 83) when mentioning the proofs of monotheism and the disavowal of the divinity of the sun, the moon and the stars. Here He also described Joseph with His saying: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will,﴾ when He guided him to this stratagem. How great is the difference between the two ranks!

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ The meaning is that Joseph's brothers, peace be upon him, were learned and excellent, but Joseph surpassed them in knowledge.

Know that the Mu'tazilah (المعتزلة, a rationalist theological school) argued with this verse that God, exalted is He, is knowing through His essence, not through knowledge. They said: if He were knowing through knowledge, He would be one possessing knowledge, and if that were so, there would exist above Him one who knows, holding fast to the generality of this verse. This is false.

Know that our companions (i.e., the Ash'ariyyah) said: the other verses establish knowledge for God, exalted is He, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, with God is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ (Luqman: 34), and ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ (al-Nisa': 166), and ﴿They do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾ (al-Baqarah: 255), and ﴿No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ (Fussilat: 47). When there is a contradiction, we apply the verse the opponent relies upon to the event of Joseph and his brothers specifically. The most that this entails is the specification of a general statement, but it is necessary to resort to this, because the knower (al-'alim, "the one who knows") is derived from knowledge ('ilm), and the derived is compound, while that from which it is derived is simple. The existence of the compound without the existence of the simple is impossible by the self-evident judgment of reason. So the preference lies on our side.

**Al-Razi's commentary on Surah Yusuf (12), verse 77**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "If he steals, there has already stolen a brother of his before." But Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, "You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe."﴾

Know that when the drinking cup came out of the saddlebag of Joseph's brother, his brothers lowered their heads and said: "This event is strange; that Rachel bore two thieving sons!" Then they said: "O sons of Rachel, how much misfortune you have brought upon us!" Benjamin said: "How much misfortune you have brought upon us! You took my brother away and lost him in the wilderness, and then you say these words to me." They said to him: "How did the cup come out of your saddlebag?" He said: "The one who put the merchandise in your saddlebags put it in my saddlebag."

Know that the apparent meaning of the verse requires that they said to the king: "This matter is not strange coming from him, for his brother who perished was also a thief." Their purpose in this statement was that "we are not on his way, nor on his conduct," while he and his brother were specialized in this manner, because they were from a different mother. They differed concerning the theft that they attributed to Joseph, peace be upon him, into several opinions:

The first:

Said Sa'id ibn Jubayr: His maternal grandfather was an unbeliever who worshipped idols, so his mother ordered him to steal those idols and break them, so that perhaps he would give up idol worship. He did so, and this is the theft.

The second: that he used to steal food from his father's table and give it to the poor. It was also said: he stole a young goat from his father and gave it to the needy. It was also said: a hen.

The third: that his aunt loved him with an intense love, and she wanted to keep him with herself. A belt of Isaac, peace be upon him, had remained with her, and they sought blessing through it. She tied it around Joseph's waist, then claimed that he had stolen it. It was among their rulings that whoever steals is enslaved, so she sought by this stratagem to keep him with herself.

The fourth: that they lied about him and slandered him, and their hearts were filled with anger toward Joseph after those events and after the passing of that long period. This event shows that the heart of the envier never becomes entirely purified of rancor.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿But Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them.﴾ They differed concerning what the pronoun in His saying ﴿But Joseph kept it﴾ refers to, on two views:

Al-Zajjaj said: "Kept it" is a pronoun in the manner of a tafsir-anticipation (al-idmar 'ala shart al-tafsir), its explanation being "You are worse in position," and it was feminine because His saying "You are worse in position" is a sentence or a word, for they call a portion of speech a word. It is as if He said: he kept the sentence or the word which is His saying "You are worse in position." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "fa-asarra" in the masculine, meaning the saying or the speech. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi criticized this view in what he took as an objection against al-Zajjaj on two grounds:

The first ground: he said: the idmar 'ala shart al-tafsir occurs in two ways:

One of them: that it is explained by a single noun, as when we say: "Ni'ma rajulan Zayd" (how excellent a man Zayd is), where in ni'ma there is a pronoun for its agent, and "rajulan" is an explanation of that hidden agent.

The other: that it is explained by a sentence, and the origin of this occurs at the beginning, as in His saying: ﴿Then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾ (al-Anbiya': 97) and ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾ (al-Ikhlas: 1), the meaning being: the matter is that the eyes of those who disbelieved stare fixedly, and the matter is that Allah is One. Then the operators that enter upon the subject and predicate also enter upon it, such as "inna," as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ (Ta-Ha: 74) and ﴿for indeed it is not the eyes that are blind﴾ (al-Hajj: 46).

Having known this, we say: the pronoun itself, in the manner of tafsir-anticipation, in both categories is connected to the sentence from which the anticipation arose, and is not outside that sentence nor separate from it. Here the explanation is separated from the sentence from which the anticipation arose, so it ought not to be good.

The second: that He, exalted, said: ﴿You are worse in position,﴾ and this shows that he mentioned this statement; and if we said that he, peace be upon him, kept this statement hidden, then His saying that he said it would be false.

Know that this objection is weak, for several reasons:

As for the first: it does not follow from the goodness of the first two categories that a third category is ugly.

As for the second: we take that to mean that he, peace be upon him, said it in a hidden manner, and with this interpretation this question falls away.

The second view: that the pronoun in His saying ﴿But he kept it﴾ returns to the response, as if they said: ﴿If he steals, there has already stolen a brother of his before,﴾ and Joseph kept their response within himself at that time and did not reveal it to them at that moment until a second time. It is also permissible that it be an anticipation of the speech.

The meaning: Joseph kept their speech hidden, and by "the speech" is meant the object of that speech, just as by "the creation" is meant the created thing and by "the knowledge" the known thing; that is, Joseph kept within himself the manner of that theft, and did not explain to them

Page 148
how it had occurred, and that there was nothing in it that required blame or censure.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: Joseph, peace be upon him, was punished three times: for his intention regarding her he was punished with imprisonment; for his saying ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾ (Yusuf: 42) he was punished with a long imprisonment; and for their saying ﴿Indeed you are thieves﴾ (Yusuf: 70) he was punished with their saying ﴿There has already stolen a brother of his before.﴾ Then Allah, exalted, related of Joseph that he said: ﴿You are worse in position,﴾ meaning: you are worse in rank with Allah, exalted, for what you undertook of wronging your brother and disobeying your father; you took your brother and cast him into the well, then you told your father that the wolf had eaten him, and you are liars; then you sold him for twenty dirhams; then after the long period and the extended time, resentment and anger still remained in your hearts, so you hurled at him the accusation of theft.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe.﴾ He means that Joseph's theft was pleasing to Allah. In sum, none of the aspects mentioned concerning his theft requires that blame or reproach return to him. The meaning: Allah is most knowing whether what you have attributed to him makes a censure return to him or not.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 78–79:**

The Almighty's saying: ﴿They said, "O Chieftain, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿He said, "We seek refuge in Allah that we take except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾

Know that the Almighty has explained that after what they had said, "If he steals, then a brother of his stole before," they loved to agree with him and to turn to the way of intercession. Although they had acknowledged that the ruling of Allah the Exalted regarding the thief is that he be enslaved, pardon and the taking of ransom were also permissible. So they said: "O Chieftain, indeed he has an aged father," meaning in years, and it may also mean in rank and religion. They mentioned this because being the son of a man of great standing necessitates pardon and forgiveness.

Then they said: ﴿so take one of us in his place﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is by way of enslavement, and it is possible that it is by way of holding as a pledge, until we bring the ransom to you.

Then they said: ﴿Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers﴾, and regarding this there are several aspects:

First: indeed, we see you among the good-doers if you do that.

Second: indeed, we see you among the good-doers toward us, since you honored us, gave us abundant provision, fulfilled our need in the best manner, and returned to us the price of the food.

Third: it has been related that when the famine became severe upon the people and they found nothing with which to buy food, and they were selling themselves to him, this led to most of the people of Egypt becoming his slaves. Then he freed them all. So perhaps they said: "Indeed, we see you among the good-doers" to the common people by freeing them, so be a good-doer also to this man by freeing him from this trial. Then Yusuf said: ﴿We seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning, I seek refuge in Allah with a seeking of refuge, that we take except him with whom we found our property, meaning, I seek refuge in Allah that I should take an innocent person for a guilty one. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "an" (that) is in the accusative (nasb), and the meaning is: I seek refuge in Allah from taking one person for another. When the word "min" (from) was dropped, the verb became governed in the accusative by it. And His saying ﴿Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers﴾ means: we would have transgressed and wronged, if I harmed a person for a crime that proceeded from another.

If it is said: this incident, from its beginning to its end, is fabrication and falsehood. How is it permissible for Yusuf, peace be upon him, together with his prophethood, to undertake this fabrication, contrivance, and harming of people without cause? Especially since he knows that if he detains his brother with himself on this accusation, his father's grief will greatly increase and his distress will intensify. How, then, is it fitting for the infallible Messenger to exaggerate in fabrication to this extent?

[Page 149]

The answer: perhaps the Almighty commanded him to do that in order to intensify the trial upon Ya'qub, and forbade him from pardon, forgiveness, and taking a substitute, just as the Almighty commanded the companion of Musa to kill a boy who, if he had lived, would have caused his parents to transgress and disbelieve.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 78–79:**

The Almighty's saying: ﴿They said, "O Chieftain, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿He said, "We seek refuge in Allah that we take except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾

Know that the Almighty has explained that after what they had said, "If he steals, then a brother of his stole before," they loved to agree with him and to turn to the way of intercession. Although they had acknowledged that the ruling of Allah the Exalted regarding the thief is that he be enslaved, pardon and the taking of ransom were also permissible. So they said: "O Chieftain, indeed he has an aged father," meaning in years, and it may also mean in rank and religion. They mentioned this because being the son of a man of great standing necessitates pardon and forgiveness.

Then they said: ﴿so take one of us in his place﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is by way of enslavement, and it is possible that it is by way of holding as a pledge, until we bring the ransom to you.

Then they said: ﴿Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers﴾, and regarding this there are several aspects:

First: indeed, we see you among the good-doers if you do that.

Second: indeed, we see you among the good-doers toward us, since you honored us, gave us abundant provision, fulfilled our need in the best manner, and returned to us the price of the food.

Third: it has been related that when the famine became severe upon the people and they found nothing with which to buy food, and they were selling themselves to him, this led to most of the people of Egypt becoming his slaves. Then he freed them all. So perhaps they said: "Indeed, we see you among the good-doers" to the common people by freeing them, so be a good-doer also to this man by freeing him from this trial. Then Yusuf said: ﴿We seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning, I seek refuge in Allah with a seeking of refuge, that we take except him with whom we found our property, meaning, I seek refuge in Allah that I should take an innocent person for a guilty one. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "an" (that) is in the accusative (nasb), and the meaning is: I seek refuge in Allah from taking one person for another. When the word "min" (from) was dropped, the verb became governed in the accusative by it. And His saying ﴿Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers﴾ means: we would have transgressed and wronged, if I harmed a person for a crime that proceeded from another.

If it is said: this incident, from its beginning to its end, is fabrication and falsehood. How is it permissible for Yusuf, peace be upon him, together with his prophethood, to undertake this fabrication, contrivance, and harming of people without cause? Especially since he knows that if he detains his brother with himself on this accusation, his father's grief will greatly increase and his distress will intensify. How, then, is it fitting for the infallible Messenger to exaggerate in fabrication to this extent?

[Page 149]

The answer: perhaps the Almighty commanded him to do that in order to intensify the trial upon Ya'qub, and forbade him from pardon, forgiveness, and taking a substitute, just as the Almighty commanded the companion of Musa to kill a boy who, if he had lived, would have caused his parents to transgress and disbelieve.

Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately. Their eldest said: "Did you not know that your father had taken an oath from you before God, and that previously you had failed regarding Joseph? So I will not leave this land until my father permits me, or God judges for me, and He is the best of judges."﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Know that when they said, ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾ (Yusuf: 78), which was the utmost they could offer, Joseph answered them, ﴿God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property﴾. Their hope of Joseph, peace be upon him, returning him was cut off. At this point God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾, which is an intensification of their despair of his return. ﴿They withdrew to confer privately﴾ means they isolated themselves from the rest of the people to consult together. There is no doubt that what is meant is that they were consulting and seeking a course of action regarding what they had fallen into. This is because they had taken Benjamin from their father after firm covenants, and after having already been accused regarding Joseph. If they did not return him to their father, many trials would result:

One: If they did not return to their father, and he was an old man, then his remaining alone without any of his sons would be a great trial.

Two: Their household was in dire need of food.

Three: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, might have thought that his sons had been entirely destroyed, and that is a severe grief. And if they returned to their father without Benjamin, their shame would be great, for the apparent matter would suggest that they had betrayed him regarding this son just as they had betrayed him regarding the first son. It would also suggest that they had given no weight to those firm covenants. There is no doubt that this is a situation of deliberation and perplexity, and that requires discussion and consultation in seeking the most correct and proper course. So this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi said: It is narrated from Ibn Kathir that they read (istayasu) and (ḥattā idhā istayasa al-rusul) without a hamza.

For yay'asu there are two dialectal forms: ya'isa and yay'as, like ḥasiba and yaḥsabu. Whoever says istā'yasa has moved the 'ayn to the position of the fa', so it becomes istaʿfala; the original is istay'asa, and then the hamza was lightened.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: istay'asu means ya'isu (they despaired). The addition of the sin and the ta' is for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿so he sought refuge﴾, and His saying: ﴿khalasu﴾. Al-Wahidi said: It is said khalasa al-shay'u yakhlusu khulūṣan when the admixture of other things is removed from it. Then there are two views:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: khalasu means they went apart, and their brother was not with them.

The second, which the others held: they separated themselves from the strangers, and this is the more apparent view. As for His saying: ﴿najiyyan﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: najiyy has two meanings. It may mean nājin, like ʿashīr and samīr meaning mu'āshir and musāmir. From this is His saying: ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant﴾ (Maryam: 52). It may also mean the verbal noun, which is taniājī (private conferring), just as it is said najwā meaning those conferring privately. Based on this, the meaning of ﴿they withdrew to confer privately﴾ is that they withdrew and isolated themselves from the people, purely, with no one else mixing with them, ﴿najiyyan﴾, meaning conferring privately. It is narrated that (najwā) means a group, (najiyyan) means conferring privately with one another. The best interpretation is to say that they became entirely absorbed in private conference, because when the realization of a matter is complete in someone, he is described as having become something other than what he was. So when they engaged in private conference with utmost earnestness, they became, as it were, in themselves, they became the very essence of private conference in reality.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their eldest said﴾, it is said that what is meant is the eldest in age, who was Ruben. It is also said that it is the eldest in intellect, who was Judah, and he was the one who had forbidden them from killing Joseph. Then God, exalted is He, relates that this eldest said: ﴿Did you not know that your father had taken an oath from you before God, and that previously you had failed regarding Joseph?﴾ There are two issues regarding this:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: When Joseph, peace be upon him, said: ﴿God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property﴾, Judah became angry. When he became angry and shouted, no pregnant woman who heard his voice failed to give birth, and his hair would stand up on his body, and he would not calm down until one of the family of Ya'qub placed his hand on him. So he said to some of his brothers: "Take care of the markets of the people of Egypt, and I will take care of the king." Then Joseph, peace be upon him, said to a young son of his: "Touch him!" So he touched him, and his anger subsided. He was about to shout, but Joseph, peace be upon him, stamped his foot on the ground, seized his garments, and pulled him, so he fell. Thereupon he said: "O Chief (al-ʿAzīz)!" When they despaired of their intercession being accepted, they reflected and said: "Our father has taken from us a great covenant before God. Furthermore, we are accused regarding the affair of Joseph. So how can we escape this predicament?"

The second issue: The word mā in His saying ﴿you had failed﴾ has several possible interpretations:

The first: its original form is "from before this you had failed in the matter of Joseph, peace be upon him, and you did not keep your father's covenant."

The second: it is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, and its position is nominative as the subject, and its predicate is the adverbial phrase "from before", meaning: your failure regarding Joseph occurred previously.

The third: it is in the accusative, in coordination with the object of ﴿did you not know﴾, and the sense is: "Did you not know your father's taking of your covenant and your previous failure regarding Joseph?"

The fourth: it is a relative pronoun, in the sense of "and from before this, what you had done", meaning: what you had committed before in regard to Joseph of great treachery. Its position is nominative or accusative according to the two aforementioned views.

Then He said: ﴿So I will not leave the land﴾, meaning: I will not depart from the land of Egypt until my father permits me to return to him, or God judges for me to leave it, or to take my right against the one who took my brother, or to free him from his hand by some means. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, because He judges only with justice and truth. In sum, what is meant is the manifestation of an excuse by which his shame and embarrassment before his father or others would be removed. He said this, turning wholly to God, exalted is He, in order to make his excuse manifest in some way.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 81–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Go back to your father and say, "O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we bear witness only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾ ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.﴾

Page 151

Know that when they reflected on what was most correct, it became clear to them that the most correct course was to return and to tell their father the manner of the event exactly, without discrepancy. The apparent view is that this statement was said by that eldest one who said: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me.﴾ It is said that he was Ruben, and he remained in Egypt and sent the rest of his brothers to the father.

If it is asked: how did they judge him to have stolen without evidence, especially since he had answered with a conclusive reply, saying: "The one who put the cup in my baggage is the one who put the merchandise in your baggage"?

The answer to this has several aspects:

The first aspect: they had witnessed that the cup had been placed in a place that no one entered except them. So when they saw that they had taken the cup out of his baggage, it prevailed upon their assumption that he was the one who took the cup.

As for his saying, "The one who placed the cup in my baggage is the one who placed the merchandise in your baggage," the difference is clear, because there, when they returned the merchandise to them, they acknowledged that they themselves were the ones who had placed it in their baggage. But as for this cup, no one acknowledged that he had placed the cup in his baggage, so the difference became apparent. For this reason, the assumption that he had stolen prevailed upon them, so they testified on the basis of this assumption. Then He made clear that they were not certain of this matter by their saying: ﴿And we bear witness only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen.﴾

The second aspect in the answer: the sense of the statement ﴿Indeed your son has stolen﴾ is in the saying of the king and his companions, and there are many like it in the Qur'an.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ (Hud: 87), meaning in your own estimation. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ (al-Dukhan: 49), meaning in your own estimation; but in our estimation, no. So likewise here.

The third aspect in the answer: your son had something appear upon him that resembles theft, and such a thing is called theft. The application of the name of one of two similar things to the other similar thing is permissible in the Qur'an. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (al-Shura: 40).

The fourth aspect: the people were not prophets at that time, so it is not far-fetched to say that they spoke this statement recklessly, especially since they had witnessed something that gave that impression.

The fifth aspect: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, used to recite (إن ابنك سُرِّق) with the shaddah, meaning he was attributed to theft. This reading needs no interpretation, since the people attributed him to theft. However, we have mentioned in this book that such readings do not dispel the question, because the difficulty is only dispelled if we say: the first reading is false, and the correct reading is this one. But if we accept that the first reading is correct, the difficulty remains whether or not this second reading is valid. Thus it is established that one must return to one of the aspects mentioned.

As for his saying: ﴿And we bear witness only to what we know﴾, its meaning is clear, because it indicates that testimony is other than knowledge, by the evidence of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we bear witness only to what we know,﴾ and that requires that testimony be distinct from knowledge. Also, he, peace be upon him, said: "When you know something like the sun, then bear witness." That too requires what we have mentioned. Testimony is also not the same as the saying "I bear witness," because the saying "I bear witness" is a report about testimony, and a report about testimony is not the testimony itself.

Having established this, we say: testimony is an expression for the mental judgment, which the theologians call the speech of the soul.

* * *

As for his saying: ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, there are several aspects to it:

The first: we have seen that they took the cup out of his baggage, but the reality of the matter is not known to us, for the unseen is known only to Allah.

The second: Ikrimah said: its meaning is: perhaps the cup was slipped into his belongings at night, for "the unseen" is a name for the night in some dialects.

The third: Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "And we did not know that your son would steal, and had we known that, we would not have taken him to the king, nor would we have given you a covenant from Allah to return him to you."

The fourth: It is reported that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said to them: "Suppose he has stolen, but how did the king know that the law of the Children of Israel was that whoever steals is enslaved? Rather, you mentioned it to him for a purpose of your own." They said in response to this statement: "We had mentioned this ruling to him before we fell into this event, and we did not know that this event would befall us." So his saying: ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ is an indication of this meaning.

If it is asked: is it permissible for Ya'qub, peace be upon him, to strive to conceal the judgment of Allah, may He be exalted, according to this statement?

We say: perhaps that judgment was specific to the case where the one robbed was a Muslim, and therefore he disliked mentioning this ruling in the presence of the king, whom he assumed to be a disbeliever.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, related of them that they said: ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came.﴾

Know that when they were accused because of the incident of Yusuf, peace be upon him, they went to great lengths to remove the accusation from themselves, so they said: ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾. Most of them agreed that what is meant by this town is Egypt. Others said: rather, what is meant is a town at the gate of Egypt in which the matter of the theft and the search took place. Then there are two views:

The first: what is meant is "ask the people of the town," but the genitive was omitted for brevity and conciseness, and this type of metaphor is well known in the language of the Arabs. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: rejecting the permissibility of this in the language is like rejecting necessary truths and denying what is sensed.

The second: Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: the meaning is: ask the town, the caravan, the wall and the walls, for they will answer you and state to you the soundness of what we have mentioned, because you are one of the great prophets of Allah, and it is not far-fetched that Allah would make these inanimate things speak as a miracle for you, so that they inform you of the soundness of what we have mentioned.

There is also a third view: that when a matter becomes manifest with complete and perfect clarity, it may be said of it: ask the heavens and the earth and all things about it, and what is meant is that it has reached the degree of manifestness at which no room for doubt remains.

As for his saying: ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, the exegetes said: there had accompanied them a group of the Canaanites, and they said: ask them about this event.

Then, when they went to great lengths in emphasis and affirmation, they said: ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾, meaning: whether you attribute to us the accusation or do not attribute it to us, we are truthful. Their purpose was not to establish their own truthfulness by themselves, for that would be like establishing a thing by itself. Rather, when a person has first mentioned the decisive proof of the soundness of a matter, he may say after it: "And I am truthful in that," meaning: reflect upon what I have mentioned of the proofs and clear evidences so that doubt may depart from you.
