**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 83–85:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾

Know that when Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, heard that statement from his sons, he did not believe them regarding what they reported, as in the incident of Yusuf (Joseph),

[Page 153]

when he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting.﴾ He repeated this very statement in this incident, except that in the incident of Yusuf, peace be upon him, he said: ﴿And Allah is the one whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ (Yusuf 12:18). Here he said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾ There are several questions (masa'il, sing. mas'alah) concerning this.

**The first question:** Some said that his saying ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you﴾ does not mean here lying and deception, as in his saying in the incident of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you.﴾ Rather, he meant: your souls made it seem fair to you to take Binyamin (Benjamin) away from me and to bring him to Egypt seeking benefit, but harm and injury came of it, and you insisted on sending him with you, and you did not know that Allah's decree had come contrary to your planning.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Rather, your souls made a matter seem fair to you": your souls imagined to you that he had stolen, when he had not stolen.

**The second question:** It was said that when Ruwbil (Reuben) resolved to remain in Egypt, the king ordered him to go with his brothers. He said: "Leave me, or I will let out a cry such that no pregnant woman in Egypt will remain without giving birth to her burden." Yusuf said: "Let him be." When the people returned to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and informed him of the incident, he wept and said: "O my sons, do not leave my presence even once without some of you being lost. You went once and Yusuf was lost; the second time Shim'un was lost; and this third time Ruwbil and Binyamin have been lost." Then he wept and said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾

He judged this judgment for several reasons:

**First:** When his grief, affliction and trial lengthened, he knew that Allah, exalted is He, would soon grant him relief and a way out. So he said this out of good opinion of the mercy of Allah.

**Second:** Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, informed him after the trial of Yusuf that he was alive, or signs of that appeared to him. He said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ because when they took Yusuf away they were twelve; Yusuf was lost and eleven remained. When he sent them to Egypt, they returned as nine, because Binyamin was detained by Yusuf, and that elder who said: ﴿I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾ was also held back. So when the absent ones were three, he said without doubt: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ That is, He is the Knower of the realities of matters, and the Wise in them, in the manner that corresponds to grace, kindness, mercy and benefit.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 83–85:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾

Know that when Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, heard that statement from his sons, he did not believe them regarding what they reported, as in the incident of Yusuf (Joseph),

[Page 153]

when he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting.﴾ He repeated this very statement in this incident, except that in the incident of Yusuf, peace be upon him, he said: ﴿And Allah is the one whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ (Yusuf 12:18). Here he said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾ There are several questions (masa'il, sing. mas'alah) concerning this.

**The first question:** Some said that his saying ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you﴾ does not mean here lying and deception, as in his saying in the incident of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you.﴾ Rather, he meant: your souls made it seem fair to you to take Binyamin (Benjamin) away from me and to bring him to Egypt seeking benefit, but harm and injury came of it, and you insisted on sending him with you, and you did not know that Allah's decree had come contrary to your planning.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Rather, your souls made a matter seem fair to you": your souls imagined to you that he had stolen, when he had not stolen.

**The second question:** It was said that when Ruwbil (Reuben) resolved to remain in Egypt, the king ordered him to go with his brothers. He said: "Leave me, or I will let out a cry such that no pregnant woman in Egypt will remain without giving birth to her burden." Yusuf said: "Let him be." When the people returned to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and informed him of the incident, he wept and said: "O my sons, do not leave my presence even once without some of you being lost. You went once and Yusuf was lost; the second time Shim'un was lost; and this third time Ruwbil and Binyamin have been lost." Then he wept and said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾

He judged this judgment for several reasons:

**First:** When his grief, affliction and trial lengthened, he knew that Allah, exalted is He, would soon grant him relief and a way out. So he said this out of good opinion of the mercy of Allah.

**Second:** Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, informed him after the trial of Yusuf that he was alive, or signs of that appeared to him. He said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ because when they took Yusuf away they were twelve; Yusuf was lost and eleven remained. When he sent them to Egypt, they returned as nine, because Binyamin was detained by Yusuf, and that elder who said: ﴿I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾ was also held back. So when the absent ones were three, he said without doubt: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ That is, He is the Knower of the realities of matters, and the Wise in them, in the manner that corresponds to grace, kindness, mercy and benefit.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 86–87 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" And his eyes became white from grief, for he was suppressing [his anguish].﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish."﴾ ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know."﴾ ﴿O my sons, go and seek information about Joseph and his brother, and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾
Page 154

Know that when Ya'qub, peace be upon him, heard the words of his sons, his heart became very constricted, and he turned away from them and separated from them. Then, in the end, he sought them and returned to them.

As for the first state, which is that he turned away from them and fled from them, it is His saying: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!"﴾

Know that when his chest was constricted because of the speech he heard from his sons concerning Benjamin, his sorrow over Joseph, peace be upon him, grew greatly: ﴿and he said, "Alas for Joseph!"﴾ His grief over parting from Joseph at this event became greater for several reasons:

The first reason: new grief strengthens old, hidden grief, and when one arrow strikes another, it is more painful.

Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said:
"My companion blamed me at the graves for weeping, for shedding flowing tears,
He said, 'Will you weep for every grave you have seen, for a grave that dwells between al-Liwa and al-Dakadik?'
I said to him, 'Indeed grief stirs up grief, so leave me, for all of this is the grave of Malik.'"

That is because when he saw a grave, his grief for his brother Malik was renewed, so they blamed him for it, and he answered that grief stirs up grief. Another said:
"The misfortunes after him have not made me forget him, but reopening a wound with a wound is more painful."

The second reason: Benjamin and Joseph were from one mother, and the resemblance between them in form and attribute was most complete. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, used to find consolation in seeing Benjamin in place of seeing Joseph. When what happened occurred, the cause of consolation was removed, so the pain and longing grew greater.

The third reason: the calamity of Joseph was the root of his calamities, upon which all other calamities and afflictions were based, so grief over him was grief over everything.

The fourth reason: these new calamities had causes that were like matters that could be known and investigated.

As for the event of Joseph, he, peace be upon him, knew their lie concerning the cause they mentioned, but the true cause was not known to him. Also, he, peace be upon him, knew that these (sons) were alive, but Joseph, he did not know whether he was alive or dead. For these reasons his longing over his separation grew greatly and his affliction was intensified by ignorance of his state.

The second issue: Some ignorant people criticized Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for his saying: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾ They said: this is a display of impatience and is akin to complaining against Allah, and that is not permissible. The scholars have explained that the matter is not as this ignorant man supposed. The explanation is that he, peace be upon him, did not say this word and then his weeping grew great, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and his eyes became white from grief﴾. Then he restrained his tongue from wailing and from mentioning what is not fitting, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿for he was suppressing [his anguish]﴾. Furthermore, he did not reveal a complaint to any creature, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. All of this indicates that, although his calamity was great and his trial was intense, he endured, swallowed his distress, and did not reveal a complaint. Therefore he deserved great praise and great commendation.

It is reported that Joseph, peace be upon him, asked Jibril: "Do you have knowledge of Ya'qub?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And how is his grief?"
Page 155

He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers," and a bereaved mother is one who has one child and then he dies.
He said: "Does he have a reward for it?" He said: "Yes, the reward of one hundred martyrs."

If it is said: It is reported from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, who said: "An old man passed by Ya'qub and said to him: 'Are you Ibrahim?' He said: 'I am the son of his son, and worries have changed me and taken away my beauty and strength.' Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'How long will you complain to My servants? By My might and My majesty, if you did not complain to Me, I would replace your flesh with flesh better than your flesh and your blood with blood better than your blood.'" Thereafter he would say: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah." And it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Ya'qub had a brother with whom he was bonded, and he said to him: 'What has taken away your sight and bent your back?' He said: 'What took away my sight is weeping over Joseph, and what bent my back is grief over Benjamin.' Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'Are you not ashamed to complain to other than Me?' He said: 'I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah.' He said: 'O Lord, do You not have mercy on the old man? You bent my back and took away my sight; return to me my two sweet-smelling ones, Joseph and Benjamin.' Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him with good news and said: 'Had they been dead, I would have raised them for you. So prepare food for the needy, for the dearest of My servants to Me are the prophets and the needy.' When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, wished to eat lunch, he would call out his caller: 'Whoever wishes to have lunch, let him lunch with Ya'qub,' and when he was fasting, he would call out the same at the time of iftar."

It is also reported that he would raise his eyebrows with a cloth because of old age. A man said to him: "What is this that I see on you?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of griefs." Allah revealed to him: "Do you complain to Me, O Ya'qub?" He said: "O Lord, it is a sin I committed, so forgive it for me."

We say: We have shown that he did not come except with patience, steadfastness, and abandoning wailing. It is also reported that the Angel of Death entered upon Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and said to him: "Have you come to take me before I see my two beloved ones?" He said: "No, but I have come to grieve with your grief and to be sorrowful with your sorrow. As for weeping, it is not among the sins."

It is also reported that the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, wept over his son Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and said: "Indeed the heart grieves, the eye sheds tears, and we do not say what displeases the Lord. And indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved over you."

Moreover, the overwhelming of a person by grief is not by his choice, so that is not included within the obligation. As for groaning and letting weeping flow, it may reach a state where one cannot repel it. As for what has come in the narrations you mentioned, the reproach in them was only because the good deeds of the righteous are bad deeds of those brought near.

Also, there is another subtle point: when a person is in a state of bewilderment and perplexity, he must return to Allah the Exalted. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, did not know whether Joseph remained alive or had died, so he was in suspense about it, and because of his suspense he would frequently return to Allah the Exalted, and his heart would be detached from turning to anything other than Allah the Exalted, except in this event. His states in this event varied: at times he became wholly absorbed in the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, passing away from recalling this event, so that its mention was like its absence. For this reason, this event was, in relation to him, like being thrown into the fire for the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), peace be upon him, and like the slaughter of his son, the one to be sacrificed.

If it is said: Is it not better, when a severe calamity descends, to say: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and indeed to Him we will return﴾, so that one earns the great reward mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and it is those who are the guided﴾ (al-Baqarah: 157)?

We say: Some exegetes said: Allah did not give the saying of istirja' (this formula) to any community except this community, so Allah honours them when a calamity strikes them.

But this, in my view, is weak, because His saying "Indeed we belong to Allah" is an indication that we are owned by Allah, who created us and brought us into existence, and His saying "and indeed to Him we will return" is an indication that there must be resurrection and the Day of Judgment. It is impossible that a community among the nations does not know this. Whoever, upon the descent of some calamity, knows that in the end he must return to Allah the Exalted, then complete consolation is attained at that calamity. And it is impossible that a believer in Allah would not know this.
Page 156

The third issue: His saying: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾ is a call to grief (asaf), and it is like His saying "O wonder!" The implication is as if he were calling upon grief and saying: "This is the time of your arrival and the moment of your coming." We have established this meaning in many places, among them in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Allah forbid!﴾ (Yusuf: 31). And asaf (grief) is sorrow over what has been lost.

al-Layth said: If a matter comes to you and you grieve over it and cannot bear it, then you are asif, meaning sorrowful, and also mutaassif.

al-Zajjaj said: The original is "Ya asafi," except that the ya of possession may be replaced by an alif because of the lightness of the alif and the fatha.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and his eyes became white from grief﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first view: When he said "Alas for Joseph!", weeping overcame him, and at the overcoming of weeping, water increases in the eye so the eye appears as if it has become white from the whiteness of that water. His saying "and his eyes became white from grief" is a metaphor for the overcoming of weeping. The evidence for the soundness of this view is that the effect of grief is in the overcoming of weeping, not in the occurrence of blindness. So if we take the whitening to mean the overcoming of weeping, this explanation is good; if we take it to mean blindness, this explanation is not good. Therefore what we have mentioned is more appropriate. This interpretation, together with the evidence, is related by al-Wahidi in "al-Basit" from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The second view: The intended meaning is blindness. Muqatil said: He did not see with them for six years until Allah removed it from him through the shirt of Joseph, peace be upon him, which is His saying: ﴿Cast it upon my father's face; he will regain sight﴾ (Yusuf: 93).

It is said: Jibril, peace be upon him, entered upon Joseph, peace be upon him, while he was in prison, and said: "Your father's sight has gone from grief over you." So he placed his hand on his head and said: "Would that my mother had not borne me, and that I had not been a grief to my father." Those who hold this interpretation say: Constant grief necessitates constant weeping, and that necessitates blindness; so grief was the cause of blindness through this intermediary. Constant weeping causes blindness because it produces a turbidity in the dark part of the eye. Among them are those who said: he did not become blind, but he came to a state where he perceived with weak perception.

It is said: The eyes of Ya'qub did not dry from the time of separation from Joseph, peace be upon him, until the time of meeting him, and that period was eighty years, and there was no servant on the face of the earth more honoured by Allah the Exalted than Ya'qub, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from grief﴾, know that it is read "min al-huzn" with a damma on the ha and sukun on the zay, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the ha and the zay.

al-Wahidi said: They differed concerning huzn and hazan. Some people said: huzn is weeping, and hazan is the opposite of joy. Others said: they are two dialects; one says "asabahu huznun shadid" and "hazanun shadid," and this is the view of most lexicographers. Yunus related from Abu 'Amr that when it is in the accusative position they open the ha and the zay, as in His saying: ﴿they turn away while their eyes overflow with tears, grieving (hazanan)﴾ (al-Tawbah: 92), and when it is in the genitive or nominative position they put a damma on the ha, as in His saying: ﴿from grief (min al-huzn)﴾ and His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief (huzni) to Allah﴾. He said: it is in the nominative position as a subject of a nominal sentence.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he was suppressing [his anguish]﴾, it may mean "one who suppresses" (al-kazim), that is, one who holds back his grief and does not reveal it.

Ibn Qutaybah said: It may also mean "one who is suppressed" (al-maktum), and its meaning is: filled with grief while his breath is blocked, like the water-skin that is compressed when it is filled to its brim. It may also mean "filled with rage at his children."

Know that the most noble of the members of a human being are these three (the tongue, the eye, and the heart?), so He, exalted is He, made clear that they were drowned in distress; the tongue was
Page 157

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 86–87 (part 2 of 2):

...preoccupied with his saying: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾ The eye is occupied with weeping and whiteness (from weeping), and the heart with intense grief, which resembles a vessel filled to the brim and sealed so that water cannot come out of it. This is an exaggeration in describing that grief.

* * *

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become consumed or become among the perishing."﴾ There are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said, "ma ziltu af'aluhu" (I continued to do it), "ma fati'tu af'aluhu" (I did not cease doing it), and "ma bariḥtu af'aluhu" (I did not leave off doing it). These are not used except with negation.

Ibn Qutayba said: "Ma fatītu" and "ma fati'tu" are two dialects, from fatyan and futu'an, meaning when you forget something and cut off from it. The grammarians said: The negative particle here is implied, with the meaning: "You will not cease (ma tafta'u) and you will not cease (la taf'a'u)." Its omission is permissible because if affirmation were intended, it would have been with the lam and the nun, as in: "By God, you will surely do it," so when it came without the lam and the nun, it was known that the word "la" (not) is implied. They cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said, 'By God's oath, I will not leave off sitting'"

and the meaning is: "I will not leave off sitting." Similar examples are numerous.

As for the exegetes, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada said: "You will not stop remembering him." And it is reported from Mujahid: "You will not slacken in your love for him," as if he made futur (slackening) and futu' (cessation) brothers in meaning.

The second issue: al-Wahidi related from the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) that the root of ḥaraḍ (wasted condition) is the corruption of the body and the mind due to sorrow and love. And the saying "ḥarraḍtu fulānan 'alā fulān" means: I incited him against him, and I inflamed him against him. The Exalted said: ﴿Urge the believers to fighting﴾ (al-Anfal: 65).

Having understood this, we say: Describing a man as ḥaraḍ is either because it is intended that he possesses ḥaraḍ, so the noun is omitted (the construction being "one who has ḥaraḍ"), or because it is intended that he has reached such a degree of corruption and weakness that he has become the very essence of ḥaraḍ and the very substance of corruption.

As for ḥaraḍ with a kasra on the ra', it is the adjective (ṣifa). Both readings have been transmitted.

Having understood this, we say: The exegetes have several expressions concerning it:

First: ḥaraḍ and ḥāriḍ mean one who is corrupted in his body and his mind.

Second: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about ḥaraḍ, and he said: The corrupted, the one wasted by illness (al-dani f).

Third: It is one who is neither like the living nor like the dead. Abu Rawq mentioned that Anas ibn Malik recited (ḥattā takūna ḥurḍan) with a ḍamma on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', and he said: It means like the stalk of ushnan (a plant used for washing). And the Exalted's words ﴿or become among the perishing﴾ mean: among the dead. The meaning of the verse is that they said to their father: "You will not cease remembering Joseph with sorrow and weeping over him until you come to an illness by which you will not benefit yourself, or you die of grief." It is as if they said: "You are now in severe affliction, and we fear that there will come what is greater than it and stronger." And by this statement they intended to prevent him from excessive weeping and grief.

If it is asked: Why did they swear to that when they did not know it with certainty?

We say: They built this matter upon what was apparent.

If it is asked: Who are the ones who uttered this statement, namely His saying: ﴿By God, you will not cease﴾?

We say: The more apparent view is that these were not the brothers, who had turned away from him, but the group who were in the house, from among his grandchildren and servants.

[p. 158]

Then the Exalted related of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God."﴾ That is, what I mention, I do not mention it in your presence, but I mention it in the presence of God the Exalted. When a person pours out his complaint to God the Exalted, he is among the company of the realized ones, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You." And God is the one who grants success. Al-batth is dispersal, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And He dispersed in it every kind of creature﴾ (al-Baqara: 164).

So grief, when a person conceals it, is hamm (distress), and when he mentions it to others, it is batth (outpouring). They said: Batth is the most intense grief, and grief is the most intense distress. That is because whenever he is able to hold his tongue from mentioning it, that grief has not overpowered him; but when it becomes great and the person is unable to control it, and the tongue speaks of it whether he wills or not, that is batth, and this indicates that the person has become incapable of it, and it has overpowered him. So His saying: ﴿my anguish and my grief to God﴾ means: I do not mention the great grief nor the small grief except to God.

Al-Hasan read (waḥazanī) with two fathas, and (ḥuzunī) with two dammas. It is said: A man came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, your body has weakened and your frame has become thin, and you have not reached an advanced age!" He said: "What is with me is due to the abundance of my sorrows." Then God revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain of Me to My creation?" He said: "O Lord, it was a sin I committed; forgive it for me." So He forgave it for him. And after that, whenever he was asked, he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God.﴾

It is also reported that God revealed to him: "I was only displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep and a poor man stood at your door, and you did not feed him. The dearest of My creation to Me are the prophets and the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it." It was also said: He bought a slave-girl together with her son, then he sold her son, and she wept until she went blind.

Then Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I know from God what you do not know.﴾ That is: I know from His mercy and His kindness what you do not know, which is that He, the Exalted, brings relief from where I do not expect. This is an indication that he was anticipating the reunion with Joseph.

They mentioned several reasons for this expectation:

First: The Angel of Death came to him and said: "O Angel of Death, have you taken the soul of my son Joseph?" He said: "No, O Prophet of God." Then he pointed toward the side of Egypt and said: "Seek him here."

Second: He knew that Joseph's dream was true, because the signs of rectitude and perfection were manifest in Joseph, and the dream of such a person, peace be upon him, does not fail.

Third: Perhaps God revealed to him that He would reunite him with him, but He did not specify the time, so he remained in anxiety.

Fourth: al-Suddi said: When his sons told him of the king's conduct and the perfection of his condition in his sayings and actions, he hoped that he would be Joseph, and he said: It is unlikely that someone like him would appear among the disbelievers.

Fifth: He knew with certainty that Benjamin would not steal, and he heard that the king had not harmed him nor beaten him, so it became probable to his mind that this king was Joseph. This is the summary of the discussion at the first stage.

The second stage: He returned to his sons and spoke with them in a gentle manner, and that is his saying: ﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother.﴾

Know that when he, peace be upon him, hoped to find Joseph on the basis of the aforementioned signs, he said to his sons: "Search out Joseph." Tahassus is seeking a thing through the senses, and it is similar to hearing and sight. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: It is said "tahassastu 'an fulan" (I sought information about so-and-so), and it is not said "min fulan." It was said: Here it is "min Yusuf" because he placed "min" in the place of "'an." He said: It is also permissible to say that "min" is partitive, and the meaning is: Seek some information of Joseph's news, and learn some of Joseph's news; so the particle "min" was mentioned because of what it indicates of partiality. And it was read "tajassasu" with a jim, as it was read with both in al-Hujurat.

[p. 159]

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not despair of God's mercy (rawḥ).﴾ Al-Asma'i said: Rawḥ is what a person finds of the breeze of air, so he is at peace with it. The root r-w-ḥ indicates movement and stirring, so whatever a person is stirred by and delights in its existence is rawḥ.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not despair of God's rawḥ" means of God's mercy. From Qatada: of God's grace. Ibn Zayd said: of God's relief. These expressions are close in meaning. al-Hasan and Qatada read (min rūḥi Allāh) with a ḍamma, meaning: of His mercy.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of God's rawḥ except the disbelieving people.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: The believer is in good with God; he hopes for it in affliction and praises Him in ease.

Know that despair of God's mercy, the Exalted, does not arise except when a person believes that God is not capable of everything, or not knowing of all knowable things, or not generous, but rather miserly. Each of these three entails disbelief. So when despair does not arise except upon one of these three, and each of them is disbelief, it is established that despair does not arise except for one who is a disbeliever. And God knows best.

Questions remain concerning the issues of this verse:

The first question: Joseph's father's love for Joseph reaching this great degree is only fitting for one who was heedless of God, for whoever knows God loves Him, and whoever loves God, his heart is not free for love of anything other than God the Exalted. Also, one heart cannot contain an all-consuming love for two things. So when his heart was wholly absorbed in love for his son, it is impossible to say that he was wholly absorbed in the love of God the Exalted.

The second question: When the intense grief overcame him, it was obligatory for him to occupy himself with the remembrance of God the Exalted, and with entrusting himself to Him and submitting to His decree.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾, this is not fitting for the people of religion and knowledge, let alone the great prophets.

The third question: There is no doubt that Ya'qub was among the great prophets, and his father and his grandfather and his uncle were all among the famous great prophets in the entire world. Whoever is such, and then there befalls him a dreadful and severe event concerning his dearest son, that event cannot remain hidden; rather, it must reach such fame that everyone knows of it, especially since a long period has passed in it. Yet Ya'qub remained in his intense grief and his great sorrow, while Joseph was in Egypt and Ya'qub was in some part of the land of Syria near Egypt. With such closeness of distance, it is impossible for this event to remain hidden.

The fourth question: Why did Joseph, peace be upon him, not send anyone to Ya'qub to inform him that he was alive and safe? It cannot be said that he feared his brothers, because after he had become a dominant king, it was possible for him to send a messenger to him, and his brothers could not have prevented the messenger?

The fifth question: How was it permissible for Joseph, peace be upon him, to place the measuring cup in his brother's bag, then extract it from it and attach to him the accusation of theft, though he was innocent of it?

The sixth question: How did he desire to attach this accusation to him and to keep him with himself, though he knew that his father's grief would increase and grow stronger?

[p. 160]

The answer to the first: Such a severe trial removes from the heart every other thought.

Moreover, the one who undergoes such a severe trial returns much to God the Exalted and occupies himself much with supplication and humble entreaty, so that becomes a cause for complete absorption.

The answer to the second: Human impulses do not disappear in this worldly life. Sometimes he would say: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾ and sometimes he would say: ﴿So patience is fitting, and God is the one whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ (Yusuf: 18).

As for the remaining questions, al-Qadi answered them with a good general answer. He said: These events that have been related to us either can be explained according to customary circumstances, or they cannot. If the first, then there is no difficulty. If the second, we say: That time was the time of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the breaking of custom in such a time is not unlikely. So it is not impossible to say that the town of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, although it was near the town of Joseph, peace be upon him, the news of neither reached the other, by way of breaking the customary order.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 86–87 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" And his eyes became white from grief, for he was suppressing [his anguish].﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish."﴾ ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know."﴾ ﴿O my sons, go and seek information about Joseph and his brother, and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾
Page 154

Know that when Ya'qub, peace be upon him, heard the words of his sons, his heart became very constricted, and he turned away from them and separated from them. Then, in the end, he sought them and returned to them.

As for the first state, which is that he turned away from them and fled from them, it is His saying: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!"﴾

Know that when his chest was constricted because of the speech he heard from his sons concerning Benjamin, his sorrow over Joseph, peace be upon him, grew greatly: ﴿and he said, "Alas for Joseph!"﴾ His grief over parting from Joseph at this event became greater for several reasons:

The first reason: new grief strengthens old, hidden grief, and when one arrow strikes another, it is more painful.

Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said:
"My companion blamed me at the graves for weeping, for shedding flowing tears,
He said, 'Will you weep for every grave you have seen, for a grave that dwells between al-Liwa and al-Dakadik?'
I said to him, 'Indeed grief stirs up grief, so leave me, for all of this is the grave of Malik.'"

That is because when he saw a grave, his grief for his brother Malik was renewed, so they blamed him for it, and he answered that grief stirs up grief. Another said:
"The misfortunes after him have not made me forget him, but reopening a wound with a wound is more painful."

The second reason: Benjamin and Joseph were from one mother, and the resemblance between them in form and attribute was most complete. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, used to find consolation in seeing Benjamin in place of seeing Joseph. When what happened occurred, the cause of consolation was removed, so the pain and longing grew greater.

The third reason: the calamity of Joseph was the root of his calamities, upon which all other calamities and afflictions were based, so grief over him was grief over everything.

The fourth reason: these new calamities had causes that were like matters that could be known and investigated.

As for the event of Joseph, he, peace be upon him, knew their lie concerning the cause they mentioned, but the true cause was not known to him. Also, he, peace be upon him, knew that these (sons) were alive, but Joseph, he did not know whether he was alive or dead. For these reasons his longing over his separation grew greatly and his affliction was intensified by ignorance of his state.

The second issue: Some ignorant people criticized Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for his saying: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾ They said: this is a display of impatience and is akin to complaining against Allah, and that is not permissible. The scholars have explained that the matter is not as this ignorant man supposed. The explanation is that he, peace be upon him, did not say this word and then his weeping grew great, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and his eyes became white from grief﴾. Then he restrained his tongue from wailing and from mentioning what is not fitting, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿for he was suppressing [his anguish]﴾. Furthermore, he did not reveal a complaint to any creature, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. All of this indicates that, although his calamity was great and his trial was intense, he endured, swallowed his distress, and did not reveal a complaint. Therefore he deserved great praise and great commendation.

It is reported that Joseph, peace be upon him, asked Jibril: "Do you have knowledge of Ya'qub?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And how is his grief?"
Page 155

He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers," and a bereaved mother is one who has one child and then he dies.
He said: "Does he have a reward for it?" He said: "Yes, the reward of one hundred martyrs."

If it is said: It is reported from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, who said: "An old man passed by Ya'qub and said to him: 'Are you Ibrahim?' He said: 'I am the son of his son, and worries have changed me and taken away my beauty and strength.' Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'How long will you complain to My servants? By My might and My majesty, if you did not complain to Me, I would replace your flesh with flesh better than your flesh and your blood with blood better than your blood.'" Thereafter he would say: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah." And it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Ya'qub had a brother with whom he was bonded, and he said to him: 'What has taken away your sight and bent your back?' He said: 'What took away my sight is weeping over Joseph, and what bent my back is grief over Benjamin.' Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'Are you not ashamed to complain to other than Me?' He said: 'I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah.' He said: 'O Lord, do You not have mercy on the old man? You bent my back and took away my sight; return to me my two sweet-smelling ones, Joseph and Benjamin.' Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him with good news and said: 'Had they been dead, I would have raised them for you. So prepare food for the needy, for the dearest of My servants to Me are the prophets and the needy.' When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, wished to eat lunch, he would call out his caller: 'Whoever wishes to have lunch, let him lunch with Ya'qub,' and when he was fasting, he would call out the same at the time of iftar."

It is also reported that he would raise his eyebrows with a cloth because of old age. A man said to him: "What is this that I see on you?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of griefs." Allah revealed to him: "Do you complain to Me, O Ya'qub?" He said: "O Lord, it is a sin I committed, so forgive it for me."

We say: We have shown that he did not come except with patience, steadfastness, and abandoning wailing. It is also reported that the Angel of Death entered upon Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and said to him: "Have you come to take me before I see my two beloved ones?" He said: "No, but I have come to grieve with your grief and to be sorrowful with your sorrow. As for weeping, it is not among the sins."

It is also reported that the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, wept over his son Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and said: "Indeed the heart grieves, the eye sheds tears, and we do not say what displeases the Lord. And indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved over you."

Moreover, the overwhelming of a person by grief is not by his choice, so that is not included within the obligation. As for groaning and letting weeping flow, it may reach a state where one cannot repel it. As for what has come in the narrations you mentioned, the reproach in them was only because the good deeds of the righteous are bad deeds of those brought near.

Also, there is another subtle point: when a person is in a state of bewilderment and perplexity, he must return to Allah the Exalted. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, did not know whether Joseph remained alive or had died, so he was in suspense about it, and because of his suspense he would frequently return to Allah the Exalted, and his heart would be detached from turning to anything other than Allah the Exalted, except in this event. His states in this event varied: at times he became wholly absorbed in the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, passing away from recalling this event, so that its mention was like its absence. For this reason, this event was, in relation to him, like being thrown into the fire for the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), peace be upon him, and like the slaughter of his son, the one to be sacrificed.

If it is said: Is it not better, when a severe calamity descends, to say: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and indeed to Him we will return﴾, so that one earns the great reward mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and it is those who are the guided﴾ (al-Baqarah: 157)?

We say: Some exegetes said: Allah did not give the saying of istirja' (this formula) to any community except this community, so Allah honours them when a calamity strikes them.

But this, in my view, is weak, because His saying "Indeed we belong to Allah" is an indication that we are owned by Allah, who created us and brought us into existence, and His saying "and indeed to Him we will return" is an indication that there must be resurrection and the Day of Judgment. It is impossible that a community among the nations does not know this. Whoever, upon the descent of some calamity, knows that in the end he must return to Allah the Exalted, then complete consolation is attained at that calamity. And it is impossible that a believer in Allah would not know this.
Page 156

The third issue: His saying: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾ is a call to grief (asaf), and it is like His saying "O wonder!" The implication is as if he were calling upon grief and saying: "This is the time of your arrival and the moment of your coming." We have established this meaning in many places, among them in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Allah forbid!﴾ (Yusuf: 31). And asaf (grief) is sorrow over what has been lost.

al-Layth said: If a matter comes to you and you grieve over it and cannot bear it, then you are asif, meaning sorrowful, and also mutaassif.

al-Zajjaj said: The original is "Ya asafi," except that the ya of possession may be replaced by an alif because of the lightness of the alif and the fatha.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and his eyes became white from grief﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first view: When he said "Alas for Joseph!", weeping overcame him, and at the overcoming of weeping, water increases in the eye so the eye appears as if it has become white from the whiteness of that water. His saying "and his eyes became white from grief" is a metaphor for the overcoming of weeping. The evidence for the soundness of this view is that the effect of grief is in the overcoming of weeping, not in the occurrence of blindness. So if we take the whitening to mean the overcoming of weeping, this explanation is good; if we take it to mean blindness, this explanation is not good. Therefore what we have mentioned is more appropriate. This interpretation, together with the evidence, is related by al-Wahidi in "al-Basit" from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The second view: The intended meaning is blindness. Muqatil said: He did not see with them for six years until Allah removed it from him through the shirt of Joseph, peace be upon him, which is His saying: ﴿Cast it upon my father's face; he will regain sight﴾ (Yusuf: 93).

It is said: Jibril, peace be upon him, entered upon Joseph, peace be upon him, while he was in prison, and said: "Your father's sight has gone from grief over you." So he placed his hand on his head and said: "Would that my mother had not borne me, and that I had not been a grief to my father." Those who hold this interpretation say: Constant grief necessitates constant weeping, and that necessitates blindness; so grief was the cause of blindness through this intermediary. Constant weeping causes blindness because it produces a turbidity in the dark part of the eye. Among them are those who said: he did not become blind, but he came to a state where he perceived with weak perception.

It is said: The eyes of Ya'qub did not dry from the time of separation from Joseph, peace be upon him, until the time of meeting him, and that period was eighty years, and there was no servant on the face of the earth more honoured by Allah the Exalted than Ya'qub, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from grief﴾, know that it is read "min al-huzn" with a damma on the ha and sukun on the zay, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the ha and the zay.

al-Wahidi said: They differed concerning huzn and hazan. Some people said: huzn is weeping, and hazan is the opposite of joy. Others said: they are two dialects; one says "asabahu huznun shadid" and "hazanun shadid," and this is the view of most lexicographers. Yunus related from Abu 'Amr that when it is in the accusative position they open the ha and the zay, as in His saying: ﴿they turn away while their eyes overflow with tears, grieving (hazanan)﴾ (al-Tawbah: 92), and when it is in the genitive or nominative position they put a damma on the ha, as in His saying: ﴿from grief (min al-huzn)﴾ and His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief (huzni) to Allah﴾. He said: it is in the nominative position as a subject of a nominal sentence.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he was suppressing [his anguish]﴾, it may mean "one who suppresses" (al-kazim), that is, one who holds back his grief and does not reveal it.

Ibn Qutaybah said: It may also mean "one who is suppressed" (al-maktum), and its meaning is: filled with grief while his breath is blocked, like the water-skin that is compressed when it is filled to its brim. It may also mean "filled with rage at his children."

Know that the most noble of the members of a human being are these three (the tongue, the eye, and the heart?), so He, exalted is He, made clear that they were drowned in distress; the tongue was
Page 157

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 86–87 (part 2 of 2):

...preoccupied with his saying: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾ The eye is occupied with weeping and whiteness (from weeping), and the heart with intense grief, which resembles a vessel filled to the brim and sealed so that water cannot come out of it. This is an exaggeration in describing that grief.

* * *

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become consumed or become among the perishing."﴾ There are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said, "ma ziltu af'aluhu" (I continued to do it), "ma fati'tu af'aluhu" (I did not cease doing it), and "ma bariḥtu af'aluhu" (I did not leave off doing it). These are not used except with negation.

Ibn Qutayba said: "Ma fatītu" and "ma fati'tu" are two dialects, from fatyan and futu'an, meaning when you forget something and cut off from it. The grammarians said: The negative particle here is implied, with the meaning: "You will not cease (ma tafta'u) and you will not cease (la taf'a'u)." Its omission is permissible because if affirmation were intended, it would have been with the lam and the nun, as in: "By God, you will surely do it," so when it came without the lam and the nun, it was known that the word "la" (not) is implied. They cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said, 'By God's oath, I will not leave off sitting'"

and the meaning is: "I will not leave off sitting." Similar examples are numerous.

As for the exegetes, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada said: "You will not stop remembering him." And it is reported from Mujahid: "You will not slacken in your love for him," as if he made futur (slackening) and futu' (cessation) brothers in meaning.

The second issue: al-Wahidi related from the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) that the root of ḥaraḍ (wasted condition) is the corruption of the body and the mind due to sorrow and love. And the saying "ḥarraḍtu fulānan 'alā fulān" means: I incited him against him, and I inflamed him against him. The Exalted said: ﴿Urge the believers to fighting﴾ (al-Anfal: 65).

Having understood this, we say: Describing a man as ḥaraḍ is either because it is intended that he possesses ḥaraḍ, so the noun is omitted (the construction being "one who has ḥaraḍ"), or because it is intended that he has reached such a degree of corruption and weakness that he has become the very essence of ḥaraḍ and the very substance of corruption.

As for ḥaraḍ with a kasra on the ra', it is the adjective (ṣifa). Both readings have been transmitted.

Having understood this, we say: The exegetes have several expressions concerning it:

First: ḥaraḍ and ḥāriḍ mean one who is corrupted in his body and his mind.

Second: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about ḥaraḍ, and he said: The corrupted, the one wasted by illness (al-dani f).

Third: It is one who is neither like the living nor like the dead. Abu Rawq mentioned that Anas ibn Malik recited (ḥattā takūna ḥurḍan) with a ḍamma on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', and he said: It means like the stalk of ushnan (a plant used for washing). And the Exalted's words ﴿or become among the perishing﴾ mean: among the dead. The meaning of the verse is that they said to their father: "You will not cease remembering Joseph with sorrow and weeping over him until you come to an illness by which you will not benefit yourself, or you die of grief." It is as if they said: "You are now in severe affliction, and we fear that there will come what is greater than it and stronger." And by this statement they intended to prevent him from excessive weeping and grief.

If it is asked: Why did they swear to that when they did not know it with certainty?

We say: They built this matter upon what was apparent.

If it is asked: Who are the ones who uttered this statement, namely His saying: ﴿By God, you will not cease﴾?

We say: The more apparent view is that these were not the brothers, who had turned away from him, but the group who were in the house, from among his grandchildren and servants.

[p. 158]

Then the Exalted related of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God."﴾ That is, what I mention, I do not mention it in your presence, but I mention it in the presence of God the Exalted. When a person pours out his complaint to God the Exalted, he is among the company of the realized ones, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You." And God is the one who grants success. Al-batth is dispersal, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And He dispersed in it every kind of creature﴾ (al-Baqara: 164).

So grief, when a person conceals it, is hamm (distress), and when he mentions it to others, it is batth (outpouring). They said: Batth is the most intense grief, and grief is the most intense distress. That is because whenever he is able to hold his tongue from mentioning it, that grief has not overpowered him; but when it becomes great and the person is unable to control it, and the tongue speaks of it whether he wills or not, that is batth, and this indicates that the person has become incapable of it, and it has overpowered him. So His saying: ﴿my anguish and my grief to God﴾ means: I do not mention the great grief nor the small grief except to God.

Al-Hasan read (waḥazanī) with two fathas, and (ḥuzunī) with two dammas. It is said: A man came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, your body has weakened and your frame has become thin, and you have not reached an advanced age!" He said: "What is with me is due to the abundance of my sorrows." Then God revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain of Me to My creation?" He said: "O Lord, it was a sin I committed; forgive it for me." So He forgave it for him. And after that, whenever he was asked, he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God.﴾

It is also reported that God revealed to him: "I was only displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep and a poor man stood at your door, and you did not feed him. The dearest of My creation to Me are the prophets and the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it." It was also said: He bought a slave-girl together with her son, then he sold her son, and she wept until she went blind.

Then Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I know from God what you do not know.﴾ That is: I know from His mercy and His kindness what you do not know, which is that He, the Exalted, brings relief from where I do not expect. This is an indication that he was anticipating the reunion with Joseph.

They mentioned several reasons for this expectation:

First: The Angel of Death came to him and said: "O Angel of Death, have you taken the soul of my son Joseph?" He said: "No, O Prophet of God." Then he pointed toward the side of Egypt and said: "Seek him here."

Second: He knew that Joseph's dream was true, because the signs of rectitude and perfection were manifest in Joseph, and the dream of such a person, peace be upon him, does not fail.

Third: Perhaps God revealed to him that He would reunite him with him, but He did not specify the time, so he remained in anxiety.

Fourth: al-Suddi said: When his sons told him of the king's conduct and the perfection of his condition in his sayings and actions, he hoped that he would be Joseph, and he said: It is unlikely that someone like him would appear among the disbelievers.

Fifth: He knew with certainty that Benjamin would not steal, and he heard that the king had not harmed him nor beaten him, so it became probable to his mind that this king was Joseph. This is the summary of the discussion at the first stage.

The second stage: He returned to his sons and spoke with them in a gentle manner, and that is his saying: ﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother.﴾

Know that when he, peace be upon him, hoped to find Joseph on the basis of the aforementioned signs, he said to his sons: "Search out Joseph." Tahassus is seeking a thing through the senses, and it is similar to hearing and sight. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: It is said "tahassastu 'an fulan" (I sought information about so-and-so), and it is not said "min fulan." It was said: Here it is "min Yusuf" because he placed "min" in the place of "'an." He said: It is also permissible to say that "min" is partitive, and the meaning is: Seek some information of Joseph's news, and learn some of Joseph's news; so the particle "min" was mentioned because of what it indicates of partiality. And it was read "tajassasu" with a jim, as it was read with both in al-Hujurat.

[p. 159]

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not despair of God's mercy (rawḥ).﴾ Al-Asma'i said: Rawḥ is what a person finds of the breeze of air, so he is at peace with it. The root r-w-ḥ indicates movement and stirring, so whatever a person is stirred by and delights in its existence is rawḥ.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not despair of God's rawḥ" means of God's mercy. From Qatada: of God's grace. Ibn Zayd said: of God's relief. These expressions are close in meaning. al-Hasan and Qatada read (min rūḥi Allāh) with a ḍamma, meaning: of His mercy.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of God's rawḥ except the disbelieving people.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: The believer is in good with God; he hopes for it in affliction and praises Him in ease.

Know that despair of God's mercy, the Exalted, does not arise except when a person believes that God is not capable of everything, or not knowing of all knowable things, or not generous, but rather miserly. Each of these three entails disbelief. So when despair does not arise except upon one of these three, and each of them is disbelief, it is established that despair does not arise except for one who is a disbeliever. And God knows best.

Questions remain concerning the issues of this verse:

The first question: Joseph's father's love for Joseph reaching this great degree is only fitting for one who was heedless of God, for whoever knows God loves Him, and whoever loves God, his heart is not free for love of anything other than God the Exalted. Also, one heart cannot contain an all-consuming love for two things. So when his heart was wholly absorbed in love for his son, it is impossible to say that he was wholly absorbed in the love of God the Exalted.

The second question: When the intense grief overcame him, it was obligatory for him to occupy himself with the remembrance of God the Exalted, and with entrusting himself to Him and submitting to His decree.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Alas, my grief for Joseph!﴾, this is not fitting for the people of religion and knowledge, let alone the great prophets.

The third question: There is no doubt that Ya'qub was among the great prophets, and his father and his grandfather and his uncle were all among the famous great prophets in the entire world. Whoever is such, and then there befalls him a dreadful and severe event concerning his dearest son, that event cannot remain hidden; rather, it must reach such fame that everyone knows of it, especially since a long period has passed in it. Yet Ya'qub remained in his intense grief and his great sorrow, while Joseph was in Egypt and Ya'qub was in some part of the land of Syria near Egypt. With such closeness of distance, it is impossible for this event to remain hidden.

The fourth question: Why did Joseph, peace be upon him, not send anyone to Ya'qub to inform him that he was alive and safe? It cannot be said that he feared his brothers, because after he had become a dominant king, it was possible for him to send a messenger to him, and his brothers could not have prevented the messenger?

The fifth question: How was it permissible for Joseph, peace be upon him, to place the measuring cup in his brother's bag, then extract it from it and attach to him the accusation of theft, though he was innocent of it?

The sixth question: How did he desire to attach this accusation to him and to keep him with himself, though he knew that his father's grief would increase and grow stronger?

He said: These events that have been related to us either can be explained according to customary circumstances, or they cannot. If the first, then there is no difficulty. If the second, we say: That time was the time of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the breaking of custom in such a time is not unlikely. If it is asked: since Jacob ordered them to seek out the affair of Joseph and his brother, why did they turn to complaint and ask for full measure?

We say: because those who search for news seek their goal by every means, and admitting helplessness, the constraint of one's resources, the weakness of one's condition, the scarcity of wealth and the severity of need are all things that soften the heart. So they said: "We will test him by mentioning these matters. If his heart softens toward us, we will mention our real purpose to him; otherwise, we will remain silent."

For this reason they led with the mention of this situation and said, ﴿O Chief of the Realm﴾. "The Chief of the Realm" is the king, the capable, the invincible. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾ means poverty, need, the large number of dependents and the scarcity of food. By "our family" they meant those they had left behind. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾. On this there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** The meaning of *izja'* (ازجاء) in the language is to push along little by little. Its equivalent is *tazjiyah*. It is said: "The wind drives the clouds" (الريح تزجي السحاب).

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives along the clouds?﴾ (al-Nur: 43). It is also said: "I put off (zajjaytu) so-and-so with words," meaning I warded him off. And "so-and-so drives along (yuzji) his life," meaning he passes the time by means of stratagem.

**The Second Discussion:** They described that merchandise as *muzjah* either because it was small in quantity, or because it was of poor quality, or because it was both.

The commentators have mentioned all of these categories. Al-Hasan said: the *bidha'ah muzjah* is that which is few in quantity. Others said that it was of poor quality, and they differed about the nature of that poor quality. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: it was inferior dirhams, which were not accepted in payment for food. It was also said: it was torn sacks and ropes, and worn-out goods. It was also said: the goods of the Bedouins, namely wool and clarified butter. It was also said: green grain. It was also said: dried curd (aqit). It was also said: sandals and leather hides. It was also said: parched flour of the *muql* fruit. It was also said: goat's wool. It was also said: the dirhams of Egypt bore an image of Joseph stamped on them, and the dirhams they brought did not bear the image of Joseph, so they were not accepted by the people.

First: al-Zajjaj said: it derives from the expression "so-and-so drives along (yuzji) his life," meaning he gets through the time with little. The meaning is that "we have come with merchandise by which we push through the days, and which is not of any real benefit." On this view, the estimated phrase is *bidha'ah muzjah bihā al-ayyām* (merchandise by which the days are pushed along).

Second: Abu 'Ubayd said: the inferior dirhams were called *muzjah* only because they are rejected and pushed away, not accepted by the one who would spend them. He said: it is from *izja'*, and *izja'* in the Arabic usage means driving and pushing.

Third: *bidha'ah muzjah* means delayed and pushed away from being spent. No one spends such goods except one who is compelled and in need of them for lack of anything better.

The intent is leniency regarding the difference between the two prices, and that he should price the inferior goods for them just as he would price the good ones.

On this interpretation, it is as if they asked for the surplus as a charitable gift. Others denied this and said: the condition of the prophets and of the children of prophets is incompatible with asking for charity, because they disdain submission to created beings, and what predominates in them is turning exclusively to Allah, may He be exalted, and seeking help from Him alone, rather than from anyone else.

It is related from al-Hasan and Mujahid that they disliked a person saying in his supplication: "O Allah, be charitable to me." They said: this is because Allah does not give charity; rather, the one who gives charity is the one who seeks reward. One should instead say: "O Allah, give me," or "Show favor to me." Accordingly, *tasaddaqa* (to give charity) means giving alms, and *mutasaddiq* means the giver. Al-Layth permitted calling a petitioner a *mutasaddiq*, but most scholars rejected this.

As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire to be burned, but Allah saved him and made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, a knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but Allah ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then they brought me his shirt smeared with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' My eyes lost their sight from weeping for him. Then I had another son, who was his full brother from his mother, and I used to be consoled by him. They took him to you, then they returned and said: 'He has stolen, and you have detained him with you.' We are a household that does not steal, and we have not borne a thief. When Joseph, peace be upon him, read the letter, he could not contain himself, his patience gave way, and he made them aware that he was Joseph.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, related of Joseph, peace be upon him, in this situation, that he said: ﴿Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?﴾ It is said: when he read his father Jacob's letter, his joints trembled, his skin shuddered, his heart softened, and he wept greatly, and he declared that he was Joseph.

It was also said: when he saw his brothers humbling themselves before him and describing their condition of the severity of the times and the scarcity of means, compassion overcame him, and then he declared that he was Joseph. His saying: ﴿Do you know what you did with Joseph?﴾ is an interrogative that conveys the enormity of the matter. Its meaning is: how great is what you committed against Joseph! And how vile is what you undertook! It is like what is said to the wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed? Do you recognize whom you opposed?"

Know that this verse confirms His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him: you will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive﴾ (Yusuf: 15). As for His saying: ﴿and his brother﴾, the intent is what they did to him, namely exposing him to grief by separating him from his brother of the same father and mother. Also, they used to harm him. Among the forms of that harm, they said concerning him: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ (Yusuf: 77). As for His saying: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾, it functions as an excuse, as if he said: "You committed that vile and reprehensible act while you were in the ignorance of youth, or in the ignorance of delusion," meaning that now you are no longer like that. A parallel to this is what is said in interpreting His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What has deluded you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ (al-Infitar: 6). It is said: Allah mentioned this specific attribute so that it would serve as a reply, namely that the servant would say: "O Lord, Your generosity deluded me." Likewise here, he mentioned that statement only to remove their embarrassment and to ease the matter for them.

Then his brothers said: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ Ibn Kathir read *innaka* (إنك) in the form of a declarative statement. So the outcome of these readings is that some readers read it as a question, and some read it as a statement.

As for the first group, they said: when Joseph said to them, ﴿Do you know?﴾, and smiled, they saw his front teeth, which were like strung pearls, and they likened him to Joseph, so they asked him as a question: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ What confirms the validity of the interrogative reading is that he replied, "I am Joseph," and he answered them concerning what they had asked about.

When he lifted the crown, they recognized him by that mark, and they said: "Indeed you are Joseph." It is also possible that Ibn Kathir intended the interrogative, but then omitted the interrogative particle.

His saying: ﴿He said, "I am Joseph"﴾ contains two discussions:

**The Second Discussion:** He only explicitly stated his name to magnify what had befallen him through the injustice of his brothers, and what Allah compensated him with of triumph and victory. It is as if he said: "I am the one whom you wronged in the gravest manner, and Allah brought me to the highest of ranks. I am that helpless one whom you intended to kill or cast into the well; then I became as you see." For this reason he said: ﴿And this is my brother﴾, even though they were already recognizing him, because his intent was to say: "This one too was wronged as I was, and then he too became favored by Allah, may He be exalted, as you see." His saying: ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "with every honor in this world and the Hereafter." Others said: "by bringing us together after separation." His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ means: whoever fears the disobedience of Allah and is patient over the harm of people, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ The meaning: indeed whoever fears and is patient, then Allah does not waste their reward. He placed "the good-doers" in the position of the pronoun because it includes those who fear Allah. On this there are two issues:

**The First Issue:** Know that Joseph, peace be upon him, described himself in this noble situation as one who fears Allah. If he had committed what the Hashwiyya (a term for literalist and anthropomorphist extremists) claim concerning Zulaykha, this statement would be a lie on his part, and mentioning a lie in such a situation, in which the unbeliever believes and the sinner repents, is not befitting for people of intellect.

**The Second Issue:** Al-Wahidi said: it is related from Ibn Kathir, through the transmission of Qunbul, that he read *innahu man yattaqi* (إنَّهُ مَن يَتَّقِي) with the *ya'* affirmed in both states (pausal and non-pausal). Its justification is that *man* may be made to function as *alladhi* (the one who), so it does not require jussive. On this reading it is also permissible that *wa-yasbir* (ويَصْبِرْ) be in the nominative position, but the nominative vowel has been dropped for the sake of lightness, just as it is lightened in *'adud* and *sham'*. The rest read it with the *ya'* omitted in both states.
