**The Second Issue:** Al-Wahidi said: it is related from Ibn Kathir, through the transmission of Qunbul, that he read *innahu man yattaqi* (إنَّهُ مَن يَتَّقِي) with the *ya'* affirmed in both states (pausal and non-pausal). Its justification is that *man* may be made to function as *alladhi* (the one who), so it does not require jussive. On this reading it is also permissible that *wa-yasbir* (ويَصْبِرْ) be in the nominative position, but the nominative vowel has been dropped for the sake of lightness, just as it is lightened in *'adud* and *sham'*. The rest read it with the *ya'* omitted in both states.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 88–90:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they entered upon him, they said, "O Chief of the Realm, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers."﴾

Know that the commentators (mufassirun, those who explain the Qur'an) agree that there is an omitted element here. The estimated meaning is: when Jacob said to his sons, ﴿Go and search for news of Joseph and his brother﴾, they accepted this instruction from their father, returned to Egypt, and entered upon Joseph, peace be upon him, and said to him, ﴿O Chief of the Realm﴾.

If it is asked: since Jacob ordered them to seek out the affair of Joseph and his brother, why did they turn to complaint and ask for full measure?

We say: because those who search for news seek their goal by every means, and admitting helplessness, the constraint of one's resources, the weakness of one's condition, the scarcity of wealth and the severity of need are all things that soften the heart. So they said: "We will test him by mentioning these matters. If his heart softens toward us, we will mention our real purpose to him; otherwise, we will remain silent."

For this reason they led with the mention of this situation and said, ﴿O Chief of the Realm﴾. "The Chief of the Realm" is the king, the capable, the invincible. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾ means poverty, need, the large number of dependents and the scarcity of food. By "our family" they meant those they had left behind. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾. On this there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** The meaning of *izja'* (ازجاء) in the language is to push along little by little. Its equivalent is *tazjiyah*. It is said: "The wind drives the clouds" (الريح تزجي السحاب).

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives along the clouds?﴾ (al-Nur: 43). It is also said: "I put off (zajjaytu) so-and-so with words," meaning I warded him off. And "so-and-so drives along (yuzji) his life," meaning he passes the time by means of stratagem.

**The Second Discussion:** They described that merchandise as *muzjah* either because it was small in quantity, or because it was of poor quality, or because it was both.

The commentators have mentioned all of these categories. Al-Hasan said: the *bidha'ah muzjah* is that which is few in quantity. Others said that it was of poor quality, and they differed about the nature of that poor quality. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: it was inferior dirhams, which were not accepted in payment for food. It was also said: it was torn sacks and ropes, and worn-out goods. It was also said: the goods of the Bedouins, namely wool and clarified butter. It was also said: green grain. It was also said: dried curd (aqit). It was also said: sandals and leather hides. It was also said: parched flour of the *muql* fruit. It was also said: goat's wool. It was also said: the dirhams of Egypt bore an image of Joseph stamped on them, and the dirhams they brought did not bear the image of Joseph, so they were not accepted by the people.

**The Third Discussion:** Explaining why the small, inferior merchandise was called *muzjah*. On this there are several views:

First: al-Zajjaj said: it derives from the expression "so-and-so drives along (yuzji) his life," meaning he gets through the time with little. The meaning is that "we have come with merchandise by which we push through the days, and which is not of any real benefit." On this view, the estimated phrase is *bidha'ah muzjah bihā al-ayyām* (merchandise by which the days are pushed along).

Second: Abu 'Ubayd said: the inferior dirhams were called *muzjah* only because they are rejected and pushed away, not accepted by the one who would spend them. He said: it is from *izja'*, and *izja'* in the Arabic usage means driving and pushing.

Third: *bidha'ah muzjah* means delayed and pushed away from being spent. No one spends such goods except one who is compelled and in need of them for lack of anything better.

Fourth: al-Kalbi said: *muzjah* is a word of the non-Arabs (ajam). It was also said: it is from the language of the Copts. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: it is not appropriate to attribute to the Copts a word of Arabic origin whose derivation and morphology are well known.

**The Fourth Discussion:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *muzjatin* (مزجاةٍ) with imalah (the vowel leaning toward i), because its original form has a *ya'*. The rest read it with a open vowel and emphatic pronunciation (tafkhim).

Know that the sum of the discussion regarding the merchandise being *muzjah* is that it is so either because of its small quantity, or its deficiency, or both together. When they described the severity of their condition and described their merchandise as *muzjah*, they said to him: ﴿So give us full measure﴾. The intent is that he should be lenient with them, either by accepting the deficient as if it were complete, or by accepting the inferior as if it were of good quality. Then they said: ﴿and be charitable to us﴾. The intent is leniency regarding the difference between the two prices, and that he should price the inferior goods for them just as he would price the good ones.

People differed as to whether this was a request from them for charity. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: charity was permissible for the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ), by this verse.

On this interpretation, it is as if they asked for the surplus as a charitable gift. Others denied this and said: the condition of the prophets and of the children of prophets is incompatible with asking for charity, because they disdain submission to created beings, and what predominates in them is turning exclusively to Allah, may He be exalted, and seeking help from Him alone, rather than from anyone else.

It is related from al-Hasan and Mujahid that they disliked a person saying in his supplication: "O Allah, be charitable to me." They said: this is because Allah does not give charity; rather, the one who gives charity is the one who seeks reward. One should instead say: "O Allah, give me," or "Show favor to me." Accordingly, *tasaddaqa* (to give charity) means giving alms, and *mutasaddiq* means the giver. Al-Layth permitted calling a petitioner a *mutasaddiq*, but most scholars rejected this.

It is related that when they said: ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, and humbled themselves before him, his eyes filled with tears. At that point ﴿he said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?"﴾

It was also said: they handed him the letter of Jacob, in which was written: "From Jacob, Israel of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah, to the Chief of the Realm of Egypt. To proceed: we are a household upon which affliction has been decreed. As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire to be burned, but Allah saved him and made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, a knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but Allah ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then they brought me his shirt smeared with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' My eyes lost their sight from weeping for him. Then I had another son, who was his full brother from his mother, and I used to be consoled by him. They took him to you, then they returned and said: 'He has stolen, and you have detained him with you.' We are a household that does not steal, and we have not borne a thief. So if you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will invoke against you an invocation that will reach the seventh of your offspring." When Joseph, peace be upon him, read the letter, he could not contain himself, his patience gave way, and he made them aware that he was Joseph.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, related of Joseph, peace be upon him, in this situation, that he said: ﴿Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?﴾ It is said: when he read his father Jacob's letter, his joints trembled, his skin shuddered, his heart softened, and he wept greatly, and he declared that he was Joseph.

It was also said: when he saw his brothers humbling themselves before him and describing their condition of the severity of the times and the scarcity of means, compassion overcame him, and then he declared that he was Joseph. His saying: ﴿Do you know what you did with Joseph?﴾ is an interrogative that conveys the enormity of the matter. Its meaning is: how great is what you committed against Joseph! And how vile is what you undertook! It is like what is said to the wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed? Do you recognize whom you opposed?"

Know that this verse confirms His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to him: you will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive﴾ (Yusuf: 15). As for His saying: ﴿and his brother﴾, the intent is what they did to him, namely exposing him to grief by separating him from his brother of the same father and mother. Also, they used to harm him. Among the forms of that harm, they said concerning him: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ (Yusuf: 77). As for His saying: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾, it functions as an excuse, as if he said: "You committed that vile and reprehensible act while you were in the ignorance of youth, or in the ignorance of delusion," meaning that now you are no longer like that. A parallel to this is what is said in interpreting His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What has deluded you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ (al-Infitar: 6). It is said: Allah mentioned this specific attribute so that it would serve as a reply, namely that the servant would say: "O Lord, Your generosity deluded me." Likewise here, he mentioned that statement only to remove their embarrassment and to ease the matter for them.

Then his brothers said: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ Ibn Kathir read *innaka* (إنك) in the form of a declarative statement. Nafi' read *a-innaka la-anta Yusuf* (أيِنَّكَ لَأنْتَ يُوسُفُ) with an open alif, not prolonged, and with a *ya'*. Abu 'Amr read *a-ainnaka* (آيِنَّكَ) with a prolonged alif, which is the transmission of Qalun from Nafi'. The rest read *a-innaka* (أئِنَّكَ) with two hamzas. All of these are in the interrogative form. Ubayy read *aw anta Yusuf* (أوَ أنْتَ يُوسُفُ). So the outcome of these readings is that some readers read it as a question, and some read it as a statement.

As for the first group, they said: when Joseph said to them, ﴿Do you know?﴾, and smiled, they saw his front teeth, which were like strung pearls, and they likened him to Joseph, so they asked him as a question: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ What confirms the validity of the interrogative reading is that he replied, "I am Joseph," and he answered them concerning what they had asked about.

As for the one who reads it as a statement, his argument is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that Joseph's brothers did not recognize him until he removed the crown from his head, and there was a mark in his hair parting, and Jacob and Isaac had a similar mark, a sort of birthmark. When he lifted the crown, they recognized him by that mark, and they said: "Indeed you are Joseph." It is also possible that Ibn Kathir intended the interrogative, but then omitted the interrogative particle.

His saying: ﴿He said, "I am Joseph"﴾ contains two discussions:

**The First Discussion:** The *lam* is the *lam* of commencement (lam al-ibtida'), *anta* is the subject, *Yusuf* is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of *inna*.

**The Second Discussion:** He only explicitly stated his name to magnify what had befallen him through the injustice of his brothers, and what Allah compensated him with of triumph and victory. It is as if he said: "I am the one whom you wronged in the gravest manner, and Allah brought me to the highest of ranks. I am that helpless one whom you intended to kill or cast into the well; then I became as you see." For this reason he said: ﴿And this is my brother﴾, even though they were already recognizing him, because his intent was to say: "This one too was wronged as I was, and then he too became favored by Allah, may He be exalted, as you see." His saying: ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "with every honor in this world and the Hereafter." Others said: "by bringing us together after separation." His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ means: whoever fears the disobedience of Allah and is patient over the harm of people, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ The meaning: indeed whoever fears and is patient, then Allah does not waste their reward. He placed "the good-doers" in the position of the pronoun because it includes those who fear Allah. On this there are two issues:

**The First Issue:** Know that Joseph, peace be upon him, described himself in this noble situation as one who fears Allah. If he had committed what the Hashwiyya (a term for literalist and anthropomorphist extremists) claim concerning Zulaykha, this statement would be a lie on his part, and mentioning a lie in such a situation, in which the unbeliever believes and the sinner repents, is not befitting for people of intellect.

**The Second Issue:** Al-Wahidi said: it is related from Ibn Kathir, through the transmission of Qunbul, that he read *innahu man yattaqi* (إنَّهُ مَن يَتَّقِي) with the *ya'* affirmed in both states (pausal and non-pausal). Its justification is that *man* may be made to function as *alladhi* (the one who), so it does not require jussive. On this reading it is also permissible that *wa-yasbir* (ويَصْبِرْ) be in the nominative position, but the nominative vowel has been dropped for the sake of lightness, just as it is lightened in *'adud* and *sham'*. The rest read it with the *ya'* omitted in both states.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 91–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will return seeing. And bring me your entire family.﴾

Know that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned to his brothers that Allah, exalted is He, had bestowed His favour upon him, and that whoever refrains from sins and is patient over the harm of people, Allah does not waste him, they believed him concerning this and acknowledged to him his excellence and distinction. ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ Al-Asma'i said: It is said, "ātharaka (he preferred you) with īthār," meaning Allah has favoured you. And "fulan ātha'ra 'abda fulan" means when he prefers him with his bounty and his kindness. The meaning is: Allah has certainly favoured you over us with knowledge, forbearance, intellect, virtue, beauty, and sovereignty. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence that his brothers were not prophets, because all positions that differ from the position of prophethood are, in comparison to it, as nothing. Had they shared with him the position of prophethood, they would not have said: ﴿By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us.﴾ And by this reasoning the question of one who says, "Perhaps what is meant is his being greater than them in sovereignty and worldly affairs, even if they shared with him in prophethood," is dispelled, because we have explained that worldly circumstances are of no account beside the position of prophethood.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and we were certainly sinners.﴾ It has been said: the sinner (khati') is one who commits a sin deliberately, and a distinction is made between the khati' and the mukhti' (one who errs). On account of this distinction, one who strives in legal rulings and does not hit the correct answer is called mukhti', and is not called khati'. Most of the commentators hold that what they apologised for was their act of throwing him into the well, selling him, and removing him far from the house and the father. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: They did not apologise to him for that, because that occurred from them before puberty, so it is not a sin and is not apologised for. They only apologised insofar as they erred after that, by not informing their father of what they had done, so that he would know that he was alive and that the wolf had not eaten him. This statement is weak from several aspects:

The first aspect: We have explained that it is not permissible to say that they undertook those acts in their childhood, because it is unlikely for someone like Ya'qub to send a group of non-adult boys without sending with them an intelligent man who would prevent them from what is not fitting and guide them to what is fitting.

The second aspect: Suppose the matter is as al-Jubba'i mentioned. Still, we say: at most, it does not become obligatory to apologise for that, but it is possible to say that apologising for it is good. The proof of this is that when a wrongdoer repents, his punishment is removed, and then he may repeat repentance and apology a second time. Thus we know that a person may also repent when repentance is not obligatory upon him.

Know that when they acknowledged his favour upon them and their being criminals and sinners, Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you.﴾ In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: At-tathrib means reproach (tawbikh). From it is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him apply the prescribed punishment to her, and let him not reproach her (yuthrribha)," meaning, let him not shame her with the fornication. So his saying "no reproach (tathrib)" means no rebuke and no blame. The root of tathrib is from ath-thurb, which is the fat that covers the paunch. Its meaning is the removal of the fat, just as tajlid is the removal of the skin. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: Seeking needs from the young is easier than seeking them from the elders. Do you not see Yusuf's saying to his brothers, "No reproach will there be upon you," and Ya'qub's saying, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you" (Yusuf: 98)?

The second discussion: His saying "today" (al-yawm) relates to what? There are two opinions:

The first opinion: It relates to his saying "no reproach," meaning, I do not reproach you today, which is the day that is the likely occasion for reproach, so what then do you think of all other days? There is another possibility: that I have ruled on this day that there is no reproach absolutely, because "no reproach" is a negation of the essence (nafy al-mahiyya), and negation of the essence requires the negation of all its individual instances. So this was a negation encompassing every time and circumstance. The sense of the statement is: Today I have ruled with this general judgment that encompasses every time and circumstance. Then, when he had made clear to them that he had removed from them the blame of this world, he asked Allah to remove from them the punishment of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿Allah will forgive you,﴾ and what is meant by it is supplication.

The second opinion: His saying "today" relates to his saying "Allah will forgive you," as if, when he negated reproach absolutely, he gave them the good news that Allah had forgiven their sin on this day. This is because, when they were humbled, ashamed, acknowledged and repented, Allah accepted their repentance and forgave their sin. Therefore he said: ﴿Today Allah will forgive you.﴾ It is related that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, "took hold of the two posts of the door of the Ka'bah on the day of the Conquest and said to the Quraysh: 'What do you think I will do with you?' They said: 'We expect good: a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have the power.' He said: 'I will say what my brother Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach will there be upon you today.﴾'" It is also related that when Abu Sufyan came to embrace Islam, al-'Abbas said to him: "When you come to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, recite to him: ﴿He said, no reproach will there be upon you today,﴾" and he did so, and the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "May Allah forgive you and whoever taught you." It is also related that when the brothers of Yusuf recognised him, they sent to him: "You have us attend your table morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you for the harm we caused you." Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: "Although the people of Egypt, even though I have been made their ruler, look at me with their former eyes and say, 'Glory be to Him who raised a slave sold for twenty dirhams to what he has reached!' Indeed, I have become honoured now by your coming, and I have become great in the eyes, now that you have come, and the people know that you are my brothers and that I am of the descendants of Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will return seeing.﴾ The commentators said: When Yusuf recognised them, he asked them about his father, and they said: "His eyes have gone white," so he gave them his shirt. The scholars who investigate said: He knew that casting that shirt over his face would bring back the strength of sight only by revelation from Allah, exalted is He, and without revelation he would not have known this, because reason does not indicate it. It is possible to say: perhaps Yusuf, peace be upon him, knew that his father had not become blind, but that from excessive weeping and constriction of heart his sight had weakened; so when his shirt was cast upon him, his heart would surely be expanded and intense joy would arise in his heart, and that strengthens the spirit and removes weakness from the faculties, so then his sight grows strong and that deficiency departs from him. This is a matter whose truth can be known by the heart, and the medical principles indicate the soundness of this meaning.

His saying: ﴿he will return seeing (ya'ti basiran)﴾ means he will become seeing (yasir basiran). Supporting this is: ﴿and he returned seeing (fartadda basiran)﴾ (Yusuf: 96). It is also said: the meaning is "he will come to me while he is seeing." He mentioned him alone by name out of honour for him, and for the rest he said: ﴿and bring me your entire family, all of them.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: his household numbered about seventy persons. Masruq said: the people of Yusuf, peace be upon him, entered Egypt, and they were ninety-three, men and women included. It is related that Yahuda carried the message and said: "I grieved him by carrying the blood-stained shirt to him, so I will gladden him as I grieved him." It was also said that he carried it barefoot and bare-headed from Egypt to Canaan, and between them is a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Therefore he said: ﴿Today Allah will forgive you.﴾ It is related that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, "took hold of the two posts of the door of the Ka'bah on the day of the Conquest and said to the Quraysh: 'What do you think I will do with you?' They said: 'We expect good: a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have the power.' He said: 'I will say what my brother Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach will there be upon you today.﴾'" It is also related that when Abu Sufyan came to embrace Islam, al-'Abbas said to him: "When you come to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, recite to him: ﴿He said, no reproach will there be upon you today,﴾" and he did so, and the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "May Allah forgive you and whoever taught you." This is a matter whose truth can be known by the heart, and the medical principles indicate the soundness of this meaning.

His saying: ﴿he will return seeing (ya'ti basiran)﴾ means he will become seeing (yasir basiran). Supporting this is: ﴿and he returned seeing (fartadda basiran)﴾ (Yusuf: 96). It is also said: the meaning is "he will come to me while he is seeing." He mentioned him alone by name out of honour for him, and for the rest he said: ﴿and bring me your entire family, all of them.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: his household numbered about seventy persons. Masruq said: the people of Yusuf, peace be upon him, entered Egypt, and they were ninety-three, men and women included. It is related that Yahuda carried the message and said: "I grieved him by carrying the blood-stained shirt to him, so I will gladden him as I grieved him." It was also said that he carried it barefoot and bare-headed from Egypt to Canaan, and between them is a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 91–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will return seeing. And bring me your entire family.﴾

Know that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned to his brothers that Allah, exalted is He, had bestowed His favour upon him, and that whoever refrains from sins and is patient over the harm of people, Allah does not waste him, they believed him concerning this and acknowledged to him his excellence and distinction. ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ Al-Asma'i said: It is said, "ātharaka (he preferred you) with īthār," meaning Allah has favoured you. And "fulan ātha'ra 'abda fulan" means when he prefers him with his bounty and his kindness. The meaning is: Allah has certainly favoured you over us with knowledge, forbearance, intellect, virtue, beauty, and sovereignty. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence that his brothers were not prophets, because all positions that differ from the position of prophethood are, in comparison to it, as nothing. Had they shared with him the position of prophethood, they would not have said: ﴿By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us.﴾ And by this reasoning the question of one who says, "Perhaps what is meant is his being greater than them in sovereignty and worldly affairs, even if they shared with him in prophethood," is dispelled, because we have explained that worldly circumstances are of no account beside the position of prophethood.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and we were certainly sinners.﴾ It has been said: the sinner (khati') is one who commits a sin deliberately, and a distinction is made between the khati' and the mukhti' (one who errs). On account of this distinction, one who strives in legal rulings and does not hit the correct answer is called mukhti', and is not called khati'. Most of the commentators hold that what they apologised for was their act of throwing him into the well, selling him, and removing him far from the house and the father. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: They did not apologise to him for that, because that occurred from them before puberty, so it is not a sin and is not apologised for. They only apologised insofar as they erred after that, by not informing their father of what they had done, so that he would know that he was alive and that the wolf had not eaten him. This statement is weak from several aspects:

The first aspect: We have explained that it is not permissible to say that they undertook those acts in their childhood, because it is unlikely for someone like Ya'qub to send a group of non-adult boys without sending with them an intelligent man who would prevent them from what is not fitting and guide them to what is fitting.

The second aspect: Suppose the matter is as al-Jubba'i mentioned. Still, we say: at most, it does not become obligatory to apologise for that, but it is possible to say that apologising for it is good. The proof of this is that when a wrongdoer repents, his punishment is removed, and then he may repeat repentance and apology a second time. Thus we know that a person may also repent when repentance is not obligatory upon him.

Know that when they acknowledged his favour upon them and their being criminals and sinners, Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you.﴾ In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: At-tathrib means reproach (tawbikh). From it is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him apply the prescribed punishment to her, and let him not reproach her (yuthrribha)," meaning, let him not shame her with the fornication. So his saying "no reproach (tathrib)" means no rebuke and no blame. The root of tathrib is from ath-thurb, which is the fat that covers the paunch. Its meaning is the removal of the fat, just as tajlid is the removal of the skin. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: Seeking needs from the young is easier than seeking them from the elders. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 94–98:**

[Verse] Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the caravan departed, their father said: "Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph, if you did not think me senile."﴾ ﴿They said: "By Allah, you are surely in your old error."﴾ ﴿Then when the bearer of good news came, he cast it upon his face, and he regained his sight. He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

It is said: *fassala* (فَصَلَ) fulan min ʿind fulan *fusulan* (فُصُولًا), meaning he left from his presence. And *fassala* minni ilayhi kitaban means he sent a letter to him through someone. *Fassala* can be intransitive (lazim) or transitive (muta'addi). When it is intransitive, its verbal noun is *fusul*; when it is transitive, its verbal noun is *fasl*.

[Al-Razi] said: When the caravan left Egypt heading toward Canaan, Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) said to those present with him from his family, his relatives, and his grandchildren: ﴿Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph, if you did not think me senile.﴾ This statement was not made to his sons, because they were absent, as shown by his (peace be upon him) saying to them: ﴿Go and search for news of Joseph and his brother﴾ (Yusuf: 87). The scholars differed on the distance. It was said: a journey of eight days. It was said: ten days.

[p. 166]

It was also said: eighty farsakhs.

They differed on how that scent reached him. Mujahid said: a wind blew and stirred the shirt, so the fragrances of Paradise spread in this world and reached Yaʿqub, and he smelled the scent of Paradise. He (peace be upon him) knew that there was no scent of Paradise in this world except that which came from that shirt. Therefore he said: ﴿Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph.﴾

Al-Wahidi related with his chain from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "As for His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it upon my father's face; he will regain sight﴾ (Yusuf: 93): when the tyrant Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He clothed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing with him. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) then passed that shirt on to Ishaq, Ishaq passed it to Yaʿqub, and Yaʿqub passed it to Yusuf. He placed it in a silver tube and hung it around his neck, and he was thrown into the well while the shirt was around his neck." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine.⁠﴾

The verified view is that He, the Exalted, conveyed that scent to him as a manifestation of miracles, because the arrival of a scent from such a great distance contradicts the normal course of things. It is therefore a miracle, and it must be a miracle for one of the two (Yaʿqub or Yusuf). The more likely view is that it was a miracle for Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) when he reported it, and they attributed to him in this statement what was not fitting. So it became clear that the matter was as he had said, and it was thus a miracle for him.

The scholars of meaning (ahl al-maʿani) said: Allah, the Exalted, conveyed to him the scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him) at the end of the period of trial and at the coming of the time of relief and joy, from a distant place. He prevented the news from reaching him, even though the two towns were close to each other, for a period of eighty years. This indicates that every ease during a time of trial is difficult, and every difficulty during a time of prosperity is easy.

The meaning of ﴿I sense﴾ (*la-ajidu*, لَأجِدُ) is "I smell." He expressed it with the word *wujud* (وُجُود, "finding"), because it is a finding of it through the sense of smell. As for His saying: ﴿were it not that you think me senile﴾ (*lawla an tufannidun*, لَوْلا أنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ), Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: *afnada* (أفْنَدَ) is said of a man when he grieves and his mind changes, and *funnida* (فُنِّدَ) is said when he is foolish and this is attributed to him. From al-Asmaʿi: when a man's speech becomes excessive due to senility (*kharaf*, خَرَف), then he is *mufannid*.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It is said: "a shaykh who is *mufannid*," but it is not said: "an old woman who is *mufannida*," because she was not, in her youth, a person of judgment who could be made senile in her old age. So His saying: ﴿were it not that you think me senile⁠﴾ means: were it not that you attribute to me senility (*kharaf*).

When Yaʿqub mentioned this, those present with him said: ﴿By Allah, you are surely in your old error.⁠﴾

Regarding *ḍalal* (ضَلال, "error") here, there are several views.

The first: Muqatil said: by *ḍalal* here he means *shaqa'* (شَقاء, "misery"), meaning the misery of this world. The meaning is: you are surely in your ancient misery, through what you suffer of grief over Yusuf. Muqatil cited His saying: ﴿Indeed, we would then be in error and madness﴾ (al-Qamar: 24), meaning: in the misery of our worldly life.

Qatadah said: ﴿in your old error⁠﴾ means ﴿in your ancient love⁠﴾, that you do not forget him and are not distracted from him. This is like their saying: ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error⁠﴾ (Yusuf: 8).

Then Qatadah said: They used a harsh expression, which they should not have used toward a prophet of Allah. Al-Hasan said: They addressed him in this way because they believed that Yusuf had died, and Yaʿqub, in his preoccupation with remembering him, had strayed from right guidance and correctness.

His saying: ﴿Then when the bearer of good news came⁠﴾: regarding *an* (أنْ) in ﴿fa-lamma an⁠﴾ there are two views.

The first: it has no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*, إعراب). It is sometimes mentioned, as here, and sometimes omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Then when fear left Ibrahim⁠﴾ (Hud: 74). Both usages exist in the poetry of the Arabs.

The second: the Basrans said: it, together with *ma* (ما), is in a nominative position as the subject of an implied verb. Its estimate is: "then when it became apparent that the bearer of good news had come," meaning the coming of the bearer of good news became apparent, and so the implied agent was omitted.

The majority of the exegetes said: the bearer of good news was Yahuda. He said: "I went with the shirt stained with blood and said that Yusuf had been eaten by a wolf. Today I will go with the shirt and gladden him as I saddened him."

His saying: ﴿he cast it upon his face⁠﴾: meaning the bearer of good news cast the shirt upon Yaʿqub's face. Or it is said: Yaʿqub cast it upon his own face. ﴿And he regained his sight⁠﴾ means he returned to seeing. The meaning of *irtidad* (ارْتِداد) is the reversion of a thing to a state it was once in. His saying: ﴿and he regained his sight⁠﴾ means Allah made him see, just as it is said: "the palm tree grew tall," and Allah made it tall.

They differed about this. Some said: he had become completely blind. Allah made him see at this time.

Others said: rather, his sight had weakened from excessive weeping and great grief. When they cast the shirt upon his face and he was given the good news of Yusuf's life (peace be upon him), his joy grew, his chest expanded, and his griefs disappeared. At that moment his sight became strong and the deficiency left him. At this point he said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?⁠﴾

The intended meaning is his knowledge of Yusuf's life through a vision, because this meaning is the one connected to what preceded. It refers to His saying before: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know⁠﴾ (Yusuf: 86).

It is related that he asked the bearer of good news: "How is Yusuf?" He said: "He is the king of Egypt." He said: "What do I do with kingship! On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Then the sons of Yaʿqub began to apologize to him: ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."⁠﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."⁠﴾

The apparent meaning of the speech is that he did not ask forgiveness for them at that moment, but rather promised that he would ask forgiveness for them afterward. The scholars differed on the reason for this meaning in several views:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and most of the scholars said: he intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *sahar* (السَّحَر, the last part of the night), because that time is the most suitable for hoping for a response.

The second: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said in another narration: he delayed the seeking of forgiveness until the night of Friday, because it is the most suitable time for a response.

The third: he wished to know whether they had truly repented or not, and whether their repentance was accompanied by complete sincerity or not.

The fourth: he asked forgiveness for them at that moment, and His saying ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you⁠﴾ means: I continue to ask forgiveness in the future. It is related that he used to ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for more than twenty years. It was also said: he stood to pray at a certain time, and when he finished he raised his hands to the sky and said: "O Allah, forgive me my anguish over Yusuf and my weak patience with him, and forgive my sons what they did against Yusuf (peace be upon him)." Then Allah revealed to him: "I have forgiven you and all of them."

It is related that the sons of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) said to Yaʿqub, when fear and weeping had overwhelmed them: "What good will it do us if we are not forgiven?" The old man faced the qibla standing and supplicated, Yusuf stood behind him saying "Amin," and they stood behind the two of them, humble and submissive, for twenty years, until their patience ran out and they thought it was destruction. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, has answered your supplication concerning your children, and has bound their covenants after you to prophethood." People differed about their prophethood, and this is well known.
