He (peace be upon him) knew that there was no scent of Paradise in this world except that which came from that shirt. Therefore he said: ﴿Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph.﴾

Al-Wahidi related with his chain from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "As for His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it upon my father's face; he will regain sight﴾ (Yusuf: 93): when the tyrant Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He clothed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing with him. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) then passed that shirt on to Ishaq, Ishaq passed it to Yaʿqub, and Yaʿqub passed it to Yusuf. He placed it in a silver tube and hung it around his neck, and he was thrown into the well while the shirt was around his neck." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine.⁠﴾

The verified view is that He, the Exalted, conveyed that scent to him as a manifestation of miracles, because the arrival of a scent from such a great distance contradicts the normal course of things. It is therefore a miracle, and it must be a miracle for one of the two (Yaʿqub or Yusuf). The more likely view is that it was a miracle for Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) when he reported it, and they attributed to him in this statement what was not fitting. So it became clear that the matter was as he had said, and it was thus a miracle for him.

The scholars of meaning (ahl al-maʿani) said: Allah, the Exalted, conveyed to him the scent of Yusuf (peace be upon him) at the end of the period of trial and at the coming of the time of relief and joy, from a distant place. He prevented the news from reaching him, even though the two towns were close to each other, for a period of eighty years. This indicates that every ease during a time of trial is difficult, and every difficulty during a time of prosperity is easy.

The meaning of ﴿I sense﴾ (*la-ajidu*, لَأجِدُ) is "I smell." He expressed it with the word *wujud* (وُجُود, "finding"), because it is a finding of it through the sense of smell. As for His saying: ﴿were it not that you think me senile﴾ (*lawla an tufannidun*, لَوْلا أنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ), Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: *afnada* (أفْنَدَ) is said of a man when he grieves and his mind changes, and *funnida* (فُنِّدَ) is said when he is foolish and this is attributed to him. From al-Asmaʿi: when a man's speech becomes excessive due to senility (*kharaf*, خَرَف), then he is *mufannid*.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It is said: "a shaykh who is *mufannid*," but it is not said: "an old woman who is *mufannida*," because she was not, in her youth, a person of judgment who could be made senile in her old age. So His saying: ﴿were it not that you think me senile⁠﴾ means: were it not that you attribute to me senility (*kharaf*).

When Yaʿqub mentioned this, those present with him said: ﴿By Allah, you are surely in your old error.⁠﴾

Regarding *ḍalal* (ضَلال, "error") here, there are several views.

The first: Muqatil said: by *ḍalal* here he means *shaqa'* (شَقاء, "misery"), meaning the misery of this world. The meaning is: you are surely in your ancient misery, through what you suffer of grief over Yusuf. Muqatil cited His saying: ﴿Indeed, we would then be in error and madness﴾ (al-Qamar: 24), meaning: in the misery of our worldly life.

Qatadah said: ﴿in your old error⁠﴾ means ﴿in your ancient love⁠﴾, that you do not forget him and are not distracted from him. This is like their saying: ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error⁠﴾ (Yusuf: 8).

Then Qatadah said: They used a harsh expression, which they should not have used toward a prophet of Allah. Al-Hasan said: They addressed him in this way because they believed that Yusuf had died, and Yaʿqub, in his preoccupation with remembering him, had strayed from right guidance and correctness.

His saying: ﴿Then when the bearer of good news came⁠﴾: regarding *an* (أنْ) in ﴿fa-lamma an⁠﴾ there are two views.

The first: it has no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*, إعراب). It is sometimes mentioned, as here, and sometimes omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Then when fear left Ibrahim⁠﴾ (Hud: 74). Both usages exist in the poetry of the Arabs.

The second: the Basrans said: it, together with *ma* (ما), is in a nominative position as the subject of an implied verb. Its estimate is: "then when it became apparent that the bearer of good news had come," meaning the coming of the bearer of good news became apparent, and so the implied agent was omitted.

The majority of the exegetes said: the bearer of good news was Yahuda. He said: "I went with the shirt stained with blood and said that Yusuf had been eaten by a wolf. Today I will go with the shirt and gladden him as I saddened him."

His saying: ﴿he cast it upon his face⁠﴾: meaning the bearer of good news cast the shirt upon Yaʿqub's face. Or it is said: Yaʿqub cast it upon his own face. ﴿And he regained his sight⁠﴾ means he returned to seeing. The meaning of *irtidad* (ارْتِداد) is the reversion of a thing to a state it was once in. His saying: ﴿and he regained his sight⁠﴾ means Allah made him see, just as it is said: "the palm tree grew tall," and Allah made it tall.

They differed about this. Some said: he had become completely blind. Allah made him see at this time.

Others said: rather, his sight had weakened from excessive weeping and great grief. When they cast the shirt upon his face and he was given the good news of Yusuf's life (peace be upon him), his joy grew, his chest expanded, and his griefs disappeared. At that moment his sight became strong and the deficiency left him. At this point he said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?⁠﴾

The intended meaning is his knowledge of Yusuf's life through a vision, because this meaning is the one connected to what preceded. It refers to His saying before: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know⁠﴾ (Yusuf: 86).

It is related that he asked the bearer of good news: "How is Yusuf?" He said: "He is the king of Egypt." He said: "What do I do with kingship! On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Then the sons of Yaʿqub began to apologize to him: ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."⁠﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."⁠﴾

The apparent meaning of the speech is that he did not ask forgiveness for them at that moment, but rather promised that he would ask forgiveness for them afterward. The scholars differed on the reason for this meaning in several views:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and most of the scholars said: he intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *sahar* (السَّحَر, the last part of the night), because that time is the most suitable for hoping for a response.

The second: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said in another narration: he delayed the seeking of forgiveness until the night of Friday, because it is the most suitable time for a response.

The third: he wished to know whether they had truly repented or not, and whether their repentance was accompanied by complete sincerity or not.

The fourth: he asked forgiveness for them at that moment, and His saying ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you⁠﴾ means: I continue to ask forgiveness in the future. It is related that he used to ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for more than twenty years. It was also said: he stood to pray at a certain time, and when he finished he raised his hands to the sky and said: "O Allah, forgive me my anguish over Yusuf and my weak patience with him, and forgive my sons what they did against Yusuf (peace be upon him)." Then Allah revealed to him: "I have forgiven you and all of them."

It is related that the sons of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) said to Yaʿqub, when fear and weeping had overwhelmed them: "What good will it do us if we are not forgiven?" The old man faced the qibla standing and supplicated, Yusuf stood behind him saying "Amin," and they stood behind the two of them, humble and submissive, for twenty years, until their patience ran out and they thought it was destruction. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, has answered your supplication concerning your children, and has bound their covenants after you to prophethood." People differed about their prophethood, and this is well known.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 99:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself and said, "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."﴾ ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true. And He was certainly good to me when He took me out of prison and brought you from the desert after Satan had caused a breach between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise."﴾

Know that it has been related that Joseph, peace be upon him, sent to his father a provision and two hundred mounts so that he and those with him could prepare to come to him. Joseph, peace be upon him, went out, with the king, with four thousand troops, the nobles, and the people of Egypt in their entirety, to meet Jacob, peace be upon him, while he was walking, leaning on Judah. He looked at the horses and the people and said, "O Judah, is this Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said, "No, this is your son Joseph." Joseph then went to begin with the greeting, but he was prevented from doing so. Jacob, peace be upon him, said, "Peace be upon you." It is also said that Jacob and his sons entered Egypt, and they were seventy-two, men and women, and they left it with Moses, and their fighting men were six hundred thousand and five hundred and some seventy men, besides the children and the elderly.

As for His saying, ﴿he drew his parents to himself﴾, there are two discussions in it.

The first discussion: concerning what is meant by His saying "his parents," there are two opinions.

The first: what is meant is his father and his mother. According to this opinion, it is said that his mother was still alive until that time. It is also said that she had died, but Allah, exalted is He, brought her back to life and raised her from her grave until she prostrated to him, in fulfillment of the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him.

The second opinion: what is meant is his father and his maternal aunt, because his mother died in childbirth with his brother Benjamin. It is said that Benjamin in Hebrew means "son of the sorrow." When his mother died, his father married her sister. Allah, exalted is He, named her with one of the two parents, because the stepmother (rabbah) is called "mother" for taking the place of the mother, or because the maternal aunt is a mother just as the paternal uncle is a father. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾ (al-Baqarah: 133).

The second discussion: "he drew his parents to himself" means he embraced them and held them close to himself.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of their entering upon him before their entering Egypt?

We say: it is as if, when he met them, he lodged them in a house there or in a tent, so they entered upon him, and he drew his parents to himself and said to them, ﴿Enter Egypt.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security﴾, there are several discussions in it.

The first discussion: al-Suddi said that he said this statement before they entered Egypt, because he had met them. This is what we have established. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that what is meant by His saying, ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ is: remain there in security. He called staying "entering" because one of the two is connected with the other.

The second discussion: the exception, which is His saying ﴿if Allah wills﴾. There are two opinions regarding it.

The first: it refers to the security, not to the entering. The meaning: "Enter Egypt in security, if Allah wills." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ (al-Fath: 27). It is also said that it refers to the entering, according to the opinion we mentioned, that he said these words to them before they entered Egypt.

The third discussion: the meaning of His saying ﴿in security﴾ is: concerning yourselves, your wealth, and your families, you fear no one. They had previously feared the kings of Egypt. It is also said: secure from famine, hardship, and poverty. And it is said: secure from fear that Joseph would harm them for the earlier crime.

[Page 169]

As for His words, ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾, the lexicographers said: *al-ʿarsh* (throne) is a high couch. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And she has a great throne﴾ (al-Naml: 23). The *ʿarsh* here means the couch on which Yusuf used to sit. As for His words, ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, there is a difficulty in it, because Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, was Yusuf's father, and the right of fatherhood is great. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to parents﴾ (al-Isra: 23). So He joined the right of parents with His own right. Also, he was an old man, and a young man must honour an old man.

The third view: he was one of the great prophets. Although Yusuf was a prophet, Yaʿqub was higher in rank than him.

The fourth view: Yaʿqub's striving and diligence in multiplying acts of obedience were greater than Yusuf's. Since these many aspects were combined, it would require that Yusuf exert himself greatly in serving Yaʿqub. How, then, could Yusuf permit that Yaʿqub prostrate to him? This is the statement of the question.

The answer to it comes in several aspects.

The first aspect, which is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta: the meaning of this verse is that they fell down *for him*, that is, on account of his finding (his brothers and parents reunited with him), and they prostrated to Allah the Exalted. The essence of the matter is that this prostration was a prostration of thanks. The one prostrated to was Allah, but that prostration was done on his account. The evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is that His words, ﴿and he raised his parents upon the throne and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, indicate that they climbed that couch and then prostrated to Him. Had they prostrated to Yusuf, they would have prostrated to him before climbing the couch, because that would be more expressive of humility.

If they say: this interpretation does not match His words, ﴿O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾, and what is meant by it is His words, ﴿I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ (Yusuf: 4).

We say: rather, this matches, and what is meant by His words ﴿and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ is *for my sake*, that is, that they prostrated to Allah seeking my welfare and striving to raise my station. Since this is a possibility, the question falls away.

In my view this interpretation is the necessary one, because it is not improbable, given Yusuf's intellect and religion, that he would be content for his father to prostrate to him, in light of his father's precedence in the rights of begetting, old age, knowledge, religion, and perfection of prophethood.

The second aspect of the answer is to say: they made Yusuf like a *qibla* (direction of prayer), and they prostrated to Allah in thanks for the blessing of finding him. This interpretation is fine, for one says, "I prayed to the Kaʿba," just as one says, "I prayed towards the Kaʿba."

Hassan said in verse:

*I did not know that the matter had turned away from Hashim, then from them, from Abu al-Hasan.*
*Was he not the first to pray towards your qibla, and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the sunan?*

This shows that it is permissible to say, "So-and-so prayed to the qibla," and likewise it is permissible to say, "He prostrated to the qibla." His words, ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, mean that they made him like the qibla, then they prostrated to Allah in thanks for the blessing of finding him.

The third aspect of the answer: prostration is sometimes used to mean humility, as in the saying:

*You see the hills before them prostrating to the hooves [of the horses].*

Humility was what was meant here. However, this is problematic, because Allah the Exalted said, ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, and "falling down" to the prostration indicates performing the prostration in its most complete form. It is answered that "falling down" may mean merely "passing by." Allah the Exalted said, ﴿they did not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ (al-Furqan: 73), meaning, they did not pass by them.

[Page 170]

The fourth aspect of the answer: we say that the pronoun in His words, ﴿and they fell down before him﴾, is certainly not referring to the two parents. Otherwise He would have said, "and they fell down before him in prostration." Rather, the pronoun refers to his brothers and all others who used to enter upon him to congratulate him. The implied meaning is: ﴿and he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ as an exaggeration in honouring them both. As for the brothers and the rest of those who entered, they fell down before him in prostration.

If they say: this does not fit His words, ﴿O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾.

We say: the interpretation of a dream need not match the dream in form and description in every respect. The prostration of the stars, the sun, and the moon is an expression of the honour that the great among people give him. There is no doubt that Yaʿqub's journey with his sons from Kanaan to Egypt for his sake was in the utmost honouring of him. This degree is enough for the dream's fulfilment. As for the interpretation being exactly equal to the dream in description and form, no intelligent person has ever required this.

The fifth aspect of the answer: perhaps the act that signifies greeting and honour at that time was prostration, and their intention in the prostration was to honour him. This is extremely far-fetched, because exaggeration in honouring was more fitting for Yusuf than for Yaʿqub. Had the matter been as you say, it would have been obligatory for Yusuf to prostrate to Yaʿqub, peace be upon him.

The sixth aspect: it may be said that perhaps his brothers were moved by pride and haughtiness not to prostrate to him in humility. Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, knew that if they did not do this, it would become a cause for the stirring up of strife and the emergence of old hatreds after they had been dormant. So he, peace be upon him, despite his lofty station and great right by reason of fatherhood, old age, precedence in religion and prophethood, and knowledge, performed that prostration, so that their witnessing of it would become a cause for the removal of pride and aversion from their hearts. Do you not see that when a great sultan appoints a *muhtasib* (market inspector), when he wishes to install him, he empowers him to establish the *hisba* (enjoining good and forbidding wrong in the market) over them, so that no one in the heart retains any dispute with that muhtasib over establishing the hisba? Likewise here.

The seventh aspect: perhaps Allah the Exalted commanded Yaʿqub to perform that prostration for a hidden wisdom that none knows but Him, just as He commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam for a wisdom that none knows but Him. Yusuf was not content with this in his heart, but when he knew that Allah had commanded him to do so, he remained silent.

Then the Exalted related that when Yusuf saw this state, ﴿he said: O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said that when he saw the prostration of his parents and brothers, it terrified him and his skin shivered, and he said to Yaʿqub, "This is the interpretation of my dream from before." I say: this strengthens the seventh aspect. It is as if he is saying: "O my father, it is not fitting for one of your stature in knowledge, religion, and prophethood to prostrate to his son. However, this is a matter you were commanded, a duty you were charged with, for the dreams of prophets are true, just as the dream of Ibrahim, that he slaughter his son, became the cause for that slaughter to become obligatory upon him in wakefulness. Likewise, this dream that Yusuf saw and related to Yaʿqub became the cause for that prostration to become obligatory." For this reason, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, relates that when Yusuf, peace be upon him, saw that, it terrified him and his skin shivered, but he said nothing. I say: it is not far-fetched that this was part of the completion of Allah the Exalted's testing of Yaʿqub. It is as if it were said to him: "You were always eager to be united with him and always grieved at separation from him. So when you find him, prostrate to him." Thus the command to that prostration was part of the completion of the test. And Allah knows best the realities of matters.

[Page 171]

The second discussion: they differed about the length of time between this moment and the dream. It was said: eighty years; it was said: seventy; it was said: forty, and this is the view of most. For this reason they say: the interpretation of the dream came true only after forty years. It was said: eighteen years. From al-Hasan: he was thrown into the well when he was seventeen years old, and he remained in slavery and prisons for eighty years, then he reached his father and relatives, and he lived after that for twenty-three years, so his lifespan was one hundred and twenty years. And Allah knows best the realities of matters.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and He has been good to me﴾, that is, *to* me. One says, "He was good *to* me" and "He was good *with* me."

Kuthayyir said:

*Treat us ill or treat us well, you are not blameworthy among us, nor are you disliked when you turn away.*

﴿when He brought me out of the prison﴾, and he did not mention his being brought out of the well, for several reasons.

The first: he said to his brothers, ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, and had he mentioned the incident of the well, that would have been a rebuke to them, so his omission of it was a form of generosity.

The second: when he came out of the well, he did not become a king; rather they made him a slave. But when he came out of the prison, they made him a king, so this release was closer to being complete favour.

The third: when he was brought out of the well, he fell into the harms caused by the accusation of the woman. When he was brought out of the prison, he reached his father and brothers and the accusation was removed. So this was closer to benefit.

The fourth: al-Wahidi said: the blessing in his release from prison is greater, because his entry into prison was due to a sin he had intended, and this should be understood as a matter of natural inclination and the soul's desire. Although this falls within the scope of pardon as regards others, it may have been a cause for being taken to account in his case, because the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of the near ones (*muqarrabun*).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: concerning the verse there are two views.

The first view: "brought you from the desert," that is, from the beginning. Al-Wahidi said: *al-badw* (desert) is the open expanse of land where a person appears from afar. Its root is from *bada yabdu budūwan*, then the place was named with the verbal noun, so one says *badw* and *hadar* (settled land). Yaʿqub and his sons were in the land of Kanaan, people of livestock and open country.

The second view: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Yaʿqub had moved to Bada and settled there, and from there he came to Yusuf. He had a mosque there beneath its mountain.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Bada is the name of a known place. It is said that it lies between Shaghb and Bada, and these are two places which Kuthayyir mentioned together, saying:

*You are the one who made Shaghb beloved to me, and Bada; and my homelands are other lands than these two.*

On this view, *al-badw* means intending this place, which is called Bada. One says, "The people went to Bada, badwan," just as one says, "The people went to the lowland, ghawran," meaning they went to the lowland. So the meaning of the verse is: "and brought you from the intention of Bada." On this view, Yaʿqub and his sons were townspeople (*hadariyyun*), because *al-badw* was not meant as the desert but as the intention to Bada. Up to here is the statement of al-Wahidi in *al-Basit*.

The second issue: our companions (the Ashʿarites) used this verse to show that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah the Exalted. For Yusuf attributed his coming out of the prison to himself in His words, ﴿when He brought me out of the prison﴾, and their coming from the desert he attributed to Himself, glorified be He, in His words, ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾. This is explicit that the very act of the servant is the act of Allah the Exalted. (Those who oppose this) interpret it as meaning that this occurred through Allah the Exalted's empowerment and facilitation, a departure from the apparent meaning.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿after Satan had stirred up discord between me and my brothers﴾. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *nazagha* means he corrupted between us and led astray. Its root is from *nazagha al-rākid al-dābba*, when the rider spurred the mount and urged it to run. One says, "nazaghahu" and "nasaghahu," when he pricked him.

Know that al-Jubbaʾi, al-Kaʿbi, and al-Qadi argued with this verse against determinism (*jabr*). They said: Allah the Exalted related of Yusuf, peace be upon him, that he attributed the kindness to Allah and attributed the stirring of discord to Satan. Had that (discord) also been from the All-Merciful, it would have been necessary that it not be attributed except to Him, as with the blessings.

The answer: attributing this act to Satan is figurative, for according to you, Satan cannot reach hidden speech. Yet Allah has related of him, saying, ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me﴾ (Ibrahim: 22). So it is established that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires attributing this act to Satan, although that is not the case.

Moreover, if a person's committing disobedience is due to Satan, then Satan's committing disobedience, if it is due to another satan, would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. And if it is not due to another satan, then the same should be said regarding the human being. Thus it is established that a person's engaging in ignorance and wickedness is not due to Satan. Nor is it due to himself, because no one's nature inclines toward choosing ignorance and wickedness which bring about blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. And since his falling into disbelief and wickedness must have a cause that brings it about, and both divisions have been refuted, nothing remains except that it is from God, exalted is He. Furthermore, what confirms this is that the verse preceding this verse, which is His saying: ﴿When He brought me out of the prison and brought you from the desert﴾, is explicit that everything is from God, exalted is He.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾. The meaning is that the gathering together of Joseph with his father and brothers, along with affection, love, a pleasant life and peace of mind, was, from the standpoint of reason, extremely remote; however, He, exalted is He, is Subtle, so when He wills the occurrence of something, He facilitates its causes, and it occurs, even if it was extremely remote from occurring.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾. I mean that His being Subtle in His actions is only because He is All-Knowing of all the possible considerations, which have no end. Thus He knows the manner by which that difficult matter is made easy to attain. And "Wise" means: firm in His action (muhkim), judging in His decree (hakim), wise in His actions, free from futility and falsehood. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 101–105 (part 1 of 2)**

[Page 173]

God the Exalted says: ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom and taught me [some] of the interpretation of events, Originator of the heavens and the earth. You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die in submission [to You], and join me with the righteous.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** It is narrated that Yusuf, peace be upon him, took Ya'qub (Jacob) by the hand and walked him through his treasuries. He showed him the treasuries of gold and silver, the treasuries of jewelry, the treasuries of garments, and the treasuries of weapons. When he brought him to the storehouses of papers (qarati's), he said: "My son, how heedless you are! Here are these papers, and what you wrote to me from eight stages away!" [Ya'qub] said: "Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, forbade me from it." [Yusuf] said: "Ask him about the reason." [Ya'qub] said: "You are closer to him than I am." So [Yusuf] asked him, and Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "God commanded me to do that because of your saying: 'I fear that the wolf will eat him' (12:13). Why did you not fear Me?"

It is also narrated that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, stayed with him for twenty-four years. When his death drew near, he instructed [Yusuf] to bury him in al-Sham (Syria), beside his father Ishaq (Isaac). [Yusuf] went himself, buried him, and then returned to Egypt. He lived after his father for twenty-three years. At that point he wished for the kingdom of the Hereafter, and so he wished for death. It was said: no prophet wished for it before him or after him. God then caused him to die in a good and pure state. The people of Egypt disputed over his burial, each one wishing to bury him in their own quarter, until they were on the verge of fighting. They then judged that the best course was to make for him a chest of marble, place him in it, and bury him in the Nile at a place where the water flows over him, and then reaches Egypt, so that his blessing would reach everyone. Ephraim (Ifra'im) and Misha were born to him; Nun was born to Ephraim; and Yusha' (Joshua), the servant of Musa (Moses), was born to Nun. Yusuf was then buried there until God raised up Musa, who brought his bones out of Egypt and buried them beside the grave of his father.

**The second issue:** The word *min* ("of") in His saying ﴿of the kingdom﴾ and ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'id), because he was given only part of the kingdom of this world, or part of the kingdom of Egypt, and part of the interpretation [of events]. Al-Asamm said: He only said "of the kingdom" because there was a king above him.

Know that the levels of existing things are three. The first is the Influencer that is not influenced, and that is God, Exalted and Sanctified. The second is that which is influenced but does not influence, and that is the world of bodies, for they are receptive to shaping, forming, various attributes and contrary accidents, and so they have no influence on anything at all. These two categories are very far apart. Between them lies a third category, which both influences and is influenced, and that is the world of spirits. The distinctive property of the substance of spirits is that they receive effect and direction from the world of the light of the majesty of God. Then, when they turn toward the world of bodies, they act upon it and affect it. Thus the spirit is connected to the world of bodies through direction and management of it, and it is connected to the world of divine matters through knowledge and recognition.

God's saying ﴿You have given me [some] of the kingdom﴾ points to the soul's attachment to the world of bodies, and His saying ﴿and taught me [some] of the interpretation of events﴾ points to its attachment to the presence of the majesty of God. Since there is no limit to the degrees of these two kinds in perfection and deficiency, in strength and weakness, in clarity and obscurity, it is impossible for a human to attain from them anything but a finite measure. Therefore what is actually attained is a part of the parts of kingship and a part of the parts of knowledge. For this reason He used the word *min*, because it indicates partiality.

Then He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions.

**First discussion:** On the linguistic meaning of the word *fatir*.

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "I did not know the meaning of *fatir* until two Bedouins brought a dispute to me about a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who *fatartuha* (originated it), and I began digging it.'"

The lexicographers said: The root meaning of *fatr* in the language is splitting. It is said: *fatara nab al-ba'ir* when the tusk of the camel appeared; *fatartu al-shay'* and *infatara* means I split it and it split; and the earth *tafattarat* with plants, and the tree with leaves, when it cracked open. This is its original meaning in the language. Then it came to be used as an expression for bringing into existence, because that thing, in its state of non-existence, is as though in darkness and concealment; when it enters existence, it is as though it has split away from non-existence, and that thing has come out of it.

**Second discussion:** The word *fatir* may be thought to be an expression for bringing a thing into being out of pure non-existence, based on the derivation we have mentioned. However, the truth is that it does not indicate this, and there are several proofs for this:

The first: He said ﴿Praise belongs to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ (35:1), and then God made clear that He created them from smoke, when He said: ﴿Then He turned to the sky when it was smoke﴾ (41:11). This shows that the word *fatir* does not indicate that He produced that thing from pure non-existence.

The second: He said, ﴿the nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾ (30:30), although God created mankind from dust. He said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out a second time﴾ (20:55).

The third: A thing comes into existence only when its matter and form are both present, like a jug. A jug exists only when that particular matter has become characterized by that particular attribute. When the form is absent, that composite does not exist; and when that form is brought into being, [the maker] becomes the one who brings that jug into being. We therefore know that being the one who brings about the *form* does not necessitate being the one who brings about the *matter* of the jug. It is thus established that the word *fatir* does not indicate that God is the one who brought into being the components from which the heavens and the earth were composed. Rather, we come to know that He brought them into being through rational proofs, not through the wording of the Qur'an.

Know that His saying ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ gives the impression that the creation of the heavens precedes the creation of the earth, according to those who hold that the particle *waw* (and) indicates sequence. Reason also confirms this, because the determination of the encompassing thing necessitates the determination of the center, but the determination of the center does not necessitate the determination of the encompassing thing, since it is possible for countless encompassing things to surround a single center; whereas for one encompassing thing only one specific center can exist.

Also, the wording indicates that the heavens are many and the earth is one. The wisdom behind this we have already mentioned in His saying ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ (6:1).

**Third discussion:** Al-Zajjaj said: Its (*fatir*'s) accusative case has two possibilities:

The first: it is an adjective of ﴿Lord﴾, which is a vocative construction in the accusative position.

The second: it may be placed in the accusative as a second vocative.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The meaning is: You are the One who takes charge of the setting right of all my affairs in this world and the Hereafter. Thus He joined the perishable kingdom to the enduring kingdom. This indicates that faith and obedience are a word from God, the Exalted, for if they came from the servant, then the one who manages his welfare would be the servant himself, and in that case the generality of His saying ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom﴾ would be nullified.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Cause me to die in submission [to You], and join me with the righteous.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the Prophet, peace be upon him, related from Jibril, peace be upon him, from the Lord of Might, that He said: "Whoever is occupied with remembering Me instead of asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." For this reason, whoever wishes to supplicate must first offer praise to God. Here, Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he wished to mention supplication, put praise before it, which is His saying ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom and taught me [some] of the interpretation of events, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. Then after it he mentioned the supplication, which is His saying ﴿Cause me to die in submission [to You], and join me with the righteous.﴾ A parallel to this is what the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), may the blessings of God be upon him, did in His saying: ﴿The One who created me, and He guides me﴾ (26:78), up to His saying ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom﴾ (26:83). Everything from the beginning to there is praise of God, and then His saying ﴿My Lord, grant me...﴾ through to the end of the speech is supplication. So it is here as well.

**The second issue:** They differed over whether His saying ﴿Cause me to die in submission﴾ is a request from him for death or not. Qatada said: He asked his Lord to join him [to the righteous, in the hereafter], and no prophet had ever wished for death before him. Many of the commentators follow this view. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said, in the narration of Ata, meaning: "When You cause me to die, then let my death be upon the religion of Islam." This is thus a request that God make his death occur in Islam, and there is nothing in it indicating that he asked for death itself.

Know that the wording is suitable for both meanings, and it is not far-fetched for a rational man, when his intellect is perfected, to wish for death and to greatly desire it, for several reasons. Among them: the perfection of the human soul, as we have explained, lies in being knowledgeable of divine matters, and in being a king and an owner who directs material things. We have stated that the degrees of variation in these two kinds are unlimited, and that absolute perfection in them belongs to God alone, while everything below that is deficient. When the deficient one becomes aware of its deficiency and tastes the pleasure of absolute perfection, it remains in restlessness and the pain of seeking. Since absolute perfection belongs only to God, and its attainment is impossible for a human, it follows that the human will remain forever in the restlessness of seeking and the pain of toil. When a human recognizes this condition, he realizes there is no way to relieve his soul of this toil except through death, and at that point he wishes for death.

The second reason for wishing for death is that the orators and eloquent speakers, although they expand at length in condemning this world, the essence of their speech comes down to three matters:

The first: these pleasures are quick to vanish, close to extinction, and the pain that occurs when they disappear is greater than the pleasure experienced when they are possessed.

The second: they are not pure, but are mixed with troubles and disturbances.

The third: base people share in them with the excellent, and indeed the portion of the base is often far greater than the portion of the excellent. These three aspects make one averse to these pleasures. When the wise person realizes that there is no way to obtain these pleasures except along with these three repellent aspects, he inevitably wishes for death so as to be freed from these afflictions.

The third reason, which is the strongest according to the verifying scholars (may God have mercy on them all), is that these bodily pleasures have no real substance; their essence is only the removal of pains. Thus the pleasure of eating is an expression for the removal of the pain of hunger, and the pleasure of intercourse is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the tingling that arises from the discharge of semen into its receptacles.

The pleasure of command and leadership is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the desire for revenge and the pursuit of leadership. Since the essence of these pleasures is nothing but the removal of pain, they are inevitably regarded by intelligent people as lowly, base, debased, and deficient. At that point, a person wishes for death in order to be freed from the need for these base conditions.

The fourth reason: the avenues of worldly pleasures are few, and they are of three kinds: the pleasure of eating, the pleasure of intercourse, and the pleasure of leadership. Each one of them has many defects.

As for the pleasure of eating, it has the following defects:

The first: these pleasures are not strong, for the feeling of the pain of severe colic—God forbid—is stronger than the feeling of the pleasure obtained from eating food.

The second: this pleasure cannot last, for when a person eats he becomes satiated, and when he is satiated his desire to enjoy eating no longer remains. Thus this pleasure is weak, and in addition to its weakness it is not lasting.

The third: in itself it is base, for eating is nothing but the moistening of that food with the saliva gathered in the mouth, and there is no doubt that this is something repellent and disgusting. Then, when it reaches the stomach, its transformation into decay, stench, and rot becomes apparent, and this too is repellent.

[p. 176]

Fourth: all base animals share in these pleasures. Dung is to the dung beetle what sweets are to a human being. Just as a human being dislikes eating the beetle's food, the beetle dislikes eating human food. As for pleasure, it is shared among people.

Fifth: eating is only enjoyable when hunger is intense, and such hunger is a severe need, and need is a considerable deficiency.

Sixth: eating is despised by intelligent people. It has been said: "Whoever's aspiration is what enters his belly, his worth is what leaves his belly." This is the brief indication of the faults of eating.

As for the pleasure of marriage, everything we have mentioned about eating applies here, along with other things. Marriage is a cause of children, and then the number of persons increases, so the need for wealth increases. Because of this, a person must resort to scheming in seeking wealth by endless means, and he may perhaps perish in the pursuit of wealth. As for the pleasure of leadership, its faults are many. What we mention here concerns one cause: everyone naturally dislikes being a servant who is commanded, and loves to be a master who commands. When a person strives to become a commanding leader, this indicates opposition to everyone else, as if he is contending with all creation for it. Meanwhile, the people of East and West are trying to nullify and repel it. There is no doubt that the multiplicity of causes makes the achievement of an effect stronger. Since this is so, obtaining this leadership is almost impossible. And even if it is obtained, it will be on the brink of loss at every moment and time, through every kind of cause. Its possessor, upon obtaining it, lives in intense fear of losing it, and upon losing it, in great grief and severe sorrow because of that loss.

Know that when the intelligent person reflects on these meanings, he knows with certainty that there is no good for him in pursuing these pleasures and striving after these goods at all. Then, the soul was created naturally inclined to seek them, with intense love for them and a complete desire to reach them. At this point a syllogism (qiyas) is formed: as long as a person is in this corporeal life, he will be seeking these pleasures; and as long as he seeks them, he is in the very midst of calamities and in the depths of regrets. This consequent is disliked, so the antecedent is also disliked. Therefore, he wishes for the end of this corporeal life. The reason that motivates desire for death is that the causes of this bodily pleasure are repetitive and cannot be increased beyond what they are, and repetition produces weariness. As for the felicities of the Hereafter, they are of many kinds, without limit.

Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, the author of this book, may God illuminate his proof, said: I am a possessor of this state and immersed in it. Had I opened the door and exaggerated in describing the faults of these bodily pleasures, I might have written volumes and still not reached a small part of them. For this reason, I have been constantly persistent, for most of my time, in remembering that which Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾

Fifth issue: Our companions relied upon His saying ﴿cause me to die as a Muslim﴾ to demonstrate that faith comes from God Most High. Its explanation: if the attainment of Islam and its continuation were from the servant, then asking God for it would be corrupt. Its explanation is as if he were saying: "Act, O You who does not act!" The Mu'tazilah constantly criticize us and say: "If the act is from God, how is it permissible to say to the servant, 'Act!' when you are not the doer?" So we say here too: if the attainment of faith and its continuation are from the servant and not from God Most High, how can he ask that from God? Al-Juba'i and al-Ka'bi said: its meaning is: "Ask for grace (lutf) for me to remain upon Islam until I die upon it." (Lutf: divine grace that facilitates obedience.)

This answer is weak, because the request was for Islam itself, so interpreting it as grace is a departure from the apparent meaning. Also, every grace that is within the scope of power has already been bestowed by Him, so asking Him for it would be impossible.

Sixth issue: Someone may say: the prophets, peace be upon them, know that they will certainly die upon Islam, so this supplication amounts to seeking the attainment of what is already attained, and that is impermissible.

Response: The best that has been said regarding it is that the perfection of the state of a Muslim is to submit to the judgment of God Most High in such a manner that his heart is firmly settled upon that Islam, he is content with the decree and destiny of God, and he is tranquil in soul, with an open breast and a broadened heart in this matter. This state is additional to Islam, which is the opposite of disbelief. Therefore, what is sought here is Islam in this sense.

Seventh issue: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was among the great prophets, peace be upon them, and righteousness is the first rank of believers. So how is it fitting for one who has reached the goal to seek the beginning? Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and other exegetes said: it means "with his forefathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub." The meaning is: "Join me with them in their reward, their stations, and their ranks."

Here is another interpretation of this verse, according to the people of unveiling (ashab al-mukashafat). When separated souls are illuminated by divine lights and sacred flashes, and they are harmonious and similar, the light in each one of them is reflected onto the other because of that closeness and kinship. Thus those lights grow greater and those radiances become stronger. The example of these states is a polished, pure mirror placed in such a position that when the sun shines upon it, the light is reflected from each of them to the other. Then the light grows stronger and the radiance becomes perfect, and it reaches a degree of brilliance, glitter and sparkle that weak eyes and sights cannot endure. So it is here as well.

Thus the pleasure of eating is an expression for the removal of the pain of hunger, and the pleasure of intercourse is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the tingling that arises from the discharge of semen into its receptacles.

The pleasure of command and leadership is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the desire for revenge and the pursuit of leadership. Since the essence of these pleasures is nothing but the removal of pain, they are inevitably regarded by intelligent people as lowly, base, debased, and deficient. At that point, a person wishes for death in order to be freed from the need for these base conditions.

The fourth reason: the avenues of worldly pleasures are few, and they are of three kinds: the pleasure of eating, the pleasure of intercourse, and the pleasure of leadership. Each one of them has many defects.

As for the pleasure of eating, it has the following defects:

The first: these pleasures are not strong, for the feeling of the pain of severe colic—God forbid—is stronger than the feeling of the pleasure obtained from eating food.

The second: this pleasure cannot last, for when a person eats he becomes satiated, and when he is satiated his desire to enjoy eating no longer remains. Thus this pleasure is weak, and in addition to its weakness it is not lasting.

The third: in itself it is base, for eating is nothing but the moistening of that food with the saliva gathered in the mouth, and there is no doubt that this is something repellent and disgusting. Then, when it reaches the stomach, its transformation into decay, stench, and rot becomes apparent, and this too is repellent.

[p. 176]

Fourth: all base animals share in these pleasures. Dung is to the dung beetle what sweets are to a human being. Just as a human being dislikes eating the beetle's food, the beetle dislikes eating human food. As for pleasure, it is shared among people.

Fifth: eating is only enjoyable when hunger is intense, and such hunger is a severe need, and need is a considerable deficiency.

Sixth: eating is despised by intelligent people. It has been said: "Whoever's aspiration is what enters his belly, his worth is what leaves his belly." This is the brief indication of the faults of eating.

As for the pleasure of marriage, everything we have mentioned about eating applies here, along with other things. Marriage is a cause of children, and then the number of persons increases, so the need for wealth increases. Because of this, a person must resort to scheming in seeking wealth by endless means, and he may perhaps perish in the pursuit of wealth. As for the pleasure of leadership, its faults are many. What we mention here concerns one cause: everyone naturally dislikes being a servant who is commanded, and loves to be a master who commands. When a person strives to become a commanding leader, this indicates opposition to everyone else, as if he is contending with all creation for it. Meanwhile, the people of East and West are trying to nullify and repel it. There is no doubt that the multiplicity of causes makes the achievement of an effect stronger. Since this is so, obtaining this leadership is almost impossible. And even if it is obtained, it will be on the brink of loss at every moment and time, through every kind of cause. Its possessor, upon obtaining it, lives in intense fear of losing it, and upon losing it, in great grief and severe sorrow because of that loss.

Know that when the intelligent person reflects on these meanings, he knows with certainty that there is no good for him in pursuing these pleasures and striving after these goods at all. Then, the soul was created naturally inclined to seek them, with intense love for them and a complete desire to reach them. At this point a syllogism (qiyas) is formed: as long as a person is in this corporeal life, he will be seeking these pleasures; and as long as he seeks them, he is in the very midst of calamities and in the depths of regrets. This consequent is disliked, so the antecedent is also disliked. Therefore, he wishes for the end of this corporeal life. The reason that motivates desire for death is that the causes of this bodily pleasure are repetitive and cannot be increased beyond what they are, and repetition produces weariness. As for the felicities of the Hereafter, they are of many kinds, without limit.

Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, the author of this book, may God illuminate his proof, said: I am a possessor of this state and immersed in it. Had I opened the door and exaggerated in describing the faults of these bodily pleasures, I might have written volumes and still not reached a small part of them. For this reason, I have been constantly persistent, for most of my time, in remembering that which Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾

Its explanation: if the attainment of Islam and its continuation were from the servant, then asking God for it would be corrupt. Its explanation is as if he were saying: "Act, O You who does not act!" This state is additional to Islam, which is the opposite of disbelief. Therefore, what is sought here is Islam in this sense.

The meaning is: "Join me with them in their reward, their stations, and their ranks."

Here is another interpretation of this verse, according to the people of unveiling (ashab al-mukashafat). When separated souls are illuminated by divine lights and sacred flashes, and they are harmonious and similar, the light in each one of them is reflected onto the other because of that closeness and kinship. Thus those lights grow greater and those radiances become stronger. The example of these states is a polished, pure mirror placed in such a position that when the sun shines upon it, the light is reflected from each of them to the other. Then the light grows stronger and the radiance becomes perfect, and it reaches a degree of brilliance, glitter and sparkle that weak eyes and sights cannot endure. So it is here as well.

It is also narrated that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, stayed with him for twenty-four years. When his death drew near, he instructed [Yusuf] to bury him in al-Sham (Syria), beside his father Ishaq (Isaac). [Yusuf] went himself, buried him, and then returned to Egypt. The lexicographers said: The root meaning of *fatr* in the language is splitting. It is said: *fatara nab al-ba'ir* when the tusk of the camel appeared; *fatartu al-shay'* and *infatara* means I split it and it split; and the earth *tafattarat* with plants, and the tree with leaves, when it cracked open. This is its original meaning in the language. Then it came to be used as an expression for bringing into existence, because that thing, in its state of non-existence, is as though in darkness and concealment; when it enters existence, it is as though it has split away from non-existence, and that thing has come out of it.

It is thus established that the word *fatir* does not indicate that God is the one who brought into being the components from which the heavens and the earth were composed. Rather, we come to know that He brought them into being through rational proofs, not through the wording of the Qur'an.

Reason also confirms this, because the determination of the encompassing thing necessitates the determination of the center, but the determination of the center does not necessitate the determination of the encompassing thing, since it is possible for countless encompassing things to surround a single center; whereas for one encompassing thing only one specific center can exist.

Also, the wording indicates that the heavens are many and the earth is one. The wisdom behind this we have already mentioned in His saying ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ (6:1).

The second: it may be placed in the accusative as a second vocative.

Therefore what is actually attained is a part of the parts of kingship and a part of the parts of knowledge. For this reason He used the word *min*, because it indicates partiality.

Then He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions.

**First discussion:** On the linguistic meaning of the word *fatir*.

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "I did not know the meaning of *fatir* until two Bedouins brought a dispute to me about a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who *fatartuha* (originated it), and I began digging it.'"

The lexicographers said: The root meaning of *fatr* in the language is splitting. It is said: *fatara nab al-ba'ir* when the tusk of the camel appeared; *fatartu al-shay'* and *infatara* means I split it and it split; and the earth *tafattarat* with plants, and the tree with leaves, when it cracked open. This is its original meaning in the language. Then it came to be used as an expression for bringing into existence, because that thing, in its state of non-existence, is as though in darkness and concealment; when it enters existence, it is as though it has split away from non-existence, and that thing has come out of it.

**Second discussion:** The word *fatir* may be thought to be an expression for bringing a thing into being out of pure non-existence, based on the derivation we have mentioned. However, the truth is that it does not indicate this, and there are several proofs for this:

The first: He said ﴿Praise belongs to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ (35:1), and then God made clear that He created them from smoke, when He said: ﴿Then He turned to the sky when it was smoke﴾ (41:11). This shows that the word *fatir* does not indicate that He produced that thing from pure non-existence.

The second: He said, ﴿the nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾ (30:30), although God created mankind from dust. He said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out a second time﴾ (20:55).

The third: A thing comes into existence only when its matter and form are both present, like a jug. A jug exists only when that particular matter has become characterized by that particular attribute. When the form is absent, that composite does not exist; and when that form is brought into being, [the maker] becomes the one who brings that jug into being. We therefore know that being the one who brings about the *form* does not necessitate being the one who brings about the *matter* of the jug. It is thus established that the word *fatir* does not indicate that God is the one who brought into being the components from which the heavens and the earth were composed. Rather, we come to know that He brought them into being through rational proofs, not through the wording of the Qur'an.

Know that His saying ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ gives the impression that the creation of the heavens precedes the creation of the earth, according to those who hold that the particle *waw* (and) indicates sequence. Reason also confirms this, because the determination of the encompassing thing necessitates the determination of the center, but the determination of the center does not necessitate the determination of the encompassing thing, since it is possible for countless encompassing things to surround a single center; whereas for one encompassing thing only one specific center can exist.

Also, the wording indicates that the heavens are many and the earth is one. The wisdom behind this we have already mentioned in His saying ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ (6:1).

**Third discussion:** Al-Zajjaj said: Its (*fatir*'s) accusative case has two possibilities:

The first: it is an adjective of ﴿Lord﴾, which is a vocative construction in the accusative position.

The second: it may be placed in the accusative as a second vocative.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The meaning is: You are the One who takes charge of the setting right of all my affairs in this world and the Hereafter. Thus He joined the perishable kingdom to the enduring kingdom. This indicates that faith and obedience are a word from God, the Exalted, for if they came from the servant, then the one who manages his welfare would be the servant himself, and in that case the generality of His saying ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom﴾ would be nullified.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Cause me to die in submission [to You], and join me with the righteous.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the Prophet, peace be upon him, related from Jibril, peace be upon him, from the Lord of Might, that He said: "Whoever is occupied with remembering Me instead of asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." For this reason, whoever wishes to supplicate must first offer praise to God. Here, Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he wished to mention supplication, put praise before it, which is His saying ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom and taught me [some] of the interpretation of events, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. Then after it he mentioned the supplication, which is His saying ﴿Cause me to die in submission [to You], and join me with the righteous.﴾ A parallel to this is what the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), may the blessings of God be upon him, did in His saying: ﴿The One who created me, and He guides me﴾ (26:78), up to His saying ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom﴾ (26:83). Everything from the beginning to there is praise of God, and then His saying ﴿My Lord, grant me...﴾ through to the end of the speech is supplication. So it is here as well.

**The second issue:** They differed over whether His saying ﴿Cause me to die in submission﴾ is a request from him for death or not. Qatada said: He asked his Lord to join him [to the righteous, in the hereafter], and no prophet had ever wished for death before him. Many of the commentators follow this view. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said, in the narration of Ata, meaning: "When You cause me to die, then let my death be upon the religion of Islam." This is thus a request that God make his death occur in Islam, and there is nothing in it indicating that he asked for death itself.

Know that the wording is suitable for both meanings, and it is not far-fetched for a rational man, when his intellect is perfected, to wish for death and to greatly desire it, for several reasons. Among them: the perfection of the human soul, as we have explained, lies in being knowledgeable of divine matters, and in being a king and an owner who directs material things. We have stated that the degrees of variation in these two kinds are unlimited, and that absolute perfection in them belongs to God alone, while everything below that is deficient. When the deficient one becomes aware of its deficiency and tastes the pleasure of absolute perfection, it remains in restlessness and the pain of seeking. Since absolute perfection belongs only to God, and its attainment is impossible for a human, it follows that the human will remain forever in the restlessness of seeking and the pain of toil. When a human recognizes this condition, he realizes there is no way to relieve his soul of this toil except through death, and at that point he wishes for death.

The second reason for wishing for death is that the orators and eloquent speakers, although they expand at length in condemning this world, the essence of their speech comes down to three matters:

The first: these pleasures are quick to vanish, close to extinction, and the pain that occurs when they disappear is greater than the pleasure experienced when they are possessed.

The second: they are not pure, but are mixed with troubles and disturbances.

The third: base people share in them with the excellent, and indeed the portion of the base is often far greater than the portion of the excellent. These three aspects make one averse to these pleasures. When the wise person realizes that there is no way to obtain these pleasures except along with these three repellent aspects, he inevitably wishes for death so as to be freed from these afflictions.

The third reason, which is the strongest according to the verifying scholars (may God have mercy on them all), is that these bodily pleasures have no real substance; their essence is only the removal of pains. Thus the pleasure of eating is an expression for the removal of the pain of hunger, and the pleasure of intercourse is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the tingling that arises from the discharge of semen into its receptacles.

The pleasure of command and leadership is an expression for the removal of the pain caused by the desire for revenge and the pursuit of leadership. Since the essence of these pleasures is nothing but the removal of pain, they are inevitably regarded by intelligent people as lowly, base, debased, and deficient. At that point, a person wishes for death in order to be freed from the need for these base conditions.

The fourth reason: the avenues of worldly pleasures are few, and they are of three kinds: the pleasure of eating, the pleasure of intercourse, and the pleasure of leadership. Each one of them has many defects.

As for the pleasure of eating, it has the following defects:

The first: these pleasures are not strong, for the feeling of the pain of severe colic—God forbid—is stronger than the feeling of the pleasure obtained from eating food.

The second: this pleasure cannot last, for when a person eats he becomes satiated, and when he is satiated his desire to enjoy eating no longer remains. Thus this pleasure is weak, and in addition to its weakness it is not lasting.

The third: in itself it is base, for eating is nothing but the moistening of that food with the saliva gathered in the mouth, and there is no doubt that this is something repellent and disgusting. Then, when it reaches the stomach, its transformation into decay, stench, and rot becomes apparent, and this too is repellent.

[p. 176]

Fourth: all base animals share in these pleasures. Dung is to the dung beetle what sweets are to a human being. Just as a human being dislikes eating the beetle's food, the beetle dislikes eating human food. As for pleasure, it is shared among people.

Fifth: eating is only enjoyable when hunger is intense, and such hunger is a severe need, and need is a considerable deficiency.

Sixth: eating is despised by intelligent people. It has been said: "Whoever's aspiration is what enters his belly, his worth is what leaves his belly." This is the brief indication of the faults of eating.

As for the pleasure of marriage, everything we have mentioned about eating applies here, along with other things. Marriage is a cause of children, and then the number of persons increases, so the need for wealth increases. Because of this, a person must resort to scheming in seeking wealth by endless means, and he may perhaps perish in the pursuit of wealth. As for the pleasure of leadership, its faults are many. What we mention here concerns one cause: everyone naturally dislikes being a servant who is commanded, and loves to be a master who commands. When a person strives to become a commanding leader, this indicates opposition to everyone else, as if he is contending with all creation for it. Meanwhile, the people of East and West are trying to nullify and repel it. There is no doubt that the multiplicity of causes makes the achievement of an effect stronger. Since this is so, obtaining this leadership is almost impossible. And even if it is obtained, it will be on the brink of loss at every moment and time, through every kind of cause. Its possessor, upon obtaining it, lives in intense fear of losing it, and upon losing it, in great grief and severe sorrow because of that loss.

Know that when the intelligent person reflects on these meanings, he knows with certainty that there is no good for him in pursuing these pleasures and striving after these goods at all. Then, the soul was created naturally inclined to seek them, with intense love for them and a complete desire to reach them. At this point a syllogism (qiyas) is formed: as long as a person is in this corporeal life, he will be seeking these pleasures; and as long as he seeks them, he is in the very midst of calamities and in the depths of regrets. This consequent is disliked, so the antecedent is also disliked. Therefore, he wishes for the end of this corporeal life. The reason that motivates desire for death is that the causes of this bodily pleasure are repetitive and cannot be increased beyond what they are, and repetition produces weariness. As for the felicities of the Hereafter, they are of many kinds, without limit.

Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, the author of this book, may God illuminate his proof, said: I am a possessor of this state and immersed in it. Had I opened the door and exaggerated in describing the faults of these bodily pleasures, I might have written volumes and still not reached a small part of them. For this reason, I have been constantly persistent, for most of my time, in remembering that which Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾

Fifth issue: Our companions relied upon His saying ﴿cause me to die as a Muslim﴾ to demonstrate that faith comes from God Most High. Its explanation: if the attainment of Islam and its continuation were from the servant, then asking God for it would be corrupt. Its explanation is as if he were saying: "Act, O You who does not act!" The Mu'tazilah constantly criticize us and say: "If the act is from God, how is it permissible to say to the servant, 'Act!' when you are not the doer?" So we say here too: if the attainment of faith and its continuation are from the servant and not from God Most High, how can he ask that from God? Al-Juba'i and al-Ka'bi said: its meaning is: "Ask for grace (lutf) for me to remain upon Islam until I die upon it." (Lutf: divine grace that facilitates obedience.)

This answer is weak, because the request was for Islam itself, so interpreting it as grace is a departure from the apparent meaning. Also, every grace that is within the scope of power has already been bestowed by Him, so asking Him for it would be impossible.

Sixth issue: Someone may say: the prophets, peace be upon them, know that they will certainly die upon Islam, so this supplication amounts to seeking the attainment of what is already attained, and that is impermissible.

Response: The best that has been said regarding it is that the perfection of the state of a Muslim is to submit to the judgment of God Most High in such a manner that his heart is firmly settled upon that Islam, he is content with the decree and destiny of God, and he is tranquil in soul, with an open breast and a broadened heart in this matter. This state is additional to Islam, which is the opposite of disbelief. Therefore, what is sought here is Islam in this sense.

Seventh issue: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was among the great prophets, peace be upon them, and righteousness is the first rank of believers. So how is it fitting for one who has reached the goal to seek the beginning? Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and other exegetes said: it means "with his forefathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub." The meaning is: "Join me with them in their reward, their stations, and their ranks."

Here is another interpretation of this verse, according to the people of unveiling (ashab al-mukashafat). When separated souls are illuminated by divine lights and sacred flashes, and they are harmonious and similar, the light in each one of them is reflected onto the other because of that closeness and kinship. Thus those lights grow greater and those radiances become stronger. The example of these states is a polished, pure mirror placed in such a position that when the sun shines upon it, the light is reflected from each of them to the other. Then the light grows stronger and the radiance becomes perfect, and it reaches a degree of brilliance, glitter and sparkle that weak eyes and sights cannot endure. So it is here as well.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 12, verses 101–105 (part 1 of 2)**

So [Yusuf] asked him, and Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "God commanded me to do that because of your saying: 'I fear that the wolf will eat him' (12:13). Why did you not fear Me?"

It is also narrated that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, stayed with him for twenty-four years. When his death drew near, he instructed [Yusuf] to bury him in al-Sham (Syria), beside his father Ishaq (Isaac). [Yusuf] went himself, buried him, and then returned to Egypt. He lived after his father for twenty-three years. At that point he wished for the kingdom of the Hereafter, and so he wished for death. It was said: no prophet wished for it before him or after him. God then caused him to die in a good and pure state. The people of Egypt disputed over his burial, each one wishing to bury him in their own quarter, until they were on the verge of fighting. They then judged that the best course was to make for him a chest of marble, place him in it, and bury him in the Nile at a place where the water flows over him, and then reaches Egypt, so that his blessing would reach everyone. Ephraim (Ifra'im) and Misha were born to him; Nun was born to Ephraim; and Yusha' (Joshua), the servant of Musa (Moses), was born to Nun. Yusuf was then buried there until God raised up Musa, who brought his bones out of Egypt and buried them beside the grave of his father.

**The second issue:** The word *min* ("of") in His saying ﴿of the kingdom﴾ and ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'id), because he was given only part of the kingdom of this world, or part of the kingdom of Egypt, and part of the interpretation [of events]. Al-Asamm said: He only said "of the kingdom" because there was a king above him.

Know that the levels of existing things are three. The first is the Influencer that is not influenced, and that is God, Exalted and Sanctified. The second is that which is influenced but does not influence, and that is the world of bodies, for they are receptive to shaping, forming, various attributes and contrary accidents, and so they have no influence on anything at all. These two categories are very far apart. Between them lies a third category, which both influences and is influenced, and that is the world of spirits. The distinctive property of the substance of spirits is that they receive effect and direction from the world of the light of the majesty of God. Then, when they turn toward the world of bodies, they act upon it and affect it.
