Know that when the intelligent person reflects on these meanings, he knows with certainty that there is no good for him in pursuing these pleasures and striving after these goods at all. Then, the soul was created naturally inclined to seek them, with intense love for them and a complete desire to reach them. At this point a syllogism (qiyas) is formed: as long as a person is in this corporeal life, he will be seeking these pleasures; and as long as he seeks them, he is in the very midst of calamities and in the depths of regrets. This consequent is disliked, so the antecedent is also disliked. Therefore, he wishes for the end of this corporeal life. The reason that motivates desire for death is that the causes of this bodily pleasure are repetitive and cannot be increased beyond what they are, and repetition produces weariness. As for the felicities of the Hereafter, they are of many kinds, without limit.

Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, the author of this book, may God illuminate his proof, said: I am a possessor of this state and immersed in it. Had I opened the door and exaggerated in describing the faults of these bodily pleasures, I might have written volumes and still not reached a small part of them. For this reason, I have been constantly persistent, for most of my time, in remembering that which Yusuf, peace be upon him, mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾

Fifth issue: Our companions relied upon His saying ﴿cause me to die as a Muslim﴾ to demonstrate that faith comes from God Most High. Its explanation: if the attainment of Islam and its continuation were from the servant, then asking God for it would be corrupt. Its explanation is as if he were saying: "Act, O You who does not act!" The Mu'tazilah constantly criticize us and say: "If the act is from God, how is it permissible to say to the servant, 'Act!' when you are not the doer?" So we say here too: if the attainment of faith and its continuation are from the servant and not from God Most High, how can he ask that from God? Al-Juba'i and al-Ka'bi said: its meaning is: "Ask for grace (lutf) for me to remain upon Islam until I die upon it." (Lutf: divine grace that facilitates obedience.)

This answer is weak, because the request was for Islam itself, so interpreting it as grace is a departure from the apparent meaning. Also, every grace that is within the scope of power has already been bestowed by Him, so asking Him for it would be impossible.

Sixth issue: Someone may say: the prophets, peace be upon them, know that they will certainly die upon Islam, so this supplication amounts to seeking the attainment of what is already attained, and that is impermissible.

Response: The best that has been said regarding it is that the perfection of the state of a Muslim is to submit to the judgment of God Most High in such a manner that his heart is firmly settled upon that Islam, he is content with the decree and destiny of God, and he is tranquil in soul, with an open breast and a broadened heart in this matter. This state is additional to Islam, which is the opposite of disbelief. Therefore, what is sought here is Islam in this sense.

Seventh issue: Yusuf, peace be upon him, was among the great prophets, peace be upon them, and righteousness is the first rank of believers. So how is it fitting for one who has reached the goal to seek the beginning? Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and other exegetes said: it means "with his forefathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub." The meaning is: "Join me with them in their reward, their stations, and their ranks."

Here is another interpretation of this verse, according to the people of unveiling (ashab al-mukashafat). When separated souls are illuminated by divine lights and sacred flashes, and they are harmonious and similar, the light in each one of them is reflected onto the other because of that closeness and kinship. Thus those lights grow greater and those radiances become stronger. The example of these states is a polished, pure mirror placed in such a position that when the sun shines upon it, the light is reflected from each of them to the other. Then the light grows stronger and the radiance becomes perfect, and it reaches a degree of brilliance, glitter and sparkle that weak eyes and sights cannot endure. So it is here as well.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verses 106–107:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen, which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they resolved on their affair while they were scheming.﴾

Know that ﴿That﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿among the tidings of the unseen﴾. ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ is a second predicate. ﴿And you were not with them﴾ means you were not with the brothers of Yusuf. ﴿When they resolved on their affair﴾ means they determined upon their plan. We have discussed this expression at His words ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾. ﴿While they were scheming﴾ means against Yusuf. Know that the purpose of this is to inform about the unseen, and so it is a miracle.

The proof that it is a report of the unseen is that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not study books, did not become a student of anyone, and the town was not a town of scholars. So his bringing this long story in a manner in which there is no distortion or error, without studying or learning, and without anyone saying that he was present with them, must be a miracle. How could it not be a miracle, when the establishment of this premise has been mentioned in this book many times?

His words ﴿And you were not with them﴾ mean "you were not there." It is mentioned as a form of mockery of them, because everyone knows that Muhammad (ﷺ) was not with them.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, even if you were eager﴾. ﴿And you do not ask them for any payment for it. It is not but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ ﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth which they pass by, yet they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except while they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿Then are they secure from the overwhelming punishment of Allah coming upon them, or the Hour coming upon them unawares while they do not perceive?﴾

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is that the disbelievers of Quraysh and a group of the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for this story as a way of challenge. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) believed that if he related it, they might perhaps believe. When he related it, they persisted in their disbelief, so this verse was revealed. It seems to be an allusion to what Allah the Exalted mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ (al-Qasas: 56).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: The answer to (law, "if") is omitted, because the answer to (law) cannot precede it. So it is not permissible to say: "I stood up if you stood up."

Al-Farra' said in "al-Masadir": It is said: harasa yahrisu hirsan. Another, anomalous dialect is: harasa yahrisu harisan. The meaning of hirs is seeking a thing with the utmost effort possible.

His words ﴿And you do not ask them for any payment for it﴾ have an apparent meaning. His words ﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾ mean that it is a reminder to them concerning the proofs of monotheism, justice, prophethood, the return, stories, obligations and acts of worship. The meaning is that this Qur'an contains these great benefits, and you do not ask them for wealth or reward. So if they were intelligent, they would have accepted and not rebelled.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth which they pass by, yet they turn away from it﴾ mean: there is no wonder if they do not reflect upon the proofs that indicate your prophethood, for the world is filled with proofs of monotheism, power and wisdom. Then they pass by them and do not pay attention to them.

Know that the proofs of monotheism, knowledge, power, wisdom and mercy must necessarily come from perceptible things, and these are either the celestial bodies or the elemental bodies. As for the celestial bodies, they are of two kinds: either the spheres (aflak) or the stars (kawakib). As for the spheres, one may take as evidence their specific measures for the existence of the Creator, or the fact that some of them are above others or below them, or the states of their movements, either because their movements are preceded by non-existence, so there must be a capable mover, or because of the manner of their movements in speed and slowness, or because of the differences in the directions of those movements.

As for the stellar bodies, sometimes the existence of the Creator is inferred from their measures, their spaces and their movements, sometimes from their colours and lights, and sometimes from their effects in producing light, shadows, darkness and brightness.

As for the proofs drawn from the elemental bodies: they are either taken from simple (basa'it) things, which are the wonders of land and sea, or from compound (mawalid) things, which are of several kinds:

The first: the upper phenomena, such as thunder, lightning, clouds, rain, snow, wind and the rainbow.

The second: minerals, with their differing natures, qualities and states.

The third: plants, and the properties of wood, leaves and fruit, and the peculiarity of each of them with a specific nature, a specific taste and a specific property.

The fourth: the differences in the states of animals in their shapes, natures, voices and creation.

The fifth: the dissection of human bodies and the dissection of human faculties, and the explanation of the benefit obtained from them. These are the comprehensive proofs.

From this category also are the stories of the ancients and the accounts of the earlier peoples, and that the kings who seized the earth, ruined the lands and oppressed the servants died, and no report or trace of them remains in the world, yet the burden and punishment remain upon them. This is the summary of the types of these proofs. The book that contains the explanation of these proofs is an explanation of the whole of the higher world and the lower world, and the human intellect cannot encompass it. For this reason Allah the Exalted mentioned it in a general way.

The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: It has been read as (wa al-ardu) with a nominative case, as a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿they pass by them﴾ is its predicate. Al-Sudd (al-Suddi) read (wa al-arda) with an accusative case, on the assumption that his words ﴿they pass by them﴾ are explained by our statement "they circle around it." In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is (wa al-ardu yamshuna alayha) with the nominative case of al-ardu.

As for His words ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except while they associate others with Him﴾, the meaning is that they were acknowledging the existence of God, as evidenced by His words:

[Page 179]

﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ (Luqman: 25), except that they used to ascribe to Him a partner in worship. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are those who liken Allah to His creation. It is also reported from him that he said: this verse was revealed concerning the talbiyah of the polytheists of Arabia, for they used to say, "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, You own him and what he owns." 

It is also reported from him that the people of Mecca said: "Allah is our Lord alone, without partner; the angels are His daughters." So they did not affirm His unity, but rather associated others with Him. The worshippers of idols said: "Our Lord is Allah alone, and the idols are our intercessors with Him." The Jews said: "Our Lord is Allah alone, and Uzayr is the son of Allah." The Christians said: "Our Lord is Allah alone, without partner, and the Messiah is the son of Allah."

The worshippers of the sun and the moon said: "Our Lord is Allah alone, and these are our lords." The Muhajirun and the Ansar said: "Our Lord is Allah alone, and there is no partner with Him."

The Karramiyya (a theological sect) argued from this verse that faith is merely the affirmation by the tongue, because He, Exalted is He, judged them to be believers while they were polytheists, and this indicates that faith is nothing but the mere affirmation by the tongue. Its refutation is well known.

As for His words ﴿Then are they secure from the overwhelming punishment of Allah coming upon them﴾, that is, a punishment that will cover them, spread over them and overwhelm them, ﴿or the Hour coming upon them unawares﴾, that is, suddenly.

The word (baghtatan, "unawares") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). It is said: "The matter took them by surprise (baghatahumu al-amru bagtan wa baghtatan) when it came upon them unexpectedly, from a direction they did not anticipate." His words ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ serve as an emphasis of His words ﴿unawares﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 108:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me. And glory be to Allah; and I am not of the polytheists.﴾

The exegetes said: Say, O Muhammad, to them: This call to which I summon, and the path upon which I stand, is my way (sabili), my sunnah and my manhaj (method). The religion is called a "way" (sabil) because it is the road that leads to reward. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ (al-Nahl: 125).

Know that sabil in the original language means the road, and they likened beliefs to it, since a person passes along them to Paradise. ﴿I call to Allah with insight﴾, that is, with proof (hujjah) and evidence (burhan), I and whoever follows me, in my conduct (sirah) and my path and the conduct of my followers in calling to Allah; for everyone who mentions the proof and answers the doubt has called to Allah to the extent of his capacity.

This indicates that calling to Allah, exalted is He, is only good and permissible on this condition, namely that one be upon insight into what he says, upon guidance and certainty. If he is not like this, then it is pure delusion (gharur). The Prayer and peace be upon him said: "The scholars are the trustees of the Messengers over the servants of Allah, insofar as they guard what you call them to." It has also been said: it is permissible for the speech to end at His saying ﴿I call to Allah﴾, and then he begins, saying: ﴿upon insight, I and whoever follows me﴾. His saying ﴿And glory be to Allah﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿This is my way﴾, meaning: Say, "This is my way," and say, "Glory be to Allah," declaring Allah far above what they associate with Him. ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾, who take with Allah a rival (didd), an equal (nidd), a peer (kufu) and a son (walad).

This verse indicates that the craft of kalam (dialectical theology) and the science of usul (foundations of religion) are the craft of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and that Allah sent them to creation only for its sake.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 109:**

Allah's words: ﴿We sent none before you except men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns. Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are god-fearing. Will you not then understand?﴾

Know that Hafs, from ʿAsim, read نُوحِي (*nūḥī*, "We reveal") with the nūn, while the rest read it with the yāʾ (*yūḥī*). Regarding ﴿Will they not understand?﴾, Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Hafs's transmission from ʿAsim read تَعْقِلُونَ (*taʿqilūn*, "you understand") with the tāʾ, as direct address (*khiṭāb*), while the rest read it with the yāʾ, as third person (*ghāʾib*). (These variant readings are known as *qirāʾāt*, the canonical recitations.)

Know also that among the objections of those who denied his prophethood, peace be upon him, was that if Allah wanted to send a messenger, He would have sent an angel. So Allah said: ﴿We sent none before you except men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns.﴾ Since all of them were like this, how then did they marvel at your case, O Muhammad? The verse indicates that Allah did not send a messenger to the truth from among women, and also that He did not send a messenger from the people of the desert (*al-bādiyah*).

He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever goes out to the desert becomes coarse, and whoever pursues game becomes heedless."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen?﴾ the ruined places of the nations that denied, and His words ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ mean the abode of the final state (*dār al-ḥāla al-ākhira*), because people have two states: the state of this world and the state of the Hereafter. Similar to this is His saying (ﷺ), "ṣalāt al-ūlā," meaning the first obligatory prayer (*ṣalāt al-farīḍah al-ūlā*). As for demonstrating that the Hereafter is better than the first (life), we have mentioned its proofs many times before.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 12, verse 110:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whoever We willed was delivered. And Our punishment is not averted from the guilty people.﴾

Know that ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read (kudhibū) with light pronunciation (takhfif) and a kasra on the dhāl, while the rest read it with emphasis (tashdid). The meaning of the light reading is in two respects:

The first: the thinking (ẓann) falls upon the people, meaning: until the messengers despaired of the faith of the people, and the people thought that the messengers had lied in what they promised of help and victory.

If it is said: the people to whom they were sent have not been mentioned in what precedes, so how is it proper for this pronoun to refer to them?

We say: the mention of the messengers indicates those to whom they were sent. And if you wish, you may say that their mention has occurred in His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ (Yusuf: 109), so the pronoun refers to those before them, the deniers of the messengers. Here, the thinking (ẓann) carries the meaning of supposition and presumption.

The second respect: that the meaning is that the messengers thought that they had been denied in what they had been promised. This interpretation is related from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. They said: the matter was only so because of the weakness of human nature. However, this is far-fetched, because a believer may not think that Allah would lie; rather, by that he would leave faith. How then can the like of that be permitted for the messengers? As for the reading with emphasis, it has two aspects:

The first: that thinking (ẓann) carries the meaning of certainty (yaqīn), meaning: they were certain that the nations had denied them with a denial after which faith would not come from them. Then they prayed against them, and there Allah, glorified is He, sent down upon them the punishment of annihilation.

The use of thinking in the sense of knowledge is frequent in the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 46), meaning, they are certain of that.

The second: that thinking carries the meaning of presumption, and the sense is: until, when the messengers despaired of the faith of their people, the messengers thought that those who had believed in them had denied them. This interpretation is related from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and it is the best of the aspects mentioned in the verse.

It is narrated that Ibn Abi Mulayka related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "And the messengers thought that they had been denied, because they were humans. Do you not see His saying: ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him say, 'When is the help of Allah?'﴾ (al-Baqarah: 214)?" He said: "I mentioned that to ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and she denied it, and said: 'Allah did not promise Muhammad (ﷺ) anything except that He knew He would fulfil it for him, but trial did not cease for the prophets until they feared that those who had believed in them would deny them.'" This rejection and interpretation from ʿĀʾishah is in the utmost excellence.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Our help came to them﴾, meaning: when the situation reached the limit mentioned, ﴿Our help came to them, and whoever We willed was delivered.﴾ ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read: (fa-nujjiya man nashāʾu) with one nun, a shadda on the jīm, and a fatḥa on the yāʾ, in the passive form (mā lam yusammi fāʿiluh), and Abu ʿUbayda preferred it because it is written in the muṣḥaf with one nun.

It is related from al-Kisāʾī that he assimilated one of the two nuns into the other, and read with one nun, a shadda on the jīm, and a sukūn on the yāʾ. Some of them said: this is an error, because the nun is vowelled, so it cannot be assimilated into a sukūn, and it is not permissible to assimilate the nun into the jīm. The rest read with two nuns, a light jīm, and a sukūn on the yāʾ, with the meaning: "and We do this to them."

Know that this is a narration of a state. Do you not see that the story concerns what is past, yet he narrated the present act, just as His saying: ﴿from his own party, and this is from his enemy﴾ (al-Qasas: 15) is a reference to the present, while the story is in the past?

The Qur'an: ﴿Certainly in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding. It was not a narration that could be invented, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Know that *i'tibar* (drawing a lesson, reflecting on what is observed) is an expression for crossing from the known end to the unknown end, and what is meant by it is contemplation and reflection. The reasons for drawing a lesson from their stories are several:

The first: the One who was able to honour Joseph after he was thrown into the well, to raise him after he was imprisoned, to give him power over Egypt after they had thought he was their slave, and to reunite him with his parents and brothers as he wished after a long period, is certainly able to honour Muhammad (ﷺ) and to exalt his word.

The second: the report about him takes the place of reports about the unseen, so it is a miracle that indicates the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The third: at the beginning of the surah He said: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ (Yusuf 12:3), and then at its end He said: ﴿Certainly in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding.﴾ This is an indication that the excellence of this story lies in the fact that lessons are drawn from it, and in knowledge of wisdom and power.

What is meant by "their stories" is the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brothers and father. Some people said: what is meant is the stories of the Messengers, because the Qur'an had earlier mentioned the stories of the other Messengers. However, the better view is that what is meant is the story of Joseph, peace be upon him.

If it is asked: why did He say ﴿a lesson for people of understanding﴾ when the people of Muhammad (ﷺ) were people of intellect and reason, and many of them did not draw a lesson from it?

We say: all of them were able to draw a lesson, and what is meant by describing this story as a lesson is that it is such that an intelligent person can draw a lesson from it. Or we say: what is meant by "people of understanding" are those who drew lessons, reflected, contemplated it and benefited from knowing it, because *ulu al-albab* (people of understanding) is a term that denotes praise and commendation, so it fits only what we have mentioned. Know that He, exalted is He, described this story with attributes:

The first attribute: that it is ﴿a lesson for people of understanding﴾, which has already been explained.

The second attribute: His saying ﴿it was not a narration that could be invented﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: what is meant is that what was brought by Muhammad (ﷺ) cannot be fabricated by him, because he did not read the books, was not taught by anyone, and did not associate with scholars. So it is impossible that he would invent this story in such a way that it matches what is in the Torah without any discrepancy.

The second: what is meant is that he does not lie in himself, because lying is not possible for him. Then He, exalted is He, affirmed that it is not invented, saying: ﴿but a confirmation of what came before it﴾. This is an indication that this story came in a form that agrees with what is in the Torah and the other divine books. The word *tasdiq* (confirmation) is put in the accusative on the presumption of: "but it was a confirmation of what came before it," like His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but the Messenger of God﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:40). This was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Then he said: according to grammatical analogy it is also permissible to put it in the nominative, in the sense of: "but it is the confirmation of what came before it."

The third attribute: His saying ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: what is meant is: and a detailed explanation of all things concerning the event of Joseph, peace be upon him, with his father and brothers.

The second: that it refers to the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ (al-An'am 6:38). Making this attribute a description of the whole Qur'an is more fitting than making it a description of the story of Joseph alone, and what is meant is that it includes what is lawful and unlawful and all that relates to the religion.

Al-Wahidi said, regarding both interpretations together: it is from the general term by which the specific is intended, like His saying: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ (al-A'raf 7:156), meaning: every thing that can enter into it. And His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ (al-Naml 27:23).

The fourth and fifth attributes: that it is guidance in this world and a means of obtaining mercy in the Hereafter ﴿for a people who believe﴾. He specified them by mention because they are the ones who benefited from it, as we explained in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:2). And God knows best what is right, and to Him is the return and the final destination.

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed, by the praise of God, on Wednesday, the seventh of Sha'ban, concluded with goodness and divine pleasure, in the year six hundred and one. I had been very distressed because of the death of my righteous son Muhammad, may God envelop him in mercy and forgiveness and grant him the degrees of grace and goodness. I recited these verses as a brief elegy for him:

[p. 183]

If the decrees of fate were subject to us, we would have ransomed you from your protection with soul and body.

And if the angels could be bought with a bribe, we would have submitted to them in servitude, in rule and in name.

But it is a decree: when its time comes, it passes from the seat of the Throne into the depths of the sea.

I shall weep for you all my life with blood, constantly, and I shall not turn from that in quality or quantity.

Peace be upon a grave in whose dust you were buried, and may the Merciful grant you abundant generosity.

Nothing has prevented me from making my eyelid your grave for your body except that it pours forth without ceasing.

I swear that if they touch my bones and my remains, they will feel the fire of grief in the hiding place of the bone.

My life and my death are one after your absence; indeed, death is better than the persistence of sorrow.

I am content with what God has decreed by His judgment, knowing that my judgment does not exceed me.

I advise whoever reads my book and benefits from its precious and lofty fruits to devote a recitation of the Fatihah to my son and to me, and to pray for mercy and forgiveness for one who has died in a distant land, far from brothers, father and mother, for I too have often prayed for whoever did that on my behalf. May God bless our master Muhammad, his family and his companions, and grant them abundant peace. Amen, and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
